How DynEarthSol compares with analytical, theoretical and independent solutions, and the regression and functional tests that guard its results.
A prestressed, sealed fault patch slips at 1 m/s under 50 MPa normal compression. Plastic dissipation heats the mixture; expanding water raises pore pressure and reduces shear resistance.
documents.s: Fault-zone heating at fixed normal traction

documents.t: A pressurized cell sheared at yield sees its loading rate rise tenfold. Rate-and-state friction jumps by $a\ln10$, then decays over the slip distance $D_c$ to the new steady state ($b>a$: velocity weakening).
documents.s: Rate-and-state friction under a velocity step

documents.t: Let an oceanic-plate temperature profile cool for 60 million years in 2D and 3D and compare it with the error-function solution.
Shorten a Maxwell viscoelastic square at a constant rate and compare the stress with the closed-form Maxwell response, element row by element row.
documents.s: Maxwell stress build-up in pure shear

documents.t: A circular opening concentrates stress in an elastic solid under isotropic compression.

A circular tunnel is excavated in rock under uniform in-situ stress: the support pressure on its wall is lowered to zero, and a ring of rock around the opening yields. Salençon’s solution gives the stresses, the plastic radius and the wall convergence for a perfectly plastic Mohr–Coulomb material.
Shorten a Mohr–Coulomb cell under uniaxial strain and compare the axial stress with the closed-form elastic and plastic path.
Poromechanics is not yet merged into DynEarthSol. It is under review in GeoFLAC/DynEarthSol#134 and is being merged in parts. Until then, build DES from the source revision named on each page.
Theis confined-aquifer pumping reference.

Fluid at pressure $p_w$ enters a borehole wall: it loads the wall and diffuses into the rock, which changes the stresses around the hole as it goes. The axisymmetric part of Detournay and Cheng’s borehole problem, on a finite annulus.
documents.s: Fluid injection into a poroelastic borehole

documents.t: Two pressure modes drain from a square; scalar permeability and directional anisotropy change together at 0.5 s.
A well pumps a confined aquifer covered by a leaky aquitard. Water drawn down through the aquitard limits the drawdown, which approaches a steady cone.
documents.s: Hantush–Jacob pumping from a leaky aquifer

documents.t: A smooth pressure pulse drains through two zero-pressure ends while the side faces remain sealed.
documents.s: Open boundaries: a draining pressure pulse

documents.t: One point supplies water and heat while another extracts them, over time windows that end inside time steps.
documents.s: Scheduled water and heat sources in a closed box

documents.t: A well pumps a confined aquifer and then shuts in. The drawdown spreads radially and recovers.
documents.s: Theis pumping and recovery in a confined aquifer

documents.t: Two wells extract water and one injects it into a confined slab; all stop after 40 s and the pressure recovers.
documents.s: Several wells: pumping, injection and recovery

documents.t: Water in a porous box heated from below becomes lighter at the base. Above a critical Rayleigh number buoyancy overturns it into a convection cell; below it, a disturbance decays.
All problems
All problems
documents.s: Heating a drained cell with changing water mass

documents.t: A porous layer heated from below over part of its base grows plumes that
Steady groundwater carries heat from a hot inlet along a saturated column while conduction spreads the front.

Injected water carries its temperature. DES adds the injected enthalpy relative to the local temperature, which with fluid mass conservation makes its advective heat equation conserve energy. Two checks: radial hot-water injection against Avdonin’s solution, and a sealed doublet against an independent heat ledger.
documents.s: Hot-water injection: Avdonin solution and heat ledger

documents.t: The drained surface of a fluid-saturated half-space is suddenly heated. Pore water expands more than the grains, so pressure rises below the surface while it drains upward, and the solid heaves.
All problems
documents.s: Warm-water mixing in a drained cell

documents.t: Above onset the heated porous cell settles into a steady convection roll that carries several times the conductive heat flow. Its Nusselt number has no closed form; an independent fine-grid solution supplies it.
A porous cell deforms at a prescribed pure-shear rate. Plastic work in aging rate-and-state plasticity heats the cell and expands the sealed fluid.
documents.s: Plastic shear heating and sealed pressurization

documents.t: Uniform supplied heat warms a rigid, sealed porous material. The temperature rise and fluid expansion give independent heat and pressure references.
documents.s: Thermal pressurization in a sealed cell

documents.t: Water is injected at a constant rate at a point. Pressure diffuses outward and the solid swells, changing the stress that a nearby fault would feel.
documents.s: Fluid injection into a poroelastic solid: Rudnicki

documents.t: A sealed porous column is compressed through Mohr–Coulomb yield. Total volume change fixes its mean pressure independently of the plastic stress return.

Rising pore pressure lowers the effective stress until the ground yields, the mechanism of injection- and rainfall-induced failure. In a laterally confined layer the yield pressure at each depth is exact, so a yield front moving down can be compared element by element.
documents.s: Pressure-driven yielding of a confined layer

documents.t: An affine material cell is extended in one direction and compressed equally in another, at fixed pore pressure. Effective stress must control its shear yield load.
A well pumps a thin poroelastic aquifer. The drawdown spreads radially and the layer contracts, splitting its volume change between areal and vertical strain.
Water enters a laterally confined elastic column through its base and leaves through a pressure-controlled top. Pressure and deformation independently measure its stored fluid.
documents.s: Water balance in a deforming column

documents.t: A drained poroelastic sphere is suddenly loaded on its surface. The shell drains and contracts first, squeezing the core, so the centre pressure rises before it decays.
Rigid frictionless plates squeeze a drained poroelastic strip. The edges drain first, load shifts to the undrained core, and the centre pressure rises before it decays.
documents.s: Mandel consolidation under a rigid plate

documents.t: All problems
documents.s: Finite-density water in a sealed cell

documents.t: A sudden load compresses a saturated column. Water drains through the top, the pressure falls and the column settles.
A small initial velocity sets a sealed saturated column oscillating; compression raises the pressure and expansion lowers it.
documents.s: Undrained wave in a sealed column

documents.t: Build DES

A constant inflow from the top produces a steady suction profile above a water table at the base. The Brooks–Corey law stays saturated up to its air-entry suction, so the profile has a kink where desaturation begins.
The water table under a laterally confined elastic column drops. Above it the soil drains; suction weighted by the effective saturation tightens the skeleton, and the drained soil becomes lighter.
documents.s: Bishop effective stress: lowering the water table

documents.t: A sealed, partly saturated soil cell is compressed slowly. Without drainage, the pore pressure follows the strain through the Bishop rate equation. The fixed-stress coupling of the PT solver must recover it as the time step shrinks, including where the Bishop pressure $S_ep$ decreases with suction.
documents.s: Bishop coupling in a sealed cell under compression

documents.t: A saturated sand column drains through its base: the top desaturates, pore pressure falls below zero and the column settles under the Bishop effective stress and its lighter weight, as in the Liakopoulos experiment. No closed form exists; an independent solver of the same continuum supplies the reference.
documents.s: Drainage of a saturated column into the unsaturated state

documents.t: Water infiltrates a partly saturated column from the top while the base stays at the water table.

A constant inflow from the top produces a steady suction profile above a water table at the base. The van Genuchten law has no air-entry pressure, so the soil desaturates as soon as the pressure falls below zero.
Run DES's two-element simple-shear benchmark and compare elastoplastic, steady-state and aging-law RSF stress with their closed-form solutions.
documents.s: Checking the friction law in simple shear

documents.t: Extend a brittle crust from a weak seed and compare the shear bands of static friction, velocity-strengthening and velocity-weakening rate-and-state friction.
documents.s: Shear bands with and without rate-and-state friction

A reservoir stands at the crest of the embankment and the slope is saturated. When the reservoir is drawn down quickly the water no longer supports the face, while the pore pressure inside falls only as the slope drains: the classic critical case for the upstream slope of a dam.
documents.s: Rapid drawdown of a reservoir against an embankment

documents.t: The standard slope-stability problem of geotechnical practice: how far can the strength of a homogeneous embankment be reduced before it slides? Strength reduction answers it with a deforming model that finds its own mechanism; limit-equilibrium methods of slices answer it on a trial slip circle.

documents.t: Rain falls on a partly saturated soil layer over impermeable bedrock. The water spreads down to the bedrock, a perched water table rises, and the slope fails when the pore pressure on the bedrock is high enough.

A well field pumps a soft confined aquifer for six months, rests for six months and repeats. The ground subsides around the wells, partly rebounds in each rest season and keeps a growing subsidence farther out.

A 2 m soil layer on 20° bedrock is loaded by its own weight and then by pore pressure rising from the bedrock. Plastic flow starts at the base and spreads along it, and the basal slip accelerates as the pressure rises.

Each benchmark runs DES on a problem with a known answer, an analytical solution, a theoretical prediction or an independent calculation, and shows how close DES comes and where the comparison stops. The inputs are in the DynEarthSol repository; each page says how to run them and what to expect. DynEarthSol is also checked against stored results to catch unintended changes, and by functional tests that run in continuous integration; both are listed below.

These checks compare DES with a reference solution inside a tutorial or a functional test. Check What it tests Where Documented in Confined elastic loading (PT) Stress and strain of a confined cell against the constrained-modulus solution, for both PT schemes PT tutorial bundle Elastic loading and equilibrium Maxwell creep (PT) Continued creep under a held load against a discrete Maxwell reference PT tutorial bundle Maxwell creep Plane-strain elastic update The 2D plane-strain stress update, including the out-of-plane stress tests/functional/plane_strain_elastic/ – Homogeneous initial stress ic.initial_stress_option = 1 produces the prescribed tensor tests/functional/initial_stress/ Initial stress RSF controls Slip-rate options and the state-change time-step limit tests/functional/rsf_controls/ Rate-and-state friction Under tests/residual-assembly-test/, component checks call the production routines directly. They cover nodal force assembly (cancellation, traction, gravity, damping), PT constraints and failed constitutive trials, with OpenMP, AddressSanitizer and OpenACC builds.

tests/regression/ guards against unintended changes in results. A run of a reference case is stored, and later runs are compared field by field: cd tests/regression make set # run once with the current executable and store the result make cmp # rerun and compare with the stored result make fresh-restart-cmp # run, restart from a checkpoint and compare: restart determinism CASE selects the input (default test-3d-equ-tiny.cfg), NDIMS the dimension and OMP the thread count. The comparison script compare.py reports the relative difference of every field and fails above 10−8 or on a non-finite value. A change to the solver that may alter results is checked by make set with the parent revision and make cmp with the change; see Testing.

Every pull request to DynEarthSol builds the code with several compilers and options (GCC 8–15, C++20 compatibility, macOS, NVHPC for OpenACC, MMG, ExodusII and GoSPL builds) and runs the functional tests: a 3D elasto-visco-plastic model with remeshing and a temperature dome, and its restart determinism; a 2D elastoplastic model on an irregular mesh with remeshing, and its restart determinism; the plane-strain elastic update and homogeneous initial stress checks; a subset of the RSF simple-shear benchmark; rejection of malformed input files; a 3D run in a debug build to catch memory errors.

A prestressed, sealed fault patch slips at 1 m/s under 50 MPa normal compression. Plastic dissipation heats the mixture; expanding water raises pore pressure and reduces shear resistance. At 100 mm slip, shear resistance falls 34.9%, temperature rises 70.15 K and pore pressure reaches 22.56 MPa. Saved-frame shear errors are 0.0011% of the initial resistance against the differential reference. At a glance Dimension 2D Build make ndims=2 from the poromechanics source (not yet merged; DynEarthSol #134) Inputs fault-heat.zip Reproduce with DynEarthSol 3774df0

documents.t: Geometry and motion. 10 mm square, four nodes and two triangles; plane strain and fixed reference mesh. The base is fixed; both sides impose a linear horizontal velocity from zero at the base to 1 m/s at the top. The top normal platen is free under 50 MPa compression. Initial material. Normal stresses −50 MPa, shear stress 25.866 MPa at yield; T=300 K, p=0. Mohr–Coulomb: K=20 GPa, G=10 GPa, cohesion 1 MPa, friction 30°, dilation zero. Physical mixture density 2360 kg/m³; damping and PT off. Water and heat. All faces sealed and insulated, gravity zero. Porosity 0.2, Biot coefficient 0.8, grain/fluid moduli 100/2.2 GPa. Fixed mixture heat capacity C=2,996,000 J/(m³ K), β=4×10⁻⁵/K; permeability, conductivity and solid expansion zero.

Every file this example needs is in fault-heat.zip. Run from that folder: # Slides at 1 m/s to 0.1 s (100 mm). Saves 600 time intervals; physical timestep is selected from the mixture mass. dynearthsol2d input.cfg

Setting Value What it does here control.has_shear_heating true converts accepted plastic work to heat, with unit heat fraction control.has_thermal_pressurization true expanding sealed water raises pressure control.has_fluid_thermal_advection true selects mixture heat capacity; this sealed case has zero Darcy flux control.is_quasi_static false false: use physical saturated mixture mass control.has_PT false false: ordinary explicit mechanics, with no PT solve control.damping_option 0 zero: no damping in the physical case control.fixed_dt 0.0 zero: automatic physical wave timestep control.dt_fraction 0.2 0.2: fraction of the mechanical stability bound bc.vbc_z1 8 8: the top has a uniform free normal velocity under its applied load bc.stress_val_z1 -50000000.0 −50 MPa total normal traction bc.vbc_val_x1 1.0 top horizontal velocity; the configured ratios give a linear profile on both sides mat.rheology_type elasto-plastic constant-friction Mohr–Coulomb plasticity, zero dilation input.cfg holds all 80 settings that differ from DES’s defaults; dynearthsol2d -h lists every option with its default.

See Running the examples for output files, the Python reader and ParaView conversion. Field What to look at stress σxz is shear resistance; σzz checks departure from imposed normal equilibrium temperature mixture temperature minus the initial 300 K pore pressure sealed thermal pressurization with normal compliance shear heating last accepted plastic power density, W/m³ pending shear heat accepted heat awaiting its thermal update, J/m per element in 2D strain trace gives the normal volume change in the fluid-content ledger

(a) Shear resistance under fixed total normal traction; the dashed line is the zero-water-expansion reference. (b) Temperature rise from plastic work. (c) Sealed pore pressure. Black curves solve the independent continuous MC/Jaumann equations; markers are ordinary explicit DES with physical mass and zero damping. Ordinary explicit mechanics with physical mixture inertia and zero damping follows the thermal weakening path. Companion GVS runs and slow-to-fast physical restarts check the mass/timestep transition and retain pending plastic heat separately from kinetic energy. S=ϕ/Kf+(α−ϕ)/Ks. The reference imposes normal equilibrium and checks that σyy=−N+ℓεv−αp stays the intermediate principal.

The independent continuous reference solves normal equilibrium and yield consistency for the volume strain rate and plastic multiplier. It integrates total stress, fluid content, temperature and work; it does not call or duplicate the DES return algorithm. Zero dilation gives opposite plastic normal strains. The stress equations include the Jaumann spin from simple shear; the sealed fluid law retains normal compliance. ϵxxp​′=ra/2,ϵzzp​′=−ra/2,γp′=rb A closed-form stiff-skeleton limit takes q≈τ, r≈1 and εv≈αp/(ℓ+G). It explains exponential thermal weakening; the plotted reference retains the finite-modulus equations above. Λ=β/[S+α2/(ℓ+G)],τ≃τ0​e−αsinϕΛγ/C Pending heat is included in accepted work. Exact power integration is checked only for cases saving every physical interval, including the first 20 intervals after switching slow GVS to physical mass. ET​+Epending​=n∑​VΔtn​qn​ Independent differential Mohr–Coulomb/Jaumann and sealed fluid/energy solution in fault_heat.py; a tighter integrator tolerance changes normalized stress by less than 1.6×10⁻¹⁰. Thermal-pressurization motivation: Rice (2006), doi:10.1029/2005JB004006. Full derivation and controls are in the supporting note.

A uniform two-triangle local patch with one normal mechanical mode, constant friction and fixed capacity. Saved-frame stress errors do not bound every wave peak. Fast GVS controls all reach the speed cap; they do not prove arbitrary scaling independence. Manual slow-to-fast restart does not establish automatic events, long tectonic clock handling, a spatial rupture or a full earthquake cycle.

A pressurized cell sheared at yield sees its loading rate rise tenfold. Rate-and-state friction jumps by aln10, then decays over the slip distance Dc​ to the new steady state (b>a: velocity weakening). DES follows its exact discrete recursion to round-off at every step (state and friction identical, stress within 9e-16), so the state is updated once per physical time step, not once per PT iteration. Against the continuum solution the largest friction error after the step is 9.56e-04, 4.67e-04, 2.31e-04, 1.15e-04 for steps of 1, 0.5, 0.25, 0.125 s: first order, against a jump of 0.0230. At a glance Dimension 2D Build make ndims=2 from the poromechanics source (not yet merged; DynEarthSol #134) Inputs rsf.zip Reproduce with DynEarthSol 3774df0
documents.s: Rate-and-state friction under a velocity step

documents.t: Cell. The material-strength unit cell: every node prescribed, normal extension rates ±e˙, plane strain, initial stress −CI with C=1 MPa and a fixed pore pressure of 0.8 MPa (α=1), cohesion 100 kPa, no dilation. Friction. EP-RSF with the aging law: a=0.01, b=0.015, Dc​=1 mm, μ0​=tan30∘, V0​=V1​, so the cell starts and stays at steady state; slip rate V=2wϵ˙II​ (total-strain-rate projection). Rate step. After 64 s at e˙1​=7.8×10−6 s−1 the cell restarts from its last checkpoint at 10e˙1​ for another 64 s. What is compared. Friction, state and principal shear stress at every step against the exact discrete recursion and the continuum solution, for steps of 1, 0.5, 0.25 and 0.125 s.

Every file this example needs is in rsf.zip. Run from that folder: # Loads the 2D cell at the slow rate for 512 steps of 0.125 s (64 s) and writes cell.save.* and cell.chkpt.* at every step; the last checkpoint (frame 512) is the starting point of the second stage. dynearthsol2d input.cfg # Restarts from cell frame 512 with ten times the boundary velocity and runs to step 1024 (another 64 s), writing step.save.*; no checkpoint is shipped, so the first stage must be run first. dynearthsol2d step.cfg

Setting Value What it does here mat.rheology_type elasto-plastic-rate-state-friction elasto-plastic-rate-state-friction: Mohr–Coulomb plasticity whose friction coefficient follows rate-and-state friction mat.state_var_model 1 1: aging law for the state variable θ mat.direct_a [0.01] direct-effect parameter a = 0.01: the instant friction jump at the rate step is a ln 10 mat.evolution_b [0.015] evolution parameter b = 0.015 > a, so the material is velocity weakening and the new steady friction is lower by (b − a) ln 10 mat.characteristic_distance [0.001] slip distance D_c = 1 mm over which friction relaxes to the new steady state mat.characteristic_velocity [1.1048543456039805e-05] reference slip rate V0, set equal to the initial slip rate V1 so the cell starts at steady state with μ = tan 30° control.rsf_slip_rate_projection_option 1 1: slip rate V = 2w ε̇_II from the total deviatoric strain rate (w is the element's minimum altitude) monitor.output_state_variable true writes the state variable and the dynamic friction coefficient to every frame bc.vbc_val_x1 7.8125e-06 extension rate of the cell (right face velocity); step.cfg multiplies it by 10 bc.vbc_val_z1 -7.8125e-06 equal shortening rate on the top; step.cfg multiplies it by 10 ic.pore_pressure_value 800000.0 fixed pore pressure 0.8 MPa (uniform, pore_pressure_option 2) ic.initial_stress [-1000000.0, -1000000.0, 0.0] isotropic total stress of −1 MPa control.fixed_dt 0.125 time step 0.125 s, the finest step of the study sim.checkpoint_frame_interval 1 1: a checkpoint at every frame, so the rate step can restart from the last one input.cfg holds all 70 settings that differ from DES’s defaults; dynearthsol2d -h lists every option with its default.

See Running the examples for output files, the Python reader and ParaView conversion. Field What to look at dynamic friction coefficient element friction coefficient μ, plotted across the rate step in panel (a) friction state variable element state θ; compared with the exact forward-Euler recursion at every step stress element total stress; half the principal-stress difference is the shear stress at yield in panel (b)

(a) Friction coefficient across the tenfold step in loading rate, against time from the step: solid line, continuum solution; thin stepped line, the forward-Euler recursion at the same time step; symbols, DES at the finest time step. (b) Principal shear stress at yield, which follows the friction coefficient through the Mohr–Coulomb load. (c) Largest friction error against the continuum solution after the step, for each time step, with a first-order reference slope. This verifies the evolving rate-and-state friction of the effective-stress plasticity, which the strength page checks only at constant friction. To reproduce the whole study behind this figure, from the DES source folder: python3 tests/functional/hydromechanics/check_rsf_step.py dynearthsol2d OUT --refinements 1 2 4 8 The study’s full numbers: record.json.

documents.t: μ=μ0​+alnV0​V​+blnDc​V0​θ​θ˙=1−Dc​Vθ​θ(t)=V2​Dc​​+(V1​Dc​​−V2​Dc​​)e−V2​(t−t1​)/Dc​,t>t1​τ=min(2Ge, ccosϕ+(C−αp)sinϕ),tanϕ=μ θ is the state variable, V the slip rate, w the element's minimum altitude and τ half the principal-stress difference. DES advances θ by forward Euler, once per physical step.

With V held constant the aging law is linear in θ and integrates to the exponential above; at t1​ friction jumps by aln10 through the direct effect and relaxes to the new steady state, a net change of (a−b)ln10. With every node prescribed and no dilation, the stress is elastic until yield and then equals the Mohr–Coulomb load at the current friction. The discrete reference repeats DES’s forward-Euler update; the continuum one is exact. Dieterich (1979), Journal of Geophysical Research 84(B5), 2161–2168; Ruina (1983), Journal of Geophysical Research 88(B12), 10359–10370. Original reference.
Aging law and the total-strain-rate slip projection only; constant pore pressure; no dilation, no elastic interaction (every node prescribed), so stick–slip instability is not tested.

A half-space whose surface is suddenly held cold cools by conduction along the error-function profile T(z,t)=Ts​+(Tm​−Ts​)erf(2κt​∣z∣​), the classic model for the cooling of oceanic lithosphere with age. This benchmark starts DES from the profile of a 1-million-year-old plate and lets it cool to 100 million years. At a glance Dimension 2D and 3D, same input Build make ndims=2 and make ndims=3 Run time 6 s (2D) and 41 s (3D) on 8 threads Inputs benchmarks/heat/half-space-cooling/diffusion.cfg in the DynEarthSol repository Checked with DynEarthSol 68cc2a0

Setting Value Domain 10 km wide (and 10 km long in 3D), 250 km deep; element size about 2 km Temperature Ts​ = 273 K held at the top; insulated sides and base; initial profile of a plate 1 Myr old with Tm​ = 1600 K (ic.temperature_option = 0) Thermal properties k = 3 W/m/K, cp​ = 1000 J/kg/K, ρ0​ = 3000 kg/m³, so κ=k/(ρ0​cp​)=10−6 m²/s Mechanics elastic, no gravity, a very small characteristic speed so that the thermal time step controls Output a frame every 1 Myr to 100 Myr At 100 Myr the cooling front, 2κt​, is 112 km deep, well above the insulated base at 250 km, so the half-space solution applies.

cd benchmarks/heat/half-space-cooling ../../../dynearthsol2d diffusion.cfg ../../../dynearthsol3d diffusion.cfg Each run writes diffusion.save.*. Frame n is the plate at age 1+n Myr. benchmarks/heat/half-space-cooling/diffusion-plot.py plots frames 0, 9 and 59 against the error function; it was written for Python 2 and the earlier output reader.

Plate age Largest difference, 2D Largest difference, 3D With mat.alpha = [0], 2D With mat.alpha = [0], 3D 1 Myr (initial) 2.6 K 2.6 K 0.0 K 0.0 K 10 Myr 8.3 K 9.1 K 1.2 K 1.1 K 60 Myr 9.6 K 9.7 K 0.21 K 0.26 K DES follows the error function in both dimensions, within 10 K of a 1327 K range. Most of that difference is not numerical. The input does not set mat.alpha, so the default thermal expansion, 3×10−5 K⁻¹, makes the density, and so the diffusivity, depend on temperature, while the error function assumes a constant diffusivity. The same input with alpha = [ 0 ] in [mat] comes within 1.2 K at 10 Myr and 0.3 K at 60 Myr. Even the initial profile differs by up to 2.6 K, because DES evaluates it with the density of the first element.
Conduction only. There is no advection, heat source or shear heating. One resolution. The element size is fixed at about 2 km; the near- surface gradient at 1 Myr is resolved by about five elements.

A Maxwell material loaded at a constant strain rate first responds elastically, then its stress approaches the viscous value 2ηε˙ over the Maxwell time η/G. This benchmark shortens a square of Maxwell material in pure shear and compares the stress with that response. It uses DES's explicit mechanics with mass scaling, not the PT solver; for PT see Maxwell creep under a held load. At a glance Dimension 2D Build make ndims=2 Run time about 7 minutes, 8 threads (2.2 million steps) Inputs benchmarks/mechanics/maxwell/maxwell.cfg in the DynEarthSol repository Checked with DynEarthSol 68cc2a0
documents.s: Maxwell stress build-up in pure shear

documents.t: Setting Value Domain 1 m × 1 m, element size 0.05 m (441 elements) Loading the right side moves inward and the base moves down, each at v=10−14 m/s; the left side and the top cannot move normal to themselves Material rheology_type = maxwell, G = 10 GPa, K = 1000 GPa (nearly incompressible), η=1022 Pa s, so η/G=1012 s Mechanics explicit, inertial_scaling = 1e6, characteristic_speed = 1e-14 Duration 3×1012 s, three Maxwell times, a frame every 104 steps The input uses standard velocity conditions (vbc_x1 = 1, vbc_val_x1 = -1e-14, vbc_z0 = 1, vbc_val_z0 = -1e-14) and stops at max_time_in_yr = 95000. Earlier versions of this input used a boundary type that needed a source patch. With the side lengths Lx​=1−vt and Lz​=1+vt, the strain rates are −v/Lx​ and +v/Lz​, and the stress difference D=σxx​−σzz​ of a Maxwell material obeys dtdD​=2G(−Lx​v​−Lz​v​)−ηG​D. The reference integrates this equation. Its limit is 4ηv=400 MPa in magnitude.
cd benchmarks/mechanics/maxwell ../../../dynearthsol2d maxwell.cfg

DES Reference Interior elements (median), after 3η/G 387 MPa 380 MPa Largest relative difference after η/G, interior median 1.9 % Top element row (median), after 3η/G 172 MPa 380 MPa The elements below the top row follow the Maxwell response: the stress rises elastically, bends over after about one Maxwell time and approaches 4ηv. Their median stays within 2 % of the reference; individual interior elements scatter by up to about ±15 % at the end. The 29 elements that touch the top surface do not. Their stress stops rising after about 1.5 Maxwell times and then falls; they shorten by about 40 % of the imposed strain. Exchanging the roles of top and base, holding the base and moving the top up, gives the same result: only the row at the top surface lags. The cause is not identified; the behaviour is reported here as found.

Top surface. As described above, the top element row departs from the homogeneous solution; compare the interior only. Explicit mechanics only. The PT solver is checked separately in Maxwell creep under a held load.

A circular opening concentrates stress in an elastic solid under isotropic compression. Radial/hoop stress RMS errors: 0.148% / 0.169% of P; largest local error 2.15%. At a glance Dimension 2D Build make ndims=2 from the poromechanics source (not yet merged; DynEarthSol #134) Inputs kirsch.zip Reproduce with DynEarthSol 3774df0

Geometry and load. A quarter annulus has opening radius a = 1 m and outer radius R = 20a. The opening is free; the outer curved face carries isotropic compressive traction P = 100 kPa. Constraints. The two straight symmetry cuts have zero normal displacement. This is a dry plane-strain problem with gravity and transport disabled. Material and comparison. K = G = 1 GPa. Stress and strain are compared over 1.1a≤r≤5a with the finite-annulus reference; the analytical curve remains visible and DES markers are thinned for display.

Every file this example needs is in kirsch.zip. Run from that folder: # Meshes the quarter annulus from annulus.poly (shipped alongside) at 0.025 m inner spacing, solves one quasi-static step to equilibrium and writes kirsch.save.* and kirsch.chkpt.*, with kirsch.info listing the frames. dynearthsol2d input.cfg

Setting Value What it does here mesh.meshing_option 90 90: mesh the polygon read from poly_filename mesh.poly_filename annulus.poly annulus.poly: quarter annulus a = 1 m to R = 20 m; its boundary flags make the vertical cut x0, the opening x1, the horizontal cut z0 and the outer arc z1 mesh.resolution 0.025 0.025 m element size, the finest mesh of the study mesh.min_angle 28 28°, keeps triangles well shaped along the curved boundaries bc.stress_bc_z1 4 type 4: normal stress on facets of any orientation, here the curved outer arc bc.stress_val_z1 -100000.0 P = 100 kPa isotropic compression on the outer arc (tension positive, so negative) bc.vbc_x1 0 0: the opening (flag x1) is free bc.vbc_z0 1 1: zero normal displacement on the horizontal symmetry cut (the vertical cut x0 uses the default 1) mat.rheology_type elastic elastic mat.bulk_modulus [1e9] K = 1 GPa mat.shear_modulus [1e9] G = 1 GPa mat.is_plane_strain true 2D plane strain; the out-of-plane stress σyy is not zero control.gravity 0 no gravity: the outer traction is the only load sim.max_steps 1 1: one step solved to equilibrium by PT is the static answer input.cfg holds all 46 settings that differ from DES’s defaults; dynearthsol2d -h lists every option with its default.

See Running the examples for output files, the Python reader and ParaView conversion. Field What to look at stress element stress, rotated to radial and hoop components and compared over 1.1a ≤ r ≤ 5a in panel (a) strain element strain, rotated to radial and hoop components in panel (b)

(a) Radial and hoop compression, scaled by P, against distance from the opening centre: lines, the finite-annulus solution; symbols, DES elements (thinned for display). (b) Radial and hoop elastic strain, scaled by P/G. (c) RMS stress error, scaled by P, against the inner mesh spacing. This checks dry elastic stress, strain, curved-surface traction and symmetry constraints. Plasticity and excavation history remain separate checks; poroelastic injection is on the borehole page. To reproduce the whole study behind this figure, from the DES source folder: python3 benchmarks/poromechanics/kirsch_reference.py python3 tests/functional/hydromechanics/check_kirsch.py dynearthsol2d OUT --spacings .2 .1 .05 .025 The study’s full numbers: record.json.

documents.t: A0​=−PR2/(R2−a2)B0​=−Pa2R2/(R2−a2)σrr​=A0​−B0​/r2σθθ​=A0​+B0​/r2ur​=2(λ+G)A0​r​+2GrB0​​λ=K−2G/3ϵrr​=ur′​ϵθθ​=ur​/rσyy​=ν(σrr​+σθθ​) Stress and displacement are tension/outward positive; σyy​ is the out-of-plane stress. ν=λ/[2(λ+G)]. Displacement is measured from an unloaded annulus, rather than from a precompressed excavation state.

Radial equilibrium and the isotropic plane-strain Hooke law give the displacement Cr+D/r. The boundary stresses determine the two integration constants. dσrr​/dr+(σrr​−σθθ​)/r=0 Substitute zero radial stress at the opening and -P at the outer wall. As the wall moves to infinity, the finite solution approaches the isotropically loaded Kirsch limit. σrr​(a)=0σrr​(R)=−P Finite-annulus solution derived from radial equilibrium; evaluated and checked in kirsch_reference.py and check_kirsch.py.

Isotropic, small-strain, dry elasticity. The finite outer wall changes the opening hoop stress by 0.251% relative to infinite-domain Kirsch. Anisotropic loading, plasticity, excavation history and poroelastic injection remain separate tests.

A circular tunnel is excavated in rock under uniform in-situ stress: the support pressure on its wall is lowered to zero, and a ring of rock around the opening yields. Salençon’s solution gives the stresses, the plastic radius and the wall convergence for a perfectly plastic Mohr–Coulomb material. On the 0.05 m mesh the hoop stress is within 1.57% of P (RMS), the displacement within 0.21% of the wall convergence, and the plastic radius within 0.34%. The radial strain error, 3.88% of P/G, is concentrated within half a radius of the wall. At a glance Dimension 2D Build make ndims=2 from the poromechanics source (not yet merged; DynEarthSol #134) Inputs salencon.zip Reproduce with DynEarthSol 3774df0

Geometry and load. A quarter annulus with opening radius a=1 m and outer radius R=20a, in plane strain. The rock starts under uniform compression P=500 kPa in all three directions. The support pressure on the opening wall is lowered from P to zero in 16 equal steps, while the outer boundary keeps the pressure P. Constraints. The two straight symmetry cuts have zero normal displacement. Gravity, fluid flow and heat are off, and the mesh does not move. Material. Perfectly plastic Mohr–Coulomb: c=100 kPa, ϕ=30∘, associated flow (ψ=30∘), G=10 GPa, K=21.7 GPa (ν=0.3). No softening and no weak zone. What is compared. Radial, hoop and out-of-plane stress, radial and hoop strain, and radial displacement for 1.05a≤r≤5a after the support is removed, on meshes refined near the opening to 0.2, 0.1 and 0.05 m, against the finite-annulus Salençon solution.

Every file this example needs is in salencon.zip. Run from that folder: # Meshes annulus.poly (0.05 m near the opening, coarser outward) and writes the initial state: uniform 500 kPa compression, the wall still supported at 500 kPa, frame 0 with a checkpoint. dynearthsol2d seed.cfg # Fifteen unloading steps, load-001.cfg to load-015.cfg in order. Each restarts from the previous one and lowers the wall support pressure by P/16 (load-path.json lists them); one PT step per file brings the rock to equilibrium. ls load-0*.cfg | xargs -n 1 dynearthsol2d # The last step removes the support completely; this is the state compared with Salençon. input.cfg is the same file, and the shipped load-015 frame lets you run it without the earlier steps (but the displacement in the figure sums the velocities of every step). dynearthsol2d salencon.cfg

Setting Value What it does here ic.initial_stress [-500000.0,-500000.0,0] uniform in-situ compression of 500 kPa in x and z (the out-of-plane stress starts equal) bc.stress_bc_x1 4 normal traction on the opening wall: the support pressure bc.stress_val_x1 -0.0 support pressure in this step, negative in compression; it is −500 kPa in seed.cfg, steps down by 31.25 kPa per load file, and is zero here bc.stress_bc_z1 4 normal traction on the outer boundary bc.stress_val_z1 -500000.0 the outer boundary keeps the in-situ 500 kPa compression throughout bc.vbc_z0 1 the straight cut along x has zero normal velocity (symmetry); vbc_x0 does the same for the other cut mat.rheology_type elasto-plastic Mohr–Coulomb elasto-plasticity mat.cohesion0 [100000.0] cohesion 100 kPa; cohesion1 is the same, so there is no softening mat.dilation_angle0 [30.0] dilation 30°, equal to the friction angle: associated flow control.has_PT true each step is solved to equilibrium by PT; the material is rate independent, so the 1 s step has no physical meaning control.PT_relative_tolerance 1e-9 tight equilibrium tolerance for every unloading step control.is_using_mixed_stress true smooths element pressure after the plastic return; needed here, because without it the plastic ring next to the wall develops an alternating pressure between neighbouring elements and diverges control.has_moving_mesh false small strain: the mesh stays in its original position mesh.poly_filename annulus.poly the quarter-annulus outline, with a finer region within 3a of the centre input.cfg holds all 57 settings that differ from DES’s defaults; dynearthsol2d -h lists every option with its default.

See Running the examples for output files, the Python reader and ParaView conversion. Field What to look at stress radial and hoop stress at element centres, rotated to polar components (panel a) stressyy out-of-plane stress; written in the checkpoint (salencon.chkpt.*), not the .save frame (panel a) velocity times the 1 s step and summed over every step, it gives the radial displacement (panel b) strain total strain from the initially compressed state, compared as radial and hoop strain plastic strain marks the yielded ring; its outer edge is the plastic radius

(a) Radial, hoop and out-of-plane stress against r/a after the support is removed, finest mesh: DES at element centres (dots) and Salençon (lines); the dashed line marks the analytical plastic radius. (b) Inward radial displacement of the nodes, scaled by the analytical wall convergence, with the analytical curve. (c) RMS errors of hoop stress, displacement and radial strain over 1.05a≤r≤5a against the inner mesh spacing. This checks Mohr–Coulomb plasticity with dilation around an opening: the stress redistribution, the extent of the plastic zone and the wall convergence that support design relies on. To reproduce the whole study behind this figure, from the DES source folder: python3 tests/functional/hydromechanics/check_salencon.py dynearthsol2d OUT --spacings .2 .1 .05 --dilation 30 --mixed --refined --load-steps 16 # Figure sources: des3d/docs/benchmarks/poromechanics/img/_src/qualify_salencon.py The study’s full numbers: record.json.

documents.t: N=1−sinϕ1+sinϕ​q=2cN​sr​=CrN−1−N−1q​,sθ​=Nsr​+q(a≤r≤b)C=aN−1Pi​+q/(N−1)​sr​=A−B/r2,sθ​=A+B/r2(b≤r≤R)CbN−1−N−1q​=(N+1)R2−(N−1)b2(2P−q)R2+qb2​ sr​ and sθ​ are radial and hoop stress, compression positive (DES output is tension positive). Pi​ is the support pressure on the wall, here zero at the end, and b the plastic radius: 1.39575 m for R=20a (1.39405 m for an infinite domain). A and B follow from continuity of sr​ at b and sr​=P at R. The displacement integrates the plastic flow rule inside b and the elastic solution outside it; the derivation gives it.

Inside the plastic zone, radial equilibrium sr′​+(sr​−sθ​)/r=0 with the yield condition sθ​=Nsr​+q gives a power law in r; the wall pressure Pi​ fixes C. Outside it the Lamé solution holds. Requiring the elastic stress at b to reach yield gives the scalar equation for b, solved numerically. sr′​+(sr​−sθ​)/r=0 For the displacement, the plastic strains follow the flow rule ϵrp​=−Mϵθp​ with M=(1+sinψ)/(1−sinψ), and the out-of-plane plastic strain is zero. Adding the elastic strains of plane-strain Hooke’s law gives u′+Mu/r as a known function of r; integrating from b, where u matches the elastic solution, gives u in the plastic zone. Strain and displacement are measured from the initially compressed state. u′+rM​u=ere​+Meθe​ Salençon (1969), Contraction quasi-statique d’une cavité à symétrie sphérique ou cylindrique dans un milieu élastoplastique, Annales des Ponts et Chaussées 4, 231–236; the solution as given in the Itasca verification example for a cylindrical hole in a Mohr–Coulomb material. Original reference.

The tunnel comparison also needs a correct material-point return. This check uses tension-positive stress, unlike the compression-positive tunnel reference above. In the order (xx,zz,yy), define C=λ11T+2GI,A=(N0​0N​−1−1​). The rows of B replace the friction factor N by the dilation factor M. If the trial reaches both adjacent shear faces, the independent reference solves the two active constraints together: (ACBT)η=Aσtr−q1,σ=σtr−CBTη. The multipliers must be nonnegative and the returned principals ordered. The tensile cap must also hold. DES keeps the existing single-face return when its principals remain ordered; otherwise its shared shear routine checks both adjacent edges and restores the repeated eigenvalue. For the same rock, an associated trial with sorted principals (169,185,200) kPa exceeds the tensile cap T=173.205 kPa, yet its admissible shear return is (165.347657,170.585939,170.585939) kPa. Both shear multipliers are positive and the tensile constraint is inactive. Therefore the trial maximum alone cannot select tensile clipping. Both 2D plane strain and 3D test the uncut shear return before accepting a tensile/composite branch. Rotated material-point tests and 1/16/64-increment paths check the stress and plastic history independently of stress smoothing. These controls qualify constant strength; they do not establish general apex, mixed tensile/shear or evolving-strength accuracy.
documents.s: Component check: return to a shear edge

documents.t: With no mixed-stress smoothing, the coarse tunnel develops alternating pressure between elements with an edge and a vertex on the wall. The out-of-plane stress remains the intermediate principal until the apex, so the shear-edge correction does not explain this spatial mode. Mixed stress suppresses the alternating pressure, but projects stress after the plastic return. The projected state can leave local yield and return again at the next step. This is a plausible explanation of the load-hold drift, rather than a demonstrated defect in the local return. At fixed mesh, the 16/32/64-stage sequences do not demonstrate convergence in the load increment. At the matching 32 stages, refining 0.05 to 0.025 m reduces hoop error from 3.09% to 1.24% and displacement error from 0.372% to 0.113%, while radial-strain error remains 4.44% of P/G. The selected 16-stage result must be read with this limit. No correction of both spatial effects has been qualified.
documents.s: Why small force residuals do not establish convergence

documents.t: Dry, isotropic loading, small strain, perfectly plastic. The radial strain misses a 3% target (3.88% of P/G on the finest mesh), almost all of it within half a radius of the wall. With mixed stress (needed here) the stored stress readjusts slightly at every step, so the result depends on the number of unloading steps: on the 0.05 m mesh, 16, 32 and 64 steps give hoop errors of 1.57%, 3.09% and 6.71%. Use the 16 steps shipped here, and do not hold the final load for many extra steps. Without mixed stress the coarse mesh diverges near the wall. Zero dilation is not covered.

An oedometer shortens a sample in one direction while its other sides cannot move. The strain is uniaxial, so the stress follows a closed-form path: elastic up to yield, then a straight plastic branch whose slope depends on the friction and dilation angles. This benchmark checks DES's Mohr–Coulomb return on that path. At a glance Dimension 2D, plane strain Build make ndims=2 Run time about 1 s Inputs benchmarks/mechanics/oedometer/oedometer-2d.cfg in the DynEarthSol repository Checked with DynEarthSol cd1042c

Setting Value Cell 1 m × 1 m, two triangles, plane strain (is_plane_strain = yes) Loading the right side moves inward at 10−5 m/s; the left, top and bottom sides cannot move normal to themselves Elasticity K=G=200 MPa Strength cohesion c = 1 MPa, friction angle ϕ = 10°, dilation angle ψ = 10°, no softening, tension cut-off 5.67 MPa Other no gravity; fixed time step 1 s, 2000 steps (20 mm of shortening) With E1​=K+4G/3 and E2​=K−2G/3, the axial stress rises elastically as Δσxx​=E1​Δε and the lateral stresses as E2​Δε. With Nϕ​=(1+sinϕ)/(1−sinϕ), the cell yields at ∣σxx​∣=E1​−E2​Nϕ​2cNϕ​​E1​​, here after 6.41 mm of shortening. Both lateral stresses are equal, so the return lies on the edge of two Mohr–Coulomb faces. With Nψ​=(1+sinψ)/(1−sinψ) the plastic branch has slope dεd∣σxx​∣​=E1​+2r(E2​Nψ​−E1​),r=(E1​+E2​)Nϕ​Nψ​−2E2​(Nϕ​+Nψ​)+2E1​E1​−E2​Nϕ​​. The reference evaluates this path at the true strain DES applies, ε=∑vΔt/(1−u) with u the shortening at the start of each step, because DES updates the cell's geometry every step.

cd benchmarks/mechanics/oedometer ../../../dynearthsol2d oedometer-2d.cfg The run writes 51 frames, result.save.*, one every 40 steps. benchmarks/mechanics/oedometer/oedometer-2d-plot.py plots the shortening of the right side against σxx​ with a reference path; it was written for an older Matplotlib and needs small changes to run with a current one. Its path takes each step's strain at the end-of-step shortening and changes slope only at a whole step, which puts its final stress 0.03 % above the closed form.

DES Reference Axial stress after 20 mm 7.0868 MPa 7.0864 MPa Largest relative difference, elastic branch 0.017 % Largest relative difference, plastic branch 0.014 % DES follows the path on both branches. The two elements carry the same stress, so the cell deforms uniformly, as the reference assumes.

One stress path. Uniaxial strain tests the two-face edge return and the dilation angle, but not the apex or the tension cut-off. No softening. Cohesion and friction stay constant; see the shear-band benchmark for softening.

note Poromechanics is not yet merged into DynEarthSol. It is under review in GeoFLAC/DynEarthSol#134 and is being merged in parts. Until then, build DES from the source revision named on each page. Benchmarks of coupled fluid flow, heat and deformation in DES. Each page sets up one problem, gives the input file and the commands to run it, says which output to look at, and compares the result with an analytical or independent reference solution, with the limits of that comparison. The applications built on these checks, slides, rapid drawdown, embankment stability and land subsidence, are in the Groundwater and slopes tutorials. Every example ships its input file and any mesh or restart files it needs, so it runs as is with DES built from this source. See Running the examples. Terms: DES is DynEarthSol. PT is its pseudo-transient solver, which iterates each time step to mechanical equilibrium by dynamic relaxation; a physical step is one model time step, as opposed to a PT iteration. The explicit form is ordinary explicit mechanics with inertial (mass) scaling, and GVS is that form with global velocity scaling. Pressure feedback means that deformation changes the pore pressure, so flow and mechanics are coupled both ways. EP is elasto-plastic Mohr–Coulomb plasticity, and EP-RSF the same with rate-and-state friction. Pressure is compression-positive; stress and volumetric strain are tension/expansion-positive. These examples need DynEarthSol built from the poromechanics source.

Finite-density water in a sealed cell. Heat and pressure in a drained cell. Injection and mixing in a storing cell. Three-dimensional convection cells. The figures use recorded runs. Each download keeps its executable and data hashes; reproduction_revision names the public source to build for reproducing the example. Version and file hashes.

Theis confined-aquifer pumping reference. Hantush–Jacob pumping from a leaky aquifer. Several wells: pumping, injection and recovery. Open boundaries: a draining pressure pulse. Anisotropic flow with changing permeability. Closed-box fluid and heat sources. van Genuchten steady infiltration. Brooks–Corey steady infiltration. Gardner transient infiltration. Bishop effective stress: lowering the water table. Bishop coupling in a sealed cell under compression. Drainage of a saturated column into the unsaturated state. Water balance in a deforming column. Terzaghi consolidation. Mandel consolidation under a rigid plate. Cryer consolidation of a sphere. Generalized Bear–Corapcioglu aquifer reference. Application: seasonal pumping and land subsidence. Factor of safety of an embankment by strength reduction. Application: rapid drawdown of a reservoir against an embankment. Application: pore pressure triggers a translational slide. Application: rainfall triggers a shallow slide. Fluid injection into a poroelastic solid. Physical-inertia undrained wave. Pore pressure and material strength. Rate-and-state friction under a velocity step. Plastic shear heating and sealed pressurization. Fault-zone heating at fixed normal traction. Water balance through plastic yielding. Pressure-driven yielding of a confined layer. Elastic circular opening: Kirsch limit. Plastic tunnel: Salençon solution. Fluid injection into a poroelastic borehole. Groundwater heat transport: Ogata–Banks. Thermal pressurization in a sealed cell. Thermal pressurization: McTigue surface heating. Onset of hydrothermal convection. Steady hydrothermal convection: Nusselt number. Hot-water injection: Avdonin solution and heat ledger.

Fluid at pressure pw​ enters a borehole wall: it loads the wall and diffuses into the rock, which changes the stresses around the hole as it goes. The axisymmetric part of Detournay and Cheng’s borehole problem, on a finite annulus. On the 0.05 a mesh: pressure within 0.06% of pw​ at every node for 1.05 a ≤ r ≤ 4 a and all four times; total stress rms 0.16% (hoop) with a largest element error of 1.06%. At a glance Dimension 2D Build make ndims=2 from the poromechanics source (not yet merged; DynEarthSol #134) Inputs borehole.zip Reproduce with DynEarthSol 3774df0
documents.s: Fluid injection into a poroelastic borehole

documents.t: Geometry. A quarter annulus a=1 m, R=20a, plane strain, with symmetry rollers on both cuts; meshes refined out to 5a. Loading. At t=0+ the wall takes fluid at pw​=1 MPa: pore pressure pw​ (a 1 ms ramp) and normal traction −pw​. The outer arc is sealed and traction-free. The rock starts unstressed at p=0; gravity is off. Material. K=200 MPa, G=100 MPa, α=1, 1/M=ϕ/Kf​=10−9 Pa−1, k/μ=10−9 m2/(Pas); diffusivity c=0.25 m2/s. What is compared. Nodal pressure and element total radial and hoop stress for 1.05a≤r≤4a at 9, 18, 27 and 36 s, relative to pw​.

Every file this example needs is in borehole.zip. Run from that folder: # Meshes the quarter annulus from annulus.poly (shipped alongside) at 0.05 m inner spacing and runs 144 steps of 0.25 s (36 s), saving hole.save.* every 36 steps (9, 18, 27 and 36 s) with hole.info listing the frames. dynearthsol2d input.cfg

Setting Value What it does here mesh.meshing_option 90 90: mesh the polygon read from poly_filename mesh.poly_filename annulus.poly annulus.poly: quarter annulus a = 1 m to R = 20 m with a refined ring to 5a; flags: vertical cut x0, borehole wall x1, horizontal cut z0, outer arc z1 mesh.resolution 0.05 0.05 m element size near the wall, the finest mesh of the study bc.hbc_x1 2 type 2: pore pressure prescribed on the borehole wall from hbc_pressure bc.hbc_pressure [0,1000000.0,0,0,0,0] the x1 (wall) entry is the fluid pressure p_w = 1 MPa bc.stress_bc_x1 4 type 4: normal stress on the curved wall bc.stress_val_x1 -1000000.0 −p_w: the wall fluid pushes on the rock (tension positive) bc.num_hbc_schedule 2 two schedule points for the wall pressure bc.hbc_schedule_time_in_yr [0, 3.168876453507857e-11] yr = [0, 0.001] s 0 and 1 ms: the wall pressure ramps on almost instantly bc.hbc_schedule_ratio [0, 1] 0 to 1, then held at p_w mat.hydraulic_perm [1e-12] k = 1e-12 m²; with water viscosity 1e-3 Pa s the mobility k/μ is 1e-9 m²/(Pa s) mat.fluid_bulk_modulus [200000000.0] K_f = 200 MPa; with porosity 0.2 the storage 1/M = φ/K_f is 1e-9 /Pa mat.bulk_modulus [200000000.0] K = 200 MPa (shear modulus 100 MPa); together they give diffusivity c = 0.25 m²/s sim.output_step_interval 36 36 steps: frames at 9, 18, 27 and 36 s, the four compared times input.cfg holds all 57 settings that differ from DES’s defaults; dynearthsol2d -h lists every option with its default.

See Running the examples for output files, the Python reader and ParaView conversion. Field What to look at pore pressure nodal pressure, binned by radius and compared with the reference in panel (a) stress element total stress, rotated to radial and hoop components in panel (b)

(a) Pore pressure, scaled by the wall pressure p_w, against distance from the borehole centre at the four saved times: lines, the finite-annulus poroelastic solution; symbols, DES. (b) Total radial and hoop stress, scaled by p_w, at the last saved time. (c) Largest pressure and stress errors against mesh spacing. This checks the coupled poroelastic response around an opening: diffusion from a curved boundary, the pressure-driven hoop stress and the wall load together. To reproduce the whole study behind this figure, from the DES source folder: python3 benchmarks/poromechanics/borehole_reference.py python3 tests/functional/hydromechanics/check_borehole.py dynearthsol2d OUT/mesh --spacings 0.2 0.1 0.05 python3 tests/functional/hydromechanics/check_borehole.py dynearthsol2d OUT/steps --spacings 0.1 --steps 576 The study’s full numbers: record.json.

documents.t: Spt​+2αC˙1​=μk​r1​∂r∂​(r∂r∂p​)S=M1​+αm,m=λ+2Gα​σrr​=−2Gmr2J​+2(λ+G)C1​−2Gr2C2​​σθθ​=2Gm(r2J​−p)+2(λ+G)C1​+2Gr2C2​​J(r)=∫ar​pr′dr′σrr​(a)=−pw​,σrr​(R)=0 Tension positive. The radial displacement is u=mJ/r+C1​r+C2​/r, so the volumetric strain is mp+2C1​; C1​(t) and C2​(t) follow from the two traction conditions and are linear in pw​ and J(R).

Radial symmetry makes the displacement irrotational, so equilibrium integrates once: the volumetric strain is mp plus a uniform term 2C1​. Fluid mass, αε˙v​+p˙​/M=∇⋅(k∇p/μ), then gives the diffusion equation above. On a finite annulus C1​=0 and depends on J(R), which couples the pressure to its own integral; it moves the pressure by about 1% of pw​ here. In Laplace space the pressure is a Bessel (I0​, K0​, I1​, K1​) solution plus a uniform part −2αCˉ1​/S, with Cˉ1​ from one scalar equation; Stehfest inversion agrees with an independent Crank–Nicolson solution to 5×10−6 of pw​. Detournay and Cheng (1988), International Journal of Rock Mechanics and Mining Sciences 25(3), 171–182, axisymmetric loading modes; the finite annulus is solved in borehole_reference.py. Original reference.

Axisymmetric loading only (no deviatoric in-situ stress), linear poroelasticity, small strain. The finite annulus is part of the reference; the infinite-medium Detournay–Cheng solution is its R→∞ limit.

Two pressure modes drain from a square; scalar permeability and directional anisotropy change together at 0.5 s. Maximum pressure error 0.0900% of P₀; spatial orders 2.008 and 2.014 between successive meshes. Halving the time step halves the change in the solution (ratio 2.00004): first order in time. A restart inside the second phase reproduces the uninterrupted run exactly. At a glance Dimension 2D Build make ndims=2 from the poromechanics source (not yet merged; DynEarthSol #134) Inputs anisotropic-time.zip Reproduce with DynEarthSol 3774df0

Domain and drainage. A 1 m square, 0<x<1, −1<z<0; all four sides hold p=0. Gravity, heat and mesh motion are off. Initial pressure. Two sine modes have relative amplitudes 1 and 0.35. Their different horizontal wave numbers distinguish the two directional diffusivities. Coefficient change. At ts​=0.5 s, scalar permeability doubles and the axis-aligned tensor changes. Pressure and storage are continuous. The second phase is a restart at ts​ with the new coefficients; a further restart part-way through it reproduces the uninterrupted run.

Every file this example needs is in anisotropic-time.zip. Run from that folder: # First phase: restarts from the shipped seed.save.000000, seed.chkpt.000000 and seed.info, whose frame 0 holds the two-mode initial pressure, and runs 40,000 steps of 1.25e-5 s to t_s = 0.5 s with the first permeability tensor. DES writes first.* frames and checkpoints at 0.25 and 0.5 s. dynearthsol2d input.cfg # Second phase: restarts from frame 2 of the first run (0.5 s) with doubled scalar permeability and the new tensor, and runs to 1 s. DES writes second.* frames at 0.75 and 1 s. It needs the first.* checkpoint written by the previous command. dynearthsol2d continuation.cfg

Setting Value What it does here sim.is_restarting true starts from a saved state instead of the built-in initial condition sim.restarting_from_modelname seed the shipped seed files, which hold the two sine modes; continuation.cfg restarts from first instead sim.max_steps 40000 40,000 steps of 1.25e-5 s end the first phase at 0.5 s; continuation.cfg counts on to 80,000 steps (1 s) sim.output_step_interval 20000 a frame every 20,000 steps (0.25 s), each with a checkpoint for the restart control.fixed_dt 1.25e-05 physical step of 1.25e-5 s, inside the elastic stability limit control.is_quasi_static false off: mechanics runs with its physical inertia, without mass scaling control.has_poroelastic_pressure_feedback false off: deformation does not change the pressure, so pressure obeys pure diffusion control.gravity 0 no gravity bc.hbc_x0 2 type 2: the side x = 0 is held at the pressure in bc.hbc_pressure, here 0; x = 1 m, top and bottom are the same, so every side drains bc.hbc_z0 2 type 2: the bottom is held at p = 0 mat.hydraulic_perm [1e-15] scalar permeability k_0 = 1e-15 m² in the first phase; continuation.cfg doubles it mat.permeability_tensor [4, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0] dimensionless tensor multiplying hydraulic_perm, [xx, yy, zz, xy, xz, yz]; in 2D xx is horizontal and zz vertical. [4, 1, 1] gives k_x = 4k_0, k_z = k_0; continuation.cfg uses [1, 1, 9] with 2k_0, i.e. k_x = 2k_0, k_z = 18k_0 mat.porosity [0.3] with the fluid and grain moduli, sets the storage S_0 mat.bulk_modulus [1e7] soft skeleton (1e7 Pa, as the shear modulus), which sets the elastic step limit input.cfg holds all 58 settings that differ from DES’s defaults; dynearthsol2d -h lists every option with its default.

See Running the examples for output files, the Python reader and ParaView conversion. Field What to look at pore pressure pressure along mid-depth, compared with the two-mode solution; the two mode amplitudes are projected from it coordinate node positions for the mid-depth profile

(a) Pressure p/P_0 along mid-depth (z = −0.5 m) at the four saved times of the two phases: DES nodes (circles) and the two-mode solution (lines). (b) Amplitudes of the two sine modes, projected from the DES pressure (circles), against their exponential decay (lines); the dotted line marks the permeability change at 0.5 s. (c) Maximum pressure error relative to P_0, in percent, against mesh spacing for the mesh study at 20,000 steps, the finest mesh at 80,000 steps (diamond), and a slope-2 guide. This checks directional diffusion, a prescribed change of permeability during a run, and a restart after that change. Permeability that evolves with the state, rotated tensors that change in time and coupled fluid-content budgets are not covered. P0​=1000 Pa, a1​(0)=1, a2​(0)=0.35, k0​=10−15 m², μ=1.002×10−3 Pa s, ϕ=0.3, α=1, Kf​=2.17 GPa and Ks​=37 GPa.

Each sine mode vanishes on the drained faces. Substitution into the diffusion equation gives its scalar decay rate; the different horizontal wave numbers make both tensor components observable. Integrate the decay rate in each time interval and carry the amplitude continuously through the coefficient jump. This gives the exponential formula without fitted parameters. The reference stored fluid volume (pressure storage only) is S0​∫pdV=4S0​P0​a1​/π2: the second horizontal mode integrates to zero. This excludes deformation storage because its feedback is disabled. Separation of variables for the stated linear diffusion equation; the independent reference is implemented in check_anisotropic_flow.py.

Prescribed, homogeneous, axis-aligned tensors; fixed storage and geometry. Mechanical pressure feedback is off, so deformation does not change the pressure; pressure still loads the solid, so the time step must stay within the elastic stability limit. This tests the flow equation, not coupled deformation or a general fluid-content budget.

A well pumps a confined aquifer covered by a leaky aquitard. Water drawn down through the aquitard limits the drawdown, which approaches a steady cone. Largest drawdown error: 0.410% of CQ​, over 10≤r≤30 m and eight times through pumping and recovery. Leakage changes the drawdown by up to 53% of CQ​ from Theis. At a glance Dimension 3D Build make ndims=3 from the poromechanics source (not yet merged; DynEarthSol #134) Inputs hantush.zip Reproduce with DynEarthSol 3774df0
documents.s: Hantush–Jacob pumping from a leaky aquifer

documents.t: Geometry and well. A quarter box, 0≤x,y≤75 m. An aquifer B=2.5 m thick lies under an aquitard one element thick (b′=h) whose top is held at p=0. A well on the corner edge, screened through the aquifer only, pumps Q/4 (Q=10−4 m3/s) for 200 s and then shuts in. Layers. The aquitard is a second material whose vertical leakance kz′​/(μb′) is the same on every mesh, so λ=15 m throughout; it stores a thousandth of the aquifer water per volume. Vertical permeability is ten times horizontal in both layers, so the aquifer has negligible vertical resistance, as the theory assumes. What is compared. The pressure drawdown at the aquifer nodes with 10≤r≤30 m, at eight times through pumping and recovery, against the superposed Hantush–Jacob solution. The skeleton is stiff and pressure feedback is off.

Every file this example needs is in hantush.zip. Run from that folder: # Runs the 3D quarter box with the one-element aquitard on top: 160 steps of 2 s, pumping for 200 s, then recovery to 320 s. DES writes hantush.save.* frames every 20 steps (40 s). On one thread this mesh takes about 45 minutes. dynearthsol3d input.cfg

Setting Value What it does here control.has_hydraulic_diffusion true turns on Darcy flow of pore pressure; wells need it control.has_poroelastic_pressure_feedback false off: deformation does not change the pressure, so only flow is tested control.gravity 0 no gravity, so the drawdown is compared directly in pressure sim.max_steps 160 160 steps of 2 s end the run at 320 s: 200 s of pumping and 120 s of recovery bc.hbc_z1 2 type 2: the top of the aquitard is held at the pressure given in bc.hbc_pressure, here 0, so water leaks down through the aquitard bc.well_rate [2.5e-05] extraction rate of the quarter well, Q/4 with Q = 1e-4 m³/s bc.well_z_top [-0.625] the screen starts one element below the top, so the well draws from the aquifer only, not the aquitard bc.well_schedule_ratio [1, 1, 0] rate multipliers 1, 1, 0 at 0, 200 s, 200 s: full rate, then shut in ic.layer_mattypes [1, 0] material 1 (the aquitard) on top of material 0 (the aquifer) ic.mattype_layer_depths [0.2] the aquitard is the top 0.2 of the 3.125 m height, i.e. one 0.625 m element mat.hydraulic_perm [1.1463636364386364e-13, 7.96085858637942e-17] aquifer and aquitard permeabilities; the aquitard value is set so that the leakage factor λ is 15 m mat.permeability_tensor [1, 1, 10.0, 0, 0, 0] vertical permeability ten times horizontal in both layers, so the aquifer has negligible vertical resistance mat.porosity [0.25, 0.0001] aquifer 0.25 and aquitard 1e-4 (with Biot coefficient 0.3), so the aquitard stores almost no water, as Hantush–Jacob assume mat.bulk_modulus [1000000000000.0, 1000000000000.0] very stiff skeleton (1e12 Pa) in both layers, so the solid barely moves input.cfg holds all 60 settings that differ from DES’s defaults; dynearthsol3d -h lists every option with its default.

See Running the examples for output files, the Python reader and ParaView conversion. Field What to look at pore pressure drawdown s_p = p(frame 0) − p at the aquifer nodes 10–30 m from the well, compared with Hantush–Jacob coordinate gives the radius from the well and selects the nodes on the aquifer base

(a) Drawdown s_p/C_Q along the aquifer base on the y = 0 plane at four times during pumping: DES nodes (circles) and the Hantush–Jacob solution (lines). The dashed grey curve is the Theis solution without leakage at the last of these times, and the band marks the compared range 10–30 m. (b) Drawdown history at r ≈ 10 m and r ≈ 20 m: Hantush–Jacob (solid), Theis without leakage (dashed) and DES (circles); the dotted line marks shut-in. (c) Maximum and RMS drawdown error against mesh spacing, with a slope-2 guide. This checks a layered aquifer system: an aquitard of a second material leaking from a fixed-pressure top, with the well, storage and radial diffusion of the Theis case. On the finest mesh the aquitard stores 0.03% of the aquifer's water, close to the no-storage assumption. Mechanical pressure feedback is disabled in this flow-isolation test. To reproduce the whole study behind this figure, from the DES source folder: python3 benchmarks/poromechanics/hantush_reference.py python3 tests/functional/hydromechanics/check_hantush.py dynearthsol3d OUT --spacings 2.5 1.25 0.625 The study’s full numbers: record.json.

documents.t: Tp​=κB/μ,Sp​=BSB​,λ2=κz′​κBb′​Sp​∂t​sp​=Tp​(∂r2​sp​+r1​∂r​sp​)−λ2Tp​​sp​sp​(r,t)=4πTp​Q​W(4Tp​tr2Sp​​,λr​)W(u,β)=∫u∞​y1​exp(−y−4yβ2​)dyW(u,0)=E1​(u)W(0,β)=2K0​(β) sp​=pinitial​−p is the pressure drawdown, κ and κz′​ the horizontal aquifer and vertical aquitard permeabilities, and SB​ the fixed-stress storage of the Theis page. Shut-in is superposed as in Theis. Errors are fractions of CQ​=Q/(4πTp​).

With no aquitard storage the aquitard pressure is linear in z, so it leaks a flux (κz′​/μb′)sp​ into the aquifer. Integrating over the aquifer thickness adds this sink to the Theis equation. qleak​=μb′κz′​​sp​=λ2Tp​​sp​ The Laplace transform in time and the line-sink limit at r→0 give the leaky well function W, which tends to Theis at early time and to the steady cone 2K0​(r/λ) at late time. hantush_reference.py checks both limits, the identity W(u,β)+W(β2/4u,β)=2K0​(β) and the equation itself. Hantush and Jacob (1955), Non-steady radial flow in an infinite leaky aquifer, Trans. AGU 36, 95-100. Evaluated in hantush_reference.py by quadrature. Original reference.

Hantush and Jacob neglect aquitard storage, horizontal aquitard flow and vertical resistance in the aquifer. Their dimensionless measures here are SB′​b′/Sp​≤0.12%, (b′/λ)2/10≤0.28% and B2/(20λ2)=0.14%, the first two falling with h. SB′​ is aquitard storage per volume and Sp​=BSB​ aquifer storage per area. Line well, no wellbore storage; the axis r<10 m is excluded.

A smooth pressure pulse drains through two zero-pressure ends while the side faces remain sealed. Maximum pressure error: 0.0424% of the initial amplitude; storage error 0.0509%. Stored fluid plus outflow equals the initial volume within 1.19e-21 m³ (independent integration). documents.t: Geometry. A 10 m column has a 1 m² cross-section. Both end faces hold zero pressure; the lateral faces are sealed. Initial condition. Pressure is Psin(πx/L), with P=1000 Pa and L=10 m. The run restarts from the shipped seed checkpoint, whose frame 0 holds this field. Material and mechanics. Diffusivity is 1 m²/s and pressure capacity is constant. Mechanical pressure feedback, gravity and heat are disabled.

Every file this example needs is in open-flow.zip. Run from that folder: # Restarts from the shipped seed.save.000000, seed.chkpt.000000 and seed.info, whose frame 0 holds the initial sine pulse, and runs 200 steps of 0.05 s to 10 s. DES writes a pulse.save.* frame at every step. To build the seed yourself, run the study command: it runs one step, then writes the pulse into frame 0. dynearthsol3d input.cfg

Setting Value What it does here sim.is_restarting true starts from a saved state instead of the built-in initial condition sim.restarting_from_modelname seed the shipped seed files, which hold the sine pulse sim.restarting_from_frame 0 frame 0 of the seed, the initial pulse sim.max_steps 200 200 steps of 0.05 s, to 10 s sim.output_step_interval 1 a frame at every step, so every step enters the pressure, storage and budget checks control.has_hydraulic_diffusion true turns on Darcy flow of pore pressure control.has_poroelastic_pressure_feedback false off: deformation does not change the pressure, so storage stays constant control.gravity 0 no gravity, so the pulse drains by diffusion alone control.fixed_dt 0.05 outer step of 0.05 s; DES splits it into stable flow substeps by itself bc.hbc_x0 2 type 2: the end face x = 0 is held at the pressure in bc.hbc_pressure, here 0 bc.hbc_x1 2 type 2: the end face x = 10 m is also held at 0; the other faces are sealed (type 0) mat.porosity [0.25] with the fluid bulk modulus, sets the constant storage mat.hydraulic_perm [1.1463636364386364e-13] chosen so that the diffusivity is 1 m²/s mat.bulk_modulus [1000000000000.0] very stiff skeleton (1e12 Pa), so the solid barely moves input.cfg holds all 46 settings that differ from DES’s defaults; dynearthsol3d -h lists every option with its default.

(a) Pressure p/P along the column axis at 0, 1, 5 and 10 s: DES nodes (circles) and the decaying sine (lines). (b) Stored fluid and cumulative outflow, each divided by the initial analytical storage M_0: DES (circles; stored fluid from pressure and element volumes, outflow from the boundary term of the fluid balance) against the exponential reference (lines). (c) Maximum pressure error relative to P and stored-volume error relative to M_0 against mesh spacing. Storage is constant here; unsaturated coupling, changing storage and remeshing are not covered. Stored fluid is computed from the element volumes and nodal pressures, independently of DES’s own fluid balance.

The sine is the first eigenfunction of the diffusion equation with zero pressure at each end. Separation of variables supplies its exponential decay. pt​=Dpxx​p(0,t)=p(L,t)=0 Integrating the sine over the column gives the stored volume. Darcy outflow at the two ends supplies its equal and opposite loss. dM/dt=−λMdVout​/dt=λM Separation-of-variables solution of the stated diffusion problem; pressure, storage and the boundary budget of every time step are checked in check_open_flow.py.
Constant-capacity saturated flow on a fixed mesh. Variable storage, unsaturated coupling, deforming volume and remapping need separate open-system fluid budgets.

Largest stored-volume error: 1.6×10−16 and largest stored-heat error: 4.5×10−13 of the final net supply. documents.s: Scheduled water and heat sources in a closed box

documents.t: Closed domain. Unit 3D box; all water and conductive-heat boundaries sealed. Normal motion fixed on every face. Initial pressure 0 Pa, temperature 300 K. Two signed sources. Point 1: (0.37, 0.43, −0.53) m, fluid +8×10⁻⁸ m³/s and heat +4000 W, active 0.25–2.75 s. Point 2: (0.61, 0.57, −0.41) m, fluid −3×10⁻⁸ m³/s and heat −1500 W, active 0.8–2.1 s. Isolated balance. κ = λ = 0; mechanical pressure feedback and thermal expansion disabled. This case compares integrated volume and heat; it does not claim a spatial point-source solution.

Every file this example needs is in sources.zip. Run from that folder: # Runs the closed 3D box for 4 steps of 1 s with the two scheduled water and heat sources. DES writes fresh.save.* frames at every step. dynearthsol3d input.cfg

Setting Value What it does here control.has_hydraulic_diffusion true turns on the pore-pressure equation that receives the water sources control.has_poroelastic_pressure_feedback false off: deformation does not change the pressure, so stored water is storage times pressure change control.has_fluid_thermal_advection true turns on groundwater heat transport with the combined rock and water heat capacity, which receives the heat sources control.fixed_dt 1 steps of 1 s, so the source windows start and end inside steps sim.max_steps 4 4 steps of 1 s, to 4 s mat.hydraulic_perm [0] zero permeability: water stays where it is supplied, so only the totals are tested mat.therm_cond [0] zero conductivity: heat stays where it is supplied mat.alpha [0] no thermal expansion of the solid (mat.fluid_alpha is also 0), so heat does not change the pressure mat.fluid_heat_capacity [4000] 4000 J/(kg K); with the rock values it gives C = 2.95e6 J/(m³ K) injection.points_x [0.37,0.61] x of the two source points; points_y and points_z complete their positions (heat_injection uses the same points) injection.rate [8e-08, -3e-08] water rates +8e-8 and −3e-8 m³/s: the first point supplies, the second extracts injection.start_time_in_yr [7.922191133769641e-09, 2.5351011628062857e-08] yr = [0.25, 0.8] s start times 0.25 s and 0.8 s, in years (also used by heat_injection) injection.end_time_in_yr [8.714410247146606e-08, 6.6546405523665e-08] yr = [2.75, 2.1] s end times 2.75 s and 2.1 s, in years heat_injection.rate [4000, -1500] heat rates +4000 W and −1500 W at the same points and times input.cfg holds all 68 settings that differ from DES’s defaults; dynearthsol3d -h lists every option with its default.

(a) Net water supplied to the closed box, in µL: the DES storage change from the saved pore pressure (circles) against the time integral of the two signed source schedules (line). (b) The same for heat, in kJ, from the saved temperature and the combined heat capacity. This checks that every source acts exactly once over each integration interval. The plotted run has C=(1−ϕ)ρs​cs​+ϕρf​cf​=2.95×106 J/(m³ K), K∗​=K in 3D. In 2D the in-plane mean-stress split uses K∗​=K+G/3 and rates are per unit out-of-plane thickness. A point rate is shared among the nodes of the element that contains it by the element shape functions. They sum to one, so the nodal loads add up to the requested signed rate. A source window that starts or ends inside a time step is integrated over its exact overlap with the step, so every source acts exactly once. fn(i)​=Ri​Nn​(xi​),n∑​Nn​(xi​)=1,∫0t​ri​(τ)dτ=Ri​[ℓi​(t)−ℓi​(0)] Summing the lumped nodal update cancels internal transport contributions. With sealed boundaries, fixed capacities and the mechanical source disabled, only the prescribed source integrals remain. Apply the same argument to thermal mass and heat rate. A total-amount schedule uses rate equal to amount divided by (bi−ai). Direct time integral of the supplied schedules plus the assembled closed-domain storage/heat balances; independently evaluated from simplex volumes and saved fields in check_point_sources.py.

This is an exact integral balance for an isolated component test with fixed capacity and mechanical pressure feedback disabled. It does not qualify the spatial singular solution, nonlinear storage, the enthalpy of injected fluid (see the injection-temperature page) or conservative remesh transfer. Fluid volume and heat sources are independent inputs. Separate forced-remesh runs check source relocation and continuation.

documents.t: Geometry and well. A quarter box, 0≤x,y≤60 m, of thickness B=5 m. A fully penetrating well on the corner edge pumps Q/4, a quarter of the total rate Q=10−4 m3/s, for 80 s and then shuts in for 80 s. Boundaries and mechanics. All faces are sealed; the symmetry planes x=0, y=0 make the corner well radial. The far sides stay beyond the drawdown: its reference value there is below 10−3 of the pressure scale. The skeleton is stiff and mechanical pressure feedback is off, so the storage is the fixed-stress value SB​. What is compared. The pressure drawdown sp​=pinitial​−p at every node with 10≤r≤30 m, at eight times through pumping and recovery, against the superposed Theis solution. Errors are fractions of CQ​=Q/(4πTp​).

Every file this example needs is in theis.zip. Run from that folder: # Runs the 3D quarter box: 80 steps of 2 s, the well pumping for the first 80 s and shut in for the last 80 s. DES writes theis.save.* frames every 10 steps (20 s); frame 0 is the initial state. dynearthsol3d input.cfg

Setting Value What it does here control.has_hydraulic_diffusion true turns on Darcy flow of pore pressure; wells need it control.has_poroelastic_pressure_feedback false off: deformation does not change the pressure, so the storage stays at the fixed-stress value S_B and pressure obeys the Theis diffusion equation control.gravity 0 no gravity, so there is no hydrostatic gradient and the drawdown is compared directly in pressure control.fixed_dt 2.0 physical step of 2 s; DES splits it into stable flow substeps by itself sim.max_steps 80 80 steps of 2 s end the run at 160 s: 80 s of pumping and 80 s of recovery sim.output_step_interval 10 a frame every 10 steps (20 s), so eight frames are compared with Theis bc.num_wells 1 one rate-controlled vertical well bc.well_x [0.0] with bc.well_y, puts the well on the corner edge x = y = 0; the sealed symmetry planes make it one quarter of a full well bc.well_rate [2.5e-05] extraction rate of the quarter well, Q/4 with Q = 1e-4 m³/s, spread uniformly over the 5 m screen bc.well_schedule_time_in_yr [0.0, 2.5351011628062854e-06, 2.5351011628062854e-06] yr = [0, 80, 80] s schedule times 0, 80 s, 80 s (in years); the repeated time makes a step change at 80 s bc.well_schedule_ratio [1, 1, 0] rate multipliers 1, 1, 0: full rate until 80 s, then shut in mat.bulk_modulus [1000000000000.0] very stiff skeleton (1e12 Pa), so the mechanical storage α²/K is negligible and the solid barely moves mat.porosity [0.25] with the fluid bulk modulus, sets the pressure storage φ/K_f of the aquifer mat.hydraulic_perm [1.1463636364386364e-13] chosen so that the pressure diffusivity κ/(μS_B) is 1 m²/s input.cfg holds all 50 settings that differ from DES’s defaults; dynearthsol3d -h lists every option with its default.
