documents.t: Tp​=κB/μ,Sp​=BSB​,SB​=S0​+α2/KCQ​=Q/(4πTp​),u=r2Sp​/(4Tp​t),sp​(r,t)=QE1​(u)/(4πTp​)E1​(u)=∫u∞​e−v/vdv,sp​(r,0)=0(r>0)sp​(r,t)=t>tk​∑​ΔQk​G(r,t−tk​)sp​(x,t)=j∑​k∑​4πTp​ΔQjk​​E1​(ujk​)ujk​=∣x−xj​∣2Sp​/[4Tp​(t−tjk​)],t>tjk​ sp​=pinitial​−p is pressure drawdown in Pa and G=E1​(u)/(4πTp​) the drawdown of a unit-rate well. Tp​ has units m3/(Pas), Sp​ has units m/Pa, and Q is total discharge in m3/s. Here S0​=ϕ/Kf​+(α−ϕ)/Ks​. Disabling mechanical pressure feedback retains the selected fixed-stress storage SB​. Terms are zero before each rate change ΔQk​ at time tk​. This pressure formulation remains valid at zero gravity; it uses no conversion from pressure to head.

Away from the well, integrate pressure diffusion through thickness B and use zero initial drawdown. The inward discharge at r→0 supplies the line-sink boundary. Integrating the radial diffusion Green function in time gives E1​. Sp​∂t​sp​=Tp​r−1∂r​(r∂r​sp​),−2πrTp​∂r​sp​⟶Q Differentiate the solution to check the well limit. Storage inside an observation circle supplies the remaining discharge; linearity permits pumping/shut-in and multiwell superposition. −2πrTp​∂r​sp​=Qe−u Theis (1935), evaluated with the exponential integral in theis_reference.py; the same module superposes changes of rate. Original reference.

Confined, homogeneous, isotropic aquifer with constant properties; a line well without wellbore storage; the singular axis r<10 m is excluded. Pressure only: the stiff skeleton removes poroelastic coupling, which the averaged-aquifer page addresses.

documents.t: Geometry and wells. A 160 by 160 by 5 m confined slab contains full-height wells at (60,80), (100,80) and (80,100) m. Their rates are Q, 0.6Q and -0.25Q, with Q=10−4 m³/s. Water boundaries and initial state. All faces are sealed, initial pressure is zero, and every well stops at 40 s. The comparison ends at 80 s, before the pressure front reaches the far walls. The pressure diffusion equation is linear in both pressure and well rate. A well switched off at 40 s is the sum of a positive step at zero and its negative at 40 s. Summing those responses over the three well locations gives the pressure reference. Integrating the pressure equation over sealed boundaries gives the signed volume budget independently of the pointwise solution. Theis superposition, evaluated in theis_reference.py and check_theis_wells.py; the saved combined run is also compared with three independent single-well DES runs. Original reference.

Infinite-aquifer reference, compared inside a sealed finite slab before its walls matter. Linear storage and constant properties; this does not establish superposition for nonlinear or evolving-property flow.

Water in a porous box heated from below becomes lighter at the base. Above a critical Rayleigh number buoyancy overturns it into a convection cell; below it, a disturbance decays. Fitted onset: Ra=39.54 against 4π2=39.48, 0.14% apart; largest growth-rate error: 0.105λ/(CH2) over 5 Rayleigh numbers. The unseeded box stays at rest to round-off: ∣T−Tc​∣≤5.7×10−15ΔT. At a glance Dimension 2D Build make ndims=2 from the poromechanics source (not yet merged; DynEarthSol #134) Inputs convection.zip Reproduce with DynEarthSol 3774df0

Heating and water boundaries. A square porous box is heated from below: T=T0​+ΔT at the base and T=T0​ at the top. All four sides are sealed, qn​=0; the sides are insulated, ∂T/∂n=0. Initial state. Steady conduction Tc​ with the hydrostatic pressure of the temperature-dependent water density, plus a 1 mK Gaussian seed centred at x=0.25 m, mid-depth. What is compared. The amplitude of the temperature mode cos(πx/W)sin(πz/H). Its growth or decay rate σ is fitted over the second half of each run and compared with linear stability theory. A seed-free run must stay at rest.

Every file this example needs is in convection.zip. Run from that folder: # Runs the seeded 2D box at Ra = 2 Ra_c for 400 steps of 1000 s and writes box.save.* and box.chkpt.* every 10 steps, with box.info listing the frames. dynearthsol2d input.cfg

See Running the examples for output files, the Python reader and ParaView conversion. Field What to look at temperature nodal temperature; its departure from the conductive profile, projected on cos(πx/W) sin(πz/H), is the mode amplitude in panel (b), and is mapped in panel (c)

(a) Fitted growth rate of the first convective mode against Ra/Ra_c: line, linear stability theory; symbols, DES. (b) Mode amplitude against time for each Rayleigh number: symbols, DES; dashed lines, the theoretical rate over the second half of each run. (c) Temperature departure from conduction at the end of the most supercritical run, showing the single convection cell. This checks Boussinesq buoyancy in Darcy flow together with heat advection, and that the conductive state stays at rest. It does not test finite-amplitude convection (see the Nusselt-number page) or 3D cells; the fastest run reaches a temperature departure of 10.7% of ΔT, so its late growth is only approximately linear. To reproduce the whole study behind this figure, from the DES source folder: python3 tests/functional/hydromechanics/check_convection.py dynearthsol2d OUT/h0.05 --spacing 0.05 --ratios 0.5 0.9 1.1 1.5 2 python3 tests/functional/hydromechanics/check_convection.py dynearthsol2d OUT/h0.025 --spacing 0.025 --ratios 0.5 0.9 1.1 1.5 2 The study’s full numbers: record.json.

Conduction with no flow is the base state, Tc​=T0​+ΔT(1−z/H), with the hydrostatic pressure of ρf​(Tc​). Perturb it by θ and q. Taking the curl of Darcy’s law twice removes the pressure: the vertical Darcy flux w is driven only by horizontal buoyancy gradients. The square box (a=π) has the smallest single-cell onset, Rac​=4π2≈39.48. w^=μκρf0​gαf​​K2a2​θ^Cσ=H2λ​(RaK2a2​−K2) Horton and Rogers (1945); Lapwood (1948); Nield and Bejan, Convection in Porous Media, section 6.2. Evaluated in convection_reference.py; no DES output or fitted parameter enters the reference. Original reference.

Linear stability of the incompressible Boussinesq limit: small disturbances, constant properties, and a rigid matrix without pore-pressure feedback. DES keeps a small water storage; pressure diffuses about 103 times faster than heat, so the incompressible reference applies. 3D cells, temperature-dependent viscosity and the Elder transient-plume problem are not yet verified.

At a glance Dimension 3D Inputs convection-3d.zip Reproduce with DynEarthSol 3774df0 A unit porous cube heated from below supports a temperature mode that varies in all three directions. Its growth changes sign at a known Rayleigh number. At 1/32 m spacing, growth-rate errors are 0.62%, 2.44%, 1.55% below and above onset. Halving the physical timestep changes the selected growth rate by 0.0067%. The unseeded cube stays exactly at conduction.

Geometry. Unit cube, rigid saturated matrix and fixed tetrahedral mesh. All faces are impermeable; vertical faces are thermally insulated. Temperature. The base is at 283 K and top at 273 K. A 0.1 mK Gaussian perturbs the conductive profile; its projection onto the (1,1,1) mode measures growth or decay. Pressure storage. The fluid bulk modulus is deliberately scaled to 10 Pa for an economical explicit test. The analytical solution retains this finite storage; this is not a realistic water-property application. Comparison. Three meshes, three Rayleigh numbers, an unseeded rest case and a separate halved physical timestep. No material or seed fitting.

Every file this example needs is in data/convection-3d/. Run from that folder: # Runs the selected cube for 200,000 s in 400 explicit physical steps. DES subcycles transport within those intervals. dynearthsol3d input.cfg

(a) Late growth rate against the finite-storage analytical eigenvalue. (b) DES amplitudes normalized at dimensionless time 0.1; lines use the analytical slope with that one amplitude anchor. (c) Temperature departure at y/H=0.25 and dimensionless time 0.2 on the selected mesh. Rates and all refinement controls are in the accompanying table. This checks three-dimensional buoyancy and heat advection, growth and decay, a rest state, and separate spatial/time controls. The amplitude in panel (b) is normalized at dimensionless time 0.1; only the analytical growth slope is compared. It does not qualify nonlinear steady planforms or realistic water compressibility. Linearize Darcy flow about the conductive hydrostatic state. The pressure disturbance has the same horizontal cosines and a vertical cosine. Its diffusion equation couples to the vertical derivative of the temperature mode, giving the first amplitude equation. The background vertical temperature gradient converts the perturbed vertical Darcy flux into heat advection. Adding thermal diffusion gives the second amplitude equation. Set the determinant of the two-mode system to zero for its eigenvalues. Its positive or least negative root gives the late growth rate. At zero growth the storage cancels, so onset is the same as in incompressible Darcy convection. λ2+b1​λ+b0​=0 As pressure diffusion becomes infinitely fast, eliminate P to recover the incompressible result. The implementation checks this limit, zero-Rayleigh diffusion and the exact neutral point independently. λ+​⟶Raa2/Km2​−Km2​(D→∞) Separation of the linear Darcy–Boussinesq pressure and heat equations, evaluated in convection_reference.py. The (1,1,1) mode extends the Horton–Rogers–Lapwood layer reference to a cube with finite pressure storage.

Linear 3D cell growth and decay with deliberately scaled storage, fixed properties and a rigid matrix. The reference retains finite storage; it must not be replaced by the incompressible expression at D around 10. This does not establish nonlinear steady cells, realistic compressibility or mechanical coupling.

At a glance Dimension 2D Inputs drained-heat.zip Reproduce with DynEarthSol 3774df0 A rigid saturated cell receives uniform heat while every face holds zero pore pressure. Thermal expansion expels water, reducing retained heat capacity and exporting sensible heat. Temperature errors at 100 and 200 steps are 0.000845 and 0.000422 K. Retained energy plus measured boundary export closes against supplied heat within 20 microjoules.

documents.t: Geometry and constraints. Rigid unit cell, every face at p=0, no gravity or solid thermal expansion. All thermal faces are insulated. Heat source. Uniform supplied power 30 MW per metre thickness for 5 s; no conduction or fluid point injection. Exchange. Expanded water leaves the pressure-controlled boundary at the current cell temperature. The original solid inventory and its heat capacity stay fixed.

Every file this example needs is in data/drained-heat/. Run from that folder: # Supplies 30 MW of heat for 5 s in 200 steps while the pressure-controlled boundary exports expanding water. dynearthsol2d input.cfg

2D unit volume per metre thickness, 30 MW supplied for 5 s, 200 steps, no gravity, solid expansion or conduction. (a) total supplied heat; (b) exported sensible heat. The reference uses the actual exponential water density. At zero pressure and zero bulk strain this isolates open-system sensible heat without mechanical boundary work. Owned solid heat capacity stays fixed while fluid mass changes. It does not qualify full thermodynamic pressure work or a thermal plume. T0​=273 K, M0​=250 kg, Cs​=1.9875 MJ/K, cf​=4180 J/(kg K) and αf​=2×10−4 K−1. Values refer to unit volume per metre thickness.

At fixed zero pressure, zero bulk strain and zero solid expansion, porosity stays fixed. Exponential thermal expansion gives the retained fluid mass directly. Differentiate retained sensible energy. Its c_f T dM term cancels the outflow enthalpy, leaving a temperature-dependent heat capacity. Integrating from the initial temperature gives Q(T); invert Q=power times time for the temperature history. The independent reference accounts for water leaving at the changing cell temperature. Subtracting retained energy gain from supplied heat gives its cumulative export. No pressure or strain boundary work occurs in this control. Direct integration of the declared exponential-density sensible-heat model in mass_reference.py.

A rigid zero-pressure open-system control. Sensible heat is measured from the stated temperature origin. Pressure work, thermoelastic caloric energy, phase changes and recovery energy are outside this model; spatial thermal-plume accuracy is not established here.

A porous layer heated from below over part of its base grows plumes that rise, merge and spread under the cold top. Elder (1967) studied this problem in a Hele-Shaw cell; Voss and Souza (1987) later made its saline version a standard test of variable-density flow codes. It has no closed- form solution, and van Reeuwijk et al. (2009) showed that at its Rayleigh number of 400 several flow patterns are possible, so solutions depend on the grid. This page therefore compares DES with an independent solution of the same equations on several grids and shows both as they come out; nothing is tuned to make them agree. The two finest reference grids follow the same plume branch. Against it, the finest DES mesh reaches the same plume pattern at τ = 0.05 and 0.1, with the heat content of the layer differing by about 1 %. Early, while the first plumes form, DES grows more of them and its heat content is up to 14 % higher. At a glance Dimension 2D Build make ndims=2 from the poromechanics source (not yet merged; DynEarthSol #134) Inputs elder.zip; reference benchmarks/poromechanics/elder_reference.py Run time 33 s, 6 min and 1 h 45 min on 8 threads for the three meshes Reproduce with DynEarthSol 3774df0

Extract elder.zip and run from its folder with OMP_NUM_THREADS=8 dynearthsol2d input.cfg. It contains the selected 1/64 m input and elder.poly; the source commands below reproduce the full grid study.

PDF schematic · PNG schematic Box. The symmetric half of Elder's box: 2 m wide and 1 m high, with the symmetry axis at x=0. The base is held 10 K above the top over 0≤x≤1 m (the heater, bc.tbc_z0 on its own boundary flag in a .poly mesh) and insulated beyond it (a slant boundary n0). The top is held at T0​; the axis and the far wall are insulated; every boundary is impermeable. The fluid starts at T0​. Equations. Boussinesq Darcy flow with heat conduction and advection, with the material constants of the onset benchmark, so that κ=10−6 m²/s, σ=1 and τ=κt/(σH2)=10−6t/s. The permeability gives Ra=μκρ0​gαΔTkH​=400. The matrix is rigid and does not feed back on the pressure; a fluid bulk modulus of 100 Pa makes pressure diffuse about 800 times faster than heat, close to the incompressible limit of the reference. Runs. Three DES meshes (h = 1/16, 1/32 and 1/64 m; 1028, 3992 and 15692 nodes) with a fixed step of 50 s, to τ = 0.1. Voss and Souza's times of 1, 2, 4, 10, 15 and 20 years correspond to τ = 0.005, 0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.075 and 0.1. Reference. elder_reference.py solves the same equations, written for the stream function, with central differences on uniform grids of 32 × 64, 64 × 128, 128 × 256 and 256 × 512 cells and third-order Runge–Kutta steps. It checks its own heat budget without buoyancy and that plumes form with it. For dimensionless upward z, temperature θ=(T−T0​)/ΔT and stream function ψ, the reference solves ∇2ψ=−Ra∂x​θ,(u,w)=(∂z​ψ,−∂x​ψ),∂τ​θ+u∂x​θ+w∂z​θ=∇2θ. Impermeable walls have ψ=0. The heater has θ=1, the top θ=0, and the remaining thermal boundaries have zero normal temperature gradient. This is an independent numerical reference, not an analytical solution.

PDF result The selected comparison uses DES h=1/64 m and the 256 × 512 reference: τ Heat content, finest DES mesh Reference 0.005 0.093 0.089 0.02 0.299 0.262 0.05 0.501 0.506 0.1 0.597 0.590 Supporting mesh and reference-grid comparisons τ Heat content, DES h = 1/16 1/32 1/64 Reference 256 × 512 0.005 0.110 0.094 0.093 0.089 0.02 0.386 0.314 0.299 0.262 0.05 0.628 0.523 0.501 0.506 0.1 0.758 0.617 0.597 0.590 Convergence. DES approaches the reference as the mesh is refined; the coarsest mesh carries too much heat at every time. Late times. At τ = 0.05 and 0.1 the finest DES mesh and the two finest reference grids show the same pattern: at τ = 0.05 a plume on the axis, a second plume over the heater and the outer plume bent out under the top, which by τ = 0.1 have become one broad plume on the axis spreading under the top. The two coarsest reference grids and the coarsest DES mesh show a plume away from the axis instead: the pattern itself depends on resolution, in both codes. The largest temperature difference from the finest grid is 0.14 at τ = 0.05 and 0.23 at τ = 0.1 (RMS 0.03 and 0.05). Early times. At τ = 0.01–0.02 DES grows more and narrower plumes along the heater, and its heat content is 4–14 % higher. Where the first plumes start depends on small disturbances; an unstructured triangle mesh and a regular grid seed them differently. The reference itself. Its 64 × 128 and 128 × 256 grids differ by up to 0.6 in temperature after τ = 0.05, where their plume patterns differ; its 128 × 256 and 256 × 512 grids differ by at most 0.12 at every time, and their heat contents agree within 0.5 %.

Other branches. The two finest reference grids agree on one branch within τ≤0.1, but at this Rayleigh number other flow patterns exist, and coarser grids of both codes fall onto them; later times were not compared. Half box. The symmetric half excludes asymmetric patterns of the full box. Slightly compressible fluid. The reference is incompressible; DES uses a fluid bulk modulus of 100 Pa so that the runs finish in hours.

Elder, J. W. (1967). Transient convection in a porous medium. Journal of Fluid Mechanics, 27(3), 609–623. van Reeuwijk, M., Mathias, S. A., Simmons, C. T., & Ward, J. D. (2009). Insights from a pseudospectral approach to the Elder problem. Water Resources Research, 45, W04416. Voss, C. I., & Souza, W. R. (1987). Variable density flow and solute transport simulation of regional aquifers containing a narrow freshwater-saltwater transition zone. Water Resources Research, 23(10), 1851–1866.

Steady groundwater carries heat from a hot inlet along a saturated column while conduction spreads the front. Largest temperature error: 1.306% of the imposed 1 K jump, over all nodes and five saved times; the pressure stays exactly steady. At a glance Dimension 3D Build make ndims=3 from the poromechanics source (not yet merged; DynEarthSol #134) Inputs heat.zip Reproduce with DynEarthSol 3774df0

Steady groundwater flow. p(x)=2−x Pa, κ/μ=1 m²/(Pa s), qx​=1 m/s; gravity zero. Pressure is prescribed at both ends. Temperature and mechanical conditions. Initially T0​=273.15 K. At t=0 the left end is set to Tin​=274.15 K. Sides and right end have zero conductive heat flux; heat can advect out. Normal motion is fixed on every face. Reference regime. Constant properties and steady Darcy flux; fixed mesh, no mechanical pressure feedback. Deliberately scaled coefficients isolate transport; this is not an aquifer application.

Every file this example needs is in heat.zip. Run from that folder: # Runs the 3D column (1 m long, 2×2 elements across) for 8192 steps to 0.47 s and writes column.save.* and column.chkpt.* every 2048 steps, with column.info listing the five frames. dynearthsol3d input.cfg

Setting Value What it does here control.has_fluid_thermal_advection true turns on heat transport by the Darcy flux, with the combined rock–water heat capacity bc.hbc_x0 2 type 2: pressure prescribed at the inlet end bc.hbc_x1 2 type 2: pressure prescribed at the outlet end bc.hbc_pressure [2,1,0,0,0,0] 2 Pa at x = 0 and 1 Pa at x = 1 m: a steady pressure drop that drives q_x = 1 m/s ic.pore_pressure_option 1 1: start from the linear pressure profile between the two prescribed ends, so the flow is steady from the start bc.tbc_x0 1 1: fixed temperature at the inlet bc.tbc_val_x0 274.15 inlet temperature T_in = T_0 + 1 K bc.tbc_z1 0 0: the top is insulated, like the other sides and the outlet ic.temp_background 273.15 initial temperature T_0 = 273.15 K mat.hydraulic_perm [1] 1 m², with fluid_visc = 1 Pa s: mobility κ/μ = 1 m²/(Pa s) mat.fluid_bulk_modulus [1e-6] deliberately tiny, which makes the hydraulic storage large without changing the steady flux mat.therm_cond [23500.0] λ chosen with the capacities to give thermal diffusivity D = 0.005 m²/s mat.heat_capacity [2000.0] solid specific heat; with rho0, porosity and fluid_heat_capacity it sets the bulk capacity C = 4.7 MJ/(m³ K) mat.fluid_heat_capacity [4000.0] water specific heat; ρ_f c_f q_x / C sets the front speed v_T input.cfg holds all 60 settings that differ from DES’s defaults; dynearthsol3d -h lists every option with its default.

See Running the examples for output files, the Python reader and ParaView conversion. Field What to look at temperature nodal temperature, normalized as (T − T_0)/(T_in − T_0) and plotted along the column pore pressure checked to stay on the steady linear profile at every saved time

Normalized temperature along the column at the last saved time: line, the Ogata–Banks solution moving at the bulk-capacity speed v_T; symbols, DES nodes (about 40 shown). This checks Darcy heat advection and the mixed solid–fluid heat capacity: the front moves at the bulk-capacity speed, not the pore-water velocity. It does not test enthalpy conservation with evolving storage. To reproduce the whole study behind this figure, from the DES source folder: python3 tests/functional/hydromechanics/check_heat_transport.py dynearthsol3d OUT/3d --spacings 0.0125 0.00625 0.003125 --steps 8192 --restart python3 tests/functional/hydromechanics/check_heat_transport.py dynearthsol2d OUT/2d --spacings 0.025 0.0125 0.00625 0.003125 --steps 8192 --restart python3 tests/functional/hydromechanics/check_heat_transport.py dynearthsol2d OUT/2d-steps --spacings 0.0125 --steps 512 1024 2048 4096 --restart The study’s full numbers: record.json.

documents.t: C=(1−ϕ)ρs​cs​+ϕρf​cf​,vT​=ρf​cf​qx​/C,D=λ/Cθ=(T−T0​)/(Tin​−T0​)θt​+vT​θx​=Dθxx​a=(x−vT​t)/(2Dt​),b=(x+vT​t)/(2Dt​)θ=21​[erfc(a)+evT​x/Derfc(b)] C is bulk volumetric heat capacity, cf​ and cs​ fluid and solid specific heat capacities, λ thermal conductivity and qx​ Darcy flux. Here ϕ=0.3, C=4.7×106 J/(m3K), vT​=0.851064 m/s and D=0.005 m2/s; the final front position is vT​t=0.4 m.

For constant C and divergence-free steady flux, the bulk sensible-heat balance reduces to the equation above. Dividing by C shows that the thermal front travels at vT, rather than at qx or qx/φ. CTt​+ρf​cf​qx​Tx​=λTxx​ Laplace-transform the normalized equation in time with its zero initial condition. Reject the growing spatial root and impose the unit step at x = 0. Inverting this transform gives the two complementary-error-function terms above. θ(x,s)=s−1exp[2DvT​−vT2​+4Ds​​x] Ogata and Banks (1961), USGS Professional Paper 411-A; the transport solution is applied here to normalized temperature. Evaluated stably using erfcx in check_heat_transport.py. Original reference.

The analytical solution is semi-infinite: θ(0,t)=1, θ(x,0)=0 for x>0 and θ(∞,t)=0. The numerical domain ends at x=1 m with zero conductive flux, so the comparison uses early times before the front reaches that boundary. Constant-capacity, divergence-free flow is tested; general evolving-storage enthalpy conservation is not established. The intentionally tiny fluid modulus makes the hydraulic storage large without changing the steady flux.

Injected water carries its temperature. DES adds the injected enthalpy relative to the local temperature, which with fluid mass conservation makes its advective heat equation conserve energy. Two checks: radial hot-water injection against Avdonin’s solution, and a sealed doublet against an independent heat ledger. Avdonin on the 0.1 m mesh: largest nodal error 1.50% of Tin​−T0​ at 5.8 d (rms 0.28%). Doublet: stored heat follows the ledger within 0.019% after the first step, through breakthrough (producer at 78% of Tin​−T0​). At a glance Dimension 2D Build make ndims=2 from the poromechanics source (not yet merged; DynEarthSol #134) Inputs injection-temperature.zip Reproduce with DynEarthSol 3774df0
documents.s: Hot-water injection: Avdonin solution and heat ledger

documents.t: Option. injection.temperature gives the temperature Tin​ of the fluid of each point source; it requires fluid thermal advection. Unset, the injected fluid carries no heat, and any heat source must be given separately. (a) Avdonin. A line source injects q=2×10−5 m2/s at Tin​=333 K into a layer at T0​=283 K. DES models a quarter plane, 8 m square, with the source at its corner, sealed and insulated symmetry sides, drained far sides and a stiff skeleton without pressure feedback. (b) Doublet. An 8 m sealed, insulated box with an injector at Tin​ and a producer 4 m away at the same rate q=10−4 m2/s. The hot front reaches the producer, so heat leaves at a changing temperature. What is compared. (a) Nodal temperature against the similarity solution at four times; stored against injected heat. (b) Stored heat against the independent ledger of injected minus extracted heat at every step.

Every file this example needs is in injection-temperature.zip. Run from that folder: # Avdonin case: injects hot water at the corner of the 8 m quarter plane (0.1 m mesh) for 500 steps of 1000 s (5.8 d), saving hot.save.* every 125 steps (four times) with hot.info listing the frames. dynearthsol2d input.cfg # Doublet case, run in its own directory because both inputs write files named hot.*: 400 steps of 1500 s in the sealed 8 m box, saving every step. mkdir -p doublet && cp input-doublet.cfg doublet/ && (cd doublet && dynearthsol2d input-doublet.cfg)

Setting Value What it does here injection.enabled true turns on scheduled point sources of fluid injection.points_x [0] source at x = 0, the corner of the quarter plane (points_z = 0, the top) injection.rate [5e-06] a quarter of the line-source rate q = 2e-5 m²/s, since the model is a quarter plane (input-doublet.cfg: +1e-4 injector, −1e-4 producer) injection.temperature [333.0] T_in = 333 K, the temperature of the injected water; the injecting node gains ρ_f c_f Q (T_in − T) control.has_fluid_thermal_advection true turns on heat transport by the Darcy flux, required by injection.temperature bc.hbc_x1 2 type 2: the far side x = 8 m is drained (pressure from hbc_pressure, 0 Pa), so water and heat can leave bc.hbc_z0 2 type 2: the bottom is drained in the same way; the two symmetry sides stay sealed (input-doublet.cfg seals all four) bc.tbc_z1 0 0: insulated top; all boundaries are insulated, and heat leaves only with the outflowing water ic.temp_background 283.0 initial temperature T_0 = 283 K mat.hydraulic_perm [1e-13] k = 1e-13 m² mat.bulk_modulus [1000000000000.0] 1e12 Pa (shear modulus too): a nearly rigid skeleton control.has_poroelastic_pressure_feedback false off: deformation does not change the pressure mat.heat_capacity [900.0] rock specific heat; with the water's it sets the bulk capacity C mat.therm_cond [2.0] λ = 2 W/(m K) input.cfg holds all 66 settings that differ from DES’s defaults; dynearthsol2d -h lists every option with its default.

See Running the examples for output files, the Python reader and ParaView conversion. Field What to look at temperature nodal temperature: along the symmetry edge against the Avdonin solution in panel (a), and summed with the heat capacity into the stored heat in panel (b)

(a) Temperature rise against distance from the injection point along a symmetry side at four times: lines, Avdonin's solution; symbols, DES. (b) Hot doublet: heat gained by the box (DES) against the ledger of injected minus extracted heat. (c) Errors against mesh spacing: largest Avdonin temperature error, as a percentage of T_in − T_0, and doublet heat-ledger error, as a percentage of injected heat. This checks the injected-enthalpy term with open outflow (Avdonin) and with outflow at a changing temperature (doublet), measured against energy conservation rather than inferred from the equation. To reproduce the whole study behind this figure, from the DES source folder: python3 benchmarks/poromechanics/avdonin_reference.py python3 tests/functional/hydromechanics/check_injection_temperature.py dynearthsol2d OUT/mesh --spacings 0.2 0.1 python3 tests/functional/hydromechanics/check_injection_temperature.py dynearthsol2d OUT/mesh-coarse --spacings 0.4 python3 tests/functional/hydromechanics/check_injection_temperature.py dynearthsol2d OUT/steps200 --spacings 0.2 --steps 200 python3 tests/functional/hydromechanics/check_injection_temperature.py dynearthsol2d OUT/steps1000 --spacings 0.2 --steps 1000 python3 tests/functional/hydromechanics/check_injection_energy.py dynearthsol2d OUT/doublet --spacings 0.2 0.1 --steps 400 The study’s full numbers: record.json.

documents.t: CTt​+ρf​cf​q⋅∇T=∇⋅(λ∇T)+ρf​cf​Q(Tin​−T)Tin​−T0​T−T0​​=Γ(ν)Γ(ν,u)​u=4λtr2C​,ν=4πλρf​cf​q​E(t)−E(0)=ρf​cf​q∫0t​(Tin​−Tprod​)ds C is the bulk heat capacity, Q the injected volume rate per unit volume, Γ(ν,u) the upper incomplete gamma function and E=∑n​CAn​Tn​ the stored sensible heat. Tprod​ is the temperature at the producer, interpolated with the element's shape functions.

The conservative balance ∂t​(CT)+∇⋅(ρf​cf​qT)=∇⋅(λ∇T)+ρf​cf​QTin​ gives the advective form above once fluid mass conservation, ∇⋅q=Q, removes ρf​cf​T∇⋅q. Extraction removes fluid at the local temperature, which the advective term already carries, so extracting points add nothing. For radial flow q=qr^/(2πr) the equation has a similarity solution in u; the injected heat ρf​cf​q(Tin​−T0​)t is all stored, since none leaves. avdonin_reference.py checks both. Avdonin’s radial thermal-injection problem (1964). The similarity solution is derived here and checked against the equation and the heat balance in avdonin_reference.py; the ledger follows from energy conservation alone.

Fixed heat capacity: heat carried by fluid that goes into storage is not tracked, so a sealed cell storing all its injection is outside the scope. No pressure work, dissipation or thermal expansion. Thermal advection uses the Darcy flux at the start of each step, which loses part of the first step of heat when a source starts from rest and that step needs several thermal substeps.

The drained surface of a fluid-saturated half-space is suddenly heated. Pore water expands more than the grains, so pressure rises below the surface while it drains upward, and the solid heaves. Largest errors over all saved times on the 0.00625 m mesh with 400 steps: pressure 0.46% of its peak, temperature 0.04% of ΔT, vertical strain 1.03% and surface heave 0.91%. At a glance Dimension 2D Build make ndims=2 from the poromechanics source (not yet merged; DynEarthSol #134) Inputs mctigue.zip Reproduce with DynEarthSol 3774df0

Column and heating. A laterally confined column 0≤z≤1 m (depth z) of fluid-saturated rock starts at T0​. At t=0+ its top is raised to T0​+ΔT, ΔT=10 K, and held there; the top is drained (p=0) and traction-free. Other boundaries. Sides and base are sealed, insulated and fixed normally. Heat conducts without advection and gravity is off. Both diffusion lengths stay well inside the column, so it behaves as a half-space. What is compared. Pressure and temperature at the nodes, vertical strain in each element layer and the surface heave, at eight times to 40 ks. DES applies a boundary temperature present at initialization as part of the initial state, so the run restarts from a checkpoint at T0​ with the hot surface.

Every file this example needs is in mctigue.zip. Run from that folder: # Zero-step run of the column at the uniform initial temperature T_0; it writes start.save.000000, start.chkpt.000000 and start.info. These three files are shipped, so this stage can be skipped. dynearthsol2d start.cfg # Restarts from start frame 0 with the surface held at T_0 + 10 K and runs 400 steps of 100 s (40 ks), saving mctigue.save.* every 50 steps (eight times). dynearthsol2d input.cfg

Setting Value What it does here sim.is_restarting yes starts from the checkpoint written by start.cfg rather than from a fresh initial state sim.restarting_from_modelname start start: the zero-step run at T_0 bc.tbc_val_z1 283.0 surface temperature T_0 + ΔT = 283 K (273 K in start.cfg). A boundary temperature present at initialization becomes part of the initial state, so the step is applied through the restart control.has_thermal_pressurization true couples thermal expansion of water and solid to the fluid content and stress bc.hbc_z1 2 type 2: the top is drained, pore pressure held at its hbc_pressure entry (0 Pa) mat.hydraulic_perm [1e-19] k = 1e-19 m²: a tight rock, so pressure diffuses about five times slower than heat (c/κ = 0.21) mat.therm_cond [2.65] λ = 2.65 W/(m K); with the default rock heat capacity and density it gives κ = 1e-6 m²/s mat.biot_coeff [0.8] α = 0.8 mat.bulk_modulus_s [5000000000.0] grain modulus K_s = 5 GPa, part of the storage S_0 mat.porosity [0.2] φ = 0.2 mat.bulk_modulus [1000000000.0] K = 1 GPa (shear modulus also 1 GPa) control.fixed_dt 100.0 100 s; 400 steps reach 40 ks sim.output_step_interval 50 50 steps: eight saved times compared with the solution control.gravity 0 no gravity: only heating drives pressure and strain input.cfg holds all 55 settings that differ from DES’s defaults; dynearthsol2d -h lists every option with its default.

documents.t: ε=Hαp+Kαs​T​H=K+34​Gζ=αε+S0​p−βTβ=ϕαf​+(α−ϕ)αs​Spt​−μk​pzz​=SγTt​,S=S0​+Hα2​,γ=Sβ−αKαs​/H​,c=μSk​T=ΔTerfc2κt​z​p=1−c/κγΔT​[erfc2κt​z​−erfc2ct​z​]w(t)=π​2​[HKαs​ΔT​κt​+H(1−c/κ)αγΔT​(κt​−ct​)] Stress is tension positive and p compression positive. αs​ and αf​ are volumetric thermal expansions, κ the thermal diffusivity, S0​=ϕ/Kf​+(α−ϕ)/Ks​ and w the upward surface heave. The runs use K=G=1 GPa, α=0.8, ϕ=0.2, Kf​=2.2 GPa, Ks​=5 GPa, k=10−19 m2, μ=10−3 Pa s, αs​=3×10−5 K−1, αf​=2.07×10−4 K−1 and κ=10−6 m2/s, so γ=101 kPa/K and c/κ=0.21.

Uniaxial strain with a traction-free surface keeps the vertical total stress zero, which fixes the strain from p and T. Substituting it into the fluid content and Darcy flow gives a pressure diffusion equation forced by the heating rate. σzz​=Hε−αp−Kαs​T=0 Each erfc term solves its own diffusion equation, so a difference of the thermal and hydraulic erfc solves the forced equation and vanishes at the drained surface and at t=0. Integrating the strain over depth gives the heave. mctigue_reference.py checks the equation, the conditions, the heave integral and an independent Crank–Nicolson solution. McTigue (1986), Thermoelastic response of fluid-saturated porous rock, J. Geophys. Res. 91(B9), 9533-9542. Evaluated in mctigue_reference.py. Original reference.

Linear thermo-poroelasticity with constant properties, small strain and conduction only (no Darcy heat advection, no temperature-dependent fluid properties). A finite column stands for the half-space while both diffusion lengths stay well inside it. DES couples pressure and mechanics sequentially, so the earliest frames carry the one-step lag.

At a glance Dimension 2D Inputs mixing.zip Reproduce with DynEarthSol 3774df0 Warm water enters a pressure-controlled, well-mixed saturated cell. Natural outflow removes water at the cell temperature; inlet and retained water have different EOS densities. Maximum temperature error is 0.000545 K at 200 steps and falls with timestep refinement. Retained energy equals injected sensible heat minus boundary export within 20 microjoules.
documents.s: Warm-water mixing in a drained cell

documents.t: Cell. Rigid unit cell at p=0, initially 273 K, insulated and without gravity. Uniform distributed sources keep the temperature spatially uniform. Injection. 0.01 m³/s enters at 323 K for 5 s. Its mass rate uses density at the inlet temperature. Outflow. Natural boundary reaction carries water at the changing cell temperature; it balances injection and the loss of retained mass from thermal expansion.
Every file this example needs is in data/mixing/. Run from that folder: # Injects 323 K water for 5 s in 200 steps into a drained, initially 273 K unit cell. dynearthsol2d input.cfg

Setting Value What it does here control.hydraulic_content_model 1 selects the finite-density saturated inventory law mat.porosity_model 1 evolves Eulerian Biot porosity from the accepted strain and pressure control.fixed_dt 0.025 physical coupling interval; transport can subcycle within it mat.fluid_bulk_modulus [1e8] constant fluid compressibility in the exponential density law mat.bulk_modulus_s [1e9] grain compressibility in the porosity law mat.fluid_alpha [0.0002] volumetric fluid thermal expansivity sim.output_step_interval 1 saved-frame interval; ledger entries belong to individual physical steps input.cfg holds all 79 settings that differ from DES’s defaults; dynearthsol2d -h lists every option with its default.

2D unit cell, 0.01 m³/s inlet at 323 K, initial 273 K, 0–5 s, 200 steps. (a) temperature and the independent integral solution; (b) injected, exported and retained sensible heat. This checks inlet-temperature ownership, injection density, outflow enthalpy and changing retained fluid storage together. Sources are distributed uniformly by nodal volume, so it is a mixing control rather than a spatial plume benchmark. Cs​=1.9875 MJ/K, cf​=4180 J/(kg K), M0​=250 kg and αf​=2×10−4 K−1. The inlet density is lower than the initial cell density.

Water balance sets the outward mass rate. In the sensible-energy balance, the retained c_f T dM term cancels the matching part of boundary export, giving the displayed temperature equation. Separate variables to obtain the independent integral solution. Its integrand is evaluated after a logarithmic distance-to-inlet-temperature substitution, avoiding an endpoint pole. With zero expansivity the solution reduces to an exponential. T=Ti​−(Ti​−T0​)e−cf​M˙i​t/(Cs​+cf​M0​) The reported budget uses actual inlet density, actual retained fluid mass and boundary enthalpy at cell temperature. It includes no numerical fixed-stress buffer in the heat capacity. Independent integral solution and constant-density exponential limit in mass_reference.py.
Uniform well-mixed sensible heat at zero pressure and zero strain. This control does not resolve a local well singularity, a thermal front or a buoyant plume.

Above onset the heated porous cell settles into a steady convection roll that carries several times the conductive heat flow. Its Nusselt number has no closed form; an independent fine-grid solution supplies it. DES Nusselt numbers on the 0.0125 H mesh: Ra = 100: 2.6506 against 2.6459 (0.17%); Ra = 200: 3.8415 against 3.8098 (0.83%). At a glance Dimension 2D Build make ndims=2 from the poromechanics source (not yet merged; DynEarthSol #134) Inputs nusselt.zip Reproduce with DynEarthSol 3774df0

Cell. The Horton–Rogers–Lapwood square cell of the onset page, 0≤x,z≤H: impermeable walls, base at T0​+ΔT, top at T0​, insulated sides, Boussinesq Darcy flow with heat conduction and advection. Run. Each run starts from conduction with a seeded roll at Ra=100 or 200 and continues until the heat transport stops changing. Storage does not enter the steady state, so a compressible pore fluid shortens the transient. What is compared. The steady Nusselt number, from the volume form below and from the temperature gradient at the top, against an independent steady solution on three fine grids, extrapolated.

Every file this example needs is in nusselt.zip. Run from that folder: # Runs the 2D cell at Ra = 200 on the 0.0125 m mesh for 1600 steps of 1000 s, until the heat transport is steady, saving box.save.* every 50 steps with box.info listing the frames. dynearthsol2d input.cfg

Setting Value What it does here control.has_fluid_thermal_advection true turns on heat transport by the Darcy flux mat.fluid_alpha [0.001] water thermal expansion α_f = 1e-3 /K; with the default gravity it drives buoyancy mat.hydraulic_perm [2e-09] permeability chosen to give Ra = 200 (the study also runs Ra = 100) bc.tbc_z0 1 1: fixed temperature at the base bc.tbc_val_z0 283.0 base temperature T_0 + ΔT = 283 K bc.tbc_val_z1 273.0 top temperature T_0 = 273 K; the sides are insulated ic.temperature_option 5 5: linear conduction profile plus a Gaussian seed ic.temp_anomaly_amplitude 0.5 0.5 K seed, large enough to start a single roll quickly mat.fluid_bulk_modulus [10.0] a very compressible pore fluid; storage only sets the transient, so this shortens the run without changing the steady state control.has_poroelastic_pressure_feedback false off: a rigid matrix mesh.resolution 0.0125 0.0125 m, the finest mesh of the study sim.max_steps 1600 1600 steps of 1000 s, long enough for Nu to stop changing sim.output_step_interval 50 50 steps: the Nu history in panel (b) input.cfg holds all 60 settings that differ from DES’s defaults; dynearthsol2d -h lists every option with its default.

See Running the examples for output files, the Python reader and ParaView conversion. Field What to look at temperature nodal temperature; isotherms in panel (a) and the heat transport in the Nusselt number pore pressure with the temperature, rebuilds the Darcy flux used in the volume form of Nu

(a) Isotherms of the steady roll at Ra = 200: solid, DES; dashed, the independent fine-grid solution. (b) Nusselt number (volume form) against time as the cell approaches steady transport. (c) Nusselt-number error against mesh spacing for both Rayleigh numbers. This checks finite-amplitude Darcy convection: buoyancy, heat advection by the Darcy flux and conduction together, through the heat they carry. Storage only sets the transient, so a compressible pore fluid shortens the runs; the transient itself is not compared. To reproduce the whole study behind this figure, from the DES source folder: python3 benchmarks/poromechanics/convection_steady.py python3 tests/functional/hydromechanics/check_convection_nusselt.py dynearthsol2d OUT --spacings 0.05 0.025 0.0125 The study’s full numbers: record.json.

∇2ψ=−Raθx​uθx​+wθz​=∇2θu=ψz​, w=−ψx​Ra=μλρf2​cf​gαf​ΔTkH​Nu=−H1​∫0H​∂z∂θ​​z=H​dx=1+λΔTρf​cf​H​⟨qz​T⟩ θ=(T−T0​)/ΔT, lengths are scaled by H and ψ is the dimensionless streamfunction; qz​ is the vertical Darcy flux and ⟨⋅⟩ the volume mean. The second form of Nu follows from the steady heat balance at every height, averaged over the cell; it is the one evaluated on DES fields, with q rebuilt from the saved pressure and temperature.

Taking the curl of Darcy’s law with Boussinesq buoyancy removes the pressure and gives the streamfunction equation; the energy balance is steady advection–diffusion. convection_steady.py solves both with second-order central differences on 322, 642 and 1282 grids by relaxed Picard iteration and extrapolates Nu (observed order 1.99). Below onset it returns the conductive Nu=1; at Ra = 100 it gives 2.6459, matching published values near 2.65. Horton and Rogers (1945); Lapwood (1948); steady values as in Caltagirone (1975). Computed independently in convection_steady.py. Original reference.
Steady state only: the transient depends on storage, which is chosen for speed. Single-roll solution, as seeded; Boussinesq, constant properties, no mechanical coupling.

A porous cell deforms at a prescribed pure-shear rate. Plastic work in aging rate-and-state plasticity heats the cell and expands the sealed fluid. At Δt = 0.0002 s, temperature and pressure differ from the continuum reference by at most 0.124% and 0.161% of their final reference rises. Both errors converge at first order. Heat plus pending energy matches accepted plastic work to round-off. At a glance Dimension 2D Build make ndims=2 from the poromechanics source (not yet merged; DynEarthSol #134) Inputs plastic-heat.zip Reproduce with DynEarthSol 3774df0
documents.s: Plastic shear heating and sealed pressurization

documents.t: Geometry and loading. Unit square, −1 ≤ z ≤ 0; plane strain. Prescribed normal velocities give ε̇xx=0.5/s, ε̇zz=−0.5/s, zero spin and zero volume strain. Four nodes and two triangles; mesh motion disabled. Initial state. T=300 K, p=0, isotropic compression 30 MPa; K=20 GPa, G=1 GPa, cohesion 10 MPa. Aging EP-RSF: a=0.01, b=0.015, Dc=0.01 m, V0=0.001 m/s, θ0=Dc/V0. Water and heat. Every face sealed and insulated. Porosity 0.2, Biot coefficient 0.8, zero permeability/conductivity, grain/fluid moduli 100/2.2 GPa. Fixed mixture capacity C=2,996,000 J/(m³ K); β=4×10⁻⁵/K. Numerical method. PT option 1; mixed stress disabled; 1000 physical steps of 0.0002 s. Heat is deposited on the following physical interval; pending energy and pressure are separate numerical reservoirs.
Every file this example needs is in plastic-heat.zip. Run from that folder: # Runs 1000 steps to 0.2 s; every physical step is saved under cell. dynearthsol2d input.cfg

Setting Value What it does here control.has_shear_heating true converts accepted nonelastic work into heat; unit heat fraction control.has_thermal_pressurization true couples fluid thermal expansion to sealed pore pressure control.has_fluid_thermal_advection true uses the combined solid and water heat capacity; zero flux here control.has_hydraulic_diffusion true enables pressure evolution; zero permeability prevents drainage control.fixed_dt 0.0002 0.0002 s, the finest of three separately checked physical steps control.is_using_mixed_stress false off, so this reference checks the constitutive work before mixed-stress projection mat.rheology_type elasto-plastic-rate-state-friction plasticity with evolving aging rate-and-state friction mat.direct_a [.01] direct velocity dependence; b is larger, giving velocity weakening mat.evolution_b [.015] state-dependent friction evolution mat.characteristic_distance [.01] sets the state relaxation distance bc.vbc_val_x1 0.5 right-face extension velocity; bottom velocity provides matching compression input.cfg holds all 77 settings that differ from DES’s defaults; dynearthsol2d -h lists every option with its default.

This checks plastic earthquake heating, including evolving EP-RSF strength, without introducing inertia or a rupture-front error. P=30 MPa is effective confinement, Q heat per volume, and V=2wϵ˙ with w=1/2​ m. The integral reference uses tight numerical quadrature of the analytical aging solution; Q=0 before first yield.

Solve the aging ODE at constant slip rate. The decreasing yield strength intersects the elastic predictor once; after this point the cell stays at yield. θ˙=1−Vθ/Dc​,τ=min(Gγ,τy​) Boundary work is τ dγ. Subtract the change in elastic shear energy τ²/(2G) to obtain plastic heat; unit heat fraction is assumed. dQ=τdγ−d(τ2/2G) Fixed volume and sealed fluid give zero content. With constant capacity and no heat loss, temperature follows Q/C. DES’s pending-pressure reservoir vanishes under time refinement. ζ=S0​p−βΔT=0 Direct boundary-work/elastic-storage identity and analytical aging law, evaluated in plastic_heat.py. Integration of the nonelastic work proposed in Eh Tan’s PR #88; thermal fault weakening motivates further fault-scale models (Rice, 2006, doi:10.1029/2005JB004006).

A material-level earthquake-heating qualification with constant effective confinement. It does not demonstrate thermal weakening at fixed total normal stress, a propagating rupture, general enthalpy conservation with changing storage, or a complete earthquake cycle.

Uniform supplied heat warms a rigid, sealed porous material. The temperature rise and fluid expansion give independent heat and pressure references. The 10 K pulse raises the pore pressure to 154.799 kPa. Pressure and stored heat match their references to round-off. At a glance Dimension 2D Build make ndims=2 from the poromechanics source (not yet merged; DynEarthSol #134) Inputs thermal-cell.zip Reproduce with DynEarthSol 3774df0
documents.s: Thermal pressurization in a sealed cell

documents.t: Geometry. Rigid unit material cell, zero gravity, fixed mesh and constant porosity. Every water boundary is sealed in the selected result. Heating. Temperature starts at 273 K. A uniform supplied power raises it at 40 K/s for 0.25 s, followed by a hold through 1 s. Coefficients. No conduction, Darcy permeability or solid thermal expansion. The heat is supplied by one point source per node, each proportional to the volume that node represents.

Every file this example needs is in thermal-cell.zip. Run from that folder: # Heats the 2D cell for 100 steps of 0.01 s (1 s) with ordinary explicit mechanics and writes heated.save.* and heated.chkpt.* at every step, with heated.info listing the frames. dynearthsol2d input.cfg

Setting Value What it does here control.has_thermal_pressurization true couples thermal expansion of water and solid to the fluid content and stress control.has_fluid_thermal_advection true uses the combined rock–water heat capacity C_0 (there is no flow to advect heat here) heat_injection.enabled true turns on scheduled point heat sources heat_injection.num_points 9 nine sources, one at each node of the 3×3-node mesh heat_injection.points_x [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0] x coordinates of the nine nodes heat_injection.points_z [-1.0, -0.5, -0.0, -1.0, -0.5, -0.0, -1.0, -0.5, -0.0] z coordinates of the nine nodes heat_injection.rate [10108333.333333332, 10108333.333333332, 10108333.333333332, 10108333.333333332, 40433333.33333333, 10108333.333333332, 10108333.333333332, 10108333.333333332, 10108333.333333332] heat supplied at each node (W per metre of thickness in 2D), proportional to the volume the node represents, so the cell warms uniformly at 40 K/s heat_injection.duration_in_yr [7.922191133769641e-09, 7.922191133769641e-09, 7.922191133769641e-09, 7.922191133769641e-09, 7.922191133769641e-09, 7.922191133769641e-09, 7.922191133769641e-09, 7.922191133769641e-09, 7.922191133769641e-09] yr = [0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.25] s 0.25 s of heating (in years), followed by a hold to 1 s bc.vbc_x0 3 type 3: every velocity component fixed; with the other faces also 3 the cell is rigid mat.therm_cond [0] 0: no conduction, so the temperature stays uniform mat.fluid_alpha [0.0002] water thermal expansion α_f = 2e-4 /K, the source of the pressure mat.alpha [0] 0: no solid thermal expansion mat.biot_coeff [0.98] α = 0.98 = 1 − K/K_s mat.fluid_bulk_modulus [100000000.0] K_f = 100 MPa; with porosity and K_s it sets the storage S input.cfg holds all 67 settings that differ from DES’s defaults; dynearthsol2d -h lists every option with its default.

See Running the examples for output files, the Python reader and ParaView conversion. Field What to look at temperature nodal temperature; its volume-weighted mean is the temperature rise in panel (a) and gives the stored heat in panel (b) pore pressure nodal pressure; its volume average is the sealed pressure in panel (a)

(a) Pore pressure of the sealed, rigid cell against its temperature rise: line, the sealed linear reference βθ/S; symbols, DES. (b) Heat stored in the cell (symbols, DES) and heat supplied by the sources (line) against time. This checks thermal pressurization of pore water and the heat equation with a supplied heat source. The same comparison holds in 2D and 3D, for several time steps and across restarts. With PT the pressure lags the heating by a first-order amount. A drained version of the cell misses 10,450 J (0.03446% of the supplied heat) because the heat capacity stays fixed while water leaves, so the energy balance of open systems such as thermal plumes is not covered. C0​=3.0325 MJ/(m³ K). L=α2/B is the PT stabilizer, with B=K+G/3 in 2D and B=K in 3D. RE​ is the separate drained control’s retained-fluid enthalpy residual.

For a sealed rigid cell, total volumetric strain and fluid-content change vanish. This gives the physical pressure directly. ζ=Sp+αεv​−βθ=0 The fixed-capacity heat equation integrates the supplied pulse exactly. The selected explicit pressure follows the physical content equation. PT instead retains its pending increment; the displayed recurrence is exact for that split, and its physical-pressure error is first order for small timesteps. For the additional drained rigid cell, all vertices hold zero pressure. Fluid expansion must leave through the boundary reaction. Vo​=Vβθ The retained fluid mass changes the heat capacity. Outflow carries enthalpy at the changing cell temperature. C(θ)=C0​−aθHo​=Va(T0​θ+θ2/2) Use retained mass in the energy change, rather than integrating the original fixed capacity. ΔEret​=V[(C0​−aθ)(T0​+θ)−C0​T0​] Adding outflow enthalpy and subtracting the supplied heat produces the displayed negative half-quadratic deficit. At 10 K it is −10,450 J, or 0.03446% of supplied heat, independent of timestep. There is no strain work or pressure-boundary work in this rigid, zero-pressure control. Linear Biot thermal expansion and integration of the stated heat pulse; the retained-fluid deficit is derived for the implemented linear fluid-content law.

This sealed cell checks thermal pressurization and the fixed-capacity heat equation. With PT the pressure can lag noticeably during rapid heating even when the force balance converges. In a drained cell a small, persistent energy deficit remains, so open systems such as thermal plumes are not covered; shear heating is not included.

Water is injected at a constant rate at a point. Pressure diffuses outward and the solid swells, changing the stress that a nearby fault would feel. Largest RMS errors once the front reaches the band (t>40 s): 1.45% in pressure, 2.11% in radial strain and 1.82% in hoop strain, over 2.5≤r≤8 m. At a glance Dimension 3D Build make ndims=3 from the poromechanics source (not yet merged; DynEarthSol #134) Inputs rudnicki.zip Reproduce with DynEarthSol 3774df0
documents.s: Fluid injection into a poroelastic solid: Rudnicki

documents.t: Source. Water is injected at a constant volume rate Q from t=0 at a point in an unbounded poroelastic solid. DES uses one octant with the scheduled point source at its corner node, injecting Q/8. Boundaries. The planes x=0, y=0 and z=0 are symmetry planes (normal displacement zero, sealed). The far faces of the 60 m box hold p=0 and zero normal displacement; the mesh is refined within 10 m of the source. What is compared. Pressure at the nodes and the radial and hoop strains at the elements for 2.5≤r≤8 m, at all saved times while the diffusion front stays well inside the box.

Every file this example needs is in rudnicki.zip. Run from that folder: # 3D. DES builds the box mesh itself, refined near the source (no mesh file needed), injects at the corner node and runs 48 steps of 5 s to 240 s, saving every fourth step as rudnicki.*. dynearthsol3d input.cfg

Setting Value What it does here injection.enabled true turns on scheduled point sources injection.points_x [0] with points_y and points_z: the source at the origin, the corner node shared by the three symmetry planes injection.rate [1.25e-05] injected volume rate: Q/8 for one octant of the full-space source, in m^3/s mesh.meshing_option 2 box mesh with a refined zone mesh.refined_zonex [0, 0.16666666666666666] with refined_zoney and refined_zonez: the refined zone is the first 10 m from the source along each axis (refined_zonez is measured downward from the top, z = 0) mesh.largest_size 1000 lets the elements grow large away from the refined zone, toward the far faces of the 60 m box bc.vbc_z0 1 with vbc_z1, vbc_y0 and vbc_y1 (and the default vbc_x0, vbc_x1): zero normal displacement on every face; symmetry on x = 0, y = 0, z = 0 bc.hbc_x1 2 with hbc_y1 and hbc_z0: the far faces hold p = 0; the symmetry planes keep the default, sealed control.gravity 0 no gravity: pressure and stress are changes caused by the injection only control.has_PT true PT keeps mechanical equilibrium at every step (quasi-static poroelasticity) mat.hydraulic_perm [1e-13] intrinsic permeability; with the storage it sets the coupled diffusivity c mat.biot_coeff [0.8] Biot coefficient 0.8: couples swelling to pressure mat.bulk_modulus_s [1000000000.0] grain bulk modulus, entering the storage 1/M control.fixed_dt 5.0 5 s time step input.cfg holds all 57 settings that differ from DES’s defaults; dynearthsol3d -h lists every option with its default.

See Running the examples for output files, the Python reader and ParaView conversion. Field What to look at pore pressure nodal pressure against distance from the source, averaged in radial bins, in (a); RMS error over 2.5 ≤ r ≤ 8 m in (c) strain element strain tensor, rotated to radial and hoop components about the source, in (b); RMS errors in (c)

(a) Pore pressure against distance from the source at four times: lines are the Rudnicki solution, symbols DES nodal pressures averaged in radial bins; the shaded band is the compared range 2.5 ≤ r ≤ 8 m. (b) Radial and hoop strain at the last saved time, DES element values binned by radius, against the solution. (c) RMS error of pressure, radial and hoop strain after the front reaches the band, against mesh spacing, with a first-order slope for reference. This checks two-way poroelastic coupling around a fluid source: the coupled diffusivity and the irrotational strain field that sets injection-induced stress on faults. It does not test the fault itself, frictional slip or the singular region next to the source. To reproduce the whole study behind this figure, from the DES source folder: python3 tests/functional/hydromechanics/check_rudnicki.py dynearthsol3d OUT --spacings 1 0.7 0.5 --steps 48 python3 tests/functional/hydromechanics/check_rudnicki.py dynearthsol3d OUT-96 --spacings 0.7 --steps 96 The study’s full numbers: record.json.

documents.t: S=M1​+K+4G/3α2​,c=μSκ​,a=2ct​p(r,t)=4πκrQμ​erfcar​ur​=r2A​[2r2​erfcar​+4a2​erfar​−2π​ar​e−r2/a2],A=4πκ(K+4G/3)αQμ​εθθ​=rur​​,εrr​=K+4G/3αp​−r2ur​​σrr​=−4Grur​​,σθθ​=2G(rur​​−K+4G/3αp​) Here r is the distance from the source, K and G are drained moduli, α the Biot coefficient, 1/M=ϕ/Kf​+(α−ϕ)/Ks​, κ the intrinsic permeability and μ the viscosity; stresses are total changes, tension positive. The runs use Q=10−4 m3/s, K=2×108 Pa, G=108 Pa, α=0.8, ϕ=0.25, Kf​=2.2 GPa, Ks​=1 GPa and κ=10−13 m2, so c=0.0387 m2/s.

For a point source in an unbounded solid the displacement is irrotational and vanishes at infinity, so the volumetric strain follows the pressure, (K+4G/3)ε=αp. The fluid content αε+p/M is then Sp, and the pressure obeys a diffusion equation with the coupled coefficient c. Spt​=μκ​∇2p+Qδ(x) Its continuous point-source solution is the erfc profile above. The radial displacement is ur​=r−2∫0r​εs2ds, which integrates in closed form; the strains and total stresses follow from ur​ and p. σij​=2G(ui,j​−δij​ε), ui​=ϕ,i​ Rudnicki (1986), Fluid mass sources and point forces in linear elastic diffusive solids, Mechanics of Materials 5, 383-393. Evaluated in rudnicki_reference.py, whose closed-form displacement is checked against direct integration.

Linear isotropic poroelasticity with constant properties and small strain; an unbounded solid approximated by a 60 m box, whose fixed far faces perturb the strain by about (r/L)3, with L=60 m (under 0.3% at r=8 m). The singular region r<2.5 m is excluded. No fault or friction is modelled: the stresses are those a fault would feel.

A sealed porous column is compressed through Mohr–Coulomb yield. Total volume change fixes its mean pressure independently of the plastic stress return. Through yield, the stored fluid content plus the pressure increment still pending in the PT step equals the imposed volume loss to round-off, and the mean pressure follows its reference recurrence to round-off. At a glance Dimension 2D Build make ndims=2 from the poromechanics source (not yet merged; DynEarthSol #134) Inputs plastic-content.zip Reproduce with DynEarthSol 3774df0

Geometry and motion. Unit column with a fixed base and fixed side-normal motion. The top moves down at 0.001 m/s for 1 s. Plane strain in 2D; zero gravity and a fixed mesh. Water boundaries. All boundaries are sealed in the selected case. Initial pressure is zero; porosity and pressure capacity remain fixed. Yield law. Mohr–Coulomb: cohesion 100 Pa, friction 20° and selected dilation 10°. Other controls use zero and negative dilation.

Every file this example needs is in plastic-content.zip. Run from that folder: # Compresses the 2D column for 100 steps of 0.01 s (1 s) and writes column.save.* and column.chkpt.* at every step, with column.info listing the frames. dynearthsol2d input.cfg

Setting Value What it does here mat.rheology_type elasto-plastic elasto-plastic: Mohr–Coulomb plasticity mat.cohesion0 [100] cohesion 100 Pa (equal to cohesion1: no weakening), small so the column yields early mat.friction_angle0 [20] friction angle 20° (friction_angle1 is the same) mat.dilation_angle0 [10] dilation angle 10° (dilation_angle1 is the same): yielding makes the skeleton dilate bc.vbc_val_z1 -0.001 the top moves down at 1 mm/s; base and sides are held normally, so the volume loss is fixed by this velocity mat.hydraulic_perm [0] zero permeability, and every hbc is 0 (no flow): the column is sealed mat.fluid_bulk_modulus [1000000.0] K_f = 1 MPa, a soft fluid, so the pressure stays small (4 kPa at 1 s) mat.porosity [0.25] φ = 0.25; with K_f it gives the storage φ/K_f mat.bulk_modulus_s [1e+20] grain modulus 1e20 Pa: incompressible grains, Biot coefficient 1 mat.bulk_modulus [20000000.0] K = 20 MPa mat.shear_modulus [10000000.0] G = 10 MPa control.has_PT true PT solves the mechanics to equilibrium every step; the pressure increment it carries to the next step is counted separately control.fixed_dt 0.01 0.01 s step; 100 steps to 1 s mat.is_plane_strain true 2D plane strain, including the out-of-plane plastic strain input.cfg holds all 62 settings that differ from DES’s defaults; dynearthsol2d -h lists every option with its default.

See Running the examples for output files, the Python reader and ParaView conversion. Field What to look at pore pressure nodal pressure; its volume average is the mean pressure in panel (a) and gives the pressure part of the stored water strain element strain; its volumetric part integrated over the mesh is the imposed volume loss plastic strain shows that the column has yielded before the balance is checked fluid balance per-step water ledger; its boundary entry stays zero in this sealed column

(a) Mean pore pressure of the sealed column against time, through yield: line, the undrained reference set by the imposed volume loss; symbols, DES. (b) Volume balance: line, the imposed pore-volume loss; symbols, DES water stored by pressure plus the pressure increment still pending in the PT step. This checks that plastic yielding neither creates nor destroys pore water: the fluid source uses the accepted volume change, not an elastic estimate. Forty-eight cases cover 2D and 3D, negative, zero and positive dilation, hydraulic substeps, open drainage, Gardner suction, EP-RSF with evolving pressure and thermal expansion. Remeshing, porosity change from plastic strain and the general energy balance are not covered. History CSV · Control tables To reproduce the whole study behind this figure, from the DES source folder: python3 tests/functional/hydromechanics/check_plastic_content.py dynearthsol2d OUT/2d python3 tests/functional/hydromechanics/check_plastic_content.py dynearthsol3d OUT/3d --ndims 3 The study’s full numbers: record.json.

D is the previous raw pressure increase consumed by mechanics. The physical pressure reaches 4 kPa at 1 s; the 0.01 s PT step leaves about 0.17% pending lag.

Integrate total volumetric strain over the actual mesh. The imposed boundary velocity fixes the volume loss even after the stress return becomes plastic. ∫V​εv​dV=−Avt Sealed linear Biot conservation gives the physical mean pressure. Adding the separately recorded pending-pressure contribution gives the exact PT recurrence shown above. Converting the stress change back to volume with the elastic moduli fails after a plastic return, including the out-of-plane plastic strain in plane strain. DES’s fixed-stress source therefore uses the accepted volumetric strain of the step and the previous raw pressure increment; pressure substeps reuse the same accepted mechanical history. With thermal expansion the direct strain source uses the full thermal fluid coefficient, without an additional elastic stress conversion. β=ϕn​αf​+(α−ϕn​)αs​ The partly saturated homogeneous Gardner control has an independent scalar content inversion at each accepted step. It checks the implemented retention-rate law; it does not establish a finite-strain porosity law. (S+L)Δp+ϕn​ΔSe​+αSe,old​Δεv​−LD=0 Additional EP-RSF controls check the independent aging update and effective-stress return while pressure evolves. Open drains include measured boundary exchange; they check material content, rather than a separate spatial Darcy-flux solution. Integral Biot conservation with prescribed boundary motion; independent scalar pressure recurrence and local effective-stress/thermal controls in check_plastic_content.py.

Fixed porosity and geometry. The pending PT term is a numerical coupling lag, not physical water. Porosity change from plastic strain (including enhancement and healing), remeshing, the energy balance of open systems and shear heating are not covered.

Rising pore pressure lowers the effective stress until the ground yields, the mechanism of injection- and rainfall-induced failure. In a laterally confined layer the yield pressure at each depth is exact, so a yield front moving down can be compared element by element. On the 0.025 m mesh with 6400 steps every element yields within 0.23% (mean 0.15%) of its exact pressure, and 96 of 160 elements yield, as predicted. DES always yields slightly late; the delay falls with both the step and the mesh. At a glance Dimension 2D Build make ndims=2 from the poromechanics source (not yet merged; DynEarthSol #134) Inputs pressure-yield.zip Reproduce with DynEarthSol 3774df0
documents.s: Pressure-driven yielding of a confined layer

documents.t: Layer. A saturated layer H=2 m deep under a drained surcharge q=20 kPa, water table at the top, an isotropic lithostatic initial stress with hydrostatic pressure. Sides and base are fixed normally and sealed. Loading. The top pressure rises linearly over 2000 s to 95% of the apex pressure; permeability is high, so the whole layer follows. Gravity acts; pressure feedback is on. Material. Elastic–perfectly plastic Mohr–Coulomb: K=100 MPa, G=60 MPa, c=10 kPa, ϕ=20∘, no dilation, α=1, ϕn​=0.3. What is compared. For each element, the pressure rise at the first step with plastic strain against the exact onset Δp∗ at its centroid depth.

Every file this example needs is in pressure-yield.zip. Run from that folder: # Runs the 2D layer (one 0.025 m element wide, 2 m deep) for 6400 steps of 0.3125 s (2000 s) and saves every step to layer.save.*, with layer.info listing the frames; it first brings the layer to gravitational equilibrium. dynearthsol2d input.cfg

Setting Value What it does here mat.rheology_type elasto-plastic elasto-plastic: elastic–perfectly plastic Mohr–Coulomb (dilation stays at its default of zero) mat.cohesion0 [10000.0] cohesion c = 10 kPa (cohesion1 equal: no weakening) mat.friction_angle0 [20.0] friction angle φ = 20° (friction_angle1 equal) bc.stress_bc_z1 3 type 3: vertical traction on the top surface bc.stress_val_z1 -20000.0 the surcharge q = 20 kPa (compression negative), which keeps the yielded top in compression bc.hbc_z1 2 type 2: the top pore pressure is prescribed from hbc_pressure bc.hbc_pressure [0,0,0,0,0,45101.03548481891] the z1 (top) entry is the final top pore pressure, 95% of the pressure that would bring the surface to the apex of the yield cone bc.num_hbc_schedule 2 two schedule points for the prescribed pressure bc.hbc_schedule_time_in_yr [0, 6.337752907015714e-05] yr = [0, 2000] s 0 and 2000 s: the top pressure ramps linearly over the run bc.hbc_schedule_ratio [0, 1] 0 to 1: the ramp starts from the hydrostatic state mat.hydraulic_perm [1e-11] high permeability, so the whole layer follows the top pressure rise almost at once control.gravity 9.81 9.81 m/s²: lithostatic stress and hydrostatic pressure set the depth dependence of the yield pressure ic.has_body_force_adjustment true brings the initial stress into equilibrium with gravity before loading control.fixed_dt 0.3125 0.3125 s; 6400 steps reach 2000 s input.cfg holds all 62 settings that differ from DES’s defaults; dynearthsol2d -h lists every option with its default.

See Running the examples for output files, the Python reader and ParaView conversion. Field What to look at pore pressure element-averaged pressure; its rise since the start, read at the first saved step with plastic strain, is each element's yield pressure plastic strain marks the first saved step at which an element has yielded stress element total stress; with the pore pressure it gives the effective-stress paths in panel (b)

(a) Depth of the yield front against the pressure rise: line, the exact onset depth; stepped lines, DES on the coarsest mesh and on the finest mesh with the most steps. (b) Effective-stress paths to yield at two depths: lines, the exact paths up to the Mohr–Coulomb line; symbols, DES elements. (c) Mean error of the yield pressure for each mesh and number of steps. This checks effective-stress plasticity in a boundary-value problem driven by pore pressure: the Biot coefficient in the effective stress, the Mohr–Coulomb return and the pressure coupling together. To reproduce the whole study behind this figure, from the DES source folder: python3 benchmarks/poromechanics/pressure_yield_reference.py python3 tests/functional/hydromechanics/check_pressure_yield.py dynearthsol2d OUT/mesh --spacings 0.2 0.1 0.05 --steps 400 python3 tests/functional/hydromechanics/check_pressure_yield.py dynearthsol2d OUT/steps1600 --spacings 0.05 --steps 1600 python3 tests/functional/hydromechanics/check_pressure_yield.py dynearthsol2d OUT/pt1-steps1600 --spacings 0.05 0.025 --steps 1600 --pt-option 1 python3 tests/functional/hydromechanics/check_pressure_yield.py dynearthsol2d OUT/pt1-steps6400 --spacings 0.025 --steps 6400 --pt-option 1 The study’s full numbers: record.json.

documents.t: σv′​=−(γ′d+q)+αΔpσh′​=−(γ′d+κq)+καΔp2σ1′​−σ3′​​+2σ1′​+σ3′​​sinϕ=ccosϕ at Δp=Δp∗(d)Δpapex​=αccotϕ+q​ Tension positive; d is depth, κ=ν/(1−ν), γ′=(ρb​−αρf​)g and σ1′​≥σ3′​ are the principal effective stresses. Δp∗(d) is the first root of the yield function of the elastic trial state.

Under uniaxial strain the horizontal stresses stay equal and change by κ times the vertical change; the total vertical stress is fixed by the weight and the surcharge, so a uniform pressure rise moves only the effective stresses, as above. Δp∗ increases with depth, so a yield front moves down. Each depth is independent under uniaxial strain, so the front stays exact after the layer above yields; the yielded state follows the cone until its apex. The surcharge keeps the top in compression: without it the yielded top reaches the apex within a few kPa of the onset. pressure_yield_reference.py checks the onset on the yield surface, the elastic state just below it, the surcharge-free closed form and the ordering of onset and apex. Terzaghi effective stress with Mohr–Coulomb yield; the uniaxial-strain stress path as in Jaeger, Cook and Zimmerman, Fundamentals of Rock Mechanics (2007). Computed in pressure_yield_reference.py.

Uniaxial strain, a uniform pressure rise, no dilation, fully saturated. The test stops short of the apex, beyond which no equilibrium exists. 3D is checked only to onset; an inclined (infinite-slope) version needs an initial-stress option DES does not have.

An affine material cell is extended in one direction and compressed equally in another, at fixed pore pressure. Effective stress must control its shear yield load. The pressurized 3D case yields at 186.603 kPa, matching the analytical load. The largest stress/plastic-strain error over 20 load paths (EP, and EP-RSF at constant friction) is 1.28e-14 of the yield load. At a glance Dimension 3D Build make ndims=3 from the poromechanics source (not yet merged; DynEarthSol #134) Inputs strength.zip Reproduce with DynEarthSol 3774df0

Material cell. Every normal velocity component is prescribed on the unit cell. Normal strains are e in x and −e in z, with zero y strain in 3D; 2D uses plane strain. Pressure and initial stress. Initial total stress is −CI. Pressure is uniform and constant; permeability and mechanical pressure feedback are zero. Gravity, mesh motion and heat are disabled. Strength law. K=G=1 GPa, cohesion c=100 kPa, friction angle 30∘ and dilation angle zero. EP-RSF is checked in the constant-friction limit a=b=0.

Every file this example needs is in strength.zip. Run from that folder: # Runs the 3D unit cell for 64 steps of 1 s (the input is 3D: six initial-stress components) and writes cell.save.* and cell.chkpt.* every 4 steps, with cell.info listing the frames. dynearthsol3d input.cfg

Setting Value What it does here mat.rheology_type elasto-plastic elasto-plastic: Mohr–Coulomb plasticity, whose strength DES evaluates with the effective stress mat.cohesion0 [1e5] cohesion c = 100 kPa; equal to cohesion1, so there is no strain weakening mat.cohesion1 [1e5] same as cohesion0: no weakening mat.friction_angle1 [30] 30°, equal to friction_angle0, so the friction angle stays fixed (dilation stays at its default of zero) mat.bulk_modulus [1e9] K = 1 GPa mat.shear_modulus [1e9] G = 1 GPa; the elastic branch of the load path is t = 2Ge ic.initial_stress_option 1 1: start from the homogeneous total stress given in initial_stress ic.initial_stress [-1000000.0, -1000000.0, -1000000.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] isotropic total stress −C with C = 1 MPa (compression negative) ic.pore_pressure_option 2 2: uniform initial pore pressure ic.pore_pressure_value 800000.0 pore pressure p = 0.8 MPa; with Biot coefficient 1 it lowers the effective confinement to 0.2 MPa control.has_poroelastic_pressure_feedback false off: deformation does not change the pore pressure, so p stays fixed bc.vbc_val_x1 7.8125e-06 the right face moves outward, extending the cell in x at strain rate e-dot bc.vbc_val_z1 -7.8125e-06 the top moves down at the same rate, shortening the cell in z; the y faces are held (vbc_y0, vbc_y1 = 1), so y strain is zero control.gravity 0 no gravity: stress and pressure are uniform input.cfg holds all 65 settings that differ from DES’s defaults; dynearthsol3d -h lists every option with its default.

See Running the examples for output files, the Python reader and ParaView conversion. Field What to look at strain element strain; its xx component, averaged over the cell, is the imposed normal strain e on the horizontal axis stress element total stress; half of (σxx − σzz), averaged over the cell, is the principal shear load t on the vertical axis

Principal shear load t (half the difference of the extreme principal stresses) against the imposed normal strain e, for the 3D elasto-plastic cell at 1 MPa total confinement and 0.8 MPa pore pressure. Line: the elastic–perfectly plastic analytical path, which yields at the effective-stress load t_y. Symbols: DES at each saved frame. This isolates the pressure-dependent strength of the skeleton and its plastic strain. EP-RSF is checked at constant friction here and with evolving friction on the rate-and-state page. Flow, dilation, tensile failure and slope or injection applications are not tested here. To reproduce the whole study behind this figure, from the DES source folder: python3 tests/functional/hydromechanics/check_pore_strength.py dynearthsol2d OUT/2d --ndims 2 python3 tests/functional/hydromechanics/check_pore_strength.py dynearthsol3d OUT/3d --ndims 3 The study’s full numbers: record.json.
