documents.t: σ′=σ+qIq=α⟨Se​(p)p⟩e​ty​=ccosϕ+(C−q)sinϕt(e)=min(2Ge,ty​)ϵp​=max[0,e−ty​/(2G)]Nϕ​=(1+sinϕ)/(1−sinϕ)Atotal​=2cNϕ​​−(Nϕ​−1)qTtotal​=T−q q=αp when saturated. t is half the extreme principal-stress difference and T the tensile cap of the skeleton. DES stores total stress, so it applies the effective-stress criterion by shifting the shear intercept and the tensile cap by q, as in the last two equations.

The effective principal stresses are -(C-q)-t and -(C-q)+t. Substituting them in Mohr-Coulomb gives the shear yield load. σmin′​−Nϕ​σmax′​+2cNϕ​​=0 Zero dilation keeps mean stress fixed on this path. Stress first follows 2Ge and then stays at the perfect-plastic yield load; the remaining strain is plastic. Closed-form Mohr-Coulomb response derived for the stated imposed path; stress and plastic strain are checked at every saved frame in check_pore_strength.py.

A uniform-strain, fixed-pressure, zero-dilation material check on the compressive shear branch. Evolving rate-and-state friction is checked on the rate-and-state page. Tensile failure, mixed-material suction, flow, dilation and slope or injection applications are not tested here.

A well pumps a thin poroelastic aquifer. The drawdown spreads radially and the layer contracts, splitting its volume change between areal and vertical strain. RMS errors: 0.71% in pressure, 1.97% in areal strain and 1.90% in vertical strain, relative to the largest analytical values. At a glance Dimension 3D Build make ndims=3 from the poromechanics source (not yet merged; DynEarthSol #134) Inputs aquifer.zip Reproduce with DynEarthSol 3774df0

DES slab. A thin quarter slab, 400×400 m and B=10 m thick, with a fully penetrating well on its corner edge pumping Q/4 (Q=0.01 m3/s). Symmetry rollers at x=0, y=0, a roller base and a traction-free top; the far sides hold the initial pressure and zero normal displacement. Reference. The thickness-averaged (generalised Bear–Corapcioglu) model: vanishing incremental vertical and vertical-shear total stress, horizontal displacement uniform through the thickness. It applies while the slab is thin compared with the radius, up to O((B/r)2). What is compared. Nodal pressure and element areal and vertical strains for 15≤r≤120 m at four times, while the pressure front stays inside the slab, on structured meshes.

Every file this example needs is in aquifer.zip. Run from that folder: # Runs the 3D quarter slab on a 5 m hexahedral mesh: the corner well pumps from t = 0 and DES writes frames slab.* at 0, 2500, 5000, 7500 and 10000 s. No mesh or restart file is needed. dynearthsol3d input.cfg

Setting Value What it does here control.has_hydraulic_diffusion true turns on Darcy flow, so the drawdown spreads from the well by diffusion control.has_PT true iterates each time step to mechanical equilibrium, so the slab deforms quasi-statically with the pressure (two-way Biot coupling) control.gravity 0 no gravity: every field is a change from the unstressed, zero-pressure initial state control.has_moving_mesh false keeps the mesh fixed (small strain), as the reference assumes mesh.meshing_elem_shape 1 structured hexahedra, so the mesh spacing follows mesh.resolution exactly bc.vbc_y0 1 symmetry plane y = 0: normal displacement fixed (the x = 0 plane is a roller by default) bc.vbc_z0 1 roller base: vertical displacement fixed, horizontal free; the top is traction-free bc.hbc_x1 1 far side x = 400 m holds its initial pore pressure (zero change) bc.hbc_y1 1 far side y = 400 m holds its initial pore pressure (zero change) bc.num_wells 1 one rate-controlled vertical well, placed on the corner edge x = y = 0 bc.well_rate [0.0025] extraction rate of the quarter well: one quarter of the full rate Q, because the model is one quarter of the slab bc.well_z_bottom [-10.0] screens the well over the whole 10 m thickness (fully penetrating) mat.hydraulic_perm [1e-12] permeability; with fluid viscosity and storage it sets the hydraulic diffusivity mat.biot_coeff [0.8] Biot coefficient, the strength of the pressure–deformation coupling input.cfg holds all 44 settings that differ from DES’s defaults; dynearthsol3d -h lists every option with its default.

See Running the examples for output files, the Python reader and ParaView conversion. Field What to look at pore pressure nodal pressure change against radius from the well at each saved time; panel (a) and the pressure error strain element strain tensor: the areal strain is the xx + yy components and the vertical strain the zz component; panel (b) and the strain errors coordinate node positions, used for the radius of nodes and element centres from the well

(a) Pressure drop against distance from the well at the first and last saved times: lines are the averaged-aquifer line-well solution, symbols the mean DES value in radius bins with the spread shaded. (b) Areal and vertical contraction at the last time against the analytical solution, which predicts the two to be equal. (c) RMS errors in pressure, areal strain and vertical strain against mesh spacing, with a first-order slope for reference. This checks two-way coupled pumping deformation against the thickness-averaged model. It does not remove the O((B/r)2) slab-model difference, which remains at the finest mesh. To reproduce the whole study behind this figure, from the DES source folder: python3 benchmarks/poromechanics/slab_refinement.py dynearthsol3d OUT --resolutions 20 10 5 The study’s full numbers: record.json.

documents.t: λ=K−2G/3,Sa​=S0​+α2/(λ+G),D=κ/(μSa​)CQ​=Qμ/(4πκB),u=r2/(4Dt),p(r,t)=−CQ​E1​(u)eh​=ϵzz​=2(λ+G)αp​,δ=−Bϵzz​Ur​=−(λ+G)rαCQ​Dt​[uE1​(u)−e−u+1] p is the pressure change (negative during extraction), Sa​ is pressure storage in Pa−1, S0​=ϕ/Kf​+(α−ϕ)/Ks​, eh​=ϵxx​+ϵyy​ is areal strain, and δ is positive downward subsidence. The plotted reference is the infinite-domain line-well limit. The full finite-annulus Laplace solution, which includes an additional spatially uniform strain function h(t), is derived below.

Thickness averaging assumes zero incremental vertical stress and negligible vertical shear. Eliminating vertical strain gives the plane-stress Lamé coefficient and uniform radial equilibrium function h(t): λ∗​=λ+2G2Gλ​,εzz​=λ+2Gαp−λeh​​,eh​=2(λ+G)αp​+h(t),εv​=λ+Gαp​+λ+2G2Gh​. Integrating areal strain and substituting fluid content give rUr​=Cw​+2(λ+G)α​∫rw​r​ρp(ρ,t)dρ+2h​(r2−rw2​),ζ=Sa​p+ch,c=λ+2G2Gα​,Sa​p˙​+ch˙=(κ/μ)∇r2​p. The well has finite radius rw​, with prescribed total extraction rate 2πrw​B(κ/μ)pr​(rw​)=Q. The outer hydraulic boundary is p(R)=0 or no flow. Either radial mechanical boundary can fix Ur​=0 or set σrr​=0, where σrr​=(λ∗​+2G)h−2GUr​/r. For the fixed inner boundary Cw​=0; for a traction-free inner boundary Cw​=rw2​(λ∗​+2G)h/(2G). In Laplace space, p​=AI0​(qr)+B0​K0​(qr)−(c/Sa​)h,q2=sSa​μ/κ. The two hydraulic conditions and outer mechanical condition form a 3×3 system for A,B0​,h. The Bessel integral in Ur​ is analytic. Exponentially scaled bases avoid overflow; a fixed 32-node Talbot inversion returns the time solution. This is the implementation in averaged_aquifer_reference.py, independent of DES's discretization. In an infinite domain h=0, recovering the closed forms above. A distant fixed boundary generally gives nonzero h before the pressure front reaches it, and its strain feeds back into storage. A finite-domain pressure therefore need not be Theis. Independent reference checks cover radial finite volumes, sealed fluid balance, the hydraulic/mechanical boundaries, kinematics, the line-well limit and steady Thiem flow: python3 tests/functional/hydromechanics/check_averaged_aquifer_reference.py -v The zero-horizontal-strain alternative has storage S0​+α2/(λ+2G) and vertical strain αp/(λ+2G). It is a different mechanical constraint. For a common pressure change, the plane-stress subsidence is (1−ν) times that value; with matching α and S0​ and both models calibrated to the same storativity, the ratio is one half.

Linear poroelasticity with constant properties; the thin-slab geometry approaches the averaged model only up to O((B/r)2), so a small model difference remains at the finest mesh. Two-way coupling with PT; no gravity. Near-well, early-time 3D pressure rises (the Noordbergum effect) are outside the averaged model. A vertical 2D slice cannot represent radial groundwater flow together with subsidence.

Water enters a laterally confined elastic column through its base and leaves through a pressure-controlled top. Pressure and deformation independently measure its stored fluid. Late pressure error is 0.0286% of the steady base pressure. In all 19 runs the stored water, including the small increment the PT solver carries into the next step, equals the net inflow to within 2.4e-15 of the injected volume. At a glance Dimension 2D Build make ndims=2 from the poromechanics source (not yet merged; DynEarthSol #134) Inputs content.zip Reproduce with DynEarthSol 3774df0
documents.s: Water balance in a deforming column

documents.t: Geometry. A 1 m confined column; 0.1 m wide on the selected 2D mesh. Fixed geometry, zero gravity, elastic skeleton. Mechanical boundaries. Base vertical motion and side-normal motion are fixed. The top has zero total normal traction: σzz​=0. Water boundaries. Initially p=0. The top stays drained; the base supplies qi​=10−6 m/s. Sides are sealed.

Every file this example needs is in content.zip. Run from that folder: # Runs the 2D column on a 0.05 m mesh for 800 steps of 0.005 s (4 s) and writes column.save.* and column.chkpt.* at every step, with column.info listing the frames. dynearthsol2d input.cfg

Setting Value What it does here control.has_hydraulic_diffusion true turns on Darcy flow, so pore pressure diffuses through the column control.has_PT true solves the mechanics to equilibrium at every step with the pseudo-transient (PT) iteration control.fixed_dt 0.005 physical time step; with max_steps it sets the 4 s simulated control.gravity 0 no gravity: all pressure comes from the water pumped in at the base bc.hbc_z0 3 type 3: the base is a prescribed-flux boundary, taking its value from hbc_flux bc.hbc_flux [0,0,0,0,-1e-06,0] the bottom (z0) entry is an outward flux; its negative value pumps water in through the base bc.hbc_z1 2 type 2: the top is drained, pore pressure held at its hbc_pressure entry (0 Pa) bc.stress_bc_z1 3 type 3: vertical traction on the top; with stress_val_z1 = 0 the top is traction-free and can rise as the column swells sim.output_step_interval 1 saves every step, so stored and drained water can be summed step by step mat.porosity [0.25] pore fraction; with the fluid and grain moduli it sets the pressure storage S mat.biot_coeff [0.8] Biot coefficient alpha: how strongly pore pressure and volume strain are coupled mat.bulk_modulus_s [1000000000.0] grain (solid) bulk modulus K_s, part of the storage S mat.fluid_bulk_modulus [100000000.0] water bulk modulus K_f, part of the storage S mat.hydraulic_perm [1e-11] intrinsic permeability k; with the viscosity it sets the mobility k/mu and the 100 Pa steady base pressure input.cfg holds all 58 settings that differ from DES’s defaults; dynearthsol2d -h lists every option with its default.

See Running the examples for output files, the Python reader and ParaView conversion. Field What to look at pore pressure nodal pressure; the vertical profile on the column centre line is compared with the series in panel (a), and its volume integral gives the pressure part of the stored water strain element strain; its volumetric part times the Biot coefficient gives the deformation part of the stored water in panel (b) fluid balance five numbers per frame for the last step: storage change, mechanical source, wells, boundary exchange and residual; the summed boundary exchange gives the drained water in panel (b)

(a) Pressure down the centre of the column at several times while it fills: lines are the series solution, symbols are DES. (b) Water stored in the column and water drained through the top, per unit cross-section, against time: lines are the reference, symbols are DES (stored water from pressure and volume strain, drained water from the boundary exchange). Stored water is computed from the pressure and volume strain integrated over the mesh, and drained water both from the boundary exchange and from the Darcy flux at the top, so the check does not reuse the pressure equation. With PT the stored water lags by about one step; the lag halves when the time step is halved. Explicit, GVS, 3D and restarted runs close the same budget. History CSV · Control tables To reproduce the whole study behind this figure, from the DES source folder: python3 benchmarks/poromechanics/fluid_content.py dynearthsol2d OUT/spatial-pt --spacings .2 .1 .05 --dt .005 --duration 4 python3 benchmarks/poromechanics/fluid_content.py dynearthsol2d OUT/time-coarse --spacings .05 --dt 0.02 --duration 1 python3 benchmarks/poromechanics/fluid_content.py dynearthsol2d OUT/time-medium --spacings .05 --dt 0.01 --duration 1 python3 benchmarks/poromechanics/fluid_content.py dynearthsol2d OUT/time-fine --spacings .05 --dt 0.005 --duration 1 The study’s full numbers: record.json.

documents.t: S=ϕ/Kf​+(α−ϕ)/Ks​Hm​=K+4G/3Co​=S+α2/Hm​m=k/μD=m/Co​kn​=(2n+1)π/(2H)p(d,t)=mqi​​[d−H2​n=0∑∞​kn2​(−1)nsin(kn​d)​e−Dkn2​t]pˉ​=mqi​​[2H​−H22​n=0∑∞​kn3​(−1)n​e−Dkn2​t]Vs​=AHCo​pˉ​Vo​=Aqi​t−Vs​Z=∫V​(Sp+αεv​)dVZsplit​=Z+e∑​Ve​L(pn​−pn−1​)​e​L=α2/BB2D​=K+G/3B3D​=K d is depth below the drain, A cross-section and H=1 m. Stress and volume strain are tension-positive. K=20 MPa, G=10 MPa, α=0.8, ϕ=0.25, Kf​=100 MPa, Ks​=1 GPa, k=10−11 m² and μ=10−3 Pa s. The steady basal pressure is 100 Pa.

Vertical equilibrium of the confined, traction-free column gives strain proportional to pressure. Insert it in physical Biot content to obtain the constrained capacity. εv​=αp/Hm​ζ=Co​p Mass balance with Darcy mobility gives diffusion and its mixed boundary conditions. Co​pt​=mpdd​p(0,t)=0mpd​(H,t)=qi​ Subtract the steady profile. The remaining field has zero value at the top and zero derivative at the base, giving the odd half-wave sine eigenfunctions. Projection of the initial negative steady profile yields the pressure series above. Integrate the pressure series for stored volume; differentiate it at the top for independent outward Darcy flux. qo​=qi​[1−H2​n=0∑∞​kn​(−1)n​e−Dkn2​t] With PT, the mechanics of each step uses the pressure increment of the previous step. The increment not yet passed to the mechanics is a small pending term, and adding it to the stored water closes the budget exactly. It is a numerical lag, not physical water, and it halves when the time step is halved. Separation of variables and mesh-independent quadrature for the stated mixed-boundary Biot diffusion problem; fluid_content.py also checks the PDE and endpoint derivatives.

Fixed geometry, saturated flow and constant material properties. This example does not check storage that changes with deformation, large-strain mass, mass conservation through remeshing, or heat. A closed budget does not by itself mean an accurate equilibrium; the two are checked separately.

A drained poroelastic sphere is suddenly loaded on its surface. The shell drains and contracts first, squeezing the core, so the centre pressure rises before it decays. Largest pressure error after ct/R2=0.05: 0.62% of p0​, and 2.12% including the first-step lag. Sampled centre peak: DES 1.4347p0​, analytical 1.4410p0​. At a glance Dimension 3D Build make ndims=3 from the poromechanics source (not yet merged; DynEarthSol #134) Inputs cryer.zip Reproduce with DynEarthSol 3774df0

Load and drainage. A poroelastic sphere of radius R receives a uniform compressive normal stress P at t=0+ on its drained surface (p=0). DES applies it as a normal stress on the curved facets. Mesh and symmetry. One octant is meshed: the three flat faces are symmetry planes (normal motion fixed, sealed), the curved surface is subdivided on the sphere. What is compared. Pressure at every node, and especially at the centre, against the series solution. The centre pressure first rises above its undrained value p0​ (Mandel–Cryer effect).

Every file this example needs is in cryer.zip. Run from that folder: # Meshes the sphere octant from octant.poly (shipped in the same folder) at 0.07 m, runs 800 steps over 0.5 R^2/c (20.9 s) and writes cryer.save.* every 20 steps, with a checkpoint every 10th frame. This is a 3D run and takes much longer than the 2D examples. dynearthsol3d input.cfg

Setting Value What it does here mesh.meshing_option 90 90: the domain boundary is read from a .poly file instead of a box mesh.poly_filename octant.poly octant.poly: one octant of a unit sphere; the curved surface carries the top (z1) boundary flag, the flat faces x = 0, y = 0 and z = 0 the x0, y0 and z0 flags mesh.resolution 0.07 target element size used when meshing the octant control.has_hydraulic_diffusion true turns on Darcy flow, so water drains out through the curved surface control.has_PT true solves the mechanics to equilibrium at every step with PT, so the sudden surface load is carried without elastic waves control.gravity 0 no gravity: only the surface load creates pressure control.fixed_dt 0.026153118474050982 physical time step, 1/800 of 0.5 R^2/c sim.max_steps 800 800 steps; this, not max_time_in_yr, ends the run bc.vbc_y0 1 fixes normal motion on the symmetry plane y = 0 (x = 0 is fixed by the default vbc_x0) bc.vbc_z0 1 fixes normal motion on the symmetry plane z = 0, which carries the z0 flag in octant.poly bc.hbc_z1 2 type 2: the curved surface is drained, pore pressure held at its hbc_pressure entry (0 Pa); the symmetry planes stay sealed bc.stress_bc_z1 4 type 4: a normal stress on facets of any orientation, here the curved sphere surface bc.stress_val_z1 -100000.0 the surface pressure; negative is compression (100 kPa) mat.hydraulic_perm [1.03e-12] intrinsic permeability; with storage and stiffness it sets the consolidation coefficient c input.cfg holds all 41 settings that differ from DES’s defaults; dynearthsol3d -h lists every option with its default.

See Running the examples for output files, the Python reader and ParaView conversion. Field What to look at pore pressure nodal pressure; the node nearest the centre gives panel (a), all nodes binned by radius give the profiles in panel (b), and the largest nodal error gives panel (c)

(a) Pressure at the centre of the sphere, scaled by the undrained pressure p0, against ct/R^2: the line is the series solution, symbols are DES; the dotted line marks p/p0 = 1, which the centre pressure first exceeds. (b) Radial pressure profiles at four times: lines are the series solution, symbols are the mean of the DES nodes in each radius bin and the shaded band their spread. (c) Largest pressure error after ct/R^2 = 0.05 against mesh spacing, one line per number of time steps. This checks 3D two-way coupling under a sudden load, the Mandel–Cryer pressure and the normal-stress load on a curved surface. It does not remove the one-step lag of the sequential coupling in the earliest frames, which falls with the time step. To reproduce the whole study behind this figure, from the DES source folder: python3 tests/functional/hydromechanics/check_cryer.py dynearthsol3d OUT/cryer-h --spacings 0.2 0.1 0.07 --steps 200 python3 tests/functional/hydromechanics/check_cryer.py dynearthsol3d OUT/cryer-t400 --spacings 0.1 --steps 400 python3 tests/functional/hydromechanics/check_cryer.py dynearthsol3d OUT/cryer-h0.1-t800 --spacings 0.1 --steps 800 python3 tests/functional/hydromechanics/check_cryer.py dynearthsol3d OUT/cryer-h0.07-t400 --spacings 0.07 --steps 400 python3 tests/functional/hydromechanics/check_cryer.py dynearthsol3d OUT/cryer-h0.07-t800 --spacings 0.07 --steps 800 The study’s full numbers: record.json.

documents.t: S=M1​+K+4G/3α2​,c=μSκ​,β=3KS(K+4G/3)4Gα2​p0​=KS(1+β)αP​3β(sinξn​−ξn​cosξn​)=(1+β)ξn2​sinξn​p0​p(r,t)​=n∑​wn​(1−rsinξn​Rsin(ξn​r/R)​)e−ξn2​ct/R2G(ξ)=3(1−ξcotξ)/ξ2,wn​=−βξn​G′(ξn​)2(1+β)​ Here K, G are drained moduli, α the Biot coefficient, 1/M=ϕ/Kf​+(α−ϕ)/Ks​, κ the intrinsic permeability and μ the viscosity. The runs use R=1 m, P=105 Pa and the material of the Mandel page, so c=0.0239 m2/s, R2/c=41.8 s and β=1.33.

Spherical symmetry makes the displacement irrotational, so (K+4G/3)ε=αp+f(t). The surface traction fixes f through the volume-average pressure ⟨p⟩, and the fluid balance becomes a diffusion equation forced by d⟨p⟩/dt. pt​−c∇2p=−βdtd⟨p⟩​ With q=s/c​, x=qR and g(x)=3(xcothx−1)/x2, the Laplace transform is closed. Its poles sn​=−cξn2​/R2 give the roots and their residues the weights wn​. The series is checked against a numerical (Stehfest) inversion of the transform. p0​p^​​=s(1+β(1−g(x)))(1+β)(1−rsinhxRsinhqr​)​ Cryer (1963); Detournay and Cheng (1993). Derived and evaluated in cryer_reference.py with the same material values; the series agrees with a Stehfest inversion to 1.3e-4. Original reference.

Small strain, linear isotropic poroelasticity with constant properties; the curved surface is a faceted approximation of the sphere. DES couples pressure and mechanics sequentially, so the earliest frames carry the one-step lag of that split. No gravity.

Rigid frictionless plates squeeze a drained poroelastic strip. The edges drain first, load shifts to the undrained core, and the centre pressure rises before it decays. Largest pressure error: 0.83% of p0​, over all nodes and times; largest relative settlement error: 0.11%. Sampled centre peak: DES 1.1257p0​, analytical 1.1265p0​. At a glance Dimension 2D Build make ndims=2 from the poromechanics source (not yet merged; DynEarthSol #134) Inputs mandel.zip Reproduce with DynEarthSol 3774df0
documents.s: Mandel consolidation under a rigid plate

documents.t: Load and plates. Rigid, frictionless, impermeable plates squeeze the strip −a<x<a with a total force 2F per unit length, applied at t=0+. DES models the top plate with a rigid platen: every top node shares one vertical velocity and slides freely. Drainage and symmetry. The faces x=±a are drained (p=0) and traction-free. One quarter is meshed: symmetry at x=0 and at the mid-plane, both sealed. What is compared. Pressure at every node and the uniform plate settlement, against the series solution. At the centre the pressure first rises above its undrained value p0​: the Mandel–Cryer effect.

Every file this example needs is in mandel.zip. Run from that folder: # Runs the quarter strip (a = b = 1 m) on a 0.05 m mesh for 800 steps over one consolidation time a^2/c (41.8 s) and writes mandel.save.* every 20 steps, with a checkpoint every 10th frame. dynearthsol2d input.cfg

Setting Value What it does here control.has_hydraulic_diffusion true turns on Darcy flow, so water drains out through the side x = a control.has_PT true solves the mechanics to equilibrium at every step with PT, so the sudden plate load is carried without elastic waves control.gravity 0 no gravity: only the plate load creates pressure control.fixed_dt 0.05230623694810197 physical time step, 1/800 of the consolidation time a^2/c sim.max_steps 800 800 steps; this, not max_time_in_yr, ends the run sim.output_step_interval 20 writes a frame every 20 steps bc.vbc_x1 0 type 0: the drained side x = a is free to move (traction-free) bc.vbc_z0 1 fixes vertical motion on the bottom edge, the mid-plane of the strip (symmetry) bc.vbc_z1 8 type 8: rigid frictionless platen; all top nodes share one vertical velocity and slide freely sideways bc.stress_bc_z1 3 type 3: the platen is pushed by a vertical traction bc.stress_val_z1 -100000.0 the plate pressure; negative is compression (100 kPa, total force F = Pa) bc.hbc_x1 2 type 2: the side x = a is drained, pore pressure held at its hbc_pressure entry (0 Pa); the other sides stay sealed mat.bulk_modulus [10000000.0] drained bulk modulus K (with G it sets the Poisson ratio and p0) mat.hydraulic_perm [1.03e-12] intrinsic permeability; with storage and stiffness it sets the consolidation coefficient c input.cfg holds all 46 settings that differ from DES’s defaults; dynearthsol2d -h lists every option with its default.

See Running the examples for output files, the Python reader and ParaView conversion. Field What to look at pore pressure nodal pressure; centre and x = a/2 histories in panel (a), profiles across the strip in panel (b), and the error at every node in panel (c) strain element strain; the vertical component averaged over the quarter gives the plate settlement, whose error is in panel (c) velocity nodal velocity; the vertical velocity of the top row should be the same at every node under the rigid platen

(a) Pressure history at the centre x = 0 and at x = a/2, scaled by the undrained pressure p0, against ct/a^2: lines are the series solution, symbols are DES; the dotted line marks p/p0 = 1, which the centre pressure first exceeds. (b) Pressure profiles across the strip at four times. (c) Largest pressure error (over all nodes and times, divided by p0) and largest relative settlement error against the time step, on log axes, with a slope-1 guide. This checks two-way poroelastic coupling under a sudden load, the non-monotonic Mandel–Cryer pressure and the rigid-platen boundary. It does not test large strain or plasticity. To reproduce the whole study behind this figure, from the DES source folder: python3 tests/functional/hydromechanics/check_mandel.py dynearthsol2d OUT/mandel-h --spacings 0.1 0.05 0.025 --steps 200 python3 tests/functional/hydromechanics/check_mandel.py dynearthsol2d OUT/mandel-t100 --spacings 0.05 --steps 100 python3 tests/functional/hydromechanics/check_mandel.py dynearthsol2d OUT/mandel-t400 --spacings 0.05 --steps 400 python3 tests/functional/hydromechanics/check_mandel.py dynearthsol2d OUT/mandel-t800 --spacings 0.05 --steps 800 The study’s full numbers: record.json.

The undrained pressure is p0​=FB(1+νu​)/(3a). The runs use a=b=1 m, F=Pa with P=105 Pa, K=G=107 Pa, ϕ=0.3, α=1, Kf​=2.17 GPa, Ks​=37 GPa and κ=1.03×10−12 m2, so c=0.0239 m2/s and a2/c=41.8 s.

A rigid frictionless plate makes εzz​(t) uniform; σxx​=0 at the drained faces and equilibrium make σxx​=0 everywhere, so the problem is one-dimensional in x. The fluid balance then contains the unknown plate strain rate, and the plate force fixes it through the integral of σzz​ over the width. ∫0a​σzz​dx=−F Separation of variables with the drained condition p(a,t)=0 and this integral constraint gives the roots αn​ and the series above; the initial undrained state fixes the coefficients. The same series gives the plate settlement. Mandel (1953); Abousleiman et al. (1996), Mandel’s problem revisited. Evaluated independently in mandel_reference.py with the same material values. Original reference.

Plane strain, small strain, linear isotropic poroelasticity with constant properties; ideal rigid frictionless plates. DES couples pressure and mechanics sequentially; the early-time error is the one-step lag of that split and falls with the time step. No gravity.

At a glance Dimension 2D Inputs mass.zip Reproduce with DynEarthSol 3774df0 A sealed saturated cell is compressed at a prescribed rate. The fluid EOS and evolving Biot porosity give an independent pressure and physical water inventory. The finest step gives 0.319% pressure error. Halving the step halves both the pressure error and physical mass defect; the separate mass-plus-buffer budget closes within 2 micrograms.
documents.s: Finite-density water in a sealed cell

documents.t: Motion. Unit cell with fixed side-normal motion and base. The top shortens at 0.01 m/s for 0.1 s; the mesh stays fixed and the inventory uses the implied bulk volume. Water and temperature. Every face is sealed, initial pressure is zero, and temperature stays at 273 K. Gravity is zero. Material. Saturated elasticity with evolving Eulerian Biot porosity and a constant-compressibility fluid EOS; no plasticity or recovery in this selected control.

Every file this example needs is in data/mass/. Run from that folder: # Compresses the sealed unit cell for 0.1 s in 4,000 steps and saves its pressure, physical water inventory and numerical buffer. dynearthsol2d input.cfg

2D unit cell, 0.01/s logarithmic compression to 0.1 s, 4,000 physical steps. (a) DES and the implicit sealed-cell solution; (b) physical water-mass residual and the split-coupling correction. The temporal table retains 1,000 and 2,000 steps. The stabilised split conserves M+R. R is a numerical lag, contributes no density or heat capacity, and must not be described as physical water. Native/HDF5, 3D, restart, remap, source and transport controls are supporting evidence. documents.t: θ=T−T0​V=V0​eεv​ρ=ρ0​ep/Kf​−αf​θϕ=α−(α−ϕ0​)e−εv​−p/Ks​+αs​θ+hM=VρϕM(p∗​,T,εv​)=M0​Ln​=ρn​Vn​α2/BRn​=Ln​(pn+1​−pn​)Mn+1​+Rn​=Mn​+Rn−1​B2D​=K+G/3B3D​=K εv​ is the tension-positive bulk strain interpreted as log volume in the inventory law; h is recovered pore dilation (zero here). α=0.98, ϕ0​=0.25, Kf​=100 MPa, Ks​=1 GPa, K=20 MPa, G=10 MPa and M0​=250 kg per metre thickness. R is an extensive numerical buffer, never physical mass.

Integrating constant fluid compressibility and expansivity gives the density law. Integrating the Eulerian porosity rate gives the displayed porosity. The sealed continuum reference is the monotone scalar root M=M0, evaluated independently in mass_reference.py. When fluid and grain moduli are equal, the implicit pressure has a closed form. The unequal-modulus reference shown here uses a bracketed root instead. p∗​=Kf​{lnαϕ0​eαf​θ+(α−ϕ0​)eαs​θ+h​−εv​} The fixed-stress pressure stabilizer leaves a separately recorded numerical mass increment. With sealed walls, physical M differs from M0 by minus R. Refining the physical timestep reduces this defect at first order; an exact M+R ledger alone does not establish exact physical mass conservation. Direct EOS and porosity integration; independent scalar root and step-refinement controls in mass_reference.py and check_mass.py.

Selected homogeneous isothermal prescribed-motion cell. The broader suite checks remapping and accepted-path spatial transport, but this figure does not establish finite-strain constitutive accuracy, unsaturated finite-density flow, buoyant hydrostatic balance or a full thermal energy equation.

A sudden load compresses a saturated column. Water drains through the top, the pressure falls and the column settles. Largest pressure error: 0.011% of the applied load; largest settlement error: 0.007% of the final drained settlement. At a glance Dimension 2D Build make ndims=2 from the poromechanics source (not yet merged; DynEarthSol #134) Inputs terzaghi.zip Reproduce with DynEarthSol 3774df0

Load and drainage. At t=0+ a compression P=100 kPa is applied; the top is drained, p=0. Constraints. Sides: zero normal displacement and zero normal water flux. Base: vertical displacement fixed, water flux zero. Initial state and comparison. Initially unloaded. The reference starts just after the instantaneous undrained load. Compare pressure and downward top settlement.

Every file this example needs is in terzaghi.zip. Run from that folder: # Runs the 10 m column on a 0.25 m mesh for 33600 steps of 0.25 s (8400 s, about 99% consolidated) and writes terzaghi.save.000000 to terzaghi.save.000007, one frame every 1200 s; frame 0 is the state before the load. dynearthsol2d input.cfg

Setting Value What it does here control.has_hydraulic_diffusion true turns on Darcy flow, so the excess pressure drains out through the top control.has_PT true solves the mechanics to equilibrium at every step with PT, so the sudden load is carried without elastic waves control.has_moving_mesh false keeps the mesh fixed (small strain); settlement is computed from the vertical strain, not from moved nodes control.gravity 0 no gravity: only the applied load creates pressure control.fixed_dt 0.25 physical time step sim.max_steps 33600 number of steps; with fixed_dt it sets the 8400 s simulated sim.output_step_interval 4800 writes a frame every 4800 steps (1200 s) bc.hbc_z1 1 type 1: the top is drained, pore pressure held at its initial value (0) bc.stress_bc_z1 3 type 3: a vertical traction is applied on the top bc.stress_val_z1 -1e5 the top load; negative is compression (100 kPa) bc.vbc_z0 1 fixes vertical motion of the base mat.bulk_modulus [1e7] drained bulk modulus K of the skeleton mat.shear_modulus [1e7] shear modulus G; with K it sets the constrained modulus K + 4G/3 mat.hydraulic_perm [1.03e-12] intrinsic permeability; with viscosity and storage it sets the consolidation coefficient c_v input.cfg holds all 39 settings that differ from DES’s defaults; dynearthsol2d -h lists every option with its default.

See Running the examples for output files, the Python reader and ParaView conversion. Field What to look at pore pressure nodal pressure; profiles against depth below the drained top are compared with the series in panel (a) strain element strain; the vertical component integrated over the column gives the top settlement in panel (b)

(a) Pressure profiles against depth below the drained top at several dimensionless times T_v: lines are the series solution, symbols are DES. (b) Settlement of the top against time over the full drainage: the line is the series solution, symbols are DES, and the dashed line is the final drained settlement. This checks fluid storage and elastic coupling together, through both pressure and settlement. It does not test a sudden load with GVS or large strain. Partial unloading and material regimes To reproduce the whole study behind this figure, from the DES source folder: python3 benchmarks/poromechanics/consolidation_refinement.py --output OUT/history-2d --dimensions 2 --spacings 1 0.5 0.25 --timesteps 1 0.5 0.25 --spatial-dt 0.25 --temporal-spacing 0.5 --duration 8400 --sample-interval 1200 --timeout 30000 python3 benchmarks/poromechanics/consolidation_refinement.py --output OUT/sanity-3d --dimensions 3 --spacings 1 0.5 0.25 --timesteps 1 0.5 0.25 --spatial-dt 0.25 --temporal-spacing 1 --duration 8400 --sample-interval 1200 --timeout 30000 The study’s full numbers: record.json.

documents.t: S0​=ϕ/Kf​+(α−ϕ)/Ks​,Hc​=K+4G/3,Sc​=S0​+α2/Hc​cv​=κ/(μSc​),km​=(2m+1)π/(2H),p0​=αP/(Hc​Sc​)p(d,t)=p0​m=0∑∞​(2m+1)π4sin(km​d)​exp(−cv​km2​t)δ(t)=Hc​PH​−Hc​αHp0​​m=0∑∞​[(2m+1)π]28exp(−cv​km2​t)​ Depth d runs downward from the drained top (0) to the base (H). P is positive compression and δ positive downward settlement; κ is intrinsic permeability, μ viscosity, ϕ porosity, and α the Biot coefficient. K, G, Kf​ and Ks​ are the drained bulk, shear, fluid and grain moduli.

Equilibrium makes the total vertical stress uniform: σzz​=−P. With tension-positive strain, Hc​εzz​−αp=−P. Substitute this strain into the fluid content ζ=αεzz​+S0​p. ζ=−αP/Hc​+Sc​pSc​pt​=(κ/μ)pdd​ Zero fluid-content change during the instantaneous load gives p0​. Thereafter p(0,t)=0 and ∂d​p(H,t)=0. The mixed-boundary eigenfunctions are sin(km​d); expanding the uniform initial pressure gives the coefficients above. Integrating compressive strain gives the settlement, including its instantaneous undrained part. δ(t)=−∫0H​ϵzz​dd=PH/Hc​−(α/Hc​)∫0H​p(d,t)dd The series and settlement follow directly from the stated one-dimensional Biot initial/boundary problem; evaluated in terzaghi_reference.py.

A separate 1 m × 1 m × 10 m confined column receives a sudden 100 kPa traction, with K=20 MPa, G=10 MPa, zero gravity, a fixed mesh, sealed sides/base and a drained top. Pressure and settlement use the same analytical series at each saved frame's actual time. PT1 uses a 1 s physical interval; shear-ceiling GVS uses scaling 105, an initial velocity scale of 10−5 m/s, fixed_dt=0 and dt_fraction=0.5. Method h (m) Late pressure / load error Late settlement / drained settlement Final free-node force / total load PT1 1 0.4915% 0.1679% 9.62×10−9 PT1 0.5 0.1706% 0.1011% 5.39×10−9 GVS shear 1 0.8916% 0.1551% 5.00×10−7 GVS shear 0.5 0.2196% 0.03967% 2.51×10−7 Late means 200–400 s; the drainage time is 2,933.74 s. Over the entire saved 40–400 s window, fine-grid pressure errors are 0.8685% (GVS) and 0.8417% (PT1). Halving the mesh also changes the automatic GVS step, so this is combined mesh/step evidence. The coarse eleven-case matrix covers PT0/PT1, ordinary explicit and both GVS ceilings at scalings 104–106. All finish, but ordinary explicit at 104 retains 2.086% late pressure error and force/load 0.01245. This does not qualify cold starts, a full 3D drainage history, Mandel/Cryer with GVS, or earthquake cycles. From a complete DES checkout, reproduce the fine comparison with: python3 benchmarks/poromechanics/mechanical_methods.py OUT \ --dimension 3 --executable ./dynearthsol3d --spacing .5 --duration 400 \ --dt-fraction .5 --pt-dt 1 --initial-speeds 1e-5 --scalings 1e5 \ --methods pt1 gvs-shear --timeout 600 --max-steps 10000000

Small-strain, homogeneous, saturated, laterally confined elasticity; constant properties, no gravity or heating. Frame 0 is written before the load is applied and is not compared. This example uses the PT solver; a sudden load with GVS is not tested here.

A small initial velocity sets a sealed saturated column oscillating; compression raises the pressure and expansion lowers it. Largest velocity error: 0.171% and largest pressure error: 0.262% of their amplitudes, over all nodes and 65 saved times. At a glance Dimension 3D Build make ndims=3 from the poromechanics source (not yet merged; DynEarthSol #134) Inputs wave.zip Reproduce with DynEarthSol 3774df0
documents.s: Undrained wave in a sealed column

documents.t: Water and displacement boundaries. All water boundaries sealed; κ = 0 throughout. End vertical displacement and side-normal displacement fixed. Initial disturbance. vz​(z,0)=Vsin[π(z+H)/H], V=10−6 m/s. Initially zero pressure, stress and strain. Physical regime and comparison. Physical mixture density; no gravity, damping, heating, PT or GVS. Compare velocity and pressure over one period.

Every file this example needs is in wave.zip. Run from that folder: # 3D. Restarts from the shipped checkpoint seed, frame 0: the column mesh with zero stress, strain and pressure and the initial sine velocity (listed in initial-velocity.csv). Runs 8192 explicit steps, one wave period, saving every 128th step as wave.* and writing a checkpoint at every saved frame. dynearthsol3d input.cfg

Setting Value What it does here sim.is_restarting true starts from the seed checkpoint, which holds the initial velocity; an input file cannot set an initial velocity, so undrained_wave.py writes it into the seed frame sim.restarting_from_modelname seed the checkpoint to start from: seed (shipped) control.is_quasi_static false dynamic run with physical (unscaled) mass, so inertial_scaling has no effect control.damping_option 0 no damping: the wave keeps its amplitude control.fixed_dt 1.4182426918901539e-07 one wave period divided by 8192 sim.max_steps 8192 8192 steps: exactly one period sim.output_step_interval 128 a frame every 128 steps: 65 saved times over the period mat.hydraulic_perm [0] zero permeability: no flow, so each point stays undrained control.has_hydraulic_diffusion true solves the pore-pressure equation; with zero permeability the pressure follows the volume change only bc.vbc_z0 1 with vbc_z1: the ends cannot move vertically; vbc_y0, vbc_y1 and the default vbc_x0, vbc_x1 fix the side-normal motion control.gravity 0 no gravity: the column is unstressed apart from the wave mesh.meshing_elem_shape 1 regular structured mesh of the 0.025 × 0.025 × 1 m column mat.bulk_modulus [10000000.0] with shear_modulus, porosity and the fluid and grain moduli, sets the undrained modulus and the wave speed control.has_moving_mesh false fixed geometry: small-strain wave input.cfg holds all 50 settings that differ from DES’s defaults; dynearthsol3d -h lists every option with its default.

See Running the examples for output files, the Python reader and ParaView conversion. Field What to look at velocity vertical component at the node nearest mid-height, normalized by the initial amplitude V, in (a); maximum error over all nodes in the result pore pressure at the base node, normalized by the pressure amplitude, in (b); maximum error over all nodes in the result strain volumetric strain, combined with the pressure to check that the local fluid content stays zero

(a) Vertical velocity at mid-height over one period, normalized by the initial amplitude V: line, eigenmode solution; symbols, DES saved frames. (b) Pore pressure at the sealed base over the same period, normalized by the pressure amplitude. This checks fluid storage and elastic wave coupling together; local fluid content is conserved to round-off. It does not test a GVS earthquake cycle. To reproduce the whole study behind this figure, from the DES source folder: python3 benchmarks/poromechanics/undrained_wave.py dynearthsol3d OUT --spacing .0125 --steps 1024 2048 4096 8192 --samples 64 --restart-check python3 benchmarks/poromechanics/undrained_wave.py dynearthsol3d OUT-h005 --spacing .05 --steps 4096 --samples 32 python3 benchmarks/poromechanics/undrained_wave.py dynearthsol3d OUT-h0025 --spacing .025 --steps 4096 --samples 32 The study’s full numbers: record.json.

documents.t: S0​=ϕ/Kf​+(α−ϕ)/Ks​,Hu​=K+4G/3+α2/S0​,ρb​=(1−ϕ)ρs​+ϕρf​cu​=Hu​/ρb​​,k=π/H,ω=kcu​,T=2H/cu​vz​=Vsin[k(z+H)]cos(ωt),ϵzz​=(V/cu​)cos[k(z+H)]sin(ωt)p=−S0​cu​αV​cos[k(z+H)]sin(ωt),σzz​=Hu​ϵzz​ z is the DES coordinate, −H at the base and 0 at the top. V is the initial velocity amplitude, ρb​ physical mixture density, Hu​ the undrained constrained modulus and T the wave period. The selected material gives T≃1.162 ms.

Sealed local fluid content remains zero because it starts at zero. Eliminate pressure from the uniaxial effective-stress relation, giving an undrained modulus in the momentum equation. ζ=αϵzz​+S0​p=0,σzz​=Hu​ϵzz​,ρb​utt​=Hu​uzz​ The fundamental sine mode vanishes at both fixed ends. Choose its amplitude to match the initial velocity V and differentiate displacement for strain; the zero-content relation then gives pressure. uz​=(V/ω)sin[k(z+H)]sin(ωt) Direct eigenmode solution of the stated sealed one-dimensional Biot wave problem; evaluated in undrained_wave.py.

A separate restart control switches a nonzero coupled state after 32 accepted steps. The unit column has a fixed base, side-normal rollers, sealed water boundaries and a constant −1 kPa top traction. Internal Darcy flow remains active. Ordinary explicit and both GVS ceilings are checked at scalings 104, 105 and 106, in 2D/3D native and HDF5 output. Both phases use strain-driven pressure ordering; this does not convert a nonzero PT pending-pressure history. The physical phase sets is_quasi_static=false, use_global_velocity_scaling=false and the neutral mass_scaling_reference_speed=shear. The independent mixture density is 2237.5 kg/m³. Minimum-simplex-altitude and undrained-wave calculations predict first physical intervals of 42.8985 µs (2D) and 35.0265 µs (3D). Every free velocity component checks the mass actually used: vi,n+1​−vi,n​=ρb​Vi​Δt​Fi,n+1​. Across the recorded 36 cases, the largest relative identity error is 4.23×10−16. Stress, strain, pressure and velocity are preserved at the switch; the reselected mass and timestep change deliberately. The closed Biot-content residual is at most 2.27×10−16 of its stored/deformation scale. A further physical restart preserves the continuation fields exactly. At unchanged velocity, physical kinetic energy is continuous. Report the change in artificial kinetic energy separately: ΔKnum​=21​i∑​(mi,physical​−mi,artificial​)∣vi​∣2. The switch neither rescales velocity nor deposits that numerical energy change as heat. Full mechanical/thermal work, event-trigger hysteresis, RSF coseismic paths and complete earthquake-cycle transitions are outside this control. Reproduce it from the DES checkout with python3 tests/functional/check_inertia_switch.py ./dynearthsol2d OUT; repeat with the 3D executable and a separate output folder.

documents.t: The standing-wave comparison uses linear small-strain, homogeneous, completely sealed, zero-permeability elasticity. The input file sets inertial_scaling, but with is_quasi_static = false DES uses the physical (unscaled) mass, so the value has no effect. This wave is a dynamic coupling check and does not establish earthquake-cycle or GVS equilibrium accuracy.

From the DES source folder: make ndims=2 # dynearthsol2d make ndims=3 # dynearthsol3d Put the executables on your PATH, or call them with their full path. For the Python reader and ParaView converter, set the source-folder path: export DES_SOURCE=/path/to/DynEarthSol export PYTHONPATH="$DES_SOURCE${PYTHONPATH:+:$PYTHONPATH}"

Each example's files come in one zip, linked in its At a glance box: input.cfg, and any mesh (.poly) or restart frames (.save, .chkpt, .info) it starts from. Unpack it somewhere writable and run the commands given in the example's "Input and how to run" section, for instance mkdir -p ~/runs && cd ~/runs unzip theis.zip cd theis export OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 dynearthsol3d input.cfg dynearthsol2d -h lists every input option with its default and meaning. Each page lists the settings that define its example.

DES names its output after sim.modelname: <model>.info lists the saved frames (frame, step, time in seconds), <model>.save.NNNNNN holds the fields of each frame and <model>.chkpt.NNNNNN the restart checkpoints. sim.output_step_interval and sim.output_time_interval_in_yr control the saved-frame cadence. HDF5 builds use the .vtkhdf suffix. import sys; sys.path.append('/path/to/DynEarthSol') from Dynearthsol import Dynearthsol model = Dynearthsol('theis') p = model.read_field(model.frames[-1], 'pore pressure') python3 "$DES_SOURCE/2vtk.py" <model> converts the frames for ParaView; add -g for a run that restarted from another, to include the frames before the restart.

The ZIPs link Python runners and references in the complete DES checkout at the stated revision. They contain inputs and dependencies, without source code copies. Each page names the script that ran the whole study behind its figure (all meshes and time steps). The scripts are in benchmarks/poromechanics/ and tests/functional/hydromechanics/. The Reproduce with row names the public source to build. Figures reuse recorded runs; their downloadable records preserve the measured executable and data hashes. The version manifest records the regression comparisons used to check the integrated source.

A constant inflow from the top produces a steady suction profile above a water table at the base. The Brooks–Corey law stays saturated up to its air-entry suction, so the profile has a kink where desaturation begins. Largest pressure error: 18.84 Pa, 1.69% of the profile range. At a glance Dimension 2D Build make ndims=2 from the poromechanics source (not yet merged; DynEarthSol #134) Inputs bc.zip Reproduce with DynEarthSol 3774df0

Water boundaries. Constant downward inflow I=1.38889×10−6 m/s at the top. Base pressure zero; sides sealed. Air entry. Pressure-based αp​=10−3 Pa−1, n=1.5 and Sr​=0.05. The material stays saturated down to p=−1/αp​=−1000 Pa. Mechanical conditions and comparison. Side-normal displacement and base vertical displacement fixed; traction-free top. Start hydrostatic and compare steady pressure, including the air-entry transition.

Every file this example needs is in bc.zip. Run from that folder: # Runs the 2D column with fixed 300 s steps for about 23 days (2e6 s), long enough to reach the steady profile. DES writes column.save.* at the start, halfway and at the end; the page compares the last frame. dynearthsol2d input.cfg

Setting Value What it does here control.has_hydraulic_diffusion true turns on Darcy flow, here partly saturated (Richards) flow control.has_PT true PT solver: mechanical equilibrium is reached by iteration within each step control.gravity 9.81 gravity drives the downward flow and sets the hydrostatic start sim.max_time_in_yr 0.06337752907015713 yr = 2e+06 s about 2e6 s in fixed 300 s steps, long enough for the column to reach steady state bc.hbc_z0 2 type 2: the base is held at the pressure in bc.hbc_pressure, here 0, the water table bc.hbc_z1 3 type 3: the top has the prescribed flux in bc.hbc_flux bc.hbc_flux [0,0,0,0,0,-1.388888888888889e-06] outward Darcy flux per face; the top value −1.389e-6 m/s is an inflow of half the saturated conductivity ic.water_table_z -1.0 starts hydrostatic with the water table at the base (z = −1 m) mat.retention_model [2] 2: Brooks–Corey retention with Burdine relative permeability mat.retention_alpha [1e-3] α_p = 1e-3 1/Pa: the soil stays saturated down to the air-entry pressure −1/α_p = −1000 Pa mat.retention_n [1.5] Brooks–Corey pore-size index 1.5 mat.residual_saturation [0.05] residual saturation S_r = 0.05 mat.fluid_bulk_modulus [40000.0] deliberately small (4e4 Pa) to allow a larger stable flow step; storage does not affect the steady profile mat.hydraulic_perm [2.8372409106354064e-13] gives saturated conductivity K_s = 2.78e-6 m/s (1 cm/h) input.cfg holds all 54 settings that differ from DES’s defaults; dynearthsol2d -h lists every option with its default.

See Running the examples for output files, the Python reader and ParaView conversion. Field What to look at pore pressure the steady pressure profile at the last frame, compared with the reference coordinate the height of each node above the base

Steady pressure (kPa) against height above the water table at the end of the run: DES nodes (circles) and the steady-infiltration reference for the Brooks–Corey law (line). The profile bends where the soil starts to desaturate at the air-entry pressure. This checks the retention-dependent conductivity and the flux boundary. It does not test transient storage or coupled slope behaviour. I is positive downward infiltration, Ks​=κρf​g/μ saturated hydraulic conductivity and J=0.5. In the saturated zone p=−γ(1−J)z; air entry occurs at zentry​=1/[αp​γ(1−J)]≃0.204 m.

At steady state qz​=−I is constant. Darcy flow with z upward includes both pressure and gravity. Rearranging and separating variables gives the integral shown above, starting from p=0 at z=0. −I=−μκkr​(p)​(pz​+γ),dz=−γ[kr​(p)−J]kr​(p)​dp For 0<J<1 the pressure decreases with elevation toward the suction at which kr​=J. The integral diverges at that limiting pressure. Storage and elastic compressibility do not enter this steady relation. The analytical relation is evaluated with an independent high-accuracy ODE solver; no DES output or fitting parameter is used. Derived from steady Darcy flow, with the saturated segment treated as part of the same pressure-dependent law; evaluated in unsaturated_reference.py.

The steady relation is implicit and its unsaturated part is evaluated numerically, rather than treated as a closed-form profile. This test checks the conductivity and air-entry transition. The fluid modulus is deliberately reduced to shorten the run; it does not alter the steady reference and does not qualify transient storage.

The water table under a laterally confined elastic column drops. Above it the soil drains; suction weighted by the effective saturation tightens the skeleton, and the drained soil becomes lighter. Largest settlement error on the 0.25 m mesh, relative to the top settlement: 0.040% in 2D and 0.041% in 3D for the van Genuchten, Brooks–Corey and Gardner laws; 0.158% and 0.172% for the column with two laws, where saturation jumps at the shared interface nodes. At a glance Dimension 2D Build make ndims=2 from the poromechanics source (not yet merged; DynEarthSol #134) Inputs bishop.zip Reproduce with DynEarthSol 3774df0
documents.s: Bishop effective stress: lowering the water table

documents.t: Column and loading. A laterally confined elastic column, 0≤z≤H with H=10 m, starts drained and at rest with a hydrostatic water table at z0​=9 m. The base pressure is then lowered to that of a table at z1​=5 m; the sealed top and sides let the column drain to the new hydrostatic state. Mechanics. Side-normal and base displacements are fixed; the top is traction-free. Gravity acts on the partly saturated bulk weight. The PT solver keeps mechanical equilibrium, with pressure feedback on. What is compared. The change in vertical displacement between the two drained states, integrated from the element strains, against the exact solution. Three retention laws are run, and a column with van Genuchten below z=7 m and Gardner above, so interface nodes are shared by two laws.

Every file this example needs is in bishop.zip. Run from that folder: # Runs the 10 m column with the van Genuchten law: 40 steps of 1e4 s. The base pressure is lowered between steps 4 and 5 and the column then drains. DES writes bishop.save.* every 4 steps; the page compares frame 1 (drained start) with the last frame. For the other laws set mat.retention_model to 2 (retention_alpha 1e-4, retention_n 0.8, residual_saturation 0.05) or 3 (retention_alpha 5.097e-5, residual_saturation 0). dynearthsol2d input.cfg

Setting Value What it does here control.has_PT true PT solver: mechanical equilibrium is reached by iteration within each step, with pressure feedback on control.gravity 9.81 gravity acts on the partly saturated bulk weight and sets the hydrostatic water table control.fixed_dt 10000.0 steps of 1e4 s, long enough for the column to drain to the new state well within the run sim.output_step_interval 4 a frame every 4 steps; frame 1 is the drained start just before the base pressure drops bc.hbc_z0 2 type 2: the base pressure is prescribed by bc.hbc_pressure and the schedule; the other faces are sealed bc.hbc_pressure [0,0,0,0,88290.0,0] base pressure 88,290 Pa = ρ_f g × 9 m, a water table 9 m above the base bc.hbc_schedule_time_in_yr [0, 0.0012675505814031427, 0.0015844382267539284] yr = [0, 40000, 50000] s the schedule holds the base pressure until step 4 and changes it by step 5 bc.hbc_schedule_ratio [1, 1, 0.5555555555555556] multipliers 1, 1, 5/9: the base pressure falls to that of a water table at 5 m ic.water_table_z -1.0 initial hydrostatic water table 1 m below the top (z = −1 m), i.e. 9 m above the base mat.bulk_modulus [20000000.0] drained bulk modulus K = 2e7 Pa (shear modulus 1e7 Pa) of the elastic skeleton mat.biot_coeff [0.9] Biot coefficient α = 0.9 mat.retention_model [1] 1: van Genuchten with retention_alpha 5e-5 1/Pa, retention_n 1.6 and residual_saturation 0.1; Bishop χ = S_e mat.fluid_bulk_modulus [100000.0] deliberately small (1e5 Pa) to allow a larger stable flow step; the drained end states do not depend on it mat.hydraulic_perm [1e-10] high permeability (1e-10 m²) so that the column drains quickly input.cfg holds all 61 settings that differ from DES’s defaults; dynearthsol2d -h lists every option with its default.

See Running the examples for output files, the Python reader and ParaView conversion. Field What to look at strain vertical strain of each element; its change between the two drained frames, integrated up from the fixed base, gives the settlement u_z pore pressure checks that the final state is drained to the new hydrostatic profile coordinate node heights for the profiles connectivity assigns element strains to the layers of the column

(a) Settlement u_z (mm) between the two drained states against height z, for the van Genuchten, Brooks–Corey and Gardner laws and the column with two laws: DES (circles, integrated from the element strains) and the exact solution (lines). The dotted lines mark the initial and final water tables. (b) Change of vertical strain against height, same key. (c) Maximum settlement error relative to the largest settlement, against mesh spacing: 2D as lines with circles, 3D as open squares, and a slope-2 guide. This checks the Bishop coupling: the effective-stress increment from each element's own retention law, including nodes shared by two laws, and gravity on the partly saturated bulk weight. Drained end states do not test the transient or the coupling term in the flow equation. To reproduce the whole study behind this figure, from the DES source folder: python3 tests/functional/hydromechanics/check_bishop_column.py dynearthsol2d OUT --spacings 1 0.5 0.25 python3 tests/functional/hydromechanics/check_bishop_column.py dynearthsol3d OUT3D --ndims 3 --spacings 1 0.5 0.25 The study’s full numbers: record.json.

documents.t: σ′=σ+αSe​(p)pχ=Se​ρ=ρs​(1−ϕ)+ρf​ϕSS=Sr​+(1−Sr​)Se​pk​(z)=−ρf​g(z−zk​)Δπ=Se​(p1​)p1​−Se​(p0​)p0​Δσzz​(z)=−ρf​gϕ(1−Sr​)∫zH​ΔSe​dz′uz​(z)=K+4G/31​[α∫0z​Δπdz′−ρf​gϕ(1−Sr​)∫0H​min(z′,z)ΔSe​dz′] Pressure p is compression positive and suction is −p; stress is tension positive. Se​ is the effective saturation of the van Genuchten, Brooks–Corey or Gardner law and S the saturation. The runs use ϕ=0.4, α=0.9, K=2×107 Pa, G=107 Pa, ρf​=1000 kg/m3, and retention αp​=1/(2×104) Pa−1, n=1.6, Sr​=0.1 (van Genuchten); 1/104 Pa−1, λ=0.8, Sr​=0.05 (Brooks–Corey); 0.5/(ρf​g) Pa−1 (Gardner).

Laterally confined uniaxial strain gives εzz​=(Δσzz​+αΔπ)/(K+4G/3). Vertical equilibrium with the changed bulk weight and a traction-free top gives the total stress change as the weight lost above z. dzdΔσzz​​=ρf​gϕΔSΔσzz​(H)=0 Integrating the strain from the fixed base and exchanging the order of integration in the weight term gives uz​(z) above. The saturated limit is the classical uz​=αΔpz/(K+4G/3). Bishop (1959); Lu, Godt and Wu (2010), χ=Se​. Evaluated in unsaturated_reference.py, checked against closed forms, an independent double integral and reversibility; the two-law column is integrated numerically in check_bishop_column.py. Original reference.

Both states are drained and at rest, so storage and permeability do not enter; the pore fluid is made compressible only to allow a larger stable flow step, which shortens the drainage run. This checks the Bishop stress and the partly saturated weight, not the transient; the transient coupling is checked separately by a sealed cell against its exact ordinary differential equation. Small strain, linear elasticity, no hysteresis.

A sealed, partly saturated soil cell is compressed slowly. Without drainage, the pore pressure follows the strain through the Bishop rate equation. The fixed-stress coupling of the PT solver must recover it as the time step shrinks, including where the Bishop pressure Se​p decreases with suction. Largest pressure error at 320 steps: 1.43% (moderate suction) and 0.64% (strong suction) in 2D; the error halves with each halving of the step. Without the Bishop correction of the fixed-stress source the scheme does not converge: the error remains 78.89% and 67.62%. At a glance Dimension 2D Build make ndims=2 from the poromechanics source (not yet merged; DynEarthSol #134) Inputs bishop-cell.zip Reproduce with DynEarthSol 3774df0

documents.t: Cell and loading. A homogeneous block, 1 m high, of partly saturated Gardner soil at uniform suction is compressed uniaxially at a constant rate to a vertical strain of −10−3 over 1000 s. All faces are sealed and the permeability is negligible, so no water moves. Two states. Moderate suction, p0​=−5 kPa with αp​=10−4 Pa−1 (αp​s=0.5), where χΠ′>0; and strong suction, p0​=−2 kPa with αp​=10−3 Pa−1 (αp​s=2, strong relative to the retention scale), where the Bishop pressure Π=Se​p decreases with suction (Π′<0). The skeleton is soft, K=G=10 kPa, so the stabilising storage is large. What is compared. The mean pore pressure along each run’s own strain path, against the exact solution of the rate equation; PT at 10 to 320 steps and the explicit strain form, in 2D and 3D, and the same scheme without the correction.

Every file this example needs is in bishop-cell.zip. Run from that folder: # Runs the moderate-suction cell: 320 PT steps of 3.125 s compress the top by 1 mm over 1000 s. DES writes cell.save.* every 32 steps. For the strong-suction state set ic.pore_pressure_value = -2000 and mat.retention_alpha = [1e-3]. dynearthsol2d input.cfg

Setting Value What it does here control.has_PT true PT solver with the fixed-stress coupling whose Bishop correction is tested; pressure feedback is on control.gravity 0 no gravity, so the cell is uniform control.fixed_dt 3.125 3.125 s steps: 320 steps over the 1000 s loading sim.max_steps 320 320 steps, the finest step count of the study sim.output_step_interval 32 a frame every 32 steps (100 s) bc.vbc_z1 1 type 1: the top moves vertically at the velocity bc.vbc_val_z1 bc.vbc_val_z1 -1e-06 −1e-6 m/s: the top moves down 1 mm in 1000 s, a vertical strain of −1e-3; the other faces are held in their normal direction ic.pore_pressure_option 2 2: uniform initial pressure ic.pore_pressure_value -5000.0 initial pressure −5000 Pa (5 kPa suction) mat.retention_model [3] 3: Gardner exponential law (retention_alpha 1e-4 1/Pa, the default); Bishop χ = S_e mat.residual_saturation [0.1] residual saturation S_r = 0.1 mat.hydraulic_perm [1e-30] negligible permeability (1e-30 m²): no water moves, so the cell is undrained mat.bulk_modulus [10000.0] soft skeleton, K = 1e4 Pa, so the fixed-stress stabilising storage is large mat.shear_modulus [10000.0] G = 1e4 Pa input.cfg holds all 53 settings that differ from DES’s defaults; dynearthsol2d -h lists every option with its default.

See Running the examples for output files, the Python reader and ParaView conversion. Field What to look at pore pressure averaged over the cell at each frame and compared with the exact rate equation strain vertical strain averaged over the cell, the path along which the exact equation is integrated coordinate identifies the vertical axis

(a) Moderate and (b) strong suction: change of mean pore pressure p − p_0 against compression −ε_zz. Line: the exact rate equation along the run's own strain path. Circles: PT at the finest step, with the corrected fixed-stress source (coloured) and without the Bishop correction (grey). Squares: the explicit strain form. (c) Maximum error relative to the pressure change against the number of PT steps over the loading, for both states in 2D, in 3D and in 2D without the correction, with a slope −1 guide. This checks the transient Bishop coupling under PT: the fixed-stress source with its correction L(χE−D), built from the increments of the last mechanical step. It does not test flow, which the column pages cover, or large strain. To reproduce the whole study behind this figure, from the DES source folder: python3 tests/functional/hydromechanics/check_bishop_cell.py dynearthsol2d OUT --steps 10 20 40 80 160 320 --explicit python3 tests/functional/hydromechanics/check_bishop_cell.py dynearthsol3d OUT3D --ndims 3 --steps 10 20 40 80 160 python3 tests/functional/hydromechanics/check_bishop_cell.py dynearthsol2d OUT-restart --restart The study’s full numbers: record.json.

documents.t: (S0​+ϕ(1−Sr​)dpdSe​​)p˙​=−αχε˙v​χ=Se​Π=Se​pΠ′=Se​+pdpdSe​​L=α2/Kb​D=p−pold​​E=Π(p)−Π(pold​)​qFS​=Kb​ΔtαχΔσm​​+ΔtL(χE−D)​S0​Δp+ϕΔS=−αχΔεv​+L(D−Δp) S0​=ϕ/Kf​+(α−ϕ)/Ks​, Kb​ is the mean-stress modulus of the fixed-stress split, and the overbars are element means of the increments of the last physical step, already applied by the mechanical solve. qFS​ is the fixed-stress source per unit volume; the mechanical stress change Δσm​ already contains −αE.

Without flow, fluid content changes only by storage, desaturation and the Bishop-weighted skeleton strain, which gives the rate equation above. The fixed-stress source reads the stress change of the last mechanical step, Kb​Δε−αE, while the scheme stores S0​+L. (S0​+L)Δp+ϕΔS=−αχΔεv​+χLE (uncorrected) Adding L(χE−D) cancels the Bishop increment inside the stress change and leaves L(D−Δp), which vanishes as consecutive increments approach each other. Clipping χΠ′ at zero is not used: where Π′<0 it would converge to a different continuum. Bishop (1959); Lu, Godt and Wu (2010). The rate equation is integrated with a high-order ODE solver in check_bishop_cell.py; the correction follows the fixed-stress split of Kim, Tchelepi and Juanes (2011) with the Bishop increment. Original reference.

Sealed and homogeneous, so flow and spatial accuracy are not tested; the column pages cover them. The remaining PT error is the one-step lag L(D−Δp), first order in the step and weighted by the soft skeleton’s large L. Small strain, linear elasticity, no hysteresis.

A saturated sand column drains through its base: the top desaturates, pore pressure falls below zero and the column settles under the Bishop effective stress and its lighter weight, as in the Liakopoulos experiment. No closed form exists; an independent solver of the same continuum supplies the reference. Largest nodal pressure error on the 0.0125 m mesh with 480 steps at 5, 20, 60 and 120 min: 0.14 / 0.02 / 0.02 / 0.01% of ρf​gH; settlement 0.24 / 0.05 / 0.02 / 0.01%. With 960 steps: 0.07 / 0.02 / 0.01 / 0.01% and 0.12 / 0.03 / 0.01 / 0.01%. At a glance Dimension 2D Build make ndims=2 from the poromechanics source (not yet merged; DynEarthSol #134) Inputs drainage.zip Reproduce with DynEarthSol 3774df0
documents.s: Drainage of a saturated column into the unsaturated state

documents.t: Column. A laterally confined sand column H=1 m high, saturated and hydrostatic with the water table at its top. Top sealed and traction-free; base fixed. Drainage. At t=0+ the base is opened to p=0 (a 1 ms ramp of the scheduled boundary pressure). Water drains out, the top desaturates and suction develops. Material. After Liakopoulos: E=1.3 MPa, ν=0.4, α=1, ϕ=0.2975, k=4.5×10−13 m2; van Genuchten αvG​=1/3000 Pa−1, n=1.8, Sr​=0.1, Mualem permeability; Bishop χ=Se​. Gravity and pressure feedback (two-way coupling) are on. What is compared. Nodal pressure and the settlement of the top at 5, 20, 60 and 120 min against an independent solution of the same continuum.

Every file this example needs is in drainage.zip. Run from that folder: # Runs the 1 m column on the 0.0125 m mesh: 480 PT steps of 15 s, 2 h in all. The base pressure drops to 0 within the first millisecond and the column drains. DES writes drain.save.* every 20 steps (5 min). dynearthsol2d input.cfg

Setting Value What it does here control.has_PT true PT solver: mechanical equilibrium within each step, with two-way pressure feedback control.gravity 9.81 gravity drives the drainage and sets the hydrostatic start control.fixed_dt 15.0 15 s steps: 480 steps over 2 h sim.output_step_interval 20 a frame every 20 steps (5 min), which includes the compared times 5, 20, 60 and 120 min bc.hbc_z0 2 type 2: the base pressure is prescribed by bc.hbc_pressure and the schedule; the top and sides are sealed bc.hbc_pressure [0,0,0,0,9810.0,0] base pressure 9810 Pa, the hydrostatic value with the water table at the top (ic.water_table_z = 0, the default) bc.hbc_schedule_time_in_yr [0, 3.168876453507857e-11] yr = [0, 0.001] s schedule times 0 and 1 ms, in years bc.hbc_schedule_ratio [1, 0] multipliers 1 and 0: the base pressure ramps to 0 over the first millisecond, opening the base ic.has_body_force_adjustment true brings the column into mechanical equilibrium under gravity before the run mat.bulk_modulus [2166666.666666667] K = 2.17e6 Pa, from E = 1.3 MPa and ν = 0.4 mat.shear_modulus [464285.7142857143] G = 4.64e5 Pa, from E = 1.3 MPa and ν = 0.4 mat.porosity [0.2975] φ = 0.2975, the Liakopoulos sand mat.hydraulic_perm [4.5e-13] intrinsic permeability 4.5e-13 m² mat.retention_model [1] 1: van Genuchten–Mualem, with retention_alpha 1/3000 1/Pa, retention_n 1.8 and residual_saturation 0.1; Bishop χ = S_e input.cfg holds all 59 settings that differ from DES’s defaults; dynearthsol2d -h lists every option with its default.

See Running the examples for output files, the Python reader and ParaView conversion. Field What to look at pore pressure pressure profiles at 5, 20, 60 and 120 min, compared with the reference strain vertical element strain; its change since frame 0, summed up the column, gives the settlement of the top coordinate node heights connectivity assigns element strains to the layers of the column

(a) Pore pressure (kPa) against height at 5, 20, 60 and 120 min: DES nodes on one side of the column (circles) and the numerical reference (lines); the dotted line is the initial hydrostatic profile. (b) Settlement of the top against time on a log scale: DES at each saved frame (circles) and the reference (line). (c) Maximum pressure error relative to ρ_f g H against mesh spacing at the four times: circles for 480 steps, diamonds for 960 steps on the finest mesh, open squares for the explicit form. This checks Richards flow and the Bishop coupling together during drainage: desaturation, suction, the effective-stress change and the lighter weight of the drying column. To reproduce the whole study behind this figure, from the DES source folder: python3 benchmarks/poromechanics/drainage_reference.py python3 tests/functional/hydromechanics/check_unsaturated_drainage.py dynearthsol2d OUT --spacings 0.05 0.025 0.0125 python3 tests/functional/hydromechanics/check_unsaturated_drainage.py dynearthsol2d OUT-explicit --spacings 0.05 --explicit python3 tests/functional/hydromechanics/check_unsaturated_drainage.py dynearthsol2d OUT-steps960 --spacings 0.0125 --steps 960 The study’s full numbers: record.json.

c(p)pt​+αSe​ε˙=−∂z​qq=−μkkr​(Se​)​(∂z​p+ρf​g)ε˙=K+34​Gσ˙+αΠ′(p)pt​​Π=Se​pσ˙(z)=−gρf​ϕ(1−Sr​)∫zH​dpdSe​​pt​dz′ c(p) is the fluid storage including ϕdS/dp; ε the vertical strain, σ the total vertical stress, which changes only by the weight of the water that leaves the column above. kr​ is the Mualem relative permeability.

Uniaxial strain makes the vertical effective-stress change equal to the constrained modulus times the strain. The Bishop stress adds αΠ, and the total stress follows the weight, so drying above a point unloads it: the storage becomes nonlocal. drainage_reference.py integrates this system with vertex-centred finite volumes, the dense coupled storage matrix and an implicit BDF method. Grid differences fall at second order (5.2 to 1.3 Pa at 300 s on 100 and 200 cells, of a 9.8 kPa scale); the comparison uses 200 cells. Liakopoulos (1965) experiment as benchmarked by Schrefler and Zhan (1993), Water Resources Research 29(1), 155–167; reference computed independently in drainage_reference.py. Original reference.
No closed form: the reference is numerical. Uniaxial strain, small strain, constant porosity, no hysteresis. The base opens instantly, so the first minutes are limited by the step.

Water infiltrates a partly saturated column from the top while the base stays at the water table. Largest error in K/Ks​: 0.714% at 7230 s and 2.52% over all saved times. At a glance Dimension 3D Build make ndims=3 from the poromechanics source (not yet merged; DynEarthSol #134) Inputs gardner.zip Reproduce with DynEarthSol 3774df0

Water boundaries. Constant downward inflow starts at the top at t = 0. Base pressure is zero; all side faces are sealed. Initial profile and gravity. Hydrostatic initial pressure p=−ρf​gz, with elevation z above the base. Gravity points downward. Mechanical conditions. Side-normal displacement and base vertical displacement fixed; traction-free top. Compare K/Ks derived from pressure. Bishop coupling is not tested here (see the Bishop pages).

Every file this example needs is in gardner.zip. Run from that folder: # Runs the 3D column for 2 h (7200 s) in fixed 30 s steps after the top inflow starts. DES writes column.save.* every 30 min; the page shows the last frame and checks all of them. dynearthsol3d input.cfg

Setting Value What it does here control.has_hydraulic_diffusion true turns on Darcy flow, here partly saturated (Richards) flow control.has_PT true PT solver: mechanical equilibrium is reached by iteration within each step control.gravity 9.81 gravity drives the downward flow and sets the hydrostatic start control.fixed_dt 30.0 fixed 30 s steps sim.max_time_in_yr 0.0002281591046525657 yr = 7200 s 7200 s (2 h) of infiltration sim.output_time_interval_in_yr 5.703977616314142e-05 yr = 1800 s a frame every 1800 s (30 min) bc.hbc_z0 2 type 2: the base is held at the pressure in bc.hbc_pressure, here 0, the water table bc.hbc_z1 3 type 3: the top has the prescribed flux in bc.hbc_flux bc.hbc_flux [0,0,0,0,0,-2.5e-06] outward Darcy flux per face; the top value −2.5e-6 m/s is an inflow of 0.9 K_s, starting at t = 0 ic.water_table_z -1.0 starts hydrostatic with the water table at the base (z = −1 m) mat.retention_model [3] 3: Gardner exponential law, S_e = k_r = exp(α_p p) mat.retention_alpha [0.0010193679918450561] α_p = 1.019e-3 1/Pa, i.e. 0.1 per cm of head mat.porosity [0.4] 0.4; with zero residual saturation the water content can change by Δθ = 0.4 mat.hydraulic_perm [2.8372409106354064e-13] gives saturated conductivity K_s = 2.78e-6 m/s (1 cm/h) input.cfg holds all 51 settings that differ from DES’s defaults; dynearthsol3d -h lists every option with its default.

See Running the examples for output files, the Python reader and ParaView conversion. Field What to look at pore pressure converted to K/K_s = exp(α_p p) at every node and compared with the series solution coordinate the height of each node above the base

Relative conductivity K/K_s = exp(α_p p), computed from the DES pore pressure (circles), against the Srivastava–Yeh series (line) along the column at the end of the run (7200 s). This checks conservative unsaturated flow against an independent transient solution. It does not test Bishop effective stress. documents.t: w=Se​=kr​=exp(αp​p),A=αp​ρf​g,Z=Az,L=AH,T=AKs​t/Δθwb​(Z)=b+(1−b)e−Z,a=Ia​/Ks​,b=Ib​/Ks​,Δθ=ϕ(1−Sr​)Fn​=1+L/2+2λn2​Lsin(λn​Z)sin(λn​L)e−λn2​T​w=wb​−4(b−a)e(L−Z)/2−T/4n=1∑∞​Fn​sin(λn​L)+2λn​cos(λn​L)=0p=log(w)/αp​ Ks​=κρf​g/μ is saturated hydraulic conductivity. αp​ is the pressure retention coefficient in Pa−1 and A its head-based value in m−1. Here A=10 m−1, Ia​=0, Ib​=2.5×10−6 m/s, Ks​=2.77778×10−6 m/s, ϕ=0.4 and Sr​=0. λn​ is the positive root in ((n−1/2)π/L,nπ/L).

For unsaturated p≤0, θ=θr​+Δθw and the upward water flux is qz​=−Ks​(wz​/A+w). Substitution into θt​+∂z​qz​=0 and nondimensionalization give a linear drift-diffusion equation. wT​=wZZ​+wZ​,w(0,T)=1,wZ​(L,T)+w(L,T)=b Before the flux change the column is at wa​=a+(1−a)e−Z. Subtract the new steady solution wb and remove the drift. Separation of variables gives a sine series and the Robin eigenvalue equation; projecting the initial difference supplies the coefficient in the reference above. w−wb​=e−Z/2−T/4f,fT​=fZZ​,f(0,T)=0,fZ​(L,T)+f(L,T)/2=0 Srivastava and Yeh (1991), homogeneous-column solution; evaluated in unsaturated_reference.py. The reference implementation is independently checked against a matrix exponential. Original reference.

This exact series solves ideal Gardner Richards flow with retention storage only. DES also retains elastic/compressible storage, so it is a reference-limit comparison, not an exact solution of every active DES term. The displayed error includes that model difference. It does not validate ponding or a seepage-face switch.

A constant inflow from the top produces a steady suction profile above a water table at the base. The van Genuchten law has no air-entry pressure, so the soil desaturates as soon as the pressure falls below zero. Largest pressure error: 5.69 Pa, 0.96% of the profile range. At a glance Dimension 2D Build make ndims=2 from the poromechanics source (not yet merged; DynEarthSol #134) Inputs vg.zip Reproduce with DynEarthSol 3774df0

Water boundaries. Constant downward inflow I=1.38889×10−6 m/s at the top. Base pressure zero; sides sealed. Retention law. Pressure-based αp​=5×10−4 Pa−1, n=2, residual saturation Sr​=0.1. Gravity points downward. Mechanical conditions and comparison. Side-normal displacement and base vertical displacement fixed; traction-free top. Start hydrostatic and compare the final steady pressure profile.

Every file this example needs is in vg.zip. Run from that folder: # Runs the 2D column with fixed 300 s steps for about 23 days (2e6 s), long enough to reach the steady profile. DES writes column.save.* at the start, halfway and at the end; the page compares the last frame. dynearthsol2d input.cfg

Setting Value What it does here control.has_hydraulic_diffusion true turns on Darcy flow, here partly saturated (Richards) flow control.has_PT true PT solver: mechanical equilibrium is reached by iteration within each step control.gravity 9.81 gravity drives the downward flow and sets the hydrostatic start sim.max_time_in_yr 0.06337752907015713 yr = 2e+06 s about 2e6 s in fixed 300 s steps, long enough for the column to reach steady state sim.output_time_interval_in_yr 0.031688764535078566 yr = 1e+06 s a frame halfway and one at the end bc.hbc_z0 2 type 2: the base is held at the pressure in bc.hbc_pressure, here 0, the water table bc.hbc_z1 3 type 3: the top has the prescribed flux in bc.hbc_flux bc.hbc_flux [0,0,0,0,0,-1.388888888888889e-06] outward Darcy flux per face; the top value −1.389e-6 m/s is an inflow of half the saturated conductivity ic.water_table_z -1.0 starts hydrostatic with the water table at the base (z = −1 m) mat.retention_model [1] 1: van Genuchten retention with Mualem relative permeability (n is retention_n, default 2) mat.retention_alpha [5e-4] pressure-based retention parameter α_p = 5e-4 1/Pa mat.residual_saturation [0.1] residual saturation S_r = 0.1 mat.fluid_bulk_modulus [40000.0] deliberately small (4e4 Pa) to allow a larger stable flow step; storage does not affect the steady profile mat.hydraulic_perm [2.8372409106354064e-13] gives saturated conductivity K_s = 2.78e-6 m/s (1 cm/h) input.cfg holds all 53 settings that differ from DES’s defaults; dynearthsol2d -h lists every option with its default.
