documents.t: s=max(−p,0),m=1−1/n,Se​=[1+(αp​s)n]−m,S=Sr​+(1−Sr​)Se​kr​=Se1/2​[1−(1−Se1/m​)m]2J=I/Ks​,γ=ρf​g,dzdp​=γ(kr​(p)J​−1),p(0)=0z=γ1​∫p(z)0​kr​(ξ)−Jkr​(ξ)​dξ Elevation z runs upward from the water-table base. I is positive downward infiltration, Ks​=κρf​g/μ saturated hydraulic conductivity, J=0.5 and γ=9810 Pa/m. The integral is an implicit analytical relation, evaluated by high-accuracy integration of its equivalent first-order ODE.

At steady state qz​=−I is constant. Darcy flow with z upward includes both pressure and gravity. Rearranging and separating variables gives the integral shown above, starting from p=0 at z=0. −I=−μκkr​(p)​(pz​+γ),dz=−γ[kr​(p)−J]kr​(p)​dp For 0<J<1 the pressure decreases with elevation toward the suction at which kr​=J. The integral diverges at that limiting pressure. Storage and elastic compressibility do not enter this steady relation. The analytical relation is evaluated with an independent high-accuracy ODE solver; no DES output or fitting parameter is used. The implicit relation is derived from steady Darcy flow; evaluated by DOP853 (rtol 10⁻¹², atol 10⁻⁹ Pa) in unsaturated_reference.py.

Homogeneous, steady one-dimensional flow, constant gravity and prescribed flux. This is not a closed-form pressure profile. Storage drops out of the steady equation; the deliberately reduced fluid modulus shortens the run (a larger stable flow step) and does not test transient storage.

Before you trust an earthquake-cycle model, check that DES reproduces the friction law itself. This benchmark shears a single square cell at a known rate. With every node velocity prescribed, there is no wave, localization or mesh effect, so the stress, friction and state can be compared directly with closed-form solutions. It runs in about half a minute. The benchmark covers four groups: Group Cases Varied Elastoplastic (static friction) 3 friction angle 10°, 20°, 30° Steady-state RSF (state_var_model = 0) 3 V0​=10−6,10−5,10−4 m/s Aging-law RSF (state_var_model = 1) 3 Dc​=10−3,3×10−3,10−2 m Healing at zero slip rate 1 – See rate-and-state friction for the equations used below. At a glance Dimension 2D Build make ndims=2 Run time about 30 s for all cases, one thread Inputs benchmarks/faults-friction/simple_shear_rsf/ in the DynEarthSol repository Checked with DynEarthSol 68cc2a0
documents.s: Checking the friction law in simple shear

documents.t: Figure 1. (a) The cell: two triangles in a 1 m square. The bottom nodes are fixed and the top nodes move at vx​=10−5 m/s. (b–d) Shear stress from DES (lines) and the reference (markers), with the relative error below each panel. The inset in (d) shows the state variable relative to its steady-state value. Setting Value Cell 1 m × 1 m, two triangles, plane strain Loading top moves at vx​=10−5 m/s; bottom fixed Bulk and shear moduli 200 MPa and 200 MPa Cohesion 1 MPa, no weakening; zero dilation; no gravity RSF parameters ϕ0​=30°, a=0.2, b=0.3 Slip-rate measure strain-rate invariant (control.rsf_slip_rate_projection_option = 1) Time step fixed, 0.01 s, 200,000 steps (2000 s, shear strain 0.02) The large a and b make the differences between cases easy to see. The cell deforms isochorically and without gravity, so the mean stress stays zero and the Mohr–Coulomb shear strength is τy​=ccosϕ with ϕ=arctanμ.

Stress. The cell loads elastically and then flows at its strength: τ(t)=min(GHvx​t​, ccos(arctanμ)), with μ=tan30° for the elastoplastic cases and the RSF friction coefficient otherwise. Slip rate. In the shearing two-triangle cell the strain-rate measure gives V(t)=(1−vx​t/H)2+1​vx​​, because the element width w changes as the cell shears. Steady state. μ=μ0​+(a−b)ln(V/V0​) at the current V. Aging law. With Φ(t)=∫0t​V/Dc​dt′, the aging law has the solution θ(t)=e−Φ(t)(θ0​+∫0t​eΦ(t′)dt′),θ0​=Dc​/V0​, which the reference evaluates by quadrature. The friction follows from the full law. Healing. A separate run holds the cell still for 1546 steps of three days (Dc​=10−2 m, V0​=4×10−9 m/s). The slip rate is then the 10−16 m/s floor and the state grows almost linearly with time, θ≈θ0​+t. The check iterates DES's discrete update independently.

Build dynearthsol2d in the DES root, then: cd benchmarks/faults-friction/simple_shear_rsf python3 run_simple_shear_benchmark.py --clean --aging-transient --healing python3 plot_simple_shear_benchmark.py -o simple_shear_benchmark.png The runner writes one input file per case from simple_shear_base.cfg, which holds placeholders for the values in the table above, and runs DES in runs/<case>/. --aging-transient adds three runs with dense monitor output for the inset in panel (d); --healing adds the zero-velocity run. Pass --exe /path/to/dynearthsol2d if the executable is elsewhere. For a pass/fail check without plotting: python3 check_simple_shear_benchmark.py # one steady, one aging, healing python3 check_simple_shear_benchmark.py --all # all nine cases and healing Add --pt to run the same cases with PT mechanics. The key RSF lines in a generated input are: [control] use_global_velocity_scaling = true rsf_slip_rate_projection_option = 1 fixed_dt = 0.01 [mat] rheology_type = elasto-plastic-rate-state-friction direct_a = [0.2] evolution_b = [0.3] characteristic_velocity = [1e-05] characteristic_distance = [0.001] state_var_model = 1 [monitor] enabled = yes num_points = 2 output_stress = yes output_dynamic_friction = yes output_state_variable = yes

Each runs/<case>/ holds the input, the DES output and two monitor files, monitor_point_0.csv and monitor_point_1.csv, one per element. Their columns include stress_0, stress_1, stress_2 (σxx, σzz, σxz), dynamic_friction and state_variable. The plot script compares the mean absolute shear stress of the two elements with the reference and writes simple_shear_benchmark_metrics.csv.

In every case DES follows the reference through loading, yield and flow. The largest difference over the run is about 0.001 % of the reference stress: Case Maximum error (%) Elastoplastic, φ = 30°, 20°, 10° 0.00091, 0.00106, 0.00116 Steady state, V0​ = 10⁻⁶, 10⁻⁵, 10⁻⁴ m/s 0.00105, 0.00089, 0.00072 Aging law, Dc​ = 10⁻³, 3×10⁻³, 10⁻² m 0.00089, 0.00089, 0.00091 The checker also recovers the slip rate DES used from the monitored friction and state; it matches V(t) to a relative error of 5×10−8. The healing run matches the discrete update exactly. Things to notice in the figure: Panel (b). A lower friction angle gives a higher strength here, because τy​=ccosϕ at zero mean stress. Friction only adds strength through normal stress, and this cell has none. Panel (c). With a−b<0, a larger V0​ means the cell slides slower relative to the reference rate, so the friction is higher and the strength ccosϕ lower. Panel (d). All three Dc​ values reach nearly the same stress, but the state approaches steady state more slowly for larger Dc​ (inset): the slip needed to renew the contacts is larger.

This benchmark checks the constitutive update in a homogeneous cell with prescribed motion. It does not test localization, wave propagation, mesh dependence or the coupling between slip and elastic unloading that controls earthquake nucleation. Under PT, the prescribed motion balances the forces at the first iteration, so the PT run checks the accepted constitutive history, not iterative convergence. The earthquake-cycle tutorial adds those effects.

A brittle crust pulled apart from a weak seed localizes into shear bands. This benchmark runs the same model three times, with static Mohr–Coulomb friction (EP) and with rate-and-state friction that is velocity strengthening or velocity weakening (EP-RSF). It asks two questions: does rate-and-state friction change where and at what angle the bands form, and does it change how they slip? The inputs are the DES v2 benchmark in benchmarks/geodynamics/localization/; see rate-and-state friction for the friction law and for global velocity scaling. At a glance Dimension 2D Build make ndims=2 Run time 35 minutes (EP), 75 minutes (weakening) and 3 hours (strengthening) on 8 threads Inputs benchmarks/geodynamics/localization/ in the DynEarthSol repository Results the benchmark results given in its README
documents.s: Shear bands with and without rate-and-state friction

documents.t: Setting Value Domain 20 km × 10 km, uniform triangles of 100 m (meshing_option = 1) Loading both sides pulled outward at 0.5 cm/yr each; free top; Winkler support at the base; gravity 10 m/s² Initial state lithostatic stress; a circular seed of radius 500 m centred at (10, −9.5) km starts with plastic strain 1 Elasticity and density K = 50 GPa, G = 30 GPa, 2700 kg/m³ Strength friction angle 30°, no dilation; cohesion softening from 30 to 0.1 MPa over plastic strain 0 to 0.5 Rate-and-state aging law, Dc​ = 5 mm, V0​=10−9 m/s, strain-rate slip measure (rsf_slip_rate_projection_option = 1), state limit rsf_dtheta_max = 0.2 Mechanics explicit, global velocity scaling with c=2×105, damping factor 0.8 Duration 12,000 years, a frame every 500 years The three inputs differ only in the friction law: Input Rheology a b a/b ep_phi30_psi0.cfg elasto-plastic – – – ep_rsf_strengthening_phi30_psi0.cfg elasto-plastic-rsf 0.018 0.015 1.2 ep_rsf_weakening_phi30_psi0.cfg elasto-plastic-rsf 0.003 0.015 0.2 For a Mohr–Coulomb material with friction angle ϕ and dilation angle ψ, the Arthur angle predicts bands at 45°+(ϕ+ψ)/4 from the direction of the least compressive stress, here 45°+30°/4=52.5° from the horizontal.

Build dynearthsol2d in the DES root, then run each input from the benchmark folder: cd benchmarks/geodynamics/localization mkdir -p output OMP_NUM_THREADS=8 ../../../dynearthsol2d ep_phi30_psi0.cfg OMP_NUM_THREADS=8 ../../../dynearthsol2d ep_rsf_strengthening_phi30_psi0.cfg OMP_NUM_THREADS=8 ../../../dynearthsol2d ep_rsf_weakening_phi30_psi0.cfg Each writes to output/ under its own name: frames <name>.save.*, checkpoints, <name>.info, and three monitor files, <name>_monitor_point_0.csv to _2.csv, recorded every 1000 steps. Point 1 starts at the seed centre; points 0 and 2 lie near the side walls.

All three models break the crust along a band that rises from the seed to the surface on the right, with a fainter conjugate band on the left. The band carries most of the extension; the rest of the crust stays elastic. Model Band dip (fit over 2–8 km) EP 52.4° EP-RSF, strengthening 54.5° EP-RSF, weakening 51.2° Arthur angle, 45°+(ϕ+ψ)/4 52.5° Rate-and-state friction moves the dip by about two degrees at most. The orientation is set by the Mohr–Coulomb strength, not by the rate dependence. Velocity strengthening steepens the band slightly; velocity weakening flattens it slightly. The dip is measured from the plastic strain gained since frame 0, so the initial seed does not count. In each 200 m depth row between 2 and 8 km, take the element with the largest gain on each side of the seed, keep it if the gain exceeds a quarter of the maximum, and fit a straight line through the points: import numpy as np from Dynearthsol import Dynearthsol des = Dynearthsol('output/ep_phi30_psi0') first, last = des.frames[0], des.frames[-1] x = des.read_field(last, 'coordinate')/1e3 # km c = des.read_field(last, 'connectivity') gain = des.read_field(last, 'plastic strain') - des.read_field(first, 'plastic strain') cen = x[c].mean(axis=1) zs, xs = [], [] for z0 in np.arange(-8.0, -2.0, 0.2): row = (cen[:, 0] >= 10) & (cen[:, 1] >= z0) & (cen[:, 1] < z0 + 0.2) i = np.argmax(np.where(row, gain, -np.inf)) if gain[i] > 0.25*gain.max(): zs.append(cen[i, 1]); xs.append(cen[i, 0]) slope = np.polyfit(zs, xs, 1)[0] print('dip', np.degrees(np.arctan(1/abs(slope)))) Run it from the benchmark folder with the DES root on PYTHONPATH. It gives the dips in the table to within 0.1°. Use cen[:, 0] < 10 for the band on the left; in these runs only the right band passes the threshold over the whole depth range.

The monitor at the seed (_monitor_point_1.csv) shows three different ways of slipping on almost the same band. The stress invariant is sqrt(0.25*(stress_0 - stress_1)**2 + stress_2**2) of the seed element. Loading is the same in all three. The stress rises linearly for about 4000 years while the crust deforms elastically. EP fails once, then slides. The stress peaks at 86 MPa at 4.1 kyr. At 5.0 kyr the band breaks through to the surface in one fast slip: the seed moves about 12 m at up to 5 cm/s. After that the band slides steadily at about 78 MPa. Velocity strengthening creeps. The stress peaks lower, at 79 MPa at 4.0 kyr, and the band then slides steadily at about 68 MPa. The seed never exceeds 1 cm/s and there are no slip events. The friction coefficient in the seed element (dynamic_friction) varies between about 0.54 and 0.81 from one monitor row to the next. Velocity weakening sticks and slips. The stress reaches 85 MPa before the first event at 4.3 kyr. Then 39 events follow until 12 kyr. The gap between events shortens from about 440 years to about 180 years after 8 kyr. In a typical event the seed slips 1.3 m (0.5 to 2.0 m) in about a minute at 0.1 to 0.8 m/s, and the stress in the seed element drops by 5 MPa (up to 21 MPa). Most events are followed a few years later by a slow slip of about 0.3 m with no stress drop. Between events the stress recovers along a straight line, as in the loading phase. The boundaries pull at the same rate in all three, and the seed has moved 68 to 77 m by 12 kyr in each. What differs is when that slip happens. Global velocity scaling lets one run carry both the centuries between events and the seconds of each event: the time step falls from about 106 s between events to below 10−3 s during them.

One element. The stress and friction histories come from the seed element and the displacement from one node. They show the character of slip, not the slip distribution along the band. One resolution. All runs use 100 m elements, so the band is a few elements wide. The dips have not been checked at other resolutions. One band. Only the band on the right is clear enough to fit over 2–8 km. The conjugate band is weaker in all three models.

Change the dilation angle. Set dilation_angle0 and dilation_angle1 to 15 and compare the dips with the Arthur angle, now 56.25°. Move a/b through 1. Run a = 0.012, 0.015 and 0.016 with b = 0.015 and find where the slip events stop. Count the events. With sim.seismic_moment_calculate_output = yes the weakening case writes each event's moment to seismic_moment_magnitude.txt. Compare it with the seed slip in the monitor file.

An input parameter appears in four places in the source and one in this manual. parameters.hpp. Add the member to the struct of its section (Sim, Mesh, Control, BC, IC, Mat, Monitor, ...). input.cxx, declare_parameters. Register section.name with its type, default and help text. The help text is what users see with -h and what the parameter reference is generated from, so state the meaning, the unit and the valid values. Per-material lists are declared as text and read with get_numbers. input.cxx, validate_parameters. Reject invalid values and incompatible combinations with die(EXIT_CONFIG_VALUE, "..."), naming the parameter in the message. examples/defaults.cfg. Add a commented line with the default, in its section. Record new, changed and removed parameters in CHANGELOG.md. Then document it: add it to the parameter table of the User guide or Theory page for its feature; regenerate the parameter reference from executables built at that revision (see maintaining this manual). Parameter names come from examples/defaults.cfg or -h; never guess one in documentation or examples.
DynEarthSol is developed on GitHub at GeoFLAC/DynEarthSol. The repository's CONTRIBUTING.md is the authority for everything on this page; this is a summary.

A commit message records what the code cannot: what was wrong before, why this change and not another, and what it was measured to do. type: imperative summary, 72 characters or fewer, no period The problem and its user-visible effect. The approach, where the diff does not make it obvious, and alternatives rejected. Numbers for every claim. Co-Authored-By: Name <email> type is one of fix, feat, refactor, test, docs, ci, build or cleanup. Refer to earlier work by its subject or pull-request number, not by hash alone, since branches are rebased.

Templates under .github/ fill in when you open an issue or a pull request. Bug reports: one issue per symptom, with the version, the exact build and run commands, the smallest failing input and the output as text. Enhancements: the problem, a concrete proposal, alternatives rejected, and what closes the issue. Pull requests: one topic each, commits that each build and pass tests/regression, and a title that stands alone in git log. Report whether the change altered results (see Testing a change). Open as a draft until CI passes, then ask at least one other developer to review.

They are welcome. You are responsible for the output of the tools you use and should be able to explain every line. Disclose the tools in the pull request, name them in Co-Authored-By trailers, and reply to reviews yourself. AGENTS.md in the repository root gives an assistant the rules it cannot infer from the code.

A release updates CHANGELOG.md, CITATION.cff and .zenodo.json, is merged through a reviewed pull request, and is then tagged (v2.x.y). The tag triggers a workflow that packages the source with its submodules for a draft GitHub release and a Zenodo deposit. The steps are in CONTRIBUTING.md under "Development and release workflow".

This manual is a Docusaurus site in the GeoFLAC/des3d repository, published at https://geoflac.github.io/DynEarthSol/ when changes are merged to main. The deploy workflow pushes the build to the gh-pages branch of GeoFLAC/DynEarthSol, and the old address https://geoflac.github.io/des3d/ redirects every page to the new one.

Section Folder Contents Getting started docs/getting-started/ overview, installation, quickstart, running, visualizing, troubleshooting Theory docs/theory/ formulation and numerical methods User guide docs/user-guide/ one feature per page: model setup, numerical controls, running and output Tutorials docs/tutorial/ reproducible worked examples that build a model for a geoscience problem, each opening with an At a glance box Benchmarks docs/benchmarks/ DES compared with analytical, theoretical or independent solutions, grouped by field and listed in the overview Reference docs/reference/ configuration file and the generated parameter list Developer guide docs/developer/ this section Moved pages keep their published URL through a slug: in their front matter, and a renamed category page gets a redirect in docusaurus.config.ts. Link to other pages by relative file path, such as ../user-guide/running/restart.md, so the build can check the link.
Docusaurus needs Node 20 or later. yarn install yarn build # fails on any broken link, anchor or image yarn start # local preview at http://localhost:3000/DynEarthSol/

docs/reference/parameters.md is generated, never edited by hand. After any change to DynEarthSol's options, build both executables at that revision and run: python3 scripts/generate_parameter_reference.py \ --exe2d /path/to/dynearthsol2d --exe3d /path/to/dynearthsol3d --source <revision> --check with the same arguments reports whether the page is out of date.

docs/ is the "Latest" manual, following the current source. Each tagged release has a frozen copy under versioned_docs/. A correction that also applies to a release is made in its copy too; a page for a feature that a release did not have is not added to it. When DynEarthSol tags a release, yarn docusaurus docs:version vX.Y.Z freezes the current manual.

When a pull request is merged into DynEarthSol, a workflow opens an issue in this repository asking for a documentation review. User-visible changes (new or changed parameters, build options, output formats, breaking changes) are documented on the page for that feature; internal fixes are not. Tutorials record the DynEarthSol revision they were checked with in their At a glance box.

DynEarthSol is a single C++17 code base in the repository root. The same sources build dynearthsol2d and dynearthsol3d: the dimension is fixed at compile time (make ndims=2 or ndims=3) through NDIMS, NODES_PER_ELEM and NSTR, so every change must compile in both.

Area Files Main program and time loop dynearthsol.cxx Input parameters input.cxx (declaration, reading, validation), parameters.hpp (the Param structs and shared variables) Mesh generation and remeshing mesh.cxx, remeshing.cxx, mmg_utils.cxx, with the bundled Triangle and TetGen Field updates fields.cxx (strain rate, force, velocity, temperature), geometry.cxx (volumes, time step, nodal masses) Constitutive models rheology.cxx (stress update), matprops.cxx (material properties, friction laws) Pore fluid and sources hydraulics.cxx/.hpp (pressure, Darcy flux, inventories and hydraulic remap), unsaturated.hpp (retention and local state conversion), point_sources.cxx/.hpp (shared fluid/heat point mapper) Pseudo-transient mechanics pseudo_transient.cxx Boundary and initial conditions bc.cxx, ic.cxx, ic-read-temp.cxx Markers and phase changes markerset.cxx, phasechanges.cxx Interpolation during remeshing nn-interpolation.cxx, brc-interpolation.cxx, barycentric-fn.cxx, knn.cxx Output, checkpoints and monitors output.cxx, binaryio.cxx, monitor.cxx, ats_output_scheduler.cxx, runtime_info.cxx Earthquake tracking earthquake_state.cxx Shared helpers utils.hpp, utils.cxx (including die() and the exit codes), constants.hpp Python tools Dynearthsol.py (output reader), 2vtk.py (VTK conversion) Bundled libraries nanoflann, knn-bvh, mmg (git submodules), third_party/CLI11, triangle, tetgen

The mechanical update, transport ordering and next-step mass must refer to the same physical interval: Refresh current material properties. In the default content model, advance temperature when transport is enabled. Evaluate strain rate and its nodal mixed projection. Coupled ordinary explicit/GVS mechanics advances default-model pressure before stress, force and velocity. PT instead trials the physical constitutive interval to equilibrium and accepts one mechanical state. Commit accepted shear work once. In the default fixed-stress path, advance pressure from accepted mechanics and then update porosity. Apply phase changes on their ten-step cadence. Apply velocity constraints and update moving geometry or fixed-mesh GVS masses. The optional finite-density path advances its inventories through HydraulicStep. Its explicit/GVS correction uses the current pressure for one accepted momentum update, restoring the original interval/mass after any geometry predictor. Only then select the next GVS interval. Rotate stress with the saved current physical interval, update monitors, track events and write outputs. Check mesh quality and remesh when needed. See Poromechanics for capacity selection and PT for trial/commit ownership. Transport substeps do not repeat plastic, porosity or RSF histories.

dppressure stores pold​−pnew​, integrated over the physical interval. Each element applies its own Biot coefficient and retention law. Its Bishop increment uses Se​(pold​)pold​−Se​(pnew​)pnew​; saturated elements retain the saturated arithmetic. Hydraulic scratch increments and the next rheology call can belong to different time levels, so sharing an element calculation does not permit reusing a scratch value without checking its ownership. Checkpoints record whether the pressure increment was consumed; a pressure correction must not repeat the plastic return or consume that increment twice. PT trials restore the same constitutive baseline until acceptance. Only the accepted caller transfers nonelastic work to pending heat. This reservoir is extensive energy: changing the next timestep changes its conversion to a rate, rather than the stored energy. Checkpoints and remapping retain it separately from temperature. Physical water supplies fluid heat capacity; the numerical fixed-stress buffer supplies neither density nor sensible heat. See thermal evolution and poromechanics for the declared energy models.

The development notes in the repository's CONTRIBUTING.md are the authority. In short: Parallel loops use #pragma omp parallel for default(none) with every variable listed, and keep the paired OpenACC clauses in step. The code must also compile as C++20 and with GCC 8 or later. Errors exit through die(EXIT_...), never a bare exit(); the first digit of the code is the category (see exit codes). Bulk output uses C-style I/O; avoid creating objects in inner loops, and avoid static and global variables.

Compiling is not verification. Before a change is reported as done: Build both dimensions. make ndims=2 make ndims=3 Compare results with the parent revision whenever the change could alter them. In tests/regression/, store a reference with the executable built from the parent commit, then rebuild with the change and compare: cd tests/regression make set NDIMS=2 CASE=<case>.cfg # with the parent's dynearthsol2d # rebuild the root executables with your change, then make cmp NDIMS=2 CASE=<case>.cfg compare.py prints the relative difference of each field and fails above 10−8. A change that is meant to alter results should say so, with the case and the size of the difference, in the commit message and the pull request. make fresh-restart-cmp checks that a restart reproduces an uninterrupted run. test-tiny.cfg is a one-second smoke test. Run the tests that cover the area you changed, for example the functional tests under tests/functional/, the component checks under tests/residual-assembly-test/, or a benchmark under benchmarks/. See Benchmarks for the list. Pull requests run the same build matrix and functional tests in continuous integration, but CI cannot tell whether a change should have altered results; the pull-request template asks you to report the comparison.

This page takes you from source code to a result in a few minutes. You will build the 2D executable, run the shipped example examples/tectonics/core-complex.cfg, and look at the normal fault that forms as a brittle crust is pulled apart.

Clone DynEarthSol and build the 2D executable in its root directory (see Installation for dependencies and build options): git clone --recursive https://github.com/GeoFLAC/DynEarthSol.git cd DynEarthSol make ndims=2 This creates dynearthsol2d.

Run the example in its own folder so the output stays together: mkdir quickstart cd quickstart cp ../examples/tectonics/core-complex.cfg . OMP_NUM_THREADS=4 ../dynearthsol2d core-complex.cfg The run takes about a minute and a half with four threads. DES prints a status line as it goes and finishes with a timing summary.

Setting Value Domain 100 km wide, 10 km thick; elements of about 1 km, finer between x = 30 and 70 km Material elasto-plastic (Mohr–Coulomb), friction angle 30°, cohesion softening from 44 to 4 MPa over plastic strain 0.5 Loading both sides pulled outward at 10−9 m/s (3.2 cm/yr each), free surface with slow diffusion Seed a weak zone dipping 60°, centred at x = 50 km in the lower half of the layer, given plastic strain 0.5 Duration 50,000 years, a frame every 1500 years The weak zone seeds a fault. Cohesion softening then concentrates further slip on it, and the mesh is rebuilt as it distorts.

The run writes, under the model name result3: File Contents result3.save.000000 … 000033 34 saved frames of all fields result3.chkpt.* checkpoints for restarting result3.info one line per frame: step, time, time step, wall time, mesh size result3.manifest how and where the run was built and run (provenance) Convert the frames to VTK and open them in ParaView: ../2vtk.py result3 This writes result3.000000.vtu to result3.000033.vtu. Open the series in ParaView and colour it by plastic strain. Or plot the last frame with Python, using the reader shipped with DES: import sys sys.path.insert(0, '..') # the DynEarthSol directory import matplotlib.pyplot as plt from matplotlib.tri import Triangulation from Dynearthsol import Dynearthsol des = Dynearthsol('result3') frame = des.frames[-1] xy = des.read_field(frame, 'coordinate') / 1e3 # km conn = des.read_field(frame, 'connectivity') plstrain = des.read_field(frame, 'plastic strain') fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 1.9), constrained_layout=True) pc = ax.tripcolor(Triangulation(xy[:, 0], xy[:, 1], conn), facecolors=plstrain, vmin=0, vmax=2) ax.set_aspect('equal'); ax.set_xlabel('x (km)'); ax.set_ylabel('z (km)') fig.colorbar(pc, cax=ax.inset_axes([1.01, 0, .012, 1]), label='plastic strain') fig.savefig('plastic_strain.png', dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')

After 50,000 years the layer has extended by about 3 km. Almost all of that extension is taken up by one normal fault that grew from the weak zone, from the base of the layer near x = 43 km to the surface near x = 53 km. Its footwall has risen about 1.3 km above the original surface. The rest of the layer has hardly deformed.

Change one setting and rerun: for example vbc_val_x0 and vbc_val_x1 in [bc] for the extension rate, or cohesion1 in [mat] for how much the fault weakens. Give each run a new modelname. Read Running DynEarthSol and Visualizing outputs for more options. Continue with the rifting and subduction tutorial, which builds on this kind of model. Look up any parameter in the configuration parameters.

When a run stops, DynEarthSol prints a two-digit exit code and its category. The first digit says where to look: 1x is the input, 2x the environment (files, libraries), and 3x–6x the computation or the code itself. The full table is in exit codes.

Symptom Check HDF5 headers or library not found Install the development package (libhdf5-dev on Ubuntu, hdf5 with Homebrew). Python's h5py does not provide it. Set HDF5_INCLUDE_DIR and HDF5_LIB_DIR only if the wrong installation is picked up. Or build without it: make hdf5=0. omp.h or libomp not found on macOS brew install libomp, then rebuild. Missing nanoflann, knn-bvh or mmg sources The repository uses submodules: clone with --recursive, or run git submodule update --init. An option a page uses is not recognized The executable is from an older revision. Check ./dynearthsol2d -h and the revision a tutorial was checked with (its At a glance box). See Installation for dependencies and build options.

Symptom Check Exit 10 or 11 before the first step A configuration error: a misspelled or retired parameter, or a value out of range. The message names the parameter. Look it up in the parameter reference. Exit 12 The .poly or .exo mesh file is malformed. See making a mesh with a .poly file. .poly file not found Run from the directory that holds both the input file and the .poly file, or give its path in mesh.poly_filename. Exit 21 or 22 when restarting The checkpoint does not match this executable: it was written by an older file-format revision or lacks records this version needs. See checkpointing and restart. Exit 30 or 31 The feature is not available in this dimension, or the executable was built without the library it needs (for example MMG or GoSPL).

Symptom Check Exit 50: NaN or non-finite value The run prints the affected fields and the first bad element and node. Common causes are a time step too large (control.dt_fraction), a control.inertial_scaling so small that inertia dominates (see mass scaling), or a badly distorted mesh. Exit 54: PT did not converge See the PT controls in choosing a mechanical solver. Exit 40–42: meshing failed The mesh became too distorted for Triangle, TetGen or MMG to rebuild. Check the quality settings in [mesh] and the remeshing options. Warning that element groups may share nodes A possible OpenMP race. Increase the resolution or use fewer threads. Very slow on a small mesh Too many threads for the work: set OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 (or a few) and OMP_DYNAMIC=FALSE.

Symptom Check No .vtkhdf files VTKHDF needs an HDF5 build (hdf5=1). Otherwise convert the binary frames with 2vtk.py. 2vtk.py skips frames of a restarted run Convert with 2vtk.py -g <restarted modelname> to include the parent run's frames. See visualizing outputs. Lost .info file utils/recreate_info.py rebuilds it from the frame files.

If the problem remains, open an issue in the DynEarthSol issue tracker with the input file, the exit code and message, and the run's <modelname>.manifest, which records how the executable was built and run.

DynEarthSol (Dynamic Earth Solver, also called DES or DES3D) is an explicit Lagrangian finite element code for deforming rock in 2D and 3D. It solves the momentum balance and heat transfer for elastic, viscoelastic and elasto-visco-plastic materials on unstructured triangular and tetrahedral meshes, which it rebuilds as they distort. It was built for long-term deformation of the lithosphere, and now also covers earthquake cycles, quasi-static equilibrium and coupled surface processes. The same source builds dynearthsol2d and dynearthsol3d, for CPUs with OpenMP or GPUs with OpenACC.

Problem Main ingredients Start here Rifting, subduction and core complexes Strain-weakening plasticity, weak zones, remeshing, markers, phase changes Rifting and subduction Convergent wedges Basal décollement friction, .poly geometry Convergent wedges Earthquake cycles and slow slip Rate-and-state friction, global velocity scaling Rate-and-state friction, Creep or earthquakes Static and slowly loaded equilibrium Pseudo-transient (PT) mechanics Choosing a mechanical solver, Elastic loading Groundwater, consolidation and slopes Biot poromechanics, partly saturated flow, groundwater heat transport Poromechanics, poromechanics benchmarks, groundwater and slopes tutorials Landscape and tectonics together Coupling with GoSPL Coupling with GoSPL Thermal evolution Heat conduction in the deforming (Lagrangian) mesh Thermal evolution Strongly distorting domains Adaptive remeshing with Triangle, TetGen or MMG Remeshing, MMG

Explicit time integration. Nodal velocities are advanced from the force balance, with no global matrix to solve. Mass scaling. Inertia is scaled so that a stable explicit step spans years in tectonic models; global velocity scaling adapts it from loading to rupture. Nodal mixed discretization avoids volumetric locking of linear elements. Lagrangian mesh with remeshing. The mesh moves with the material and is rebuilt when its quality drops; markers carry material identity. Pseudo-transient mechanics (optional) iterates to equilibrium within each physical step. See Theory for the formulation.

Check Troubleshooting first. Report problems and ask questions in the DynEarthSol issue tracker. Using an AI assistant to get oriented If you're new to DES3D, one effective way to get started is working through model setup with an AI coding assistant. Point it at this documentation site and any background papers relevant to your problem, then describe the tectonic scenario you want to model in plain language, geometry, timing, boundary conditions, the processes involved, and iterate on the resulting .cfg file together. Treat its output as a draft to check against this manual and your own understanding of the parameters, not a substitute for either.

A DynEarthSol model is described by one input file in INI format, passed to the executable: dynearthsol2d model.cfg Each parameter belongs to a section, and its full name is section.parameter, for example mat.rheology_type. Inside the file it is written under its section header: [mat] rheology_type = elasto-plastic Parameters left out take their defaults. Lists are written in brackets, [1, 2, 3], with one value per material where a parameter is set per material. A single value applies to every material.

Section Controls [sim] Model name, run length, output and checkpoint intervals, restart [mesh] Domain size, mesh generation, resolution, quality checks and remeshing [markers] Lagrangian markers that carry material identity [control] Gravity, time stepping, mass scaling, damping, the PT solver, and heat and fluid transport [bc] Velocity, traction, thermal and hydraulic boundary conditions, surface processes [ic] Initial temperature, stress, weak zones and material layout [mat] Rheology and material properties, per material [monitor] Point monitors written as CSV time series [debug] Diagnostic output

The configuration parameters page lists every parameter with its type, default and description. It is generated from the executables, which remain the authoritative list for their own version. Run one with -h to print the same information for the build you are using: ./dynearthsol2d -h ./dynearthsol2d -h | grep -A2 'rsf' examples/defaults.cfg in the DynEarthSol repository lists the parameters by section with their default values and short comments. The examples/ and benchmarks/ directories contain complete working inputs. The User guide and Theory pages describe the parameters that belong to each feature: Feature Page Boundary conditions Velocity and traction, temperature Initial stress Initial stress Weak zones Weak zones Mechanical solver Choosing a mechanical solver Remeshing Remeshing, MMG Rate-and-state friction Rate-and-state friction Point monitors Point monitors Restart Checkpointing and restart An unknown or misspelled parameter stops the run with exit code 11 before any computation; see exit codes.

All parameters accepted by DynEarthSol at source revision 1c7ef34, as printed by dynearthsol2d -h and dynearthsol3d -h. A parameter is written in its section of the input file; see Configuration file. Defaults that differ between 2D and 3D are shown for both. Domain size, mesh generation, resolution, quality checks and remeshing. Parameter Type Default Description meshing_option integer 1 How to create the new mesh? 1: rectangular box with roughly uniform resolution 2: rectangular box with rectangular zone of refined resolution 90: read the bounding polygon from a .poly file 91: same as 90, but the max. element size is normalized with resolution. 95: read the mesh from from a .exo file meshing_elem_shape integer 0 Mesh layout. 0: unstructured triangles (2D) or tetrahedra (3D); 1: regular rectangular cells split into triangles/tetrahedra; 2: equilateral triangles (2D) or a regular tetrahedral layout (3D). All solver elements are simplices. meshing_verbosity integer -1 Screen output of meshing and remeshing. -1: no stage log (default). 0: the stage log ([metric], [collapse], [freeze], [unfreeze], [require], [corner], [mmg], [restore], [GPU mem] lines: what a remesh re-sized, collapsed, froze, freed and restored) and the mesher's standard report. 1-3: Triangle/TetGen -V levels on top. Warnings print at every level. meshing_sediment yes/no no Refine the elements with sediment marker during remeshing. tetgen_optlevel integer 3 Optimization level for tetgen. 0: no optimization; 1: multiple edge filps; 2: 1 & free vertex deletion; 3: 2 & new vertex insertion. High optimization level could slow down the speed of mesh generation. For 3D only. xlength real required Length of x (in meters) ylength real required Length of y (in meters), for 3D only zlength real required Length of z (in meters) resolution real required Spatial resolution (in meters) smallest_size real 0.01 The size of smallest element relative to an element with typical resolution. It sets the tiny-element remesh trigger smallest_vol = smallest_size * sizefactor * resolution^NDIMS (sizefactor 0.433 in 2D, 0.118 in 3D: a unit-edge equilateral element's measure) and two lengths, hmin = smallest_size^(1/NDIMS) * resolution and min_dist = (smallest_size * sizefactor)^(1/NDIMS) * resolution. hmin is the Triangle/TetGen node-spacing floor (a remesh deletes interior nodes closer than hmin to a retained node), with MMG in 2D the boundary-segment length below which a remesh merges the segment's two nodes (never a domain corner), and the necking-stop distance of remeshing_option 1, 11 and 13 (see remeshing_option). With options 1, 11 and 13 a remesh removes the nodes off a restored boundary that lie past it or within min_dist of it, and option 2 the interior nodes within min_dist of the new bottom; with options 1 and 10-12 Triangle keeps a boundary node whose two segments are both longer than min_dist, and in 3D TetGen's boundary edge flips move a boundary by at most min_dist; at a receiving wall, option 13 gives the side profile to new material up to min_dist inland of the old wall. With MMG it also sets MMG's size floors (see mmg_remesh_defensive_tiny_ratio). largest_size real 30 The size of largest element relative to an element with typical resolution, which also caps the coarse zone of a meshing_option = 2 mesh. With MMG it also sets the maximum edge length, hmax = largest_size^(1/NDIMS) * resolution sediment_size real 1 The size threshold of the refined sediment elements min_angle real 32 Min. angle of all triangles (in degrees), for 2D only max_steiner_factor real 30 Cap on the number of Steiner points Triangle may insert while (re)meshing, expressed as a multiple of the number of input nodes (2D only). This bounds the pathological, non-terminating segment splitting that Triangle can enter when two boundary segments meet at a very small angle (e.g. a highly distorted mesh at extreme strain), which would otherwise spin forever and exhaust memory. The cap is far above any healthy remesh, so normal meshing is unaffected. Set <= 0 to disable the cap (Triangle default: unlimited). min_tet_angle real 22 Min. dihedral angle of all tetrahedra (in degrees), for 3D only max_ratio real 2 Max. radius / length ratio of all tetrahedra, for 3D only refined_zonex list [0.4, 0.6] Refining portion of xlength ([d0,d1]; 0<=d0<=d1<=1), for meshing_option=2 only refined_zoney list [0.4, 0.6] Refining portion of ylength ([d0,d1]; 0<=d0<=d1<=1), for meshing_option=2 only, for 3D only refined_zonez list [0.8, 1] Refined depth interval [d0,d1] as fractions of zlength measured downward from the top (0 <= d0 <= d1 <= 1); meshing_option=2 only. poly_filename text mesh.poly Input polygon filename for meshing_option=90 or 91. Triangle .poly format in 2D; TetGen .poly format in 3D. Region attributes select materials when ic.mattype_option=0. Point attributes, point boundary markers and holes are not supported. Also supply mesh.xlength, mesh.ylength and mesh.zlength. exo_filename text mesh.exo Filename of the input polygon, for meshing_option=95 only. Meshing software like Trelis is supposed to be used for creating a mesh in the ExodusII format. Limitation: Only box-like domains with six sides are supported. Users still need to provide these parameters: mesh.xlength, mesh.ylength, and mesh.zlength. quality_check_step_interval integer 100 How often to check mesh quality? min_quality real 0.4 Min. mesh quality before remeshing (between 0 and 1) max_boundary_distortion real 0.25 Max. distance of boundary distortion before remeshing (in unit of mesh.resolution). remeshing_option integer 0 How to deal with the boundaries during remeshing? 0: no modification on any boundary. 1: move all bottom nodes to initial depth and delete the side-wall nodes left just above or below it; other boundaries are intact. 2: create a new bottom boundary at the initial depth, other boundaries are intact (2D only, not with MMG remeshing). 10: no modification on any boundary, except small boundary segments might get merged (in 3D with TetGen, see smallest_size). 11: move all bottom nodes to initial depth and delete the side-wall nodes left just above or below it; other boundaries are intact, except small boundary segments might get merged. 12: move all x0 (left) wall nodes to the x of the wall's top corner and delete the nodes left outside, other boundaries are intact. For a wall pushed over a fixed bottom with its push tapered toward it (vbc_x0 = 3 with bottom_shear_zone_thickness), whose foot lags its top. With MMG remeshing, 2D only. 13: move all bottom and side-wall nodes (left/right; also front/back in 3D) to initial dimensions, and give material entering through a side wall the structure recorded at that wall (its side profile). A wall receives while its nodes drift inward between remeshes (by any amount when its vbc at the remesh is inflow, else by more than min(1e-3, max_boundary_distortion) * resolution). It keeps the column (2D) or wall face (3D) recorded when it started receiving (at run start when its vbc is inflow, else at the first remesh at which it receives), and drops it when it neither receives nor has an inflow vbc. Incoming material gets the recorded temperature, layering, radiogenic source, coord0 reference and zero strain at its depth below the wall's top point less the rise surface processes gave it, and in 3D at its along-strike position (a point off the recorded face takes the values of the face's nearest point). A deposit on the wall top gets the profile top's values. Markers a remesh creates in an element at the wall take the layering at the element's centroid and time 0; in an element centred in the deposit, mattype_sediment and the time of a sediment marker of the element, else the remesh time. Temperatures are not re-conducted under a risen surface, so they can differ from the domain beside the wall by up to the near-surface temperature gradient times the rise. Requires MMG when meshing_elem_shape = 0: the restored wall accumulates sub-hmin elements that only MMG collapses. With MMG on an unstructured mesh, a Triangle/TetGen initial mesh first gets its restored-wall elements refined to ~resolution, whatever use_mmg_init says (in 3D under mattype_option 0 this can move a regional-attribute boundary inside the wall band), and every remesh caps the size target at every restored-wall node at resolution (see mmg_aniso_wall_ratio), so the walls can carry more elements than the cfg's sizes give. 14: restore selected reference-boundary components (2D unstructured meshes only; mesh.remeshing_reset_boundaries). On an unstructured mesh (meshing_elem_shape = 0), options 1, 11 and 13 stop the run at a remesh (exit 42) when a top-surface node is within smallest_size^(1/NDIMS) * resolution of the restored bottom, or below it: the domain has necked through. num_remeshing_reset_boundaries integer 0 Number of selected boundary-marker bits for remeshing_option=14. remeshing_reset_boundaries list [] Boundary-marker bits to restore, e.g. [1,16]. Single faces restore normal components; two selected faces restore their corner fully. mmg_remesh_active_plstrain real 0.01 Conservative MMG remeshing (always on with MMG): a remesh keeps quiet elements as they are (frozen) and rebuilds the rest. This key is the plastic-strain increment since the last remesh above which an element is refined: MMG may split it (not along an edge it shares with a frozen, MMG-required element) but keeps its existing nodes, so the band's plastic strain is carried verbatim. Distorted or tiny elements are repaired with node motion (see mmg_remesh_defensive_quality_ratio and mmg_remesh_defensive_tiny_ratio), and so is the mesh that restoring a boundary squashed or collapsed or that merging a short boundary segment (see smallest_size) reshaped. Elements far from their size target are freed (see mmg_remesh_size_recovery_ratio), as is the band beside a receiving or outward-drifting restored wall (remeshing_option 13). Boundary nodes stay pinned except the free-surface nodes a surface process moves by more than 1% of resolution per remesh interval (2D only, surface_process_option 1 or 102), the off-bottom nodes of unrestored side walls and slant boundaries, the nodes of repaired elements and the band nodes off an outward-drifting restored wall. Keep it > 0: at 0, incidental yielding makes quiet far-field elements splittable at every remesh. Default 0.01, heuristic: above the increment of incidental yielding, below a localizing band's increment over a remesh interval. mmg_remesh_defensive_tiny_ratio real 1.5 Gap, in element measure, between the tiny-element remesh trigger smallest_vol (see smallest_size) and the smallest elements MMG builds (usemmg=1, meshing_elem_shape = 0; remeshing and MMG-built initial meshes). MMG's minimum edge length is hmin * ratio^(1/NDIMS) (hmin: see smallest_size), so MMG aims to build every element at smallest_vol * ratio or more, which must shrink by this factor before it re-triggers, and a remesh rebuilds any element below smallest_vol * ratio. The ratio also sets MMG's metric floor one step higher, hmin * ratio^(2/NDIMS) (at most MMG's hmax), and the post-remesh quality gate at smallest_vol * sqrt(ratio). Must be >= 1 (at 1 a just-remeshed element re-triggers under any compression); a ratio at or above largest_size / smallest_size is capped just below it, with a warning. Default 1.5 (a 2/3 measure gap), heuristic. mmg_remesh_defensive_quality_ratio real 1.5 MMG remeshing repairs (unfreezes, with its nodes movable except where disjoint material bodies meet) every element of quality below min_quality * this ratio, so a marginal element is rebuilt before it crosses the min_quality remesh trigger instead of triggering another remesh a few steps later. The trigger itself stays at min_quality. Must be >= 1 (1: repair only below the trigger). Default 1.5, heuristic. mmg_remesh_size_recovery_ratio real 1.4 Size recovery in MMG remeshing. A quiet element (e.g. one that entered at ~resolution through a restored inflow wall and advected inland) is freed to coarsen when it is finer by more than this factor than the gradation envelope, the smallest size MMG's gradation (hgrad) allows there given every intentionally fine size target; an element at least 2x its own plastic-strain size target is freed to split. Neither frees an element refined for plastic-strain growth (mmg_remesh_active_plstrain), one on the top surface, one at a material interface (by its own and its neighbours' markers) or one within 4 rings of a restored wall that receives no material, and neither unpins a restored-wall or bottom node; the remesh log's '[unfreeze] size recovery' line counts the top-surface, interface and wall-band skips. On a moving mesh, a Triangle/TetGen initial mesh also gets the 2x split in its weak zone before any field exists, except on a top-surface node or a region boundary ('[weakzone]' log lines). 0 disables all three; otherwise must be > 1 (a margin against re-freeing the legal size transition). Default 1.4 ~ sqrt(2) in edge length (one 2D bisection level), heuristic. remesh_deborah_min real 1 During remeshing the element stress is a Deborah-number-weighted blend of the NN-remapped stress and the SPR recovery, De = Maxwell time / time since the last remesh. The weight is a smoothstep -- the cubic 3t^2 - 2t^3, flat at both ends -- in log10(De): high-De (cold, effectively elastic) elements keep the NN stress, preserving elastic stress memory; low-De (weak, viscous) elements take the SPR average, which suppresses element-scale noise. This sets the De at or below which the remeshed stress is purely the SPR recovery. remesh_deborah_max real 100 De at or above which the remeshed stress is purely the NN-remapped stress. The default puts the two limits two decades apart, which keeps them clear of the De = 1 crossover while remesh intervals themselves vary by a factor of a few between events; widen it to blend more of the domain, narrow it to make the switch sharper. The window width is otherwise untuned. is_discarding_internal_segments yes/no yes Discard the initial mesh's internal segments (refined-zone box, .poly internal facets)? 'no' keeps them as Triangle/TetGen constraints across remeshes, but a remesh that deletes one of their nodes (tiny-element repair, node cleanup near a restored boundary) misroutes them, which can make the mesher fail or hang; in 3D with remeshing_option 1 or 10-12 the first remesh that deletes a boundary node drops them all. MMG remeshing (usemmg=1, meshing_elem_shape = 0) requires 'yes': MMG keeps no internal segment. mmg_debug integer 0 Run MMG remesher in debug mode? No:0; Yes:1 mmg_verbose integer 0 Verbosity level of MMG remesher. For debugging, set a value greater than 4. mmg_hausd_factor real 0.01 Factor multiplied to param.mesh.resolution to set the Hausdorff distance between original and remeshed surfaces. At 0.01 MMG refines a sharply bent free surface down to its size floor and builds elements below the tiny-element trigger there, so the trigger fires at nearly every quality check: use 0.02-0.05 along a 3D fault scarp and 0.1 on the top/wall ridges next to restored side walls. MMG3D does not bound its top-surface edge swaps between pinned nodes by this distance. mmg_init_coarsening_factor real 10 Coarsening factor for the two-stage TetGen+MMG init mesh. TetGen creates a mesh with element volumes scaled by factor^NDIMS; MMG then refines to target resolution. Higher values = smaller coarse mesh = faster TetGen but more MMG work. Default: 10. use_mmg_init yes/no no Use two-stage TetGen+MMG initialization? Requires compilation with USEMMG. Set to yes for metric-aware refinement; no (default) uses plain triangle/tetgen init (MMG still refines its restored walls under remeshing_option 13 and, on a moving mesh, its weak zone: see mmg_remesh_size_recovery_ratio). Under mattype_option 0, which reads the regional attributes as mattypes, a boundary between them stays on the .poly line in 2D and can move by up to about half a coarse element in 3D (see mmg_init_coarsening_factor). mmg_metric_refine_coeff real 5 Plastic-strain sensitivity of the MMG remeshing metric: the target element volume is scaled by 1/(1 + coeff*plastic_strain), so the target edge length by that ratio^(1/NDIMS) (whether a node keeps its finest target: see mmg_metric_refine_recover). 0 disables plastic refinement from a fresh start (the metric floor, the surface-motion inflation of shrinking top elements and the option-13 restored-wall cap still apply). MMG starts from this target except at a node on a required edge (an edge of a frozen element or, in 2D, an option-13 material-interface edge) that belongs to no refined element (see mmg_remesh_active_plstrain): there it starts from the mean length of the required edges through the node, MMG's own rule. Larger values mesh a plastically strained zone finer, down to the metric floor (see mmg_remesh_defensive_tiny_ratio): a shear band can localize narrower, at more elements and, where an elastic, advection or diffusion limit sets dt, a shorter time step. Default 5. mmg_metric_refine_recover yes/no no no (default): each node keeps the finest plastic-strain size target (see mmg_metric_refine_coeff) it has had at a remesh, so a refined zone stays refined where the target coarsens, chiefly where plastic strain drops (the remap of rebuilt elements, the 2D top-element plastic-strain decay, a growing top element); the mesh can then hold more elements. Size recovery (mmg_remesh_size_recovery_ratio) measures against the kept size, and material entering through a restored side wall starts unrefined. yes: the target follows the current plastic strain. The record is checkpointed: with no, a restart that lowers mmg_metric_refine_coeff (even to 0) keeps the sizes recorded before it, and a restart that switches from yes to no holds from the last remesh's targets. mmg_aniso_wall_ratio real 0 Anisotropic MMG metric at inflow restored side walls (remeshing_option 13). 0 (default): off, isotropic. >= 1: aspect ratio; the inflow-wall elements are coarsened by this factor normal to the wall and kept fine along it, so the incoming column is carried by thin, wide elements. MMG's hmax (see largest_size) caps the aspect (~5.5 in 2D, ~3.1 in 3D at the default largest_size). Other values below 1 are rejected. Requires USEMMG. vt_size real 0.5 Cell size of the virtual-topology marker grid (in unit of mesh.resolution), used by the serpentinization grid (mat.phase_change_option 3 with mat.has_serpentinization). 0.5 = half an element edge: the one-element-thick slab crust gets its own wet-crust-dominant cell row instead of averaging with the mantle above, while a cell nominally (elements of edge mesh.resolution) holds ~2.3 markers in 2D (~4.2 in 3D) at the default 4 per element; a refined mesh puts more in each cell. Heuristic, untuned. With serpentinization on it must be > 0, and mesh.resolution * mesh.vt_size must not exceed mat.serpentinization_thickness. The grid is rebuilt at each mesh.quality_check_step_interval and after each remesh.

Assuming the width of the channel is 50 km, 5e7 ton/yr ~= 2.e-5 m^2/s has_thermal_pressurization yes/no no Couple thermal expansion to solid stress and fluid content; requires hydraulic and thermal diffusion. has_shear_heating yes/no no Convert accepted viscous/plastic work to heat. Rheology and material properties. List values hold one entry per material. Parameter Type Default Description rheology_type text required Type of rheology, either 'elastic', 'viscous' (experimental), 'maxwell', 'elasto-plastic', 'elasto-visco-plastic', 'elasto-plastic-rate-state-friction', or 'elasto-visco-plastic-rate-state-friction' (short '-rsf' aliases are also accepted) is_plane_strain yes/no no Use plane-strain constitutive updates in 2D (elastic and elasto-plastic paths). phase_change_option integer 0 What kind of phase changes? 0: no phase changes. 1: simple rules of subduction-related phase changes. See simple_subduction() in phasechanges.cxx for more details. 3: subduction phase-change rule engine (see subduction_phase_changes() in phasechanges.cxx). A marker converts to a metamorphic product when it crosses a pressure-temperature reaction boundary (pressure: see mat.phase_change_pressure_option; depth: below the local surface; chlorite-out and the first two sediment steps read depth only); each transition activates only when its target mat.mattype_* is set to a distinct material and its switch is on (mat.has_eclogitization and mat.has_serpentinization default on, mat.has_hydrous_mantle_dehydration and mat.has_sediment_metamorphism off). Transitions: oceanic crust->eclogite (Hacker 2003), mantle<->serpentinite (Ulmer & Trommsdorff 1995; serpentinization also needs wet crust -- oceanic crust, sediment or sedimentary rock -- within mat.serpentinization_thickness below the marker, and no deeper than mat.serpentinization_max_depth), hydrous mantle->mantle (Grove 2009), and sediment->sedimentary rock->metasediment->schist (compaction uses geoflac's unsourced thresholds, the next step Montanez & Crossey 2017, the last Wei 2004). 101: custom phase changes (custom_phase_change() in phasechanges.cxx). phase_change_pressure_option integer 0 The pressure the mat.phase_change_option 3 rules read (options 1 and 101 always use ref_pressure()). 0: the mean stress of the marker's element, compression positive, in 2D the in-plane mean. Tectonic over- and underpressure move the reaction boundaries. 1: the reference pressure, ref_pressure() (control.ref_pressure_option), at the marker's depth below the local surface. The phase diagrams are drawn for a lithostat, and geoflac reads one. num_materials integer 1 Number of material types mattype_ref integer 0 Index of reference material. For compute_dt(), compute_mass() and ref_pressure() mattype_mantle integer 0 Index of mantle material. For continental thermal gradient. With mat.phase_change_option 3: what serpentinizes above the slab and what serpentinite and hydrous mantle dehydrate to; no rule may start from it, and it must be set in the cfg when option 3 reads it. mattype_depleted_mantle integer 0 Index of depleted mantle material. Unused: no phase change reads it. mattype_partial_melting_mantle integer 0 Index of partial melting mantle material. Unused: no phase change reads it. mattype_continental_crust integer -1 Index of continental crust. Read only by the continental geotherm (ic.temperature_option 1), which needs it in [0, mat.num_materials). Default -1 (unset). mattype_oceanic_crust integer -1 Index of oceanic crust. Read only by mat.phase_change_option 3: the source of the eclogite rule (with mat.has_eclogitization) and wet crust for the serpentinization grid (with mat.has_serpentinization); either needs it in [0, mat.num_materials). Default -1 (unset). mattype_serpentinite integer -1 Index of serpentinite material, for mat.phase_change_option 3 with mat.has_serpentinization: what mantle above the slab turns into, and the source of serpentinite->mantle dehydration. Default -1 (unset); with serpentinization on it must be in [0, mat.num_materials) and distinct from mattype_mantle and the wet-crust materials (mattype_oceanic_crust, mattype_sediment, and mattype_sediment_rock when set). mattype_eclogite integer -1 Index of eclogite material. For the mat.phase_change_option 3 rule engine: oceanic-crust markers past the basalt->eclogite P-T boundary (Hacker 2003) convert to this. Default -1 (unset); must be set while mat.has_eclogitization is on. mattype_hydrous_mantle integer -1 Index of hydrous (chlorite-bearing) mantle material. For mat.phase_change_option 3: dehydrates to mattype_mantle above the chlorite-out boundary (Grove et al. 2009). Default -1 (unset); must be set while mat.has_hydrous_mantle_dehydration is on. mattype_sediment_rock integer -1 Index of consolidated sedimentary-rock material. For mat.phase_change_option 3: mattype_sediment compacts to this, which then metamorphoses to mattype_metasediment; when set, it is also wet crust for the serpentinization grid. Default -1 (unset); must be set while mat.has_sediment_metamorphism is on. mattype_metasediment integer -1 Index of metamorphic-sediment material. For mat.phase_change_option 3: mattype_sediment_rock -> this -> mattype_schist. Default -1 (unset); must be set while mat.has_sediment_metamorphism is on. mattype_schist integer -1 Index of schist material. For mat.phase_change_option 3: mattype_metasediment dehydrates to this (Wei et al. 2004). Default -1 (unset); must be set while mat.has_sediment_metamorphism is on. mattype_sediment integer 0 Index of sediment material. Should be the same as mattype['sediment'] in 2vtk.py for sediment time convertion. With mat.phase_change_option 3: wet crust for the serpentinization grid (with mat.has_serpentinization) and the source of the sediment chain (with mat.has_sediment_metamorphism); with either it must be set in the cfg. mattype_mor_extrusion integer 0 Index of mid-ocean-ridge extrusion material. Unused: no phase change reads it. mattype_asthenosphere integer 0 Index of asthenosphere. max_viscosity real 1e+24 Max. value of viscosity (in Pa.s) min_viscosity real 1e+18 Min. value of viscosity (in Pa.s) max_tension real 1e+09 Max. value of tensile stress (in Pa) max_thermal_diffusivity real 5e-06 Max. value of thermal diffusivity (in m^2/s) convert_rate_oceanic_crust real 1e-13 Converting rate from melting to oceanic crust. Unused: no phase change reads it. serpentinization_thickness real 10000 Thickness (in m) of the mantle layer above wet crust (oceanic crust, sediment or sedimentary rock) that turns into serpentinite (mat.phase_change_option is 3 with mat.has_serpentinization). Counted in whole background-grid cells below the marker's own cell (cell size mesh.resolution * mesh.vt_size), down to a wet-crust-dominant cell (mat.wet_crust_fraction_threshold), so the effective reach differs from it by up to two cells, and the thickness must be positive and at least one cell. Default 10e3: heuristic, untuned. serpentinization_wet_crust_margin real -1 Horizontal margin (in m) for the serpentinization wet-crust-below test. When >= 0, a wet-crust-dominant grid cell triggers conversion only if the marker's horizontal position lies within the cell's wet-crust extent (recorded per cell at grid build) widened by this margin -- suppressing the column-quantization false positive at a slab bend, where a cell is wet-crust-dominant from wet crust up to a whole cell size away horizontally. < 0 (default) disables: whole-column behavior. serpentinization_max_depth real 150000 mat.phase_change_option 3 with mat.has_serpentinization: no mantle deeper than this (in m below the local free surface) serpentinizes. It also ends the serpentinization grid, at this depth plus mat.serpentinization_thickness and one cell. Must be positive. Default 150e3, heuristic, untuned: slab dehydration, the water source, is essentially complete by ~150 km, shallower than the antigorite stability field's cold-slab extrapolation (> 200 km at 500 C). wet_crust_fraction_threshold real 0.5 mat.phase_change_option 3 with mat.has_serpentinization: a serpentinization grid cell is wet-crust-dominant, so it can serpentinize the mantle above it, when more than this fraction of its markers is wet crust. In [0, 1). A cell holds markers.markers_per_element times (cell / element measure) markers, nominally ~2.3 in 2D and ~4.2 in 3D at mesh.vt_size 0.5, so at 0.5 a two-marker cell needs both. Default 0.5, untuned: geoflac's 0.8 (of an element, with no source) leaves out the cell that straddles the slab top and cuts the serpentinite band of examples/tectonics/subduction.cfg by more than half. has_serpentinization yes/no yes mat.phase_change_option 3: enable mantle<->serpentinite (mantle above the slab serpentinizes inside the antigorite stability field; serpentinite above 550 C outside it dehydrates back to mantle). Default on. Needs mattype_serpentinite and mattype_oceanic_crust, and mattype_sediment set in the cfg. Off: no serpentinization grid is built, and the checks on its inputs are skipped: mattype_mantle, mattype_serpentinite and the wet-crust materials distinct, mattype_serpentinite in range and set, mattype_sediment set, serpentinization_thickness positive and at least one grid cell, mesh.vt_size positive. mattype_mantle and mattype_sediment stay range-checked with the other base material indices, and the rule checks still run (see the other has_* switches); every key an active rule reads must be set in the cfg. has_eclogitization yes/no yes mat.phase_change_option 3: enable oceanic crust->eclogite (Hacker 2003). Default on. Needs mattype_oceanic_crust and mattype_eclogite set, distinct, and not mattype_mantle, and mattype_sediment different from mattype_oceanic_crust (deposits would turn into eclogite). Like every has_* switch, no two active rules may start from one material. has_hydrous_mantle_dehydration yes/no no mat.phase_change_option 3: enable hydrous (chlorite) mantle->mantle dehydration (Grove 2009). Default off. Needs mattype_hydrous_mantle. has_sediment_metamorphism yes/no no mat.phase_change_option 3: enable the sediment chain sediment->sedimentary rock->metasediment->schist (compaction uses geoflac's unsourced thresholds, the next step Montanez & Crossey 2017, the last Wei 2004). Default off.
