The dynamic equation and explicit time integration below describe the default control.has_PT = no path. Both paths share the spatial force discretization. With control.has_PT = yes, pseudo-transient mechanics instead seeks equilibrium within each physical timestep. See solver selection for configuration.

DES3D solves the equation of motion, i.e., linear momentum balance equation, in the following fully dynamic form: ρu˙=∇⋅σ+ρg where ρ is the material density, u is the velocity vector, σ is the total (Cauchy) stress tensor, and g is the acceleration of gravity. The dot above u indicates total time derivative while bold face indicates a vector or tensor. The spatial gradient is denoted by ∇, the inner product between vectors is denoted by ⋅, while ∇⋅ represents the divergence operator. This equation must be complemented with appropriate initial and boundary conditions. The motion is described using a Lagrangian formulation.

The momentum equation is discretized using a two- or three-dimensional (2D or 3D), unstructured mesh. The displacement x, velocity u, acceleration a, force f, and temperature T are nodal values on linear (P1) elements while other physical quantities (e.g., stress σ and strain ϵ) and material properties (e.g., density ρ and viscosity η) are evaluated on the one-point quadrature in the elements; and thus are piecewise constant (P0). A weak form of the momentum balance equation is constructed by the standard finite element method. The velocity function u is expanded with piecewise linear basis functions: u(x)=a∑​ua​Na​(x), where Na​(x) is the basis function associated with global node number a in the mesh with the property, Ni​(xj​)=δij​ for the coordinates of j-th node, xj​. Na​(x)'s are also used as weighting functions and multipled to both sides of the equation, and the product is integrated over the domain: ∫Ω​Na​ρu˙dΩ=∫Ω​Na​(∇⋅σ+ρg)dΩ,a=0,…,N, where N+1 is the total number of nodes in a mesh. Plugging in the finite dimensional representation of u and carrying out the element-to-global assemablage, we obtain the following equation for the acceleration aa​ of every node a: ma​aa​=fa​=faint​+fabc​+faext​. ma​ is the nodal mass given by ma​=e∑​(∫Ωe​​Nea​ρf​dΩ)=e∑​(ρf​∫Ωe​​Nea​dΩ)=e∑a∈e​(M1​ρf​Ωe​), where Ωe​ is the area (volume in 3D) of the element e, Nae​ is Na​ confined to element e, and M is the number of apexes of an element (i.e., M=3 for 2D triangles and M=4 for 3D tetrahedra.) The summation should be understood as done for all the elements having node a as an apex. ☝ Two features to note Fictitious density, ρf​, instead of the true density, ρ, is used in the definition of ma​. Row-sum mass lumping is applied to obtain a diagonal mass matrix. The total force fa​ is composed of three parts: the internal, boundary, and external forces. The internal force, faint​, is defined as: faint​​=e∑​(∫Ωe​​∂x∂Nae​​⋅σdΩ)=e∑​(∂x∂Nae​​⋅σ∫Ωe​​dΩ)=e∑a∈e​(∂x∂Nae​​⋅σΩe​).​ Neumann boundary conditions are tractions prescribed on the surface of the body. These tractions yield a boundary force denoted fabc​: fabc​=e∑​(∮∂Ωe​​−Nae​σ⋅ndL)=−e∑a∈s,s∈∂Ωe​​(M−11​σs​⋅ns​Ls​). The summation is over the boundary segment s, which has a length Ls​ (surface area in 3D), the outward, unit normal vector n, and a prescribed (constant) stress σs​ on the Neumann boundary. The external force, faext​, is given by: faext​=e∑​(∫Ωe​​Nae​ρgdΩ)=e∑​(ρg∫Ωe​​Nae​dΩ)=e∑a∈e​(M1​ρgΩe​). When deriving the equations above, we utilize the fact that ρf​, ρ, ∂x∂Nae​​, σ, and g are constants on each element, and these identities: ∫Ωe​​dΩ=Ωe​,∫Ωe​​Nae​dΩ=M1​Ωe​,∮∂Ωe​​Nae​dL=M−11​Ls​.

We are interested in tectonic deformation, which can be properly simulated in a quasi-static fashion. Thus, we apply a technique called dynamic relaxation, which enables us to achieve a static equilibrium from the dynamic momentum equation by damping out the intertial force. Additionally, using mass scaling, we substitute the true density by a fictitious scaled density that allows us to increase the size of admissible stable time steps in the explicit time integration scheme. That is, using the resulting scaled acceleration and velocity, we compute an instantaneous velocity and position of each node in the mesh, which updates the model geometry at each time step.
documents.s: The rest of the explicit solution scheme

documents.t: The stress tensor is updated using the strain rate and strain tensors according to an appropriate constitutive relationship. Since the stress update calculations are performed at the element level, we drop the subscript e to simplify notation. The EVP material model is approximated by a composite rheology which uses visco-elastic and elasto-plastic sub-models. With the bulk modulus Ks​, shear modulus G, viscosity η, cohesion C, and internal friction angle ϕ, we calculate the visco-elastic stress σve​ and the elasto-plastic stress σep​. The visco-elastic stress increment Δσve​ is calculated assuming a linear Maxwell material, where a total deviatoric strain increment Δϵ is composed of the elastic and the viscous components while the deviatoric stress increment is identical for each component: dev(Δϵ)=2Gdev(Δσve​)​+2ηdev(σve​)Δt​ Substituting Δϵ with ϵt+Δt−ϵt, Δσve​ with σvet+Δt​−σt, and σve​ with (σvet+Δt​+σt)/2, the equation above is reduced to: Writing s=devσ and Δϵ=ϵt+Δt−ϵt, r=2ηGΔt​,st+Δt=1+r(1−r)st+2Gdev(Δϵ)​. The isotropic stress components are updated based on the volume change. As a result, the visco-elastic stress is: σvet+Δt​=st+Δt+(σmt​+Ks​Δεv​)I. Here Δεv​=Δttrϵ˙ and σmt​ is the old mean normal stress, using the same normal components as the deviatoric projection. Without a volumetric strain increment, the mean stress is retained. The elasto-plastic stress σep​ is computed using linear elasticity and the Mohr-Coulomb (MC) failure criterion with a general (associative or non-associative) flow rule. Following a standard operator-splitting scheme [e.g., @Lubliner1990; @SimoHugh2004; @Wilkins1964a], an elastic trial stress σelt+Δt​ is first calculated as σelt+Δt​=σt+(Ks​−32​G)tr(ϵ˙t+Δt)IΔt+2Gϵ˙t+ΔtΔt. If the elastic trial stress, σelt+Δt​, is inside or on both yield surfaces, the stress does not need a plastic correction. With the signs defined below, the admissible conditions are fs​≥0 for shear and ft​≤0 for tension. So, σept+Δt​ is set to be equal to σelt+Δt​. However, if σelt+Δt​ is outside the yield surface, we project it onto the yield surface using a return-mapping algorithm [@SimoHugh2004]. In the case of a Mohr-Coulomb material, it is convenient to express the yield function for shear failure in terms of principal stresses: fs​(σ1​,σ3​)=σ1​−Nϕ​σ3​+2CNϕ​​, where σ1​ and σ3​ are the maximal and minimal compressive principal stresses with the sign convention that tension is positive (i.e., σ1​≤σ2​≤σ3​), C is the material's cohesion, Nϕ​=1−sinϕ1+sinϕ​, Nϕ​​=1−sinϕcosϕ​, and ϕ is an internal friction angle (<90∘). The yield function for tensile failure is defined as ft​(σ3​)=σ3​−σt​, where σt​ is the tension cut-off. If a value for the tension cut-off is given as a parameter, the smallest value between the theoretical limit (C/tanϕ) and the given value is assigned to σt​. This comparison is required because the theoretical limit is not constant in the strain weakening case, where the material cohesion, C, and the friction angle ϕ may change. The classic two-principal-stress construction selects between shear and tensile return with the auxiliary function fh​(σ1​,σ3​), which bisects the obtuse angle made by two yield functions on the σ1​-σ3​ plane, as fh​(σ1​,σ3​)​=σ3​−σt​+(Nϕ2​+1​+Nϕ​)(σ1​−Nϕ​σt​+2CNϕ​​).​ In that construction, once yielding is identified, that is, fs​(σel,1​,σel,3​)<0 or ft​(σel,3​)>0, the mode of failure (shear or tensile) is decided based on the value of fh​, in other words, shear failure occurs if fh​(σel,1​,σel,3​)<0, tensile failure occurs otherwise. The current 3D and full plane-strain routines also check principal-stress ordering, the tensile cap and Mohr–Coulomb edges. An elastic trial stress above the tensile cap can still admit a pure shear return below that cap; it does not by itself establish tensile plastic flow. The equations below describe a smooth yield face; edge returns require the additional active constraints. See the Salençon benchmark. The flow rule for frictional materials is in general non-associative, that is, the direction of plastic flow in the principal stress space during plastic flow is not the same as the direction of the vector normal to the yield surface. As in the definitions of yield functions, the plastic flow potential for shear failure in the Mohr-Coulomb model can be defined as gs​(σ1​,σ3​)=σ1​−1−sinψ1+sinψ​σ3​, where ψ is the dilation angle. Likewise, the tensile flow potential is given as gt​(σ3​)=σ3​−σt​. In the presence of plasticity, the total strain increment Δϵ is given by Δϵ=Δϵel​+Δϵpl​, where Δϵel​ and Δϵpl​ are the elastic and plastic strain increments, respectively. The plastic strain increment is normal to the flow potential surface and can be written as Δϵpl​=β∂σ∂g​, where β is the plastic flow magnitude. β is computed by requiring that the updated stress state lies on the yield surface, f(σept+Δt​)=f(σt+Δσep​)=0. In the principal component representation, σA​=EAB​ϵB​ where σA​ and ϵA​ are the principal stress and strain, respectively, and E is a corresponding elastic moduli matrix with components: EAB​EAB​​=(Ks​−32​G)=(Ks​+34​G)​​if A=B,otherwise.​ By applying the consistency condition and using σelt+Δt​=σt+E⋅Δϵ (in the principal component representation), we obtain the following formulae for β β=∑B​(E1B​∂σB​∂gs​​−Nϕ​E3B​∂σB​∂gs​​)σel,1t+Δt​−Nϕ​σel,3t+Δt​+2CNϕ​​​for shear failure, and β=∂σ3​∂gt​​σel,3t+Δt​−σt​​for tensile failure. Likewise, ∂g/∂σ takes different forms according to the failure mode: ∂g/∂σ1​∂g/∂σ2​∂g/∂σ3​​=1=0=−1−sinψ1+sinψ​​(for shear failure,) and ∂g/∂σ1​∂g/∂σ2​∂g/∂σ3​​=0=0=1​(for tensile failure.) Once Δϵpl​ is computed, σep​ is updated as σep​=σelt+Δt​−E⋅Δϵpl​. in the principal component representation and transformed back to the orignal coordinate system. After the visco-elastic stress σve​ and elasto-plastic stress σep​ are evaluated, we compute the second invariant of the deviatoric components of each. If the visco-elastic stress has a smaller second invariant (J2​), σve​ is be used as the updated stress; otherwise, σep​ is used. The fundamental deformation measures in DynEarthSol are strain rates. Thus, the stress update by rate-independent constitutive models like elasto-plastic stresses need to be considered as the time-integration of the rate form of the corresponding stresses. Since a stress rate is not frame-indifferent in general, an objective (or co-rotational) stress rate needs to be constructed and integrated instead. The Jaumann stress rate is our choice for DynEarthSol among the possible objective rates because of its simplicity. The Jaumann stress rate (σ˙ˇ) is defined as σ˙ˇ=σ˙−ω⋅σ+σ⋅ω, where ω is the spin tensor, which is defined as, ωij​=21​(∂xj​∂ui​​−∂xi​∂uj​​). Based on this definition, the new objective stress (σˇt+Δt) is, σˇt+Δt=σt+Δt+Δt(σt+Δt⋅wt+Δt−wt+Δt⋅σt+Δt), where σt+Δt is the updated stress equal to either σve​ or σep​, depending on which has a lower value of J2​.

The elasto-plastic-rsf and elasto-visco-plastic-rsf rheologies use the update above with a Mohr–Coulomb friction angle set by rate-and-state friction. The friction law, the slip-rate measures (control.rsf_slip_rate_projection_option) and the state-change time-step limit (control.rsf_dtheta_max) are described in Rate-and-state friction.

This page describes damping in the default explicit momentum path (control.has_PT = no). PT's optional adaptive dynamic relaxation (PT_option = 1) has its own mass and damping construction; see Pseudo-transient mechanics. Given that our main interest is in long-term tectonic modeling, high-frequency vibrations are not relevant to the overall deformation pattern. A strong and efficient damping is necessary to achieve quasi-static solutions of the dynamic equation. Complementarily, force amplification might be needed to accelerate the transient process to achieve equilibrium. Therefore, we either damp or amplify the total net force in the discretized nodal momentum equation, ma​aa​=fa​, according to the direction of velocity (Cundall, 1989): mai​=(fdamped​)i​=fi​−0.8sgn(ui​)∣fi​∣, where subscript i denotes the i-th component of a vector and sgn denotes the signum function. The motivation for the choice of damping/amplification is based on the simple observation that in an under-damped oscillator, the direction of force is always opposite to the velocity direction, while in an over-damped system, the direction of the force is parallel to the velocity direction. We found that this choice of damping/amplification accomplishes the design goals satisfactorily (i.e., robustly and economically).

With its default moving mesh, DynEarthSol follows the deforming material: nodes move with the velocity, so every quantity below is carried by the material and time derivatives follow it. This page collects the equations and the conventions; each section links to the page that treats it in detail.

Quantity Where it lives Symbol velocity, position nodes u, x temperature nodes T pore pressure (with fluid flow) nodes p stress, strain, plastic strain elements σ, ε, εp​ material identity markers Stress and strain are positive in tension; pore pressure is positive in compression. Depth is negative z (the top of the box is at z=0). In 2D the coordinates are x and z. Elements are linear simplices (triangles in 2D, tetrahedra in 3D), so strain and stress are constant in each element.

ρI​dtdu​=∇⋅σ+ρb​g. DES integrates this equation explicitly. For slow tectonic deformation the inertia is scaled up (mass scaling) and damped (dynamic relaxation) to approach a quasistatic response, or each physical step is solved to equilibrium by pseudo-transient iteration. Scaled explicit/GVS runs still require force-balance and physical-step checks for their loading path. See Solution scheme. ρI​ constructs the inertial mass, while ρb​ supplies physical weight. Mass scaling changes the former, not the gravitational load.

The stress follows the strain history through the material's rheology: elastic, viscous, Maxwell, elasto-plastic or elasto-visco-plastic, with optional rate-and-state friction. The stress rate is objective: after the constitutive update of each step, the stress and strain are rotated by the element's spin (the Jaumann rate). See Rheology for the laws, Constitutive update for their integration and Rate-and-state friction.

Without hydraulics, the solid density of an element varies with temperature, ρ=ρ0​[1−α(T−273 K)], averaged over the materials of its markers; it does not change with pressure or volumetric strain. It enters gravity, while volume change is resisted by the bulk modulus in the constitutive law. Hydraulics adds mixture weight, with saturation-dependent fluid content; the optional finite-density mode has inventory-based weight. These physical weights are distinct from the fictitious inertial mass used by quasistatic explicit/GVS mechanics. See Poromechanics.
ρcp​dtdT​=∇⋅(k∇T)+ρH+Qs​+Qi​, with radiogenic, shear and injected heat. See Heat transport.

With control.has_hydraulic_diffusion = yes, the stress in the momentum balance is the total stress of a fluid-saturated or partly saturated solid, σ=σ′−αB​χpI for effective stress σ′ and Biot coefficient αB​. χ=1 for saturated material and χ=Se​ for the Bishop retention law. The pore pressure obeys a fluid mass balance with Darcy flow. See Poromechanics.

Markers carry material identity and change it by phase changes; the top surface erodes and receives sediment by surface processes; and the mesh is rebuilt when it distorts, with fields mapped to the new mesh (Remeshing).
Velocity, traction, temperature and pressure conditions and the initial temperature, stress and weak zones are set per model; see the User guide.

The mesh moves with the material, but it is rebuilt when it distorts, and an element then no longer holds one rock. DES therefore tracks material identity with markers: points that move with the deformation, each carrying a material index. An element's properties are the marker-weighted means described in Rheology.

Each marker stores the element that contains it and its barycentric coordinates there, so it moves exactly with the element and needs no search while the mesh only deforms. After remeshing, every marker is located in the new mesh. Initial markers. markers.init_marker_option = 1 scatters markers.markers_per_element markers randomly in each element (seeded by markers.random_seed); 2 places them on a regular grid with spacing markers.init_marker_spacing, in units of mesh.resolution. Their material comes from ic.mattype_option: 0 takes the region of a .poly mesh, 1 assigns horizontal layers at ic.mattype_layer_depths (in units of mesh.zlength), and 101 calls a custom routine in the source. Replenishment. Remeshing and stretching can leave an element with few markers. When it holds fewer than markers.min_num_markers_in_element, a marker is added. Its material follows markers.replenishment_option: 0 material 0, 1 drawn from the materials of the element and its neighbours in proportion, 2 the material of the nearest marker; the parameter reference lists the other options.

A phase change converts a marker from one material to another when its pressure and temperature cross a reaction boundary; the element properties then follow the new marker counts. mat.phase_change_option selects the rules: Option Rules 0 none (default) 1 a fixed set of subduction rules on fixed material indices 0–7 3 the subduction rule engine: rules switched on one by one, materials named by parameters 101 a custom routine in phasechanges.cxx Phase changes need at least two materials.

Each rule converts the material named by one mat.mattype_* parameter into another when its predicate holds. Depth d is measured below the current local free surface; temperature T is in °C below. The pressure P (compression positive) is the mean stress of the marker's element with mat.phase_change_pressure_option = 0, so tectonic over- and underpressure move the boundaries, or the lithostatic reference pressure at that depth with 1. Switch Conversion Boundary mat.has_eclogitization (on) oceanic crust → eclogite T≥400, d≥20 km, P≥−0.3+0.0022T GPa and P≥20.1−0.0375T GPa (Hacker et al., 2003) mat.has_serpentinization (on) mantle above wet slab crust → serpentinite inside the antigorite stability field (Ulmer & Trommsdorff, 1995) and within mat.serpentinization_thickness above oceanic crust or sediment, no deeper than mat.serpentinization_max_depth mat.has_serpentinization (on) serpentinite → mantle T≥550 and outside the antigorite field mat.has_hydrous_mantle_dehydration (off) hydrous (chlorite-bearing) mantle → mantle T≥880−3.5×10−8(d−62 km)2, d in m (Grove et al., 2009) mat.has_sediment_metamorphism (off) sediment → sedimentary rock T≥80 and d≥2 km sedimentary rock → metasediment T≥250 or d≥7 km metasediment → schist P≥0.88−0.176(710.8−T)/48.5 GPa, a metapelite dehydration boundary (Wei et al., 2004) The antigorite field is the wedge between the lines through (730 °C, 2.1 GPa)–(500 °C, 7.5 GPa) and (730 °C, 2.1 GPa)–(650 °C, 0.2 GPa). Using one field for both serpentinite rules means no pressure and temperature satisfy both, so a marker cannot flip back and forth. Where the mantle serpentinizes. Water released by the slab hydrates the mantle above it. DES finds the slab with a background grid of cells of size mesh.vt_size (in units of mesh.resolution): a cell is wet crust when more than mat.wet_crust_fraction_threshold of its markers are oceanic crust, sediment or sedimentary rock. A mantle marker serpentinizes when such a cell lies below it within mat.serpentinization_thickness, optionally only if the marker is also horizontally within the wet crust's extent plus mat.serpentinization_wet_crust_margin. Each active rule needs its source and target materials set (mat.mattype_oceanic_crust, mat.mattype_eclogite, mat.mattype_serpentinite, mat.mattype_mantle, mat.mattype_hydrous_mantle, mat.mattype_sediment, mat.mattype_sediment_rock, mat.mattype_metasediment, mat.mattype_schist); DES stops at start-up if one is missing, out of range or equal to its target. The rules and boundaries follow those of GeoFLAC. The subduction tutorial uses this option.

Option 1 uses fixed material indices: 0 mantle, 1 serpentinized mantle, 2 oceanic crust, 3 eclogite, 4 sediment, 5 schist, 6 and 7 upper and lower continental crust, and the pressure is always the lithostatic reference pressure. Oceanic crust becomes eclogite above 500 °C and P>−0.3+0.0022TK​ GPa, with TK​ in kelvin; sediment becomes schist above 650 °C deeper than 20 km; serpentinite returns to mantle above 550 °C past the (730 °C, 2.1 GPa)–(500 °C, 7.5 GPa) line. With control.has_hydration_processes = yes, crust and sediment hotter than 150 °C release water as separate hydrous markers, which rise at control.hydration_migration_speed; mantle below 550 °C that holds a hydrous marker becomes serpentinite.

Grove, T. L., Till, C. B., Lev, E., Chatterjee, N., & Médard, E. (2009). Kinematic variables and water transport control the formation and location of arc volcanoes. Nature, 459, 694–697. Hacker, B. R., Abers, G. A., & Peacock, S. M. (2003). Subduction factory Theoretical mineralogy, densities, seismic wave speeds, and H₂O contents. Journal of Geophysical Research, 108(B1), 2029. Ulmer, P., & Trommsdorff, V. (1995). Serpentine stability to mantle depths and subduction-related magmatism. Science, 268, 858–861. Wei, C., Powell, R., & Clarke, G. L. (2004). Calculated phase equilibria for low- and medium-pressure metapelites in the KFMASH and KMnFMASH systems. Journal of Metamorphic Geology, 22, 495–508.

The Courant-Friedrichs-Lewy (CFL) condition imposes a fundamental limit on the time step size for an explicit time marching scheme. In the explicit time integration used in DynEarthSol, the P-wave velocity sets the largest possible time step size. For instance, using relevant parameters for lithospheric modeling, a P-wave speed of ∼103 m/s and an element size of ∼103 m yield a stable time step size of ∼ 1 s. With this stringent upper limit for the time step size, a typical LTM simulation would take an excessively large number of time steps to reach the targeted amount of deformation (e.g., O(1013) steps for 1 Myrs of model time). To overcome this drawback, a mass scaling technique is applied. We adjust each nodal mass (density) to achieve a stable time step size which is orders of magnitude larger than the one allowed by the physical density. Increasing mass also increases inertia at a given acceleration; the approximation is useful only when the resulting inertial forces remain small relative to the mechanical loads. Check that separation for the chosen loading path. The time step size increases when the elastic wave speed, uelastic​, is made comparable to the tectonic speed, utectonic​, (∼10−9 m/s). We achieve this time-step size increase by scaling the density as follows: uelastic​=Ks​/ρf​​=c1​utectonic​, where Ks​ is the bulk modulus of the material, ρf​ is a fictitious scaled density and c1​ is a constant.

When c1​ is too small, that is, the density is scaled up too high, dynamic instabilities might occur. In this case, the fictitious elastic wave is too slow to relax the stress back to quasi-equilibrium, therefore the kinetic energy becomes too large, breaking the assumption of the quasi-static state. When the density scaling is insufficient (i.e., c1​ is too large), the simulation becomes too time consuming. The density approaches its physical value when c1​utectonic​ approaches the bulk-based speed Ks​/ρ​. There is no universal value of c1​ for this transition. control.inertial_scaling sets c1​ when control.is_quasi_static = yes with ordinary explicit/GVS mechanics. The coupled-method comparisons include 104, 105 and 106; no single value establishes equilibrium for every load, material or mesh. Compare physical-step refinement, force residuals and observables, especially for sudden traction. With is_quasi_static = no, the inertial mass is physical and this scaling parameter has no effect. PT has a separate pseudo-time relaxation.

When use_global_velocity_scaling is enabled, the mass-scaled density and the elastic time step are limited by an elastic wave speed derived from the material moduli. mass_scaling_reference_speed selects which modulus sets that ceiling: Value Ceiling Notes shear (default) G/ρ​ Historical behavior. bulk Ks​/ρ​ Uses the bulk modulus instead. Leaving the option at its default reproduces earlier results.
documents.s: Reference speed for global velocity scaling

documents.t: The linear triangular elements used in DynEarthSol2D are known to suffer volumetric locking when subject to incompressible deformations. Since incompressible plastic or viscous flow are often needed in LTM, we adopt an anti-volumetric locking correction based on the nodal mixed discretization (NMD) methodology (e.g., De Micheli and Mocellin, 2009). The strain rate of element e, ϵ˙e​, is computed from the velocity: ϵ˙e,ijt+Δt​=21​a∈e∑​(∂xi​∂Nae​​ua,jt+Δt​+∂xj​∂Nae​​ua,it+Δt​), where i, j are spatial indices. The strain rate tensor can be decomposed into the deviatoric and the isotropic parts: ϵ˙e​=dev(ϵ˙e​)+D1​tr(ϵ˙e​)I, where dev(⋅) represents an operator returning the deviatoric tensor, tr(⋅) is an operator returning the trace of the projected tensor. D=2 for the in-plane projection in 2D and D=3 in 3D. The code corrects the NDIMS diagonal strain-rate components, including in a supported 2D plane-strain update. Plane strain keeps the out-of-plane strain at zero and tracks its stress separately; it does not add a third projected strain component here. The basic idea is to average volumetric strain rate over a group of neighboring elements and then replace each element's volumetric strain rate with the averaged one. The NMD method first assigns an area (volume in 3D) average of the trace of ϵ˙e​ to each node a: ε˙a​=e∑a∈e​Ωe​e∑a∈e​tr(ϵ˙e​)Ωe​​. Then the nodal field ε˙a​ is interpolated back to the element to retrieve an averaged volumetric strain rate for an element e: ϵ˙ˉe​=a∈e∑​M1​ε˙a​, where, as before, M is the number of apexes in an element. Finally, the averaged volumetric strain rate of an element is used to modify the original strain rate tensor. The anti-locking modification replaces the isotropic part with ϵ˙ˉe​: ϵ˙e′​=dev(ϵ˙e​)+D1​ϵ˙ˉe​I This modified strain rate tensor substitutes the original strain rate tensor when updating strain tensor and in defining constitutive update. For the sake of brevity, we drop the prime and use ϵ˙ to refer the modified strain rate tensor from now on. The strain tensor ϵ is accumulated: ϵet+Δt​=ϵet​+Δtϵ˙et+Δt​

DES3D can couple the flow of one pore fluid with deformation of the solid skeleton. Pore pressure changes the effective stress and therefore the strength, and deformation changes the pore pressure. Optional extensions cover partly saturated ground, groundwater heat transport, thermal pressurization, evolving porosity and permeability, and an immobile matrix reservoir. Fluid and heat transport use explicit substeps. The mechanical solver can use ordinary explicit stepping, GVS or PT relaxation; local pressure/content conversions do not introduce a global implicit flow solve. Hydraulics is enabled with control.has_hydraulic_diffusion = yes.

Stress and strain are positive in tension, as elsewhere in DES3D. Pore pressure p is positive in compression, so suction is −p. The vertical coordinate z points up, and gravity acts in −z. The volumetric strain is εv​ and the mean stress σm​.

The skeleton responds to the effective stress (Biot, 1941): σ′=σ+αpI, where σ is the total stress and α the Biot–Willis coefficient (mat.biot_coeff). With mat.derive_biot_coeff_from_bulk_moduli = yes, DES3D sets α=1−K/Ks​ from the drained bulk modulus K (mat.bulk_modulus) and the grain modulus Ks​ (mat.bulk_modulus_s) (Biot and Willis, 1957). The plastic models use the effective stress in their yield functions. A rise in pore pressure moves the Mohr circle toward failure without changing the deviatoric stress. The stored stress remains the total stress, which balances the external loads.

The default control.hydraulic_content_model = 0 uses the linear excess fluid volume per unit bulk volume (Rice and Cleary, 1976) ζ=αεv​+Mp​−β(T−T0​),M1​=Kf​ϕ​+Ks​α−ϕ​, with porosity ϕ (mat.porosity), fluid bulk modulus Kf​ (mat.fluid_bulk_modulus) and Biot modulus M. The thermal term applies only with thermal pressurization (below). Valid materials satisfy 0≤ϕ≤α≤1.

The Darcy flux is q=−μkr​​k(∇p+ρf​gez​), where μ is the fluid viscosity (mat.fluid_visc), ρf​ the reference fluid density (mat.fluid_rho0) and kr​ the relative permeability (kr​=1 when saturated). The permeability tensor is the scalar intrinsic permeability (mat.hydraulic_perm, m²) times a dimensionless symmetric positive-definite tensor (mat.permeability_tensor = [xx,yy,zz,xy,xz,yz], isotropic by default). In 2D its x–z part is used. Fluid mass balance closes the system: ∂t∂ζ​+∇⋅q=Q, where Q is a volumetric source from wells or point sources.

For the default hydraulic model, gravity uses the mixture density ρ=(1−ϕ)ρs​+ϕSρf​, with the temperature-dependent solid density ρs​ and saturation S (S=1 when saturated). The same density loads a wet Winkler foundation. The reference solid density is mat.rho0. Without hydraulics, gravity uses the solid density alone. This gravity density must be distinguished from inertial mass. With control.is_quasi_static = yes, ordinary explicit mechanics and GVS use fictitious masses set by mass scaling. The default hydraulic model's unscaled mass and wave estimates use the saturated mixture (S=1), even when gravity uses a lower saturation. The finite-density model below has a separate inventory-based weight.

Each physical step advances mechanics once and pressure over the same interval. Which quantity drives the pressure depends on the mechanical solver. Strain-driven form (default content model). With ordinary explicit mechanics or GVS and pressure feedback enabled, pressure advances first from the strain rate projected from the current velocity: M1​p˙​=−αε˙v​−∇⋅q+Q. The stress and nodal forces then use the new pressure. Unscaled physical inertia also uses this ordering. The sealed elastic limit gives the undrained longitudinal wave; relative-fluid inertia is not integrated as a separate momentum equation. Fixed-stress form (PT mechanics). Mechanics first reaches equilibrium for the step. Pressure then follows from the accepted change in mean total stress, with the fixed-stress storage (Kim et al., 2011): Sσ​Δp=−Kb​α​Δσm​−Δt(∇⋅q−Q),Sσ​=M1​+Kb​α2​. Kb​=K in 3D. In 2D, σm​ is the in-plane mean stress and Kb​=K+G/3. The pressure change enters the effective stress in the next mechanical update. Saving it in checkpoints makes restarts exact. Because mechanics sees the pressure one step late, the coupling error is first order in Δt. control.has_poroelastic_pressure_feedback = no removes the mechanical source term (the ε˙v​ or Δσm​ term). Pressure still diffuses and still acts on the effective stress. In quasistatic explicit/GVS runs with feedback disabled, storage is Sσ​, as in the reduced fixed-stress flow model; unscaled physical inertia uses 1/M. Removing feedback therefore does not mean keeping the same diffusivity as every coupled explicit case. It does not disable the pressure's effect on skeleton strength.

The fixed-stress mechanical return samples pn​, while a completed saved frame pairs its stress with pn+1​. For a saturated Mohr–Coulomb material, let N=(1+sinϕ)/(1−sinϕ) and qc​=2cN​. The admissible slack at the sampled pressure and the saved-frame diagnostic obey fn​=σmin​+αpn​−N(σmax​+αpn​)+qc​,fsaved​=fn​−(N−1)α(pn+1​−pn​). A negative saved-frame slack during a pressure rise can therefore measure coupling lag. In the recorded pressure-driven slope, doubling 404 to 808 steps reduces the minimum in-plane saved-pressure slack from −205.617 to −102.843 Pa; using the sampled pressure gives −0.000744 and −0.000226 Pa. This timing check does not replace the three-principal material return checks. Hydraulic subcycling does not remove the mechanical lag. After plastic yielding, the pressure source uses accepted total volumetric strain, rather than converting stress through elastic moduli. The sealed plastic cell checks the matching fixed-stress recurrence. With retention, the Bishop cell checks its own rate equation and matching stabilization.
documents.s: Pressure sampled by a plastic return

documents.t: Pressure diffusion often needs smaller steps than mechanics. Within each physical step DES3D advances pressure in explicit substeps. Their size is set by the assembled lumped storage and conductance. A long physical step, including control.fixed_dt, can therefore contain many stable transport substeps. This does not make an oversized mechanical step stable or remove the coupling lag. Mechanics, porosity and other histories advance once per physical step. Scheduled flux and source amounts use their exact schedule integrals; prescribed pressures are imposed at substep endpoints.

Each face has a hydraulic type, bc.hbc_x0 to bc.hbc_z1 (y faces in 3D only): Type Condition 0 No normal flow (default) 1 Hold the initial nodal pressure 2 Prescribed pressure from bc.hbc_pressure (Pa) 3 Prescribed outward Darcy flux from bc.hbc_flux (m/s) bc.hbc_pressure and bc.hbc_flux list six values in the order x0 x1 y0 y1 z0 z1. A shared piecewise-linear multiplier, bc.hbc_schedule_time_in_yr and bc.hbc_schedule_ratio with bc.num_hbc_schedule entries, scales types 2 and 3 in time. A repeated time makes a step; the ratio is held outside the table. Two faces that meet must prescribe the same pressure at their shared nodes. ic.pore_pressure_option sets the initial pressure: Value Initial pressure 0 (default) Hydrostatic, p=−ρf​g(z−zw​) with water table zw​ = ic.water_table_z, plus ic.excess_pore_pressure away from the boundaries 1 Linear in x between the pressures prescribed on the x0 and x1 faces 2 Uniform, ic.pore_pressure_value Above the water table the hydrostatic pressure is negative (suction).

Wells are vertical screens with a prescribed volume rate: bc.num_wells, bc.well_x, bc.well_y (3D), bc.well_z_top, bc.well_z_bottom and bc.well_rate. The rate is m³/s in 3D and m²/s per unit out-of-plane length in 2D; positive extracts. The rate is spread uniformly along the screen and integrated exactly against the element shape functions. All wells share one schedule, bc.well_schedule_time_in_yr and bc.well_schedule_ratio. Each step applies the exact time average of the schedule, so the pumped volume does not depend on the step size. Point sources ([injection] section) supply or extract fluid at chosen points, with a constant rate or a total amount over a time window. Positive rates supply fluid. With fluid heat advection, an injected temperature can be set. A parallel [heat_injection] section supplies heat at points.

Setting mat.retention_model to a nonzero value per material enables Richards flow (Richards, 1931) with the gas phase at zero gauge pressure. With suction s=max(−p,0), effective saturation Se​ and residual saturation Sr​ (mat.residual_saturation), the saturation is S=Sr​+(1−Sr​)Se​: retention_model Se​ kr​ 0 1 (saturated) 1 1 van Genuchten–Mualem [1+(as)n]−m, m=1−1/n Se1/2​[1−(1−Se1/m​)m]2 2 Brooks–Corey–Burdine (as)−n for as>1, else 1 Se3+2/n​ 3 Gardner e−as Se​ Here a is mat.retention_alpha (1/Pa) and n is mat.retention_n (van Genuchten, 1980; Mualem, 1976). For Brooks–Corey, 1/a is the air-entry pressure and n the pore-size index. The pressure-dependent nodal content is ϕS(p)+sp, where s is 1/M in the strain-driven form or Sσ​ in the fixed-stress form. Mechanical source increments are assembled separately. DES3D updates this content explicitly and inverts it for pressure node by node. Its positive capacity gives one local root. Effective stress uses Bishop's form with χ=Se​ (Lu et al., 2010): σ′=σ+αSe​(p)pI. Suction therefore adds apparent cohesion to a partly saturated slope. dppressure remains the raw pold​−pnew​. Each element evaluates its own Bishop increment Se​(pold​)pold​−Se​(pnew​)pnew​ with its own retention law, averaging the nodal products over the element. This differs from multiplying an averaged saturation by an averaged pressure. Matching fixed-stress terms use the same element law. Elements saturated at both states keep the saturated arithmetic. Retention cannot yet be combined with evolving porosity or permeability, thermal pressurization, fluid heat advection or matrix exchange.

With mat.porosity_model = 1, porosity follows the deformation through an element history, the pore strain εϕ​. Each step adds Δεϕ​=Δεv​+Ks​Δp​−αs​ΔT−Δh,ϕ=α−(α−ϕ0​)e−εϕ​, where αs​ is the solid thermal expansivity (mat.alpha, used only with thermal pressurization), ϕ0​ the material porosity and Δh recovery of previously accepted plastic pore dilation (zero unless pore healing is enabled). A step that would leave 0<ϕ≤α stops the run with a diagnostic. mat.permeability_model lets permeability follow porosity: Value Permeability 0 (default) Fixed, k=k0​ 1 Kozeny–Carman k=k0​(ϕ0​ϕ​)3(1−ϕ1−ϕ0​​)2 2 power law k=k0​(ϕ/ϕ0​)n, n = mat.permeability_exponent (Costa, 2006; Yang et al., 2021).

Recovery uses signed plastic volume, including the out-of-plane stress in plane strain. Reversible pressure and thermal increments are excluded from the elastic stress change: Δεvp​=Δεv​−3Ktr3​Δσelastic​​. For remaining recoverable opening η≥0, each accepted interval uses Δh=ηn​(1−e−Δt/τ),ηn+1​=max(0,ηn​−Δh+Δεvp​). Closure precedes the new plastic increment; compaction reduces opening and is not itself healed. Elastic dilation does not enter η. With mat.pore_healing_time =τ0​>0, τ(T)=τ0​(T/T0​)exp[REa​​(T−1−T0−1​)], where mat.pore_healing_temperature is T0​ in K, mat.pore_healing_energy is Ea​ in J/mol and R=8.3144 J/(mol K). Mixed elements average recovery rates by marker count. Frozen pressure, strain and temperature give expelled pore volume δϕc​=(α−ϕn​)(eΔh−1); its negative increment enters the hydraulic source. Changing permeability alone would omit it. During a drained hold starting at the accepted state (η∗​,ϕ∗​), η(s)=η∗​e−s/τ,ϕ(s)=α−(α−ϕ∗​)eη∗​[1−e−s/τ]. Together with the chosen permeability law, this is the independent hold reference in check_recovery.py. The recorded 2D/3D controls use finite grain stiffness, signed dilation/compaction, elastic holds, restart, changed timestep and remeshing. PT trials freeze recovery; acceptance commits it once. Checkpoints require its history when enabling recovery. The qualification covers this property law and tangent Biot coupling; finite-density recovery energy and retentive remapping are outside it.

mat.matrix_storage (1/Pa per bulk volume) and mat.matrix_exchange (1/(Pa s)) add an immobile reservoir to each element, as in a double-porosity medium (Warren and Root, 1963). The reservoir exchanges fluid with the mobile pressure at the rate q=cx​(p−pm​). It starts at the mobile pressure, and the volume it gains is removed from the flow exactly. Its pressure is saved as matrix pressure.

With control.has_fluid_thermal_advection = yes, temperature is carried by the Darcy flux: CT˙+ρf​cf​q⋅∇T=∇⋅(λ∇T)+r,C=(1−ϕ)ρs​cs​+ϕρf​cf​, with fluid heat capacity cf​ (mat.fluid_heat_capacity). This is the default heat-capacity model; evolving storage requires the separate finite-density inventory below for retained sensible-energy accounting. The fluid density in Darcy gravity varies with temperature (Boussinesq), ρf​[1−αf​(T−T0​)], with αf​ = mat.fluid_alpha and T0​ the surface temperature. This drives free convection. Heat diffusion also runs in explicit substeps within each physical step. Thermal boundary types bc.tbc_x0 to bc.tbc_z1 select insulated (0) or prescribed-temperature (1) faces, with values in bc.tbc_val_* (K).

With control.has_thermal_pressurization = yes, heating expands both the solid and the pore fluid (McTigue, 1986; Rice, 2006). The solid adds a thermal stress −Kαs​ΔT to each normal component, and the fluid content gains the term −β(T−T0​) with β=ϕαf​+(α−ϕ)αs​. In a sealed or poorly drained region, heating therefore raises pore pressure and lowers effective stress. It requires hydraulic and thermal diffusion and an elastic bulk response.

After a remesh, nodal pressure is interpolated onto the new mesh like other nodal fields. For saturated material with fixed properties, DES3D then adjusts the pressure on free nodes by a common offset, so the total linear Biot content ∫ζdV is the same before and after the remesh. Prescribed-pressure nodes keep their values; domain changes and boundary reservoir reactions are accounted for separately. This is a global constraint, not conservation element by element. Partly saturated material and evolving porosity in the default model are interpolated without this adjustment. The optional inventory model has its own remap, below.

control.hydraulic_content_model = 1 selects a saturated inventory model. It requires pressure feedback, mat.porosity_model = 1, an elastic bulk response and control.is_quasi_static = yes; ordinary explicit mechanics, GVS and PT are available, but unscaled physical inertia is excluded. Retention, matrix exchange, surface processes and material phase conversion are outside this mode. All solid materials must share one fluid law. Constant compressibility and expansivity give ρf​(p,T)=ρf0​exp[p/Kf​−αf​(T−T0​)],Mf​=Vρf​ϕ. T0​ is the saved EOS temperature origin and the reference pressure is zero. This is a constitutive EOS, not a tabulated water-property model. The porosity law above is integrated over the accepted path. A moving mesh supplies V; a fixed mesh uses the virtual volume V0​exp(trε). That convention does not establish finite-strain mechanical accuracy. The forward transport step uses the starting substep's Darcy mass and sensible-heat fluxes. Converting the updated local inventories to pressure and temperature requires a local root, without a global implicit transport solve. A fixed-stress numerical mass buffer R is recorded separately: the split closes the Mf​+R budget, while physical mass alone retains a coupling defect that must decrease with physical-step refinement. R is neither fluid density nor heat capacity. For heat transport this mode requires both thermal pressurization and fluid thermal advection. Retained sensible energy is E=(Cs​+cf​Mf​)T, where Cs​ is the retained solid heat-capacity inventory. Injection uses inlet temperature and density; outflow uses the local state. Remapping transfers physical water, the numerical buffer, solid mass, Cs​, sensible energy and accepted pending shear energy, with domain and reservoir exchanges recorded separately. The constraint is global, not exact local inventory matching. Checkpoints preserve these inventories and their time levels when the next timestep changes. Full pressure work and thermoelastic caloric energy are outside this sensible-heat model. A closed ledger alone does not qualify a general thermal plume or complete earthquake-cycle energy balance.

Saved frames contain pore pressure and, when the corresponding model is active, porosity, permeability, saturation, effective saturation, relative permeability and matrix pressure. The field fluid balance lists, for the last step, the change in stored fluid, the mechanical and thermal source, well extraction, net boundary inflow and their residual. The residual measures how well the discrete update balances its own fluid volume. With content model 1, fluid mass and hydraulic split buffer separate physical mass from the numerical reservoir. The six entries of fluid mass balance are physical stored-mass change, buffer change, extraction, boundary inflow, reservoir reset and residual. With heat transport, sensible energy balance separates retained-energy change, supplied heat, well enthalpy, carried boundary heat, thermal reaction and residual. These mass and energy diagnostics are distinct from the default five-entry fluid balance.

Parameter Default Meaning control.has_hydraulic_diffusion no Enable pore-pressure transport control.has_poroelastic_pressure_feedback yes Let deformation drive pore pressure control.hydraulic_content_model 0 0 linear Biot/retention, 1 saturated finite-density inventory mat.porosity [0.0] Porosity ϕ0​ mat.hydraulic_perm [1e-14] Intrinsic permeability k0​ (m²) mat.permeability_tensor [1,1,1,0,0,0] Dimensionless anisotropy tensor mat.fluid_visc [1.002e-3] Fluid viscosity μ (Pa s) mat.fluid_rho0 [1000] Reference fluid density ρf​ (kg/m³) mat.fluid_bulk_modulus [2.17e9] Fluid bulk modulus Kf​ (Pa) mat.fluid_alpha [2.07e-4] Fluid thermal expansivity αf​ (1/K) mat.fluid_heat_capacity [4180] Fluid heat capacity cf​ (J/(kg K)) mat.biot_coeff [1.0] Biot–Willis coefficient α mat.bulk_modulus_s [37e9] Grain bulk modulus Ks​ (Pa) mat.derive_biot_coeff_from_bulk_moduli no Use α=1−K/Ks​ mat.retention_model [0] 0 saturated, 1 van Genuchten–Mualem, 2 Brooks–Corey, 3 Gardner mat.retention_alpha [1e-4] Retention parameter a (1/Pa) mat.retention_n [2] Retention exponent n mat.residual_saturation [0] Residual saturation Sr​ mat.porosity_model 0 0 fixed, 1 evolving with deformation mat.permeability_model 0 0 fixed, 1 Kozeny–Carman, 2 power law mat.permeability_exponent [3] Power-law exponent n mat.pore_healing_time [0] Recovery timescale of accepted plastic pore dilation; zero disables recovery mat.matrix_storage, mat.matrix_exchange [0], [0] Immobile reservoir storage (1/Pa) and exchange coefficient (1/(Pa s)) control.has_fluid_thermal_advection no Heat transport by Darcy flow control.has_thermal_pressurization no Thermal stress and thermal fluid content bc.hbc_x0 … bc.hbc_z1 0 Hydraulic boundary type per face bc.hbc_pressure, bc.hbc_flux zeros Face values for types 2 and 3 ic.pore_pressure_option 0 Initial pressure field ic.water_table_z 0 Initial water-table height (m)

With control.has_PT = yes, DES3D solves for quasi-static mechanical equilibrium within a physical timestep. The finite-element force assembly uses the spatial discretization shared with the explicit momentum path. PT adds an inner relaxation loop whose candidates all refer to the same physical increment. Configuration and diagnostic details are in Choosing a mechanical solver.

Let Hn​ denote the material history at the start of a physical step, Δt its physical duration, and xn​ its reference mesh. Each candidate velocity v(k) defines a constitutive trial H(k)=C(Hn​,∇v(k),Δt;xn​). C is the existing material update, including applicable plastic, viscous and frictional history. Every evaluation restores Hn​ first. Consequently, k trials do not represent kΔt of aging or viscous relaxation. Mixed stress correction is applied before candidate force evaluation. Acceptance commits the full constitutive candidate. With the default hydraulic content model, temperature advances once before a physical PT solve and remains fixed during its trials. The optional finite-density model instead advances its heat and water inventories after accepted mechanics. Hydraulic transport, mesh motion, stress rotation and remeshing remain outside the trial loop; see Poromechanics. Gradients, volumes, facet areas and normals remain on the reference mesh during mechanics. For moving-mesh physical steps, height-dependent foundation, water and side-support pressures include the candidate vertical displacement in their height argument. This is an incremental pressure-load correction, not a complete finite-deformation follower-load formulation.

Write the undamped assembled force as f=fint+fbc+fext. Let P be the orthogonal projector onto admissible homogeneous velocity perturbations, and let r be its total free rank. PT measures R=r∥Pf∥22​​​,r>0. For r=0, the free residual is defined as zero. On axis-aligned roller boundaries this removes constrained force components. Oblique constraints require projection onto their free directions. Support reactions are excluded; applied tractions, body forces and foundation loads remain. Artificial damping is excluded as well. The units are N/m in 2D and N in 3D. The affine velocity constraints enforce prescribed motion. Their homogeneous counterparts define the perturbation space. DES3D retains the ordered boundary dispatch and corner precedence of its boundary conditions; arbitrary contradictory prescriptions are not simultaneously enforced. The default acceptance threshold uses an absolute tolerance plus a relative tolerance times the first warm candidate's residual. The alternative running-scale criterion and its limitations are given in the convergence reference.
documents.s: Force balance in the admissible velocity space

documents.t: The previous physical velocity supplies the warm start. If that candidate already meets the threshold, it is accepted. Otherwise, a physical solve can also evaluate the affine prescribed velocity with zero free motion, and retain the finite candidate with the smaller residual. Both candidates evaluate the complete physical-dt constitutive response. This matters for a held elastic load: reusing the previous loading velocity could apply the same compression again. Zero free motion can represent its equilibrium. For a Maxwell material, however, zero velocity still permits constitutive relaxation over Δt and need not satisfy the imposed traction. A new equilibrium velocity must then produce continued creep. The elastic and Maxwell tutorials demonstrate the distinction.

PT_option = 0 uses localized dual-time stress/velocity relaxation. Its factors depend on mesh heights, effective viscosity, PT_CFL and PT_Re, following the effective-viscosity/dual-time approach of Räss et al. (2022). Lagged stress is solver scratch; acceptance always checks the full constitutive candidate. PT_option = 1 uses adaptive dynamic relaxation. A Gershgorin row-sum construction supplies nodal fictitious masses from the elastic/viscous velocity stiffness. A secant Rayleigh quotient estimates a low mode for adaptive damping; momentum is discarded when it opposes the current force. There is no lagged stress, and PT_CFL and PT_Re are unused. The row-sum construction bounds the magnitude of eigenvalues of the mass-scaled linear reference operator. It does not prove stability of the full nonlinear constrained problem. Both options share the force criterion, material acceptance and rollback behavior.

Initial body-force equilibration uses homogeneous supports and the instantaneous material skeleton, without transport, viscous relaxation or physical frictional aging. Plastic history is committed only for the accepted initial candidate. Maxwell and EVP initialization use their instantaneous skeletons; a pure viscous material has no such skeleton and is rejected for this initialization. Initial equilibrium precedes frame-zero output and monitor initialization, and completion is checkpointed. The saved PT residual force describes the accepted reference-geometry solve before hydraulic transport, mesh motion and stress rotation. For physical steps with thermal diffusion enabled, temperature has already been advanced. The report's stage=before_physical_updates refers to the later updates, not the preceding thermal stage. A force reconstructed from saved post-rotation stress can differ slightly, even on a fixed mesh. Remeshing invalidates this diagnostic until another solve is accepted. See PT force output. Neither relaxation scheme can produce a stable quasi-static equilibrium where the model has none. Strain softening can introduce negative stiffness; changing the numerical relaxation does not supply physical regularization. The implementation notes and validation record separate demonstrated cases from unresolved convergence limits.
documents.s: Initial equilibrium and diagnostic time level

documents.t: DES3D models faults as finite-width shear zones in a continuum. A rate-and-state friction (RSF) law sets the friction angle of the Mohr–Coulomb plastic model in every element. The friction coefficient then depends on how fast the element slips and on its slip history, so a fault can creep, heal, nucleate an instability and rupture within one simulation. The approach follows Tong and Lavier (2018); Herrendörfer et al. (2018) describe a related invariant formulation. This page gives the friction law, how DES3D measures slip rate in an element, and how the law enters the plastic update. It then describes global velocity scaling, which lets one model run through slow loading and fast rupture, and the other numerical controls. A benchmark checks the law in simple shear, and the tutorials show it at work in earthquake cycles and slip events in a shear band.

The friction coefficient is μ=μ0​+alnV0​V​+blnDc​V0​θ​, where V is the slip rate, θ the state variable (a time), V0​ a reference slip rate, Dc​ the characteristic slip distance, and a and b the direct-effect and evolution-effect parameters (Dieterich, 1979; Ruina, 1983). The reference coefficient μ0​ is the tangent of the element's Mohr–Coulomb friction angle, so μ=μ0​ when the element slides steadily at V0​. The state variable evolves by one of two laws. The aging law (Dieterich, 1979; Ruina, 1983) lets a fault heal while it is stationary: dtdθ​=1−Dc​Vθ​. The slip law (Ruina, 1983) changes the state only while the fault slips: dtdθ​=−Dc​Vθ​lnDc​Vθ​. Under both laws, steady sliding at rate V gives θss​=Dc​/V and the steady-state friction μss​=μ0​+(a−b)lnV0​V​. A material with a−b>0 is velocity strengthening: it strengthens as it slides faster and creeps stably. A material with a−b<0 is velocity weakening and can become unstable (Marone, 1998; Scholz, 1998). mat.state_var_model selects the law: Value Law Friction 0 (default) No state evolution μss​ at the current slip rate 1 Aging law full law 2 Slip law full law With 0 the friction follows the current slip rate instantly. This is steady-state friction and needs no Dc​.

The law needs a slip rate, but an element carries a strain rate. DES3D offers two measures, chosen with control.rsf_slip_rate_projection_option. Option 1: strain-rate invariant (recommended). The slip rate is the shear across one element width, V=2wε˙II​,ε˙II​=21​ε˙ij′​ε˙ij′​​, where ε˙′ is the deviatoric strain rate and w is the element's smallest altitude: twice the area divided by the longest edge in 2D, three times the volume divided by the largest face in 3D. For simple shear at engineering rate γ˙​, ε˙II​=γ˙​/2 and V=wγ˙​, the velocity jump across the element. A shear band wider than one element shares its slip among its elements, each with its own rate and state. The measure is independent of rigid motion and of the reference frame. The DES v2 benchmarks use it. Option 0: velocity projection (default, historical). The element's mean velocity is projected onto the direction of maximum shear stress, which lies at 45° to the principal stress axes. In 3D the projection is onto the plane of maximum shear. This measures the velocity of the element, not a velocity difference, so it depends on the reference frame: a block that translates rigidly reports slip. The option is kept so that earlier models reproduce. Each rate is floored at 10−16 m/s before it enters the law, so the logarithms stay finite in a locked element.
documents.s: Slip rate in a continuum element

documents.t: RSF is available as mat.rheology_type = elasto-plastic-rate-state-friction (alias elasto-plastic-rsf) and elasto-visco-plastic-rate-state-friction (elasto-visco-plastic-rsf). They are the elasto-plastic and elasto-visco-plastic models of the constitutive update with one change: the friction angle in the Mohr–Coulomb yield function is ϕ=arctanμ. A higher friction coefficient raises the yield stress. A slipping velocity-weakening element lowers its own strength, which concentrates the strain further. Cohesion, dilation angle and tension cutoff are unchanged. They still weaken with plastic strain between mat.pls0 and mat.pls1. The reference friction angle also weakens: μ0​=tanϕ0​ follows mat.friction_angle0 to mat.friction_angle1 as plastic strain grows. The normal stress that resists slip is the one in the Mohr–Coulomb criterion. It is not an input. It comes from the stress field, including lithostatic load and tectonic stress.

In each element and each step, DES3D: computes V from the current strain rate (option 1) or velocity (option 0); advances the state explicitly with the step Δt, θn+1=θn+Δtθ˙(V,θn); evaluates μ(V,θn+1) and ϕ=arctanμ; performs the elasto-plastic (or elasto-visco-plastic) stress update with that friction angle. With several materials in an element, a, b, V0​ and Dc​ are averaged over the element's markers, as are the friction angles.

The update keeps the law finite in extreme states: Quantity Bound θ 10−12 to 1012 s V in the law at least 10−16 m/s μ at least 10−6 Vθ/Dc​ in the slip law at least 10−10; a step that would make θ≤0 resets it to Dc​/V The state starts at steady state at the reference rate, θ0​=Dc​/V0​, so μ=μ0​ at the start. The initial PT equilibrium (ic.has_body_force_adjustment with control.has_PT) holds the state and friction, since it is an instantaneous response with no time for healing. The state is saved in checkpoints as friction state variable; the friction coefficient is recomputed from it on restart.

An earthquake cycle spans loading at plate rates, about 10−9 m/s for hundreds of years, and slip near 1 m/s for seconds. With physical density, an explicit step is limited by the elastic wave speed to milliseconds, and a 300-year interseismic period would need about 1012 steps. Ordinary mass scaling fixes the scaled wave speed from the boundary velocity, cvbc​. That keeps loading quasi-static, but a fault slipping 109 times faster than the boundary then moves faster than the scaled waves, and inertia dominates the event. Global velocity scaling (GVS) ties the mass scaling to the fastest motion in the model at every step. control.use_global_velocity_scaling = yes enables it, and DES3D turns it on for any RSF rheology.

At each step DES3D finds the largest speed vmax​ (nodal or boundary) and sets cf​=min(cvmax​, M/ρ​),ρf​=cf2​K​, where c is control.inertial_scaling, K the bulk modulus, ρ the physical density and M the modulus chosen by control.mass_scaling_reference_speed (shear: G, the default; bulk: K). The nodal masses are rebuilt from ρf​ every step. Below the ceiling, the prescribed scaled speed is cvmax​. This helps separate elastic relaxation from deformation, but does not establish mechanical equilibrium during acceleration or an instantaneous load. Check force residuals, deformation and physical-step convergence for the loading path. The ceiling is a speed used to construct fictitious mass, not a guarantee of the complete physical wave spectrum. At the bulk ceiling the dry inertial density reaches ρ; at the default shear ceiling it remains ρK/G.

For automatic timesteps (control.fixed_dt = 0), the elastic contribution is Δtel​=max(cvmax​0.5lmin​​, Δtfloor​),Δtfloor​=emin​5Me​/ρe​​he​​, where he​ is the element's smallest altitude and lmin​=mine​he​. Other limits, including motion, Maxwell relaxation, heat/fluid transport and the RSF state limit, can reduce the final timestep; control.dt_fraction multiplies that minimum. Coupled fluid inertia has an additional undrained-wave limit. Only while the first term controls does vmax​Δtel​ equal 0.5lmin​/c. Once the floor controls, that displacement estimate no longer holds. Neither the floor nor a velocity ceiling guarantees an accurate or stable coupled solution for arbitrary loading. For a homogeneous dry example with lmin​=100 m, c=105, G=30 GPa and ρ=2700 kg/m³ (shear speed 3.3 km/s), ignoring the other timestep limits and taking dt_fraction = 1: Stage vmax​ Capped speed used for mass Δtel​ Interseismic loading 10−9 m/s 10−4 m/s 5×105 s (6 days) Fast slip 1 m/s 3.3 km/s 6×10−3 s The automatic step can therefore span many orders of magnitude. GVS still uses its selected fictitious mass and damping; reaching its ceiling is not an automatic switch to undamped physical coseismic inertia.

Force damping (control.damping_option, default 1 with control.damping_factor = 0.8) acts in every step, including during events. Ruptures in DES3D are therefore damped, as in the quasi-dynamic simulations of Tong and Lavier (2018). control.damping_option = 0 removes the damping.

With GVS, regular output follows sim.output_time_interval_in_yr or sim.output_step_interval as usual, and events add frames every sim.earthquake_output_step_interval steps (see earthquake output). A long cycle model therefore saves sparse interseismic frames and dense coseismic frames.

The explicit state update is accurate only if the slip in one step is small compared with Dc​. While the inverse-speed term controls, the GVS displacement estimate is 0.5lmin​/c, set by the element size rather than Dc​. For the aging law, the update is stable only if ΔtV/Dc​<2. When 0.5lmin​/c is not small compared with Dc​, set control.rsf_dtheta_max =f. It adds two bounds over all elements: Δt≤fVDc​​,Δt≤fθ. The first limits the slip per step to fDc​. The second limits the fractional healing per step to f. f must lie in [0,2); 0 (default) disables the bounds. The bounds require the aging law (mat.state_var_model = 1), slip-rate option 1, adaptive stepping (control.fixed_dt = 0), and no PT solver, body-force adjustment or isostasy adjustment.

documents.t: A velocity-weakening fault is unstable only if it is softer than a critical stiffness. For a spring-slider of stiffness k under effective normal stress σ, steady sliding is unstable when k<kc​=Dc​(b−a)σ​ (Ruina, 1983). A fault in an elastic medium has stiffness of order G′/L over a slipping length L, so instability needs a patch larger than a nucleation length. For the aging law two length scales are useful (Rubin and Ampuero, 2005): Lb​=bσG′Dc​​,L∞​=π1​(b−ab​)2Lb​(0.5≲a/b<1), with G′=G for antiplane and G′=G/(1−ν) for in-plane slip. Lb​ is close to the size of the cohesive zone at a rupture tip and sets the element size. Cycle simulations need several elements across Lb​ (Lapusta et al., 2000). A velocity-weakening patch shorter than L∞​ creeps or slips slowly instead of rupturing. In DES3D the slip of an element is spread over its width w, so element size controls both the length scales above and the width of the shear zone.

DES3D detects events in RSF models from the largest speed vmax​ and plastic activity: an event starts when vmax​ exceeds sim.earthquake_start_factor (default 5) times the largest boundary speed, but at least 10−6 m/s, while plastic strain is growing; it ends when vmax​ falls below sim.earthquake_end_factor (default 2) times the boundary speed, but at least 5×10−7 m/s, or when plastic strain stops growing. During an event, fields are written every sim.earthquake_output_step_interval steps (default 50) in addition to the regular output. With sim.seismic_moment_calculate_output = yes DES3D writes each event's start and end times to seismic_moment_magnitude.txt, together with the seismic moment accumulated over the event, M0​=steps∑​e∑​2GΩe​Δεep​, where G is the shear modulus, Ωe​ the element volume and Δεep​ the element's plastic-strain increment of the step (the second invariant, γ/2 in simple shear, so each term is GΩe​γ). It needs no fault geometry: only elements that yield contribute, and rigid motion adds nothing. In 3D M0​ is in N·m and the file also gives Mw​=32​(log10​M0​−9.1) (Hanks and Kanamori, 1979). In 2D Ωe​ is the element area, so M0​ is per unit length out of the plane (N·m/m) and no Mw​ is written. In the RSF earthquake example the main events give about 1.5×1016 N·m/m, an average slip of 5 m on the 100 km layer, which matches the loading of one cycle. The point monitor can record the friction coefficient and state at chosen points with monitor.output_dynamic_friction and monitor.output_state_variable; see the point monitor tutorial.

Parameter Default Meaning mat.rheology_type – elasto-plastic-rsf or elasto-visco-plastic-rsf mat.direct_a [0.020] a per material mat.evolution_b [0.025] b per material mat.characteristic_velocity [1e-6] V0​ per material (m/s), must be positive mat.characteristic_distance [4e-3] Dc​ per material (m) mat.state_var_model 0 0 steady state, 1 aging law, 2 slip law mat.friction_angle0, mat.friction_angle1 [30], [5] reference friction angle ϕ0​ (degrees) before and after plastic weakening control.rsf_slip_rate_projection_option 0 0 velocity projection, 1 strain-rate invariant control.rsf_dtheta_max 0 state-change limit f on the time step, in [0,2) control.use_global_velocity_scaling no Global velocity scaling; forced on for RSF control.inertial_scaling 1e5 c: scaled wave speed over the fastest speed control.mass_scaling_reference_speed shear Wave-speed cap: shear (G) or bulk (K) control.damping_option, control.damping_factor 1, 0.8 Force damping sim.earthquake_start_factor, sim.earthquake_end_factor 5, 2 event thresholds relative to the boundary speed sim.earthquake_output_step_interval 50 output interval during an event (steps) sim.seismic_moment_calculate_output no write event times and seismic moment to seismic_moment_magnitude.txt

We assess the mesh quality at fixed temporal intervals and use specific quality measures to decide whether to keep using the present mesh or remesh. For example, if the smallest angle of an element is less than a certain prescribed value, we remesh.

The default mode of remeshing is to create a new mesh preserving the old mesh's boundaries. The meshing libraries linked during the build are resued: triangle for 2D and tetgen for 3D. To assist the meshing process, DES provides a point set for the meshing libraries to start with. However, a group of nodes in the deformed mesh may be removed from the point set if any of the following criteria is met: Left outside of the new boundaries when a deformed or displaced boundary is restored to the initial configuration Surrounded only by small elements Once all criteria are enforced, a final list of nodes is collected and used for constructing a new mesh. During the process, new nodes might be inserted into the mesh or the mesh topology changed through edge-flipping (see the figure below) during the triangulation. (above) Plastic strain distribution on a mesh before and after remeshing. Solid and dashed white lines are new and old element edges. Pink circles are newly added nodes. At extreme strain, a highly distorted mesh can have two boundary segments meeting at a tiny angle, which sends triangle's Steiner-point insertion into a non-terminating splitting loop. The 2D-only parameter mesh.max_steiner_factor (default 30) caps the number of Steiner points triangle may insert during remeshing at factor × npoints, bounding this runaway; set it <= 0 to restore the old unlimited behavior. It only applies when no area constraint is active, so initial meshing is unaffected.

As described in Adaptive mesh refinement with MMG, a user can choose link MMG when building DES. MMG performs mesh optimization allowing a metric-based element size variation and the metric itself can be defined in terms of one of the physical variables like accumulated plastic strain.

After the new mesh is created, the boundary conditions, derivatives of shape function, and mass matrix have to be re-calculated. Also, an inter-mesh mapping of variables is performed. For data associated to nodes (e.g., velocity and temperature), we use linear interpolation of the data from the old mesh to evaluate the field at the new nodal location. For data associated to elements (e.g., stress and strain), DES3D uses Superconvergent Patch Recovery (SPR) (Zienkiewicz & Zhu, 1992), blended with a plain nearest-neighbor (NN) remap, per element, by how elastic that element currently is: SPR first projects each element's centroid value onto the nodes of its patch by fitting a linear polynomial in patch-relative coordinates, then evaluates that polynomial at each new nodal position. This produces a smooth, higher-order-accurate nodal field that is subsequently re-sampled back to the new element centroids, eliminating the spurious velocity spikes and checkerboard stress patterns that appeared with a plain nearest-neighbor scheme. But SPR's smoothing also relaxes elastic stress that should instead carry over unchanged (a cold, slowly-deforming element's memory of past loading), so each element's stress is blended between its NN-remapped value and its SPR-recovered value by the Deborah number, De = (element Maxwell time) / (time since the last remesh): a high-De (cold, elastic) element keeps its NN stress; a low-De (weak, viscous) element takes the SPR average. The blend is a smoothstep in log10(De), controlled by two parameters: Parameter Default Meaning mesh.remesh_deborah_min 1.0 De at or below which the remeshed stress is purely the SPR recovery. mesh.remesh_deborah_max 100.0 De at or above which the remeshed stress is purely the NN-remapped stress. remesh_deborah_min must be positive and less than remesh_deborah_max, or the run exits with a config error (see Exit codes). Widen the gap to blend more of the domain; narrow it to make the switch sharper. The free surface is pinned to its exact physical condition (zero normal and shear stress) after the blend, rather than relying on SPR's one-sided, less reliable extrapolation there, and an element whose shape and neighbors are unchanged by the remesh keeps its pre-remesh stress bit-exactly rather than being re-interpolated at all. If a node's patch is geometrically degenerate (e.g., a boundary node with fewer neighbours than degrees of freedom), SPR falls back to a simple weighted average of the surrounding element centroid values. Zienkiewicz, O. C., & Zhu, J. Z. (1992). The superconvergent patch recovery and a posteriori error estimates. Part 1: The recovery technique. International Journal for Numerical Methods in Engineering, 33(7), 1331–1364. https://doi.org/10.1002/nme.1620330702
