documents.t: How to build DES with GWB, and the three input options that use a world How DES queries the world, and what a world must contain to set materials How GWB faults become DES weak zones, and two conventions of GWB faults that matter for that Three examples: a 2D subduction zone, a 3D slab, and a 2D core complex whose weak zone alone comes from GWB

✅ GWB (CMake 3.5 or newer, a C++14 compiler) built as a shared library and installed, in under a minute on 4 cores: git clone https://github.com/GeodynamicWorldBuilder/WorldBuilder.git cmake -S WorldBuilder -B WorldBuilder/build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \ -DBUILD_SHARED_LIBS=ON -DWB_ENABLE_TESTS=OFF -DWB_ENABLE_PYTHON=OFF \ -DWB_MAKE_FORTRAN_WRAPPER=OFF -DCMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX=$HOME/opt/WorldBuilder cmake --build WorldBuilder/build -j 4 cmake --install WorldBuilder/build The OFF options skip parts DES does not use; with Python on, the install also runs GWB's setup.py install into the active Python. GWB installs its library in bin/, not lib/. Its gwb-dat, which prints a world's fields at given points, is not installed and stays in WorldBuilder/build/bin/. ✅ DynEarthSol with GeoFLAC/DynEarthSol#117, which adds option 936, built with usegwb=1 (and GWB_DIR if GWB is not in ~/opt/WorldBuilder); see Build: make ndims=2 usemmg=1 usegwb=1 GWB_DIR=$HOME/opt/WorldBuilder ✅ For the figures: Python 3 with numpy and matplotlib

One input names the world, ic.gwb_filename. Option 936 of three [ic] options takes a field from it; any of them can be used alone or together with DES's other options. (936 reads as "gwb": 9 is a g, 3 on its side a w, 6 a b.) Option Field From the world temperature_option = 936 temperature of every node GWB temperature mattype_option = 936 material of every marker GWB composition i is mattype i weakzone_option = 936 weakzone_plstrain in the weak elements, uniform or (with gwb_fault_is_gaussian) a Gaussian across the fault the elements whose centroid lies in a GWB fault feature [ic] gwb_filename = gwb-subduction.wb temperature_option = 936 mattype_option = 936 weakzone_option = 936 weakzone_plstrain = 1 Where the world is queried. A point of the initial mesh lies at depth −z, since z = 0 is the surface. In 2D the world must have a cross section, and DES's x is the distance along it; in 3D, DES's x and y are the world's map coordinates and no cross section is needed. When. Only while the model is initialized; the world is then released. A restart cannot re-seed its weak zone from the world: is_restarting_weakzone = yes with weakzone_option = 936 is an error. Remeshing. Materials ride on the markers, and temperature and plastic strain are carried over as usual. With MMG, DES refines the weak zone at t = 0, so a GWB fault also gets a finer initial mesh.

GWB compositions are numbered 0, 1, 2, …; DES reads composition i as mattype i, so number them in the order of the cfg's [mat] arrays. A marker takes the composition that holds at least half of it. The world must give one to every point of the domain, the mantle included: a marker with none, or with only a composition ≥ num_materials, stops the run (exit 12) and names its position and fractions. In practice, give the mantle layer a composition of its own and fill each plate and slab below its crust: {"model":"mantle layer", "name":"mantle", "max depth":300e3, "coordinates":[...], "composition models":[{"model":"uniform", "compositions":[2]}]}, {"model":"continental plate", "name":"overriding plate", "max depth":100e3, "coordinates":[...], "composition models":[{"model":"uniform", "compositions":[1], "max depth":35e3}, {"model":"uniform", "compositions":[2], "min depth":35e3, "max depth":100e3}]} A later feature overrides an earlier one where they overlap, and a composition model replaces the compositions it does not list with zero.

Every fault feature is a weak zone. Two GWB conventions decide where: A fault starts at its min depth. Its coordinates are the trace of the fault surface at that depth, not at the surface. A fault confined to 5–10 km depth on a plane that crosses the surface at x = 50 km and dips 60° has its trace at x = 50 − 5/tan 60° = 47.113 km. Segment length plus thickness must reach the deepest point. A point deeper than the fault's total segment length plus its thickness lies outside it, even within max depth. Make the segments long enough, and let max depth end the fault. A GWB fault's thickness is measured across the fault, while DES's weakzone_halfwidth is measured horizontally: a planar DES zone of half-width h dipping at θ is a GWB fault of thickness 2 h sin θ. A fault without composition or temperature models changes neither, so a plate-interface fault can be added on top of the materials and temperatures above it. By default every element in a fault gets the same weakzone_plstrain. With ic.gwb_fault_is_gaussian = yes, the plastic strain falls off away from the fault's plane as a Gaussian, plstrain = weakzone_plstrain × exp(−d² / 2σ²) where d is the element centroid's distance from the plane (GWB measures it across the fault, like the thickness) and σ is ic.weakzone_standard_deviation, in metres. The fault's thickness still bounds the zone, so make it about 4–6 σ for the strain to fade before the edge. An element in several faults takes the largest value; GWB finds each fault's plane by its name, so the faults need distinct names.
Set bc.mantle_temperature to the world's potential mantle temperature. DES also takes the bottom temperature as the largest initial temperature.

DES starts from a lithostatic stress, the reference pressure of control.ref_pressure_option, which the side walls and the Winkler bottom also use. The examples take it from the mantle (ref_pressure_option = 0, mat.mattype_ref = 2). PREM's (option 1) is interpolated between table rows 35 km apart whose rounding gives each interval a slightly different density; the excess over the model's own weight then steps at every row, which shows as horizontal stripes, at 80, 115, 150 and 185 km depth, in a quiet model's strain rate.

examples/gwb-subduction.cfg and .wb: a 600 × 200 km cross section of a continental plate (35 km crust), an oceanic plate (7 km crust) and a slab descending from x = 450 km to about 180 km depth, with GWB's plate and mass-conserving slab temperatures, and a 12 km-thick fault along the slab top to 80 km, the plate interface. All three options are on; the materials are 0 oceanic crust, 1 continental crust and 2 mantle. The weak zone is Gaussian: weakzone_plstrain = 1 gwb_fault_is_gaussian = yes weakzone_standard_deviation = 2.5e3 # the 12 km thickness is about 5 sigma cd DynEarthSol/examples ../dynearthsol2d gwb-subduction.cfg The initial mesh has 5372 elements and 21 488 markers: 743 of oceanic crust, 2443 of continental crust and 18 302 of mantle. 154 elements lie in the fault, with plastic strain from 1 at the slab top down to 0.06 at the fault's edges, 6 km away. The ragged isotherms above the slab follow a step in the world's temperature at the slab top: at x = 330 km it drops by 285 K within 1 km at 33 km depth, from the overriding plate's geotherm to the cold slab, and the 5 km mesh samples that step. The example runs 100 kyr with fixed walls in about 8 s on 4 threads: it shows the initial fields rather than subduction.

examples/gwb-core-complex.cfg is the bundled core-complex.cfg, the model of Tectonic rifting and subduction Part 1, with only its seed fault taken from a world. Temperature and the single material stay DES's own: [ic] weakzone_option = 936 weakzone_plstrain = 0.5 gwb_filename = gwb-core-complex.wb {"model":"fault", "name":"seed fault", "min depth":5e3, "max depth":10e3, "coordinates":[[47.113e3,-100e3],[47.113e3,100e3]], "dip point":[0,0], "segments":[{"length":12e3, "thickness":[2.08e3], "angle":[60]}]} The fault reproduces the planar weak zone of core-complex.cfg: the plane through (50 km, 0) dipping 60° toward −x, between 5 and 10 km deep, with the 1.2 km horizontal half-width as a 2 × 1.2 × sin 60° = 2.08 km thickness. Both fault conventions above are at work: the trace is where the plane reaches the 5 km min depth, and the 12 km segment is longer than the 10 − 2.08 km it must reach. The two runs start from the same mesh, refined by MMG around the same 16 weak elements, and stay identical: frame 3 matches bit for bit.
documents.s: Example 2: a weak zone alone, in a core complex

documents.t: examples/gwb-slab-3d.cfg and .wb: a 200 × 100 × 100 km box with a continental plate (30 km crust) for x < 80 km, an oceanic plate (7 km crust) beyond, a slab dipping from the trench at x = 80 km, and a 10 km-thick fault along its top to 60 km depth. In 3D the world has no cross section. ../dynearthsol3d gwb-slab-3d.cfg The mesh has 10 131 elements and 40 524 markers (3089 oceanic crust, 1807 continental crust, 35 628 mantle); 427 elements lie in the fault. The front and back faces are free slip: left free, they bulge outward, since the plates and the slab weigh differently and no one reference pressure holds them all. The example runs 5 kyr in about 6 s on 4 threads. Run it longer and the dense slab sinks along the weak interface at velocities far above the 3.15 cm/yr push, and the mesh is remeshed often.

Symptom Cause exit 31: ... 936 needs the Geodynamic World Builder: build with usegwb=1 DES was built without GWB exit 11: ... 936 needs ic.gwb_filename no world named exit 20: cannot open ic.gwb_filename the world file is missing exit 11: ic.weakzone_option 936 cannot re-seed the weak zone of a restart a restart with is_restarting_weakzone = yes exit 11: Error: Geodynamic World Builder, world '...': ... GWB rejected the world; its own message follows. In 2D, a world without a cross section is one cause exit 12: ... defines no material at x = (...) mattype_option = 936 and a marker without a composition of at least 0.5 below num_materials; see Every point needs a material exit 12: ic.weakzone_option 936 needs a fault feature the world has no fault exit 12: ic.gwb_fault_is_gaussian needs the faults ... to have distinct names two faults share a name exit 11: ic.gwb_fault_is_gaussian needs ic.weakzone_standard_deviation > 0 σ is 0 or negative

DynEarthSol's GWB build workflow builds GWB at a pinned commit, builds DES in 2D and 3D with usegwb=1, and runs tests/functional/gwb/check_gwb.py. The script compares frame 0 of a 2D and a 3D world with GWB's own gwb-dat application point by point: every node temperature, every marker's material and every weak element. It also checks the error exits above.

Fraters, M., Thieulot, C., van den Berg, A. & Spakman, W. (2019). The Geodynamic World Builder: a solution for complex initial conditions in numerical modeling. Solid Earth, 10, 1785–1807. doi:10.5194/se-10-1785-2019

The [monitor] section writes a lightweight CSV time series for a handful of fixed locations, independent of the normal field output (output_time_interval_in_yr / output_step_interval). Use it when you need high-time-resolution history at a few points — a fault patch's velocity and state variable, a borehole site's temperature, a wall's stress — without paying for a full-field snapshot every step.

[monitor] enabled = yes step_interval = 10 # write every 10 solver steps num_points = 2 points_x = [50e3, 50e3] points_z = [-4e3, -6e3] # 2D: second coordinate; 3D: use points_y too points_unit = m output_prefix = output/monitor output_coord = yes output_velocity = yes output_stress = yes This writes output/monitor_point_0.csv and output/monitor_point_1.csv, one row every 10 steps, each row holding the step, time, the point's current position, the node and element sampled, the requested fields and the row kind (see Remeshing and restart). monitor.enabled = yes requires num_points > 0 and at least one output_* flag on; otherwise the run stops at input.

Each monitor point is a tracer, like a marker. It is placed at points_x/points_y/points_z, keeps its position inside its element as the mesh moves, and so follows the material through deformation, remeshing and restart. monitor.point_type chooses what a row reports: point_type Node fields (velocity, temperature, ...) Element fields (stress, plastic strain, ...) particle (default) interpolated at the point from the element that contains the point grid from the node nearest the point from the element whose centroid is nearest the point The columns query_* hold the point's current position, and matched_node/matched_elem the node and element that were sampled. A point that leaves the mesh reports NaN (particle) or its nearest node (grid), with one warning. points_x, points_z: in 2D, the two in-plane coordinates. points_x, points_y, points_z: in 3D, all three. points_unit: mm, cm, m, or km — one unit for every coordinate of every point. 2D legacy alias In a 2D build, points_y is accepted as an alias for points_z only when points_z is left empty ([]). This exists for old 2D configs written before points_y meant the 3D y-coordinate; in a 2D config, write the depth/vertical coordinate as points_z, not points_y, to avoid relying on the alias.

One file per point: <output_prefix>_point_<i>.csv, where i is the point's 0-based index in points_x/points_y/points_z. Every row has: Column(s) Always present Meaning step, time_s yes Solver step and model time (seconds) query_x[, query_y], query_z yes The point's current position (metres) matched_node, matched_elem yes The node nearest the point, and the element sampled (see How points are located) row yes, last column 0 regular, 1 before a remesh, 2 after a remesh (see Remeshing and restart) The remaining columns appear only if their output_* flag is on, between matched_elem and row. Node-based fields are interpolated at the point (particle) or read from matched_node (grid); element-based fields come from matched_elem. Any field a flag requests that the run doesn't actually have (e.g. pore pressure without poroelasticity) comes out as nan, like a missing or out-of-range match (matched_node/matched_elem = -1) would. Node-based (one column per field, or NDIMS columns for a vector): Flag Column(s) Source output_coord coord_x[_y]_z Current node position (m) output_velocity velocity_x[_y]_z Node velocity output_force force_x[_y]_z Node force output_temperature temperature output_pore_pressure pore_pressure Poroelastic models only output_bcflag bcflag Boundary-condition flag bitmask, as an integer Element-based, from the sampled element: Flag Column(s) Source output_stress stress_0...stress_{NSTR-1} See component order below output_strain strain_0...strain_{NSTR-1} output_strain_rate strain_rate_0...strain_rate_{NSTR-1} output_plastic_strain plastic_strain output_plastic_strain_rate plastic_strain_rate output_radiogenic_source radiogenic_source output_density density Current effective density, not just rho0 output_viscosity viscosity Current effective viscosity output_mesh_quality mesh_quality Same metric that triggers remeshing — see Adaptive mesh refinement with MMG output_material material Index of the material with the most markers in the element output_dynamic_friction dynamic_friction output_state_variable state_variable Rate-and-state friction's state variable — see Rate-and-state friction NSTR is 3 in 2D and 6 in 3D, in the same component order as initial_stress: 2D [xx, zz, xz], 3D [xx, yy, zz, xy, xz, yz]. Every numeric value is written in full double precision (%.17e); nan/inf/-inf are spelled out literally rather than left blank.

A remesh rebuilds the mesh, so each point is located again at the position it had just before the remesh. A remesh also remaps element fields, which smooths them slightly. To show that, the last CSV column, row, marks what each row records: row Written 0 every step_interval steps: the regular series 1 just before a remesh that falls between monitor steps 2 just after a remesh, with the remapped values (only with remesh_output = both) monitor.remesh_output = before (default) writes rows 0 and 1; both also writes row 2. A remesh on a monitor step needs no row 1: the regular row already records that state. Filter on row == 0 for an evenly spaced series, and compare rows 1 and 2 of one step to see how much a remesh changed a value. The checkpoint stores each point's position and element, so a restart continues the same points. Restarting keeps the rows a CSV already holds up to the restart step and continues the series in the same file.

The initial state is always written once. At step = 0 (a fresh start, not a restart), every point's row is written immediately, regardless of step_interval. step_interval must be >= 1; num_points must be >= 0. Rows 1 and 2 fall between monitor steps, so a series that includes them is not evenly spaced in steps or time.

Rate-and-state friction (2D) is a full worked example: it places three monitor points at known .poly vertices straddling a fault band, and its companion notebook reads the resulting monitor_point_*.csv files directly to compute across-band slip velocity, displacement, and the friction state variable through a seismic cycle.

This exercise compresses a 1 m elastic cell with a constant top traction. You will run both pseudo-transient schemes, compare the result with an analytical elastic response, and see why a held load does not produce repeated compression. Finish by restarting from a held state and applying a larger load. At a glance Dimension 2D (a 3D variant is described at the end) Build make ndims=2 hdf5=0 Run time under a second per case, one thread Inputs the PT tutorial bundle (elastic-0.cfg, elastic-1.cfg, analyze_pt.py) Checked with figures from DynEarthSol 707e481; reproduced on 68cc2a0

Use a new terminal and a separate checkout. You need Git, Make, a C++17 compiler, and Python 3. On Debian/Ubuntu, install git g++ make python3 python3-venv; on macOS, install the Xcode Command Line Tools and Homebrew's libomp and python. See installation for other platforms. The config parser is bundled with the source. git clone https://github.com/GeoFLAC/DynEarthSol.git DynEarthSol-pt-tutorial cd DynEarthSol-pt-tutorial make -j2 ndims=2 hdf5=0 ./dynearthsol2d --help make fetches the required nanoflann submodule. This exercise needs no MMG, Exodus, GPU or HDF5 build. Confirm that help includes PT_option, PT_use_running_scale and PT_absolute_tolerance. Prepare Python in the same checkout: python3 -m venv .venv source .venv/bin/activate python -m pip install numpy matplotlib export OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 export OMP_DYNAMIC=FALSE

Download the tutorial bundle and extract it into a new pt-tutorial directory inside the solver checkout. The bundle contains the four elastic/Maxwell configs, analyze_pt.py, and a README. From the checkout root, the equivalent terminal commands are: python - <<'PY' from pathlib import Path from urllib.request import urlretrieve from zipfile import ZipFile destination = Path("pt-tutorial") destination.mkdir() # Use a new directory for a fresh exercise. urlretrieve("https://geoflac.github.io/DynEarthSol/tutorial/pt/pt-tutorial.zip", destination / "pt-tutorial.zip") with ZipFile(destination / "pt-tutorial.zip") as archive: archive.extractall(destination) PY cd pt-tutorial You can also inspect option 0, option 1 and the analysis script individually. The elastic configs reproduce the upstream examples/fundamentals/pt-elastic-load.cfg with distinct output names and the selected PT_option.

The 2D domain spans 0≤x≤1 m and −1≤z≤0 m. The sides are horizontal rollers: horizontal velocity is zero, and vertical motion is free. The base is clamped. The top is free in velocity and carries a vertical traction of −100 kPa. Compression is negative in DES output. Setting Value Bulk modulus K / shear modulus G 10 MPa / 10 MPa Gravity / hydraulic diffusion / surface processes Disabled Nominal resolution 0.5 m Physical timestep / duration 0.01 s / 3 steps Mesh motion / remeshing Disabled Field and checkpoint output Every physical step, without time averaging PT convergence mode PT_use_running_scale = yes The important controls in both configs are: [control] has_PT = yes PT_option = 0 PT_max_iter = 5000 PT_use_running_scale = yes fixed_dt = 0.01 has_moving_mesh = no has_hydraulic_diffusion = no gravity = 0 surface_process_option = 0 elastic-1.cfg changes PT_option to 1 and the output name to elastic-1. The running scale keeps force precision tied to the applied load during subsequent held steps. It is an explicit tutorial setting; the solver default is no. Read its scope and limitations before using it in another problem.

From DynEarthSol-pt-tutorial/pt-tutorial, run: ../dynearthsol2d elastic-0.cfg > elastic-0.log 2>&1 ../dynearthsol2d elastic-1.cfg > elastic-1.log 2>&1 python analyze_pt.py elastic elastic-0 elastic-1 --source .. Each model writes a .info index, a .manifest, and save/checkpoint frames 0 through 3. The script reads the native output through the checkout's Dynearthsol.py. It checks all components of saved stress, strain, coordinates and velocity for finiteness, then compares axial stress, axial strain and vertical velocity against the homogeneous reference and checks convergence records. It writes elastic-0.csv, elastic-1.csv, elastic-response.svg/.png and elastic-convergence.svg/.png. For the laterally confined response, M=K+34​G=23.333333 MPa,ϵzz​=M−0.1 MPa​=−0.004285714. After the first physical step, expect approximately −100 kPa vertical stress and −0.004286 vertical strain. Steps 2 and 3 retain that compression. Both schemes should agree with this response within the solver tolerance; the checked runs have normalized field errors below 1.2×10−6. The analysis script uses a 5×10−5 acceptance limit, normalizing stress by 100 kPa, strain by 0.01, and velocity by 0.5 m/s. Because mesh motion is disabled, the coordinates remain unchanged. The equivalent top displacement is reconstructed as ∑n​vz,topn​Δt, approximately −4.286 mm. This deliberately fixed-grid constitutive exercise is not a moving-boundary compression experiment.

rg '^PT step=' elastic-0.log elastic-1.log Use grep '^PT step=' elastic-0.log elastic-1.log if ripgrep is unavailable. The checked serial runs give: Physical step Option 0 iterations / evaluations Option 1 iterations / evaluations 1: apply the load 299 / 299 25 / 25 2: hold the load 1 / 2 1 / 2 3: hold the load 1 / 1 1 / 1 Iteration counts can vary with platform and compiler. In both options, the first step needs relaxation. Step 2 compares the old loading velocity with zero free motion; the latter already meets the threshold. Step 3 starts from the retained zero velocity. One loop pass therefore means no relaxation update, while two evaluations mean two full candidates were checked. The 2D option-0 step-1 residual is about 0.0341744 N/m and its threshold is 0.0353553 N/m. The residual is a projected nodal-force RMS, not a stress in Pa. initial describes the selected candidate; warm_initial can be much larger after the candidate comparison. All records state stage=before_physical_updates. For physical steps, this label follows any thermal diffusion update and precedes hydraulic transport, mesh motion and stress rotation. The saved PT residual force has this same diagnostic time level. Saved stress includes the later physical stress rotation, so independently assembling force from it need not reproduce exactly the printed residual. See the force-output reference.

This Python block copies the option-0 config into a new restart config, selects the checkpoint at frame 2, and doubles the top traction. Run it in the same pt-tutorial directory: python - <<'PY' import configparser cfg = configparser.ConfigParser() cfg.optionxform = str cfg.read("elastic-0.cfg") cfg["sim"].update(modelname="elastic-reload", is_restarting="yes", restarting_from_modelname="elastic-0", restarting_from_frame="2") cfg["bc"]["stress_val_z1"] = "-2e5" with open("elastic-reload.cfg", "w") as stream: cfg.write(stream) PY ../dynearthsol2d elastic-reload.cfg > elastic-reload.log 2>&1 python - <<'PY' import sys sys.path.insert(0, "..") import numpy as np from Dynearthsol import Dynearthsol model = Dynearthsol("elastic-reload") stress = model.read_field(3, "stress")[:, 1] strain = model.read_field(3, "strain")[:, 1] np.testing.assert_allclose(stress, -2e5, rtol=1e-5) np.testing.assert_allclose(strain, -0.008571428571, rtol=1e-5) print("Reload passed: axial stress about -200 kPa, strain about -0.00857143") PY The changed load must produce a new deformation even though the saved velocity was zero. This is a changed-load exercise, not an exact continuation comparison. Keep output names distinct for fresh, restarted and repeated runs. The restart reference describes unchanged-control continuation.

The same elastic inputs run in 3D. From the solver checkout root, build make -j2 ndims=3 hdf5=0, copy the bundle to a new output directory, then replace ../dynearthsol2d with ../dynearthsol3d in the run commands. The analysis script detects the dimension. In 3D the cell also has roller y sides; the expected confined response is the same. The reload checking snippet above is specifically 2D (zz is component 1); in 3D it is component 2. Continue with PT Maxwell creep to see a material that keeps deforming under the same held traction. Reproducing the reference figures The bundle's README records the source version used for the reference figures. They were checked with GCC 13.3, one OpenMP thread and binary output. For an exact source match, check out that version before building.
documents.s: Repeat in 3D or continue to creep

documents.t: The elastic tutorial reaches equilibrium after the load is applied and then holds its strain. A Maxwell material continues to creep: its deviatoric stress relaxes over physical time, and additional deformation is needed to maintain the prescribed traction. This exercise checks that PT retains that time-dependent response. Use the same checked solver, Python environment, single-thread settings, and tutorial bundle as the elastic exercise. Run the commands below from DynEarthSol-pt-tutorial/pt-tutorial. At a glance Dimension 2D Build make ndims=2 hdf5=0 Run time under a second per case, one thread Inputs the PT tutorial bundle (maxwell-0.cfg, maxwell-1.cfg, analyze_pt.py) Checked with figures from DynEarthSol 707e481; reproduced on 68cc2a0
documents.s: Maxwell creep under a held load

documents.t: maxwell-0.cfg and maxwell-1.cfg retain the 1 m cell, roller sides, clamped base and −100 kPa top traction. They run 100 steps of 0.01 s with a fixed mesh and no hydraulic diffusion. The material settings are: [mat] rheology_type = maxwell is_plane_strain = yes rho0 = [2650] porosity = [0] bulk_modulus = [1e7] shear_modulus = [1e7] min_viscosity = 1e6 max_viscosity = 1e6 Both viscosity bounds fix η=106 Pa s. In 2D, is_plane_strain = yes retains the out-of-plane normal stress in the 3D constitutive state with zero out-of-plane strain. In 3D the setting has no effect. The shear relaxation time is η/G=0.1 s, so the run spans ten shear relaxation times. As in the elastic tutorial, these configs explicitly enable the optional running scale; that small-model check does not qualify its use for general viscous flow.
documents.s: Change the material, keep the loading

documents.t: ../dynearthsol2d maxwell-0.cfg > maxwell-0.log 2>&1 ../dynearthsol2d maxwell-1.cfg > maxwell-1.log 2>&1 python analyze_pt.py maxwell maxwell-0 maxwell-1 --source .. The script checks every component of stress, strain, coordinates and velocity for finiteness in each saved frame, then compares axial stress, axial strain and vertical velocity against the independent discrete reference below. It writes one CSV per model and maxwell-response.svg/.png. The checked 2D runs have maximum normalized field errors below 2.2×10−6, within the script's 5×10−5 limit. Normalizers are 100 kPa for stress, 0.01 for strain and 0.5 m/s for velocity. The axial stress stays near −100 kPa. The axial strain continues beyond the first step, reaching about −0.00991968 at 1 s, or 9.920 mm equivalent shortening. Coordinates remain fixed; the script integrates the top velocity to reconstruct displacement.

For homogeneous confined compression, let en​=ϵzz,n​, mn​=Ken​ be the signed mean normal stress, and sn​ the axial deviatoric stress, so σzz,n​=mn​+sn​. Start with e0​=m0​=s0​=0. For the prescribed axial traction T=−105 Pa, define a=2ηGΔt​,q=1+a1−a​,D=3(1+a)4G​. Crank–Nicolson integration of the Maxwell deviatoric response gives Δen​=K+DT−mn−1​−qsn−1​​,mn​=mn−1​+KΔen​,sn​=qsn−1​+DΔen​,en​=en−1​+Δen​. These are algebraic homogeneous equations, independent of the mesh force assembly. The analysis script implements this recurrence and checks all elements, rather than using one PT option as the reference for the other. This is a check against the discrete material update at the selected physical timestep. Agreement does not establish physical-time convergence. For the corresponding continuum step-load problem, the post-loading strain is e(t)=KT​[1−K+4G/34G/3​exp(−τc​t​)],τc​=Gη​KK+4G/3​. The instantaneous elastic jump is T/(K+4G/3); the long-time strain is T/K=−0.01. The first saved DES step includes a finite interval of creep, so it is not exactly that instantaneous jump. A timestep-refinement study against this continuum solution is a separate accuracy assessment. The provided plotting script expects the supplied 100-step, 0.01 s configs.

The held elastic and Maxwell runs test different physical responses. For elasticity, zero free velocity can preserve a completed loading increment. For Maxwell rheology, the same candidate still evaluates constitutive relaxation over the physical dt; a zero-velocity shortcut cannot suppress creep. Both PT schemes must recover the discrete history. For the matching 3D exercise, use the 3D build and a fresh output directory as described in the elastic tutorial. The same inputs and analysis script apply. These homogeneous, dry, fixed-grid checks do not qualify moving meshes, localized softening, arbitrary irreversible loading or hydraulic coupling. For solver controls and known convergence limits, return to Choosing a mechanical solver and the validation record.

This tutorial uses two small 2D DynEarthSol models to follow slow loading, rapid slip and recovery. You will run a uniform velocity-weakening (VW) band, then compare it with a VW patch between velocity-strengthening (VS) flanks. Figure 1 introduces the model. For each exercise, predict what you might see, run the plotting cell, and describe your observations before opening the collapsed reference result. Python plotting is provided; interpretation is the main task. At a glance Dimension 2D Build make ndims=2 hdf5=1 (VTKHDF output is required) Run time not recorded; reference outputs are included in the download Inputs the workshop files (DES-RSF-Tutorial.zip) Checked with DynEarthSol 1b4e94f
documents.s: Rate-and-state friction in a finite-width shear band

documents.t: Rate-and-state friction describes resistance that depends on sliding rate and a state variable, θ, which evolves with the deformation history. The parameters a and b control the frictional response: at steady sliding, a−b > 0 is velocity strengthening and a−b < 0 is velocity weakening. Velocity weakening can promote instability; the surrounding stiffness, loading and state evolution also matter. Here frictional deformation occupies a 2 km thick band, rather than an infinitely thin fault. Our displacement measure is the horizontal displacement of the upper band interface minus that of the lower interface. It includes elastic deformation as well as localized inelastic deformation. By the end, you should be able to connect a slip-speed peak to displacement accumulation, stress release and a reduction in the solver time step, and explain why the VS flanks creep while the central VW patch accumulates a displacement deficit and then catches up.

Download and extract the workshop files. They contain Tutorial.ipynb, a browser-readable Tutorial.html, model inputs, reference outputs and the data behind the five figures. Use Linux, macOS or Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL). On Windows, run both DES and Jupyter inside WSL. You need a C++ compiler, Make, Boost.Program_options, HDF5 and Python 3.10 or later. HDF5 development headers and libraries are required: this tutorial reads VTKHDF spatial fields, so keep hdf5=1 when building DES. Installing Python's h5py alone does not provide the system development package needed to compile DES. Install the dependencies for your operating system before building. Ubuntu 22.04 or later (including Ubuntu in WSL): sudo apt update sudo apt install -y git g++ make libboost-program-options-dev libhdf5-dev pkg-config python3 python3-venv macOS: install the Xcode Command Line Tools (xcode-select --install, if not already installed) and Homebrew, then run: brew install boost libomp hdf5 pkg-config python libomp supplies the OpenMP runtime for Apple's compiler. The pinned DES revision below automatically locates HDF5 on Ubuntu and macOS; do not pass Ubuntu-specific HDF5_INCLUDE_DIR or HDF5_LIB_DIR paths on macOS.

This exercise was checked against the public DES revision 1b4e94f1c333fdade9dc512cf9cb20e10e8e9aad. Use a separate checkout so an existing working copy is preserved. git clone --recursive https://github.com/GeoFLAC/DynEarthSol.git DynEarthSol-tutorial cd DynEarthSol-tutorial git checkout 1b4e94f1c333fdade9dc512cf9cb20e10e8e9aad git submodule update --init --recursive make config ndims=2 opt=2 openmp=1 hdf5=1 make -j2 ndims=2 opt=2 openmp=1 hdf5=1 export DYNEXE="$PWD/dynearthsol2d" export OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 export OMP_DYNAMIC=FALSE "$DYNEXE" --help Check that make config reports hdf5 1 and existing HDF5 include and library directories for your installation. The same build commands work on Ubuntu and macOS. Check that the help lists rsf_slip_rate_projection_option, rsf_dtheta_max and use_global_velocity_scaling. The executable must be a 2D HDF5 build. Keep this terminal open so DYNEXE remains defined. The mesh is small enough that one OpenMP thread is appropriate. Only if HDF5 auto-detection fails: first install the HDF5 development package listed above. If it is installed but the build still cannot find it, check its location and rerun the complete build command with explicit paths. These overrides select an existing installation; they do not install HDF5. On Ubuntu x86_64, the serial development package normally uses the paths below. Verify them before building; other architectures can use a different library directory. ls /usr/include/hdf5/serial/H5Lpublic.h ls /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/hdf5/serial/libhdf5.so make -j2 ndims=2 opt=2 openmp=1 hdf5=1 \ HDF5_INCLUDE_DIR=/usr/include/hdf5/serial \ HDF5_LIB_DIR=/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/hdf5/serial On macOS with Homebrew, use the installed formula's prefix: ls "$(brew --prefix hdf5)/include/H5Lpublic.h" ls "$(brew --prefix hdf5)/lib/libhdf5.dylib" make -j2 ndims=2 opt=2 openmp=1 hdf5=1 \ HDF5_INCLUDE_DIR="$(brew --prefix hdf5)/include" \ HDF5_LIB_DIR="$(brew --prefix hdf5)/lib" Each multi-line make block is one shell command: the trailing backslashes continue it onto the next line. Keep the path assignments on that command; do not run them as separate commands after make. Once the build succeeds, continue with the DYNEXE exports and help check above.

Change to the extracted DES-RSF-Tutorial directory, then run: export TUTORIAL_DIR="$PWD" python3 -m venv .venv source .venv/bin/activate python -m pip install -r resources/requirements.txt python -m jupyterlab Open Tutorial.ipynb and a JupyterLab terminal (File → New → Terminal). Run each example's bash block in that terminal; run its python block as a notebook cell. In the terminal, run these three commands once before Example 1, replacing the executable path with the absolute path from the build step: export DYNEXE="/absolute/path/to/DynEarthSol-tutorial/dynearthsol2d" export OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 export OMP_DYNAMIC=FALSE A JupyterLab terminal normally inherits these variables if they were exported before JupyterLab started. Repeating the commands makes the run settings explicit. Keep this terminal for both examples; repeat the three commands if you open a new terminal. To study the results without running DES, use the supplied reference paths in the notebook's setup cell. The reference figures and numerical data are included in the download; no solver is needed for that route.

The model is 100 km wide and 10 km deep. A horizontal band lies between depths of 4 and 6 km. The upper boundary moves in the positive x direction at 10⁻⁹ m/s and has zero vertical velocity; the bottom is fixed. The side boundaries do not impose a velocity. Both examples use the same geometry and loading. Figure 1. (a) Model geometry, boundary loading and monitor positions; depth is exaggerated by 2.5×. P0 and P1 sample the upper and lower faces of the band near x = 50 km, and P2 samples its interior. (b) Spatial distribution of a−b in Example 1: the entire band is VW. (c) Spatial distribution of a−b in Example 2: a central VW patch lies between VS flanks. Setting Value Domain / band thickness 100 × 10 km / 2 km Central patch x = 45–55 km Density / bulk modulus / shear modulus 2700 kg/m³ / 50 GPa / 30 GPa Band cohesion / characteristic distance 4 MPa / 0.005 m Reference and loading velocity 10⁻⁹ m/s Nominal mesh resolution 400 m Model duration 850 years

decollement.poly defines 14 vertices, 18 segments and five material regions. The band order from left to right is 3–2–1, while arrays in [mat] are indexed by material ID 0,1,2,3,4. The lower and upper hosts are IDs 0 and 4. Their very large cohesion keeps them elastic in this exercise. Case / region Material ID a b a−b Example 1: entire band 1, 2, 3 0.003 0.015 −0.012 Example 2: left VS 3 0.011 0.001 +0.010 Example 2: central VW 2 0.011 0.017 −0.006 Example 2: right VS 1 0.011 0.001 +0.010 Both examples use state_var_model=1 and the same characteristic distance. The two cfg files already contain these assignments. The .poly vertices at (50, −4) and (50, −6) km let P0/P1 match the interface at x = 50 km; they do not introduce another material division. The annotated resources/POLY_GUIDE.md in the download explains the point, segment and region blocks.

P0 and P1 provide the signed across-band horizontal speed vx(P0) − vx(P1). Figures 2–3 show its absolute value, |vx(P0) − vx(P1)|. Across-band displacement is calculated from the P0 and P1 horizontal coordinates as [x(P0,t) − x(P1,t)] − [x(P0,t_initial) − x(P1,t_initial)], where t_initial is the first saved monitor sample. This retains the sign of displacement; integrating the absolute speed would instead accumulate travel in both directions. P2 provides local shear stress and θ. Figure 5 instead interpolates displacement along both band interfaces at the same initial x positions. This lets the spatial profiles and the VS/VW time histories use exactly the same quantity.

Start in the extracted tutorial directory. Use a fresh run-directory name when repeating a calculation; mkdir below deliberately stops if it already exists. export TUTORIAL_DIR="$PWD" mkdir -p "$TUTORIAL_DIR/results" export RUN_DIR="$TUTORIAL_DIR/results/example1" mkdir "$RUN_DIR" && mkdir "$RUN_DIR/output" && \ cp resources/models/example1_uniform_vw.cfg resources/models/decollement.poly "$RUN_DIR/" sed -n '/^\[mat\]/,/^\[monitor\]/p' "$RUN_DIR/example1_uniform_vw.cfg" In [sim], max_time_in_yr=850 is physical model time. output_time_interval_in_yr=25 sets the normal field-save interval to 25 model years; output_step_interval=1000000 also requests a save after that many solver steps. earthquake_output_step_interval=1000 requests more frequent fields during a detected rapid episode. In [monitor], step_interval=10 saves monitor points every ten solver steps. These are output intervals, not the solver's physical time step.
documents.s: Step 1: prepare and inspect the inputs

documents.t: cd "$RUN_DIR" "$DYNEXE" example1_uniform_vw.cfg Wait for the solver to finish successfully. Confirm the startup log reports one OpenMP thread. Then inspect the files: head -n 2 output/monitor_point_0.csv head -n 2 output/monitor_point_1.csv head -n 2 output/monitor_point_2.csv ls output/model.save.*.vtkhdf | head printf 'Example 1 output: %s\n' "$RUN_DIR" CSV coordinates and displacement use metres, velocities m/s, times seconds and stresses Pa. Compare the requested query_x/query_z with the selected coord_x/coord_z: P0/P1 should match x = 50000 m exactly, while P2 can use a nearby interior mesh node. VTKHDF save files contain spatial fields; chkpt files are restart checkpoints.
documents.s: Step 2: run DES and inspect its output

documents.t: The notebook starts in the tutorial directory, independently of the terminal's current directory. Set RUN to your Example 1 output and SECOND to the Example 2 directory you will create below. For the no-solver route, uncomment the two reference assignments. from pathlib import Path import sys import numpy as np import h5py import matplotlib.pyplot as plt ROOT = Path.cwd().resolve() assert (ROOT / "resources/tutorial_tools.py").is_file(), "Open the notebook in the tutorial directory." sys.path.insert(0, str(ROOT / "resources")) import tutorial_tools as tt RUN = ROOT / "results/example1" SECOND = ROOT / "results/example2" # RUN = ROOT / "resources/reference/example1_uniform_vw" # SECOND = ROOT / "resources/reference/example2_vs_vw_vs" FIGURES = ROOT / "resources/figures" print(f"Example 1 analysis source: {RUN}") print(f"Example 2 analysis source: {SECOND}") # Read monitor CSVs: P0-P1 relative horizontal velocity/displacement, # plus P2 shear stress, state variable and friction histories. history = tt.band_history(RUN) # Find |vx(P0) - vx(P1)| >= 1e-3 m/s (1 mm/s). # Group exceedances separated by at most 86400 s (one model day). events = tt.find_events(history) for number, event in enumerate(events, start=1): print(f"Event {number}: {event['start_yr']:.3f} yr; " f"peak speed {event['peak_relative_speed']:.3f} m/s") start_yr is the first saved threshold-exceeding time in each group; peak_relative_speed is its largest sampled absolute relative speed. This is an analysis criterion, separate from DES's internal rapid-output trigger, not a physical definition of an earthquake. It measures motion at P0/P1, not every slipping region in the model, and can miss peaks between saved samples. The defaults are threshold=1e-3 and merge_gap_s=86400; the plotting helpers below use those same defaults internally. The plotting cells use the directories selected by RUN and SECOND. Plot your selected runs first, answer the observation questions, then open Reference result and interpretation to compare with Figures 2–5. If you selected the reference paths, you are analysing supplied results rather than a new calculation. Sections explicitly labeled supplied data always use the bundled reference arrays, independently of RUN and SECOND. The basic workshop saves fewer spatial fields than some reference runs; compare physical trends and actual saved times rather than exact images.
documents.s: Step 3: load the results in the notebook

documents.t: Before plotting, predict how speed, stress and state might change during a rapid episode. What changes would you expect in the numerical time step and pseudo-density? Plot six panels from RUN on a shared model-time axis: speed, mean solver time step, pseudo-density, displacement, stress and state. plot_history calculates the mean time step as diff(time_s) / diff(step) between consecutive monitor records and plots it at each interval's midpoint. The workshop records every 10 solver steps, so this is an interval average, not an individual step's dt. It resolves the time-step trend more densely than the spatial field saves, but can smooth short-lived extrema. Both the supplied Figure 2 and your plot use this same monitor-based calculation. The pseudo-density panel represents numerical inertia from mass scaling, not physical rock density. pseudo_density_samples(history) uses the run's cfg and estimates the global speed as the largest vector speed sqrt(vx**2 + vz**2) at P0, P1 and P2, floored by the prescribed boundary-speed bound. This is different from the across-band relative speed used to detect events. It then applies rho_pseudo = K / min(S * V_est, sqrt(M / rho))**2, where S is inertial_scaling, rho is the configured constant rho0, and M is the shear modulus by default, or the bulk modulus for mass_scaling_reference_speed=bulk. The helper requires uniform elastic moduli and physical density, as in these workshop models. With the workshop's default shear-speed ceiling, K=50 GPa, G=30 GPa and rho=2700 kg/m³, pseudo-density cannot fall below rho*K/G=4500 kg/m³. The solver uses the global maximum element-mean speed; three monitor points only approximate that value and can miss motion elsewhere. The curve is therefore labeled monitor-based estimate, not an exact record of solver pseudo-density. It provides a densely sampled view of mass-scaling changes. Mean dt alone cannot determine pseudo-density because other constraints, including the RSF state limit, also control dt. # Plot speed, mean dt, monitor-estimated pseudo-density, displacement, stress and theta. fig = tt.plot_history(history, title=f"Example 1 — {RUN.name}") plt.show() Observe before comparing. How many rapid episodes do you find? At each speed peak, describe the changes in displacement, stress and state. How do mean dt and estimated pseudo-density behave? Identify which two panels represent numerical controls rather than physical material properties. Reference result and interpretation — Figure 2 Figure 2. Six panels from the supplied Example 1 reference run. Read vertically at each event: speed rises, mean solver dt shrinks, estimated pseudo-density decreases, displacement increases abruptly, and shear stress drops. Stress then reloads. The dt curve uses monitor-interval averages; pseudo-density is estimated from the largest speed at the three monitor points. All six panels use monitor CSV data and the run's material/control settings, without reading spatial field files. The supplied Example 1 has two detected episodes, near 648.255 and 836.241 years. Here an episode groups across-band speeds of at least 1 mm/s with the one-model-day gap rule described above. Use these as comparison values, not a requirement that every modified run reproduce the same timing. Rebuild the supplied Figure 2 (PNG/PDF) and its numerical CSV data with python resources/plot_history_figure.py from the extracted tutorial directory. It uses the bundled reference run; your notebook uses RUN. Compare actual monitor sample times and physical trends when runs differ.

Choose an episode from your own event list. Before plotting its short-time history, predict when most displacement will accumulate relative to the speed peak and stress change. EVENT_INDEX = 0 # Set to 1 for the second detected episode. assert EVENT_INDEX < len(events), "No such detected episode; inspect the full history first." event = events[EVENT_INDEX] time_from_peak = history["time_s"] - event["peak_time_s"] print(f"Sampled peak speed: {event['peak_relative_speed']:.3f} m/s") print(f"Threshold-crossing envelope: {event['span_s']:.3f} s") print(f"Local stress drop to the low-rate recovery sample: " f"{event['local_shear_stress_drop_mpa']:.2f} MPa") Plot the selected episode from RUN. This helper shows a short window around the threshold-crossing interval on a linear time axis; Figure 3 uses a longer symlog window to show loading and recovery. The displacement here is zero at the first threshold-crossing sample. # Plot the selected event from 10 s before its first exceedance to 10 s # after its last; time zero is the sampled speed peak (default detection). fig_event = tt.plot_event(history, event_index=EVENT_INDEX) fig_event.suptitle(f"Example 1 — {RUN.name}; event {EVENT_INDEX + 1}") plt.show() Exercise 1. Identify loading, rapid slip and recovery in your full history and selected event plot. When is displacement accumulated relative to the speed peak? If a second episode was detected, set EVENT_INDEX=1 and rerun the event cells to compare it. Two episodes give one observed interval, not a recurrence distribution. Then compare with the reference below. Reference result and interpretation — Figure 3 Figure 3. Time is measured from the sampled speed peak. The continuous symlog axis is linear within ±10 s and logarithmic outside, so both slow tails and the rapid interval remain visible. Shading spans the first to last 10⁻³ m/s threshold exceedance in this episode. The sampled peak reaches approximately 1.92 m/s. Most displacement accumulates while the band moves rapidly and stress is released; the recovery continues well beyond the rapid interval. Equal distances along this time axis are not equal durations.

The second cfg changes the band friction values while preserving geometry, loading, cohesion and characteristic distance. The relevant arrays are: direct_a = [0.003, 0.011, 0.011, 0.011, 0.003] evolution_b = [0.015, 0.001, 0.017, 0.001, 0.015] The centre is VW and the flanks are VS. Do not overwrite Example 1's cfg. Return to the tutorial directory in the same terminal and run the second case: cd "$TUTORIAL_DIR" export SECOND_DIR="$TUTORIAL_DIR/results/example2" mkdir "$SECOND_DIR" && mkdir "$SECOND_DIR/output" && \ cp resources/models/example2_vs_vw_vs.cfg resources/models/decollement.poly "$SECOND_DIR/" cd "$SECOND_DIR" "$DYNEXE" example2_vs_vw_vs.cfg After successful completion, return to the notebook: # Read Example 2 monitors and apply the same speed/gap criteria as Example 1. second_history = tt.band_history(SECOND) second_events = tt.find_events(second_history) for number, event in enumerate(second_events, start=1): print(f"Event {number}: {event['start_yr']:.3f} yr; " f"peak speed {event['peak_relative_speed']:.3f} m/s") Plot Example 2's monitor history from SECOND before examining its spatial response. Compare the event timing and displacement jumps with Example 1. # Use the same six panels, including mean dt and pseudo-density, for Example 2. fig_second = tt.plot_history(second_history, title=f"Example 2 — {SECOND.name}") plt.show()

Before plotting, predict where plastic deformation and rapid motion will be concentrated: the VW patch, the VS flanks, or the surrounding host. To inspect your own spatial fields, the following cell uses SECOND and selects saved fields before, near the peak of, and after its first event. The upper row shows signed plastic-strain increments from the pre-event field; the lower row shows instantaneous nodal speed. These diagnostics complement the divergence/curl reference figure. Read the actual saved times printed below: a sparse save may miss the speed peak. This plot needs pre-event and recovered fields; if an input variation has no detected or recovered event, inspect its full history first. plot_snapshots chooses the last pre-event field whose maximum nodal speed is below 1e-7 m/s, the field nearest the sampled speed peak, and the first field at or after the first post-event P0/P1 relative-speed sample below 1e-7 m/s. Here "recovered" denotes that speed threshold, not proof that the band has physically locked; inspect the printed snapshot times. SPATIAL_EVENT_INDEX = 0 assert SPATIAL_EVENT_INDEX < len(second_events), "No such detected spatial episode." # Select saved fields before, nearest the sampled peak, and after recovery; # plot plastic-strain changes from the pre-event field and nodal speed. fig_spatial, selected_fields = tt.plot_snapshots( SECOND, second_history, event_index=SPATIAL_EVENT_INDEX) fig_spatial.suptitle(f"Example 2 — {SECOND.name}; event {SPATIAL_EVENT_INDEX + 1}") for label, row in selected_fields: print(f"{label}: {row['time_s'] / tt.YEAR:.6f} yr; step {row['step']}") plt.show() Exercise 2. Use your three snapshots and their printed times to describe where plastic strain accumulates and how the velocity pattern changes. Does your nearest saved field capture the rapid episode well? State what would require more frequent field output to resolve.

This separate exploration uses the bundled Figure 4 wavefield calculation, not your SECOND run. Its denser output illustrates velocity gradients; the preceding snapshot cell instead plots plastic-strain changes and speed. In the 2D x–z plane, these scalar diagnostics are div v = ∂vx/∂x + ∂vz/∂z and curl_y v = ∂vx/∂z − ∂vz/∂x, both in s⁻¹. They highlight dilatational and rotational motion around the slipping band. Derivatives are calculated directly within each linear triangular element on the current mesh, without smoothing. The next cell selects the saved reference time nearest 5.8 s after event detection and reports spatial maxima of the already-computed gradients. It does not calculate gradients from your own output. print("Source: supplied Figure 4 wavefield data") with np.load(FIGURES / "04_wavefield_data.npz") as data: offsets = data["time_after_detection_s"].copy() divergence = data["divergence"].copy() curl_y = data["curl_y"].copy() index = int(np.argmin(abs(offsets - 5.8))) print(f"Field time after detection: {offsets[index]:.3f} s") print(f"Maximum absolute divergence: {np.max(abs(divergence[index])):.3e} 1/s") print(f"Maximum absolute curl_y: {np.max(abs(curl_y[index])):.3e} 1/s") Observe before comparing. Check the selected time and the two maxima. Can these scalar maxima alone tell you where the deformation occurs? Open the reference to inspect its spatial distribution and animation. Reference result and interpretation — Figure 4 Figure 4. Top: divergence of velocity. Bottom: its out-of-plane curl. Times are seconds after the first event's analysis threshold crossing. The bracket marks the central VW interval. The full band is visible, with values beyond each fixed colour range saturated. View the velocity-gradient animation. Its frames have nonuniform physical time intervals; read their timestamps rather than interpreting playback speed as physical time. This calculation retains adaptive mass scaling and damping. The gradients show the spatial mechanical response, but do not by themselves establish physical P/S wave speeds or isolate pure wave amplitudes. Large gradients inside the band also include its localized deformation. Compare the reference snapshots and animation. Where are the largest gradients? How does the host response change as slip accelerates and decays? Distinguish evidence for spatial motion from a measurement of propagation speed.

Before plotting, predict whether the VS flanks and VW centre will accumulate displacement at the same rate between and during rapid episodes. Plot displacement profiles and VS/VW histories from SECOND using the same interface interpolation as the reference analysis. If a quiet field is available between the first event's recovery and the second event, start from the earliest such field to reveal the next loading interval and displacement jump. Otherwise, start from the earliest saved field in the run. All curves use that one common reference time, shown in the title. Markers represent saved fields, and straight connecting lines do not resolve unsaved rapid motion. The reference Figure 5 uses a post-first-event origin and dense saves around its second event; your reference time depends on the fields actually available. # List VTKHDF save files with their saved model times and solver steps. catalog = sorted(tt.field_catalog(SECOND), key=lambda row: row["time_s"]) if len(second_events) >= 2: recovered_time = second_history["time_s"][second_events[0]["quiet_index"]] next_start = second_history["time_s"][second_events[1]["start_index"]] quiet_fields = [row for row in catalog if recovered_time <= row["time_s"] < next_start] if quiet_fields: catalog = [row for row in catalog if row["time_s"] >= quiet_fields[0]["time_s"]] x_km = np.linspace(0, 100, 401) profiles = [] base_field = None for row in catalog: # Read mesh, velocity, plastic strain, material IDs and stress from VTKHDF. field = tt.read_field(row["path"]) if base_field is None: base_field = field assert np.array_equal(field["connectivity"], base_field["connectivity"]), "Mesh topology changed." assert np.array_equal(field["material"], base_field["material"]), "Material IDs changed." # Interpolate upper-minus-lower horizontal displacement at common initial x. profiles.append(tt._interface_profile(field, x_km)) profiles = np.asarray(profiles) profiles -= profiles[0].copy() field_times_yr = np.asarray([row["time_s"] / tt.YEAR for row in catalog]) positions_km = np.asarray([25., 50., 75.]) position_histories = np.asarray([np.interp(positions_km, x_km, profile) for profile in profiles]) fig_comparison, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(10, 8), layout="constrained") # Limit the legend to six profiles; the histories use every saved field. indices = np.unique(np.linspace(0, len(catalog) - 1, min(6, len(catalog)), dtype=int)) for index in indices: axes[0].plot(x_km, profiles[index], label=f"{field_times_yr[index]:.3f} yr") for left, right, name in [(0, 45, "VS"), (45, 55, "VW"), (55, 100, "VS")]: axes[0].axvspan(left, right, color="0.5", alpha=.06 if name == "VS" else .15) axes[0].text((left + right) / 200, .96, name, transform=axes[0].transAxes, ha="center", va="top") for column, label in enumerate(["Left VS (25 km)", "Central VW (50 km)", "Right VS (75 km)"]): axes[1].plot(field_times_yr, position_histories[:, column], ".-", label=label) axes[0].set(xlabel="Initial x (km)", ylabel="Across-band displacement (m)") axes[1].set(xlabel="Model time (yr)", ylabel="Across-band displacement (m)") for ax in axes: ax.grid(alpha=.18) ax.legend(fontsize=9) fig_comparison.suptitle(f"Example 2 — {SECOND.name}; common zero at {field_times_yr[0]:.3f} yr") plt.show() To save a generated figure as PNG and PDF, run, for example, tt.save_figure(fig_comparison, "example2_selected_run_displacement"). Files are written under results/figures/; using the same name again replaces those exported figures. The supplied numbered figures remain available for comparison. For denser profiles and histories, run figure5_dense.cfg in a fresh directory, set SECOND to that directory and rerun the Example 2 cells. Exercise 3. In your plots, compare displacement accumulation at the VS flanks and VW centre. Does either region develop a relative displacement deficit, and when does it change? Explain how the spatial profiles relate to the three time histories. Why would separate arbitrary displacement offsets obscure the comparison? Then open the reference below. Reference result and interpretation — Figure 5 Figure 5. Top strip: positions of the VS flanks and central VW patch. Upper plot: cumulative across-band horizontal displacement versus x at successive saved times. Blue curves show interseismic accumulation; warm colours resolve the second rapid episode. Lower plot: time histories of the same displacement at x = 25 km (left VS), 50 km (central VW) and 75 km (right VS). Circles and dotted lines identify the interseismic snapshots shown above. All curves use the same zero at 674.465 years, after the first event. VS flanks accumulate displacement steadily while the VW centre falls behind. Near 743.974 years, the centre makes a rapid displacement jump and catches up. The finite band still deforms between events: “locked” here means a relative displacement deficit, not exactly zero motion. Optional: inspect the supplied Figure 5 numerical data. This cell reads the illustrated reference run, independently of SECOND. Compare the three positions at the selected saved time with the reference figure above. print("Source: supplied Figure 5 displacement data") with np.load(FIGURES / "05_displacement_histories.npz") as data: positions = data["x_km"].copy() sample_times = data["time_s"].copy() displacements = data["displacement_m"].copy() index = int(np.argmin(abs(sample_times / tt.YEAR - 740.8))) print(f"At {sample_times[index] / tt.YEAR:.3f} yr:") for x, displacement in zip(positions, displacements[index]): print(f" x = {x:.0f} km: {displacement:.3f} m")

Copy Example 2 into a new run directory and change only the central material's evolution_b entry. Keep track of its a−b value and compare displacement histories, maximum speed and local stress release. Do not assume that every VW configuration must produce an earthquake, or that changing friction leaves the event timing unchanged. For denser observations with unchanged physical parameters, the download also includes figure2_dense.cfg, figure5_dense.cfg and figure4_wave.cfg. Copy one together with decollement.poly into a fresh directory containing output/ and pass its filename to DES, just as above. The first two run for 850 years; the wavefield case stops at 700 years and saves fields every ten steps. It can produce hundreds of megabytes of output.
