Use the supplied .poly guide to change the central patch width, or compare both detected events without changing the inputs. Keep each run separate and record one change at a time. For the broader context, see the DES documentation and Lapusta et al. (2000).

A frictional fault either creeps steadily or locks and fails in repeated earthquakes. Rate-and-state friction decides which through two quantities: the sign of a−b and the characteristic slip distance Dc​. This tutorial runs the three examples shipped in examples/earthquakes/rate_and_state_friction/, which differ only in those parameters, for 1000 years each: Case a b a−b Dc​ Outcome ep_rsf_creep 0.006 0.003 +0.003 1 mm steady creep ep_rsf_eq 0.003 0.015 −0.012 1 mm three earthquakes ep_rsf_creep_largeDc 0.003 0.015 −0.012 100 mm slow creep, no earthquake The same model also shows how global velocity scaling carries one simulation through centuries of loading and seconds of rupture. See rate-and-state friction for the equations and for global velocity scaling. At a glance Dimension 2D Build make ndims=2 Run time about 10 minutes per case on 3 threads Inputs examples/earthquakes/rate_and_state_friction/ in the DynEarthSol repository Checked with DynEarthSol 68cc2a0

Figure 1. The model, with depth exaggerated twice. The top moves right at the loading rate and the base is fixed. P is the monitor point on the top of the band at x = 50 km. Setting Value Domain 100 km × 10 km (2D), gravity 10 m/s² Band 4–6 km depth, full width, rate-and-state friction Hosts above and below the band; cohesion 1050 Pa keeps them elastic Elastic moduli and density K = 50 GPa, G = 30 GPa, 2700 kg/m³ Band strength cohesion 4 MPa, ϕ0​ = 30°, no dilation, no weakening RSF aging law, V0​=10−9 m/s, a, b and Dc​ as in the table above Loading top: vx​=10−9 m/s (3.2 cm/yr), vz​=0; base fixed; sides free Mesh rsf_long_strike_model_low_resolution.poly; about 215 m elements in the band, 300 m in the hosts; 32,091 elements Mechanics explicit, global velocity scaling with c=105, damping option 1 The .poly file divides the band into three regions (material IDs 3, 2, 1 from left to right) so that the central 10 km can be given different friction. In these examples all band materials share the same a and b.

Build dynearthsol2d in the DES root. Then: cd examples/earthquakes/rate_and_state_friction python3 run_rsf_examples.py --exe ../../../dynearthsol2d python3 plot_rsf_time_series.py -o rsf_time_series.png The runner creates one output folder per case and runs the three inputs one after another. On a laptop each case takes about 10 minutes with three OpenMP threads (OMP_NUM_THREADS=3). You can also run a single case directly: mkdir -p ep_rsf_eq OMP_NUM_THREADS=3 ../../../dynearthsol2d ep_rsf_eq.cfg The settings that matter for the cycle are: [sim] max_time_in_yr = 1000 output_time_interval_in_yr = 100 # regular frames earthquake_output_step_interval = 500 # extra frames during an event earthquake_start_factor = 5.0 # event: fastest speed > 5 x boundary speed, and > 1e-6 m/s earthquake_end_factor = 2.0 [control] use_global_velocity_scaling = true inertial_scaling = 1e5 damping_option = 1 [mat] rheology_type = elasto-plastic-rate-state-friction direct_a = [0.003, 0.003, 0.003, 0.003, 0.003] evolution_b = [0.015, 0.015, 0.015, 0.015, 0.015] characteristic_velocity = [1e-9] characteristic_distance = [1e-3] state_var_model = 1 # aging law [monitor] enabled = yes step_interval = 10 points_x = [50] points_y = [-4.0] # z in 2D points_unit = km output_velocity = yes output_stress = yes output_dynamic_friction = yes output_state_variable = yes

Each case writes to its own folder (ep_rsf_eq/, ep_rsf_creep/, ep_rsf_creep_largeDc/): <case>.save.* field frames: one every 100 years, plus one every 500 steps while an event is under way. The earthquake case has 40 frames (about 0.7 GB), the creep cases 11 (about 0.2 GB). <case>.chkpt.* checkpoints for restarting. <case>.info: one line per frame with the step, time (s) and time step (s). monitor_point_0.csv: the history at P every 10 steps, with velocity_x, velocity_z, stress_0–stress_2 (σxx, σzz, σxz), dynamic_friction and state_variable. plot_rsf_time_series.py plots the speed and displacement at P for all three cases. To read the monitor yourself: import numpy as np d = np.genfromtxt('ep_rsf_eq/monitor_point_0.csv', delimiter=',', names=True) year = 365.2422 * 86400 t = d['time_s'] / year speed = np.hypot(d['velocity_x'], d['velocity_z']) shear = np.abs(d['stress_2']) / 1e6 # MPa dt = np.diff(d['time_s']) / np.diff(d['step']) print(f'{speed.max():.2f} m/s peak; dt from {dt.min():.2g} to {dt.max():.2g} s')

Figure 2. Histories at P for the three cases: (a) speed, (b) shear stress σxz, (c) friction coefficient, (d) state variable. Loading (0–620 years). All three cases are identical. The band is still below its Mohr–Coulomb strength, so it deforms elastically, the friction law has no effect, and shear stress at P rises linearly. P moves at about 0.6 of the loading rate, its share of the elastic shear across the 10 km column. After yield (from about 620 years) the cases separate: Velocity strengthening (a−b>0). The band creeps at the loading rate and the shear stress stays near 57 MPa. Any acceleration raises friction and damps itself. Velocity weakening (a−b<0, Dc​ = 1 mm). The band fails in three earthquakes, at 632, 791 and 950 years, about 159 years apart. Peak speed at P is 0.7–1.6 m/s. Shear stress at P drops by 11–21 MPa in each event and then reloads. Velocity weakening with large Dc​ (100 mm). The band yields and then creeps while its stress slowly declines, from 59 to 53 MPa by 1000 years. No event occurs. With a 100 times larger Dc​, weakening is spread over 100 times more slip, and the critical stiffness kc​=(b−a)σ/Dc​ falls by the same factor, which favours stable sliding. Figure 3. The first earthquake at P, from 400 s before to 300 s after peak speed: (a) speed, (b) shear stress, (c) friction coefficient. Inside an event. Speed at P rises from about 10−5 m/s to 1.6 m/s in the last few seconds before the peak, and stays above 1 mm/s for about 12 s. The friction coefficient falls from 0.55 to near zero at peak slip rate, because the state collapses as the band slips many times Dc​. It then heals back toward 0.45–0.47 within minutes as slip slows. The shear stress swings below its final value and settles at 35 MPa, a static drop of about 21 MPa. Global velocity scaling at work. In the earthquake case the time step ranges from 3.9×105 s (4.5 days) during loading to 4.7×10−3 s at peak slip, a factor of 108. Each event takes about 2300–2700 steps; the whole 1000-year run takes 98,000 steps. Without the scaling the run would need about 1013 steps at the event time step.

Change a−b along the band. Give the central region (material 2) a velocity-weakening a−b and the flanks (materials 1 and 3) a velocity-strengthening one, as in the shear-band tutorial. Events then nucleate in the centre and stop in the flanks. Vary Dc​ between 1 and 100 mm. Find the value at which the earthquakes stop. Compare the recurrence interval and peak speed on the way. Record seismic moment. Set sim.seismic_moment_calculate_output = yes to write each event's start and end times and moment to seismic_moment_magnitude.txt. The moment is per unit length out of the plane in 2D (see Earthquake output). Each of the three earthquakes gives about 1.5×1016 N·m/m, that is 5 m of average slip on the 100 km layer; it is followed by a few short entries five to seven orders of magnitude smaller, as the speed crosses the thresholds again while the model rings down. Limit the state change per step. Add control.rsf_slip_rate_projection_option = 1 and control.rsf_dtheta_max = 0.5 and check how much the event changes.

One point. The monitor records the velocity of P on the top of the band, not the slip rate across it. Use the saved fields to see where an event starts and how far it spreads. Resolution. The band elements (about 215 m) are much larger than the nucleation length Lb​=G′Dc​/(bσ) of the 1 mm case, about 20 m for the lithostatic normal stress at 5 km depth. Event timing and size here are mesh dependent. In the first event the state also reaches its lower bound of 10−12 s. Damped inertia. Force damping stays on during events, and the default shear wave-speed cap keeps the scaled density above the physical density. The ruptures are therefore damped, quasi-dynamic events, not fully dynamic ones. Slip-rate measure. These inputs use the default velocity projection (rsf_slip_rate_projection_option = 0), which reads the element velocity rather than the velocity jump across it.

This tutorial walks through two classic long-term tectonic models with DynEarthSol: rifting of a brittle crustal layer, which produces a metamorphic core complex, and subduction of an oceanic plate beneath an overriding plate. Both use bundled 2D examples as a starting point, so you can run them as they are and then modify one ingredient at a time. Both cases move material a long way under divergent or convergent forcing. Deformation localizes where plastic strain accumulates, and with MMG remeshing the mesh is refined there, so faults stay sharp as the model runs. The first case takes minutes on a laptop; the second about half an hour. At a glance Dimension 2D Build make ndims=2 usemmg=1 Run time 12 minutes (rifting, to 100 kyr) and 22 minutes (subduction, to 5 Myr) on 6 threads Inputs examples/tectonics/core-complex.cfg, examples/tectonics/subduction.cfg and the tutorial package Checked with Part 1: DynEarthSol 68cc2a0 (relief, dip and element count as stated); Part 2: DynEarthSol 68cc2a0 (slab-tip depths, mesh growth and step count as stated; serpentinite and eclogite counts within 10 %; deepest trench point about 1 km deeper than stated, within the run-to-run scatter described under Exercise 3)

How a DES .cfg file is organized and which sections matter for tectonics How Mohr–Coulomb plasticity with strain softening produces faults, and how a weak zone and the wall velocities decide where and how fast How a slab-shaped initial geometry is built with a .poly file How marker phase changes add serpentinite and eclogite as the slab descends, and what the virtual-topology grid does for them How remeshing keeps a Lagrangian mesh usable, what triggers it, and how MMG refines along the faults and the plate interface How to read the output: plastic strain, topography, viscosity, temperature, material and velocity How to restart a run from a checkpoint with a changed boundary condition, and read what the model does when its forcing stops The two parts are meant to be read in order. Part 1 is the smallest model that shows a DES fault: one material, no temperature, a box mesh, a planar seed, three run steps. Part 2 keeps that skeleton and adds one ingredient at a time: Ingredient Part 1: core complex Part 2: subduction Geometry A box, refined in the middle by the config A .poly file with a slab already in the mantle Materials One Six populated, four reserved for phase-change products Rheology Elasto-plastic Elasto-visco-plastic with a geotherm Seed One planar weak zone One dipping segment along the slab top Walls Both pulled apart One pushed in, one fixed; material flows in through the wall Phase changes None Serpentinization and eclogitization on a marker grid Remeshing Bottom restored Bottom and side walls restored, which needs MMG Run time, 6 threads 12 minutes to 100 kyr 22 minutes to 5 Myr Every run time quoted on this page is the wall-clock time on 6 threads of an Apple M3 Max laptop; a 4-core machine of a few years ago takes two to three times longer. Each part has the same four steps, geometry, configuration, run, and what to look for, followed by exercises that change one parameter at a time. Workshop package For a hands-on class, download the tutorial package (12 MB). It holds a Jupyter notebook that draws every figure of this page, the configs of both parts and all exercises with the shell commands to run them, and reference results so the plots work before your own runs finish. Start with its README; resources/SETUP.md has a short build recipe.

This tutorial follows the ones before it in this section and uses what they cover. Before starting, ensure you have: ✅ DynEarthSol compiled in 2D with MMG, make ndims=2 usemmg=1; see Build and Running DES3D. MMG is a git submodule that make fetches and builds for you; the build is described in Adaptive mesh refinement with MMG ✅ Python 3 with numpy for 2vtk.py, and ParaView or another VTK viewer; see Visualizing outputs ✅ Read Making a complex mesh with .poly file: Part 2 reads its slab geometry from one ✅ Read Weak zones: Part 1 seeds a fault with a planar weak zone and Part 2 the plate interface with a segment one Velocity boundary conditions (3D) and Rate-and-state friction are not needed here: both examples are 2D with steady wall velocities and no earthquake cycles. The next tutorial, Coupling with GoSPL, adds surface processes to models like these. A default build is not enough A plain make builds the 3D executable without MMG, and that is what the build instructions and the first tutorial leave you with. This tutorial needs the 2D MMG build, make ndims=2 usemmg=1, which takes a few minutes on a laptop and leaves the 3D executable in place. Check it with ./dynearthsol2d --help | grep -c mmg, which must print a number above zero. Part 2 also needs a source tree from after 30 October 2026; see its note. Which build? Both examples are 2D; a 3D build (make) runs the same physics at a much higher cost. Part 1 runs on either build: a plain Triangle build (make ndims=2) remeshes uniformly, an MMG build refines along the fault, and the MMG box in Part 1 says what changes. Part 2 needs the MMG build, because its restored side walls (remeshing_option = 13) are only available with MMG. If you build once, build with usemmg=1.

DynEarthSol's rheology is built from three responses that can be switched on per run with rheology_type. Part 1 uses elasto-plastic; Part 2 adds viscous creep with elasto-visco-plastic. Component Controls Key parameters Used in Elastic Short-term stress build-up bulk_modulus, shear_modulus Parts 1 and 2 Plastic (Mohr–Coulomb, strain softening) Brittle faulting cohesion0/1, friction_angle0/1, dilation_angle0/1, pls0/1 Parts 1 and 2 Viscous (power-law creep) Ductile flow where it is hot visc_exponent, visc_coefficient, visc_activation_energy, min_viscosity, max_viscosity Part 2 only Temperature Viscosity through creep; density through alpha temperature_option, oceanic_plate_age_in_yr, surface_temperature, mantle_temperature Part 2 only Phase changes Marker material conversion at pressure–temperature boundaries phase_change_option, mattype_*, has_serpentinization, has_eclogitization Part 2 only

Faults in DES are bands of elements that have yielded. A band localizes only if the material gets weaker as it deforms: cohesion and friction angle drop linearly from their 0 values to their 1 values as accumulated plastic strain goes from pls0 to pls1. Fast softening (small pls1) favours one long-lived fault; slow softening spreads deformation over many short-lived faults.

In a uniform model nothing selects where the first fault forms, so the location of localization is uncontrolled and depends on mesh noise. A weak zone is a region given an initial plastic strain weakzone_plstrain, which pre-softens it and pins the first fault. Part 1 uses a planar seed (weakzone_option = 1), Part 2 a dipping multi-segment one. The other shapes are described in Weak zones.

vbc_x0 and vbc_x1 set the condition type on the left and right walls; type 1 fixes the normal velocity and leaves the shear component free. vbc_val_x0 and vbc_val_x1 are the normal velocities in m/s, positive toward +x, so a negative value on the left wall and a positive one on the right wall pull the model apart. The top is a free surface. The bottom carries a Winkler foundation, a lithostatic normal stress that lets the base move vertically.

Part 1 is isothermal. Part 2 sets an initial geotherm by half-space cooling (temperature_option = 0, oceanic_plate_age_in_yr), and temperature then evolves by conduction and advection. It feeds back into the viscosity through the creep law, which is what makes the deep slab and the mantle wedge flow. The other options are for continents: 1 is a linear continental gradient over lithospheric_thickness, 2 adds the equilibrium of crustal radiogenic heating, 3 puts an adiabatic mantle under the continental gradient, and 90 reads a temperature grid from a file.

A Lagrangian mesh follows the material, so elements distort as faults slip. When the worst element quality drops below min_quality (checked every quality_check_step_interval steps), or a boundary moves by more than max_boundary_distortion × resolution, DES rebuilds the mesh and maps the fields onto it. remeshing_option = 11 restores the bottom boundary to its initial depth. Markers carry material identity across remeshes. With MMG the rebuild is adaptive: elements are sized from accumulated plastic strain, so faults get finer elements and the quiet far field stays coarse. See Remeshing and MMG.

The bundled example examples/tectonics/core-complex.cfg stretches a single 10 km brittle layer with a pre-cut dipping fault. With strain softening the fault keeps slipping, its footwall rises and rotates, and the fault surface flattens into a dome. This is the rolling-hinge mechanism of metamorphic core complexes (Lavier, Buck & Poliakov 1999), and it is the fastest way to see every ingredient of a DES tectonic run. Setting Domain 100 × 10 km, 1 km resolution refined in the central 40 km (meshing_option = 2, refined_zonex = [0.3, 0.7]) Forcing ±1e-9 m/s (3.15 cm/yr per side, 6.3 cm/yr total) extension in x Duration 50 kyr as shipped (3.2 km of total extension), output every 1.5 kyr Rheology elasto-plastic, one material (ρ = 2700 kg/m³), cohesion 44 → 4 MPa over 0.5 plastic strain, friction 30° fixed Weak zone Planar (weakzone_option = 1), dipping 60°, 1.2 km half-width, in the lower half of the layer at x = 50 km Surface Hillslope diffusion, surface_diffusivity = 1e-7 m²/s Thermal Isothermal, 273 K
documents.s: Part 1: Rifting a brittle crust (core complex)

documents.t: Part 1 needs no mesh file. The box, its refinement and the seed fault are all set in the config: meshing_option = 2 meshes a rectangle at resolution between refined_zonex = [0.3, 0.7], 30 to 70 km, and lets elements grow to largest_size times the area outside, about 3 km on an edge. The seed is a planar weak zone through (50 km, 0) dipping 60° toward −x, 1.2 km wide and confined to the lower half of the layer, where it is given a plastic strain equal to pls1 so it starts fully softened.
documents.s: Step 1: The initial geometry and mesh

documents.t: core-complex.cfg [sim] modelname = result3 max_time_in_yr = 50000 output_time_interval_in_yr = 1500 has_output_during_remeshing = no is_outputting_averaged_fields = no [mesh] meshing_option = 2 xlength = 100e3 ylength = 10e3 zlength = 10e3 resolution = 1e3 largest_size = 10 smallest_size = 0.01 refined_zonex = [0.3, 0.7] refined_zoney = [0.0, 1.0] refined_zonez = [0.0, 1.0] quality_check_step_interval = 500 remeshing_option = 11 [control] surface_process_option = 1 surface_diffusivity = 1e-7 dt_fraction = 1.0 inertial_scaling = 1e5 [bc] vbc_x0 = 1 vbc_x1 = 1 vbc_val_x0 = -1e-9 vbc_val_x1 = 1e-9 vbc_y0 = 1 vbc_y1 = 1 vbc_val_y0 = 0 vbc_val_y1 = 0 has_water_loading = no surface_temperature = 273 mantle_temperature = 273 [ic] weakzone_option = 1 weakzone_azimuth = 15 weakzone_inclination = -60 weakzone_halfwidth = 1.2 weakzone_depth_min = 0.5 weakzone_depth_max = 1.0 weakzone_xcenter = 0.5 weakzone_ycenter = 0.5 weakzone_zcenter = 0 weakzone_plstrain = 0.5 [mat] rheology_type = elasto-plastic rho0 = [2700] alpha = [0] bulk_modulus = [50e9] shear_modulus = [30e9] pls0 = [0] pls1 = [0.5] cohesion0 = [4.4e7] cohesion1 = [4e6] friction_angle0 = [30] friction_angle1 = [30] min_viscosity = 1e24 Section by section: [sim] names the output (result3.save.*) and runs 50 kyr with a frame every 1.5 kyr. Instantaneous rather than averaged fields are written. [mesh] builds a 100 × 10 km box. meshing_option = 2 refines the central 40 % in x at resolution, and lets the flanks coarsen up to largest_size times that. ylength is read but unused in 2D. remeshing_option = 11 flattens the bottom back to 10 km depth at every remesh. [control] turns on surface diffusion and sets the mass scaling. inertial_scaling is the factor by which density is inflated to lengthen the elastic time step; see Mass scaling. With no viscosity in play, this parameter and the element size set dt. [bc] pulls the two walls apart at 3.15 cm/yr each. The vbc_y* lines matter only in 3D. Water loading is off because the surface starts at sea level and would otherwise be loaded as it subsides. [ic] cuts the seed fault. Positions are fractions of the domain: weakzone_xcenter = 0.5 is x = 50 km, and weakzone_depth_min/max = 0.5, 1.0 confines the seed to the lower 5 km. weakzone_halfwidth is in units of resolution. weakzone_plstrain = 0.5 equals pls1, so the seed starts fully softened. weakzone_azimuth is a 3D parameter and is ignored here. [mat] is one material. Cohesion softens by a factor of 11; friction does not. min_viscosity is irrelevant for elasto-plastic but must be set. The parameters you will change most often: Parameter What it sets max_time_in_yr Total extension; 100 kyr gives 6.3 km and a clear dome weakzone_inclination Dip of the seed fault; the sign picks which way it dips pls1 Plastic strain needed to fully soften; smaller localizes faster cohesion1 Strength after softening; lower = sharper fault surface_diffusivity How fast relief is smoothed; controls footwall exhumation vbc_val_x0, vbc_val_x1 Extension rate at each wall, m/s resolution, refined_zonex Element size and where it is fine

cd DynEarthSol/examples/tectonics OMP_NUM_THREADS=6 ../../dynearthsol2d core-complex.cfg As shipped the file stops at 50 kyr, which is enough to see the fault break through and the footwall start to rise. The figures below run to 100 kyr, when the dome is fully formed; to reproduce them, change one line: max_time_in_yr = 100000 The log prints one line per output_time_interval_in_yr with the step count, model time and dt, and a remeshing notice whenever the mesh is rebuilt. Output goes to result3.save.* and result3.info in the working directory. Cost on a laptop: the stock 50 kyr run takes a few minutes. To 100 kyr the MMG build took 12 minutes on 6 threads while another run shared the machine, 6.2 million steps, 23 remeshes, 720 to about 1300 elements. The Triangle build needs about the same number of steps and ends with about 1800 elements. It remeshes some 20 times for the usual reasons, but twice in the run a surface element at the fault scarp, x = 53 km, sits just below min_quality after each rebuild, so every quality check remeshes again, over 1100 times in all. Remeshing is still about 1 % of the wall time with Triangle and 0.03 % with MMG; the time step, not the mesh, is the cost. With and without MMG The runs shown below use the MMG build from the prerequisites. The same file also runs on a plain Triangle build (make ndims=2); nothing in the config changes. The difference is in how the mesh is rebuilt. MMG sizes elements from accumulated plastic strain, within a band set by two parameters the file already has: the largest edge is resolution × largest_size^(1/2) and the smallest resolution × (smallest_size × mmg_remesh_defensive_tiny_ratio)^(1/2), 3.2 km and 0.12 km here, and it is conservative, freezing elements that are not yielding, distorted or tiny so that each remesh touches mainly the fault band. Triangle rebuilds the whole mesh at the initial sizes. To 100 kyr the MMG run ends with about 1300 elements after 23 remeshes, the Triangle run with about 1800 after over 1100, nearly all of them repeats on a surface element at the fault scarp that a rebuild does not improve. The build is described in Adaptive mesh refinement with MMG. The full parameter list, with a one-line tuning rule for each, is in the [mesh] section of examples/defaults.cfg and in dynearthsol2d --help. These parameters are in DynEarthSol master since PR #95, October 2026.

python ../2vtk.py result3 Open result3.*.vtu in ParaView. Fields to look at: plastic strain, the fault, and whether it stays one band surface topography, footwall uplift and hanging-wall basin strain rate, where slip is happening now, as opposed to where it has happened the mesh itself, how element size tracks the fault after remeshing The left column is where slip has accumulated and how the mesh follows it; the right column is where slip is happening now. They differ: at 50 kyr the strain rate shows a second, antithetic band under the footwall at x = 55–65 km that never gains enough plastic strain to show on the left. The bottom row quantifies the rolling hinge: the fault band steepens to 49° while it breaks through, then rotates steadily to 35° by 100 kyr as relief grows to 3.8 km. Things to look for as the run proceeds (the figure is the reference run): Breakthrough. The seed fault cuts up to the surface at about 13 kyr and the footwall starts to rise; the velocity arrows show the footwall moving up and to the right while the hanging wall slides left. Relief. By 50 kyr the surface has a footwall crest of 1.4 km near x = 54 km and a basin of 1.2 km near x = 50 km, 2.6 km of relief; by 100 kyr the crest is 2.2 km at x = 56 km and the relief 3.8 km. The rolling hinge. The fault rotates to a shallower dip as it is exhumed, from about 47° at 25 kyr to 35° at 100 kyr; the band of high plastic strain curves from steep at depth to gentle near the surface, and its exhumed upper part drapes the footwall dome. The mesh. After a remesh the elements along the fault are smaller than in the far field with MMG, and uniform with Triangle; the MMG run grows from 720 to about 1300 elements over 100 kyr.

Run surface_diffusivity What you should see at 100 kyr Reference 1e-7 Sharp footwall crest 2.2 km high, basin 1.7 km deep, 3.8 km of relief Moderate 1e-6 The same structure a little smoothed: crest 1.8 km, basin 1.6 km, 3.4 km of relief Strong erosion 1e-5 Relief capped at 1.5 km from about 50 kyr on; the crest is planed to 1 km and the basin filled to 0.5 km while the fault keeps slipping The coloured bands are passive horizons: every node carries its initial position through remeshing in the coord0 field, so contouring the initial depth on the present mesh shows where each layer of the original crust has gone. Read them together with the surface panels: The fault is the same in all three runs. The band dips 41° to 42° at 50 kyr and 34° to 36° at 100 kyr and reaches a plastic strain of 3.7 whatever the diffusivity. Diffusion acts on the surface only. So is the exhumation. Rock from 8 km depth has risen to about 4 km depth at x = 48 km in all three, the horizons under the dome are bent the same way, and the rock exposed at the surface came from 1.4 to 2.3 km in every run. The fault sets how far the footwall rises; erosion does not add to it here. What changes is the topography. At 1e-5 m²/s the relief stops growing at about 50 kyr because the crest is planed as fast as the fault lifts it and the debris fills the basin. The same exhumation then shows as a low dome rather than a sharp crest. That is why relief alone is a poor measure of what a fault has done, and why the horizons are worth drawing. Each run took 4 to 12 minutes on 6 threads.

Requires the MMG build (make ndims=2 usemmg=1). Two parameters decide how fine the mesh becomes along the fault. smallest_size is the area of the smallest allowed element relative to one of edge resolution: with MMG it sets the floor of the refinement band, resolution × (smallest_size × mmg_remesh_defensive_tiny_ratio)^(1/2), and for every remesher it sets the tiny-element trigger, an element compressed below smallest_size of its nominal area forcing a remesh. Both scale with its square root, so a factor of 100 in smallest_size is a factor of 10 in element edge. mmg_metric_refine_coeff is the target: MMG aims for an element area of the initial one divided by 1 + coeff × plastic strain, so at the default 5 an element at a plastic strain of 4 is asked to shrink to a fifth of its initial edge. The mesh can only be as fine as the target asks and the floor allows. Run smallest_size Smallest MMG element What you should see No refinement 1 1.2 km A diffuse band 3 km wide that never sharpens; the run takes an eighth of the time Stock 0.01 0.12 km A sharp fault, about 1300 elements; 12 min Very fine 0.001 0.04 km The same mesh as stock, since the target rather than the floor limits refinement; 5 % more steps for nothing Very fine, stronger target 0.001 with mmg_metric_refine_coeff = 10 0.04 km Now the band refines: 1770 elements, 70 % more in the band, and a second fault splays into the hanging wall All four rows were run. Going up to smallest_size = 1 costs resolution: the fault still forms in the same place and the surface still domes, but the band cannot be narrower than the elements it runs through, so the strain is spread over a 3 km wide zone and the fault never sharpens. The time step is on average seven times longer, since it follows the smallest element, and the whole run takes an eighth of the time. Going down to 0.001 alone buys nothing. The smallest element in the stock run is 0.17 km, above the 0.12 km floor, so the floor was not what stopped the refinement; the target was. Lowering the floor further cannot refine the band, and what it does change is the tiny-element trigger: squeezed elements may now shrink to a third of the size before a remesh repairs them, so the time step can fall further. Here that costs only 5 % more steps, but it is a cost with nothing in return. Raising the target as well, mmg_metric_refine_coeff = 10, is what makes the lower floor useful. The band now holds 560 elements instead of the stock run's 330, at a median edge of 0.29 km instead of 0.43, and the smallest element reaches 0.12 km, still above the 0.04 km floor. The fault is drawn more sharply and the maximum plastic strain is a little higher, 4.1 against 3.7. The finer band also lets a second fault split off the main one into the hanging wall from about 50 kyr; by 100 kyr it reaches the surface at x = 45 km and opens a second, smaller basin there. Away from that splay the surface hardly notices: the three refined runs end with the same crest and basin to within 0.2 km, and only the unrefined run is lower and broader. The lesson is that the two parameters work as a pair: the target asks for refinement where plastic strain accumulates, the floor caps how far it may go, and moving one without the other changes the cost of the run more than its result. Change one parameter at a time, and keep a log of what you changed.

documents.t: core-complex.cfg has no mantle, no temperature and no viscosity. examples/tectonics/rifting-2d.cfg adds all three: a 500 × 150 km crust-over-mantle lithosphere read from a .poly file (the one used in Making a complex mesh), elasto-visco-plastic rheology, a 100 Myr half-space geotherm and a Gaussian weak zone. It runs for 2 Myr at 6 km resolution. Everything in Part 2 that is new relative to Part 1 appears there first, so it is a good intermediate step.

Part 2 needs a recent master The example below, examples/tectonics/subduction.cfg, and the phase-change engine it uses (phase_change_option = 3 on a virtual-topology marker grid) reached DynEarthSol master on 30 October 2026 with pull request #110. A clone or build from before that date does not have them: git pull and rebuild with make ndims=2 usemmg=1 first. A quick check is ./dynearthsol2d --help | grep -c serpentinization, which must print a number above zero. The example examples/tectonics/subduction.cfg with its mesh file poly-subduction.poly pushes an oceanic plate under a fixed overriding plate. A short slab is already in the mantle at the start, so the plate interface exists from the first step. Two metamorphic reactions run on the markers as the slab descends: mantle just above the slab top becomes serpentinite, a weak and light layer that lubricates the interface, and slab crust that sinks past the basalt-to-eclogite boundary becomes eclogite, dense enough to add slab pull. Everything that was missing from Part 1 appears here: several materials, viscous creep, a geotherm, a .poly geometry, phase changes and material flowing in through a side wall. Setting Domain 400 × 160 km, 6 km resolution, a 10 km halo of refined mantle around the slab (poly-subduction.poly) Initial slab Oceanic crust 7 km thick, from the trench at x = 125–139 km dipping 30° to 40 km depth Forcing Left plate pushed at +1e-9 m/s (3.15 cm/yr) into a fixed right wall (vbc_val_x1 = 0) Duration 5 Myr, a frame every 50 kyr; about 23 min alone on 6 threads, 31 min when two runs share the machine; 5.8 million steps Rheology elasto-visco-plastic, 10 materials of which 6 are populated; cohesion 40 → 4 MPa and friction 30° → 15° over 0.1 plastic strain; sediment and serpentinite at 3° Phase changes phase_change_option = 3: serpentinization and eclogitization on, the other rules off Weak zone One 30° segment along the slab top (weakzone_option = 5), seeding the plate interface Thermal Half-space cooling, 80 Myr plate; surface 273 K, mantle 1573 K Remeshing MMG required; remeshing_option = 13 restores the side walls so the incoming plate keeps its layering Surface Hillslope diffusion, surface_diffusivity = 5e-7 m²/s; deposits become sediment

A subducting slab needs a pre-existing dipping interface, which a weak zone alone cannot supply. poly-subduction.poly defines it as a region of oceanic crust already inside the mantle, following Making a complex mesh with .poly file: 0------------------------------------------7 z = 0: top, free surface 1------------------------------------------6 z = -2 km: sediment / crust 2----12--8=====9--13-----------------------5 z = -9 km: crust / mantle | \ \ 0 \ \ | | \ 10----11 15 | 10-11: slab end, cut normal to the dip | \ \ / | 12-14: halo below the slab | 14-------/ | 13-15: halo above the slab | | 3------------------------------------------4 z = -160 km: bottom Region Material Max element area What it is 0 3, sediment 4 km² The top 2 km across the whole domain 1 0, oceanic crust 8 km² 2 to 9 km depth across the whole domain 2 0, oceanic crust 8 km² The slab, 7 km thick, 30° dip, ending at 34–40 km depth 3 2, mantle 10 km² A 10 km halo around the slab, refined so the serpentinite layer is resolved 4 2, mantle 1000 km² The rest of the mantle, coarse Three things to notice: No region holds serpentinite or eclogite. Those materials exist only because the phase-change rules create them. The halo is what makes the example affordable: 6 km elements everywhere except a band where the interface needs them finer. The internal segments are discarded at the first remesh (is_discarding_internal_segments = yes). After that the slab is carried by the markers alone, which is why has_marker_output = yes is set. The grid drawn over the slab is the virtual topology used by the serpentinization rule, explained below. Its cells are half an element wide, so the one-element-thick slab crust gets its own row of crust-dominant cells instead of being averaged with the mantle.

documents.t: subduction.cfg (abridged; the file itself is fully commented) [sim] modelname = model-subduction max_time_in_yr = 5e6 output_time_interval_in_yr = 50e3 has_marker_output = yes [mesh] meshing_option = 90 poly_filename = poly-subduction.poly xlength = 400e3 zlength = 160e3 resolution = 6e3 # times vt_size = serpentinization grid cell smallest_size = 0.04 quality_check_step_interval = 1000 min_quality = 0.2 remeshing_option = 13 # restore the side walls (needs MMG) is_discarding_internal_segments = yes mmg_hausd_factor = 0.1 max_boundary_distortion = 1 mmg_aniso_wall_ratio = 2 [markers] init_marker_option = 1 replenishment_option = 12 [control] ref_pressure_option = 1 # PREM surface_process_option = 1 surface_diffusivity = 5e-7 inertial_scaling = 1e4 [bc] surface_temperature = 273 mantle_temperature = 1573 vbc_x0 = 1 vbc_x1 = 1 vbc_val_x0 = 1e-9 # +x, 3.15 cm/yr vbc_val_x1 = 0 # fixed backstop has_water_loading = no [ic] weakzone_option = 5 weakzone_plstrain = 1 weakzone_num_segments = 1 weakzone_segments_inclination = [30] weakzone_segments_halfwidth = [0.6] weakzone_segments_xcenter = [0.42] weakzone_segments_zcenter = [0.135625] weakzone_segments_depth_min = [0.000] weakzone_segments_depth_max = [0.19375] weakzone_segments_x_min = [0.275] weakzone_segments_x_max = [0.575] oceanic_plate_age_in_yr = 80e6 [mat] rheology_type = elasto-visco-plastic num_materials = 10 phase_change_option = 3 mattype_oceanic_crust = 0 mattype_mantle = 2 mattype_sediment = 3 mattype_serpentinite = 4 mattype_eclogite = 5 serpentinization_thickness = 5e3 # [ ocean0 (1) mant2 sed3 serp4 eclg5 ... ] rho0 = [ 2880, 2800, 3300, 2400, 3200, 3480, ... ] friction_angle0 = [ 30, 30, 30, 3, 3, 30, ... ] friction_angle1 = [ 15, 15, 15, 3, 3, 15, ... ] pls1 = [ 0.1 ] max_viscosity = 1e24 min_viscosity = 1e19 Section by section, with what is new relative to Part 1: [sim] writes a frame every 50 kyr and the markers with it, since the materials live on the markers once the poly segments are gone. [mesh] reads the .poly file (meshing_option = 90). remeshing_option = 13 restores the left and right walls to their initial positions at every remesh, so the plate entering through the left wall arrives with its sediment-over-crust-over-mantle layering intact. This option needs MMG. mmg_aniso_wall_ratio = 2 lets the incoming column be carried on elements twice as long normal to the wall as along it. [markers] replenishment_option = 12 refills an element that has lost its markers with its own single material, which keeps thin layers from vanishing. [control] ref_pressure_option = 1 uses the PREM reference pressure; the phase-change rules read pressure and temperature at the marker's depth below the current free surface. inertial_scaling = 1e4 lengthens the time step ten times over the default, buying speed at a known cost in accuracy, which the file's comments quantify. [bc] pushes only the left wall. The right wall is a fixed backstop, so the trench sits still in the model frame and the slab is fed from the left. The two temperatures set the half-space geotherm with the 80 Myr age in [ic]. [ic] seeds the interface with a single 30° plastic weak zone along the slab top, extending a few km into the mantle wedge. Values are fractions of the domain. [mat] has ten material slots. Five are populated by the initial mesh or the active rules: oceanic crust, mantle, sediment, serpentinite and eclogite. Slot 1 is kept free for continental crust, and four more, hydrous mantle, sedimentary rock, metasediment and schist, are the targets of rules that are switched off, so they stay empty. Each mattype_* tells the rule engine which slot plays which role. The phase-change rules​ phase_change_option = 3 runs every 10 steps over all markers. A rule fires only when its switch is on and its source and target are distinct, valid materials; the run stops at input otherwise. Transition Rule Switch Mantle → serpentinite In the antigorite pressure–temperature field (Ulmer & Trommsdorff 1995), shallower than serpentinization_max_depth (150 km), and with a grid cell within serpentinization_thickness below the marker whose oceanic crust and sediment share exceeds wet_crust_fraction_threshold (one half) has_serpentinization (on) Serpentinite → mantle Above 550 °C and outside the antigorite field has_serpentinization (on) Oceanic crust → eclogite Past the basalt–eclogite boundary (Hacker 2003); one way has_eclogitization (on) Hydrous mantle → mantle Chlorite-out boundary (Grove et al. 2009) has_hydrous_mantle_dehydration (off) Sediment → sedimentary rock → metasediment → schist Compaction, then metamorphic thresholds has_sediment_metamorphism (off) The "crust below" test is what makes serpentinization follow the slab instead of the whole mantle. DES keeps a coarse background grid of marker materials, the virtual topology, with cells of resolution × vt_size (3 km here). A mantle marker looks down through that grid as far as serpentinization_thickness, 5 km here, so one cell, and converts if it finds a cell that is mostly crust. The grid is built at the start, rebuilt after each remesh and carried through checkpoints, so a restart continues with the same cells. Two details worth knowing: the reach is counted in whole cells, so it can differ from the nominal thickness by up to two cells; and the pressure the rules read is the element mean stress, not a fixed lithostat, so tectonic over- and underpressure shift the reaction boundaries slightly. The parameters you will change most often: Parameter What it sets vbc_val_x0 Convergence rate, m/s oceanic_plate_age_in_yr Thermal age, hence strength and negative buoyancy, of the incoming plate friction_angle0/1 of sediment and serpentinite Plate-interface strength; controls dip and forearc style serpentinization_thickness How thick the weak layer above the slab can grow, in whole grid cells; must be positive and at least one cell, so "none" is has_serpentinization = no has_serpentinization, has_eclogitization Turn each reaction off for a control run rho0 of eclogite Slab pull at depth surface_diffusivity Trench fill and forearc erosion max_time_in_yr 5 Myr is about 160 km of convergence

Run from examples/tectonics/ so the .poly path resolves. The MMG build from the prerequisites is required here, since the restored side walls need it: cd DynEarthSol/examples/tectonics OMP_NUM_THREADS=6 ../../dynearthsol2d subduction.cfg The full run takes about 22 minutes on 6 threads, with the mesh growing from about 2600 to 4500 elements. Output goes to model-subduction.save.*; the step counter in the log advances about a million steps per 0.9 Myr. Smoke run first Before committing to the full run, set max_time_in_yr = 500e3 and output_time_interval_in_yr = 25e3. That is 2 to 3 minutes on 6 threads and already shows the serpentinite layer along the slab top and a sediment-filled trench, enough to confirm the build, the MMG remeshing and the phase changes all work. Then restore the two lines.

python ../2vtk.py model-subduction Open model-subduction.*.vtu in ParaView. Fields to look at: material on the markers, to see serpentinite and eclogite appear plastic strain, the plate interface and any forearc faults viscosity, the cold slab against the weak wedge temperature, the slab's thermal anomaly and the heated wedge corner Things to look for as the run proceeds (the figure is the reference run): Serpentinite from the first frame. The slab is already in place, so mantle just above its top converts at once: about 370 markers by 0.5 Myr, 3200 by 5 Myr. On the viscosity panels this layer sits at the 10¹⁹ Pa s floor and is the weakest material in the model. Eclogite starts at the slab tip. A few dozen markers have converted by 0.5 Myr, where the tip sits near 50 km; the count grows to about 380 by 5 Myr, when the deepest 30 km of the slab is eclogite. The slab tip reaches 50 km at 0.5 Myr, 85 km at 2.5 Myr and about 125 km at 5 Myr, keeping a dip of 30–35° on its way down. The cold core stays at the 10²⁴ Pa s viscosity cap and drags the isotherms down with it. The wedge corner serpentinizes wholesale. The mantle between the overriding plate's crust and the slab top lies within one grid cell of crust, so by 2.5 Myr a body 20–25 km thick and 50 km long has converted. This is the geometric rule at work, not a thermal one; Exercise 3 shows how serpentinization_thickness controls it. The trench fills with sediment and the overriding plate's crust bends down into it, while the incoming plate at the left wall keeps its three layers thanks to the restored wall. How the mesh keeps up​ The mesh grows by two thirds over the run, and the left panel shows where the new elements go. Elements with no plastic strain fall from 2500 to about 2000 as the deforming band widens into them, and they stay coarse at a median of 4.5 km. Fully softened elements, those past pls1 = 0.1, grow from none to about 1900, 42 % of the mesh, at a median size of 2.1 km against the 6 km resolution and the 1.5 km MMG floor. That is the MMG metric at work: mmg_metric_refine_coeff shrinks the target size where plastic strain has accumulated, along the plate interface and in the wedge, and nowhere else. The 200 remeshes have three triggers, each checked every quality_check_step_interval steps. A tiny element is one whose area has dropped below smallest_size times the resolution squared. Low quality is an element quality below min_quality, 0.2 here. Bottom drift is a bottom node more than max_boundary_distortion times resolution, 6 km here, from the 160 km base. The first two are the ordinary triggers and fire throughout. Bottom drift belongs to the first million years, 26 of its 28 remeshes, while the slab tip sinks through the lower mantle and the Winkler bottom adjusts; after that it stops. Each remesh moves the element count by only a few tens, because the conservative MMG mode freezes elements that are not yielding, distorted or tiny. Remeshing takes under 1 % of the wall time; the phase changes take 5 %.

serpentinization_thickness sets how far above the slab top mantle can convert, counted in 3 km grid cells. It must be positive, so the zero case is the rule switched off. Run Thickness Change What you should see None 0 km has_serpentinization = no The interface locks. The slab tip falls behind from 2 Myr on and reaches only 100 km at 5 Myr, the slab necks and tears below the overriding plate, and both plates thicken and buckle: the trench reaches 9 km at 2.5 Myr, 3 km deeper than the reference Reference 5 km serpentinization_thickness = 5e3 (one cell) Steady subduction to 125 km at 5 Myr; trench deepens to 6.5 km by 3 Myr and recovers to 4 km; about 3200 serpentinite and 380 eclogite markers Thick 10 km serpentinization_thickness = 10e3 (two cells) Half again as much serpentinite (4600 markers) in a wedge body that reaches further down the slab; trench about 1 km shallower on average, with less swing; slab tip 120 km; a quarter fewer eclogite markers What the comparison shows: The weak layer is what makes this model subduct. Without it the sediment seed alone cannot keep the interface slipping; convergence goes into thickening and buckling the plates, the slab falls behind and tears below the overriding plate, and the velocity arrows show the whole overriding plate being pushed instead of the slab sliding under it. Such a run also works the mesh hard: the thickened plates load the Winkler bottom unevenly and most of its remeshes are bottom-drift triggers, and an earlier build of this case died in a remeshing failure at 3.45 Myr. A thicker layer lubricates more. With two cells the trench is shallower by about 1 km on average and swings less, the forearc high is lower, and the wedge-corner body is larger. The slab tip ends 4 km shallower. Eclogite responds indirectly. The 10 km run has about 300 eclogite markers at 5 Myr against 380 in the reference. The rule did not change; the thicker weak layer keeps the slab crust shallower and warmer where it would otherwise cross the reaction boundary. Time step and cost barely change: 5.7 to 5.9 million steps for the two subducting runs, about 22 minutes alone on 6 threads; the locked run takes 4.3 million steps and 17 minutes because its plates move more slowly. The reference and the 10 km run were each made twice, on the pull request's branch and on master after the merge, with the same configuration. The pairs agree on everything above, but differ in detail: the 10 km trench ended 1 km shallower than the reference in one pair and 0.5 km deeper in the other, and the eclogite deficit was 40 % in one and 22 % in the other. That is the chaotic scatter of a remeshing model. Read differences of that size as suggestive, and the locking of the 0 km case, which starts by 1 Myr and grows, as robust.
documents.s: Exercise 3: change the thickness of the serpentinite layer

documents.t: A run can be continued from any checkpoint with changed settings. DES writes a checkpoint every checkpoint_frame_interval frames, 10 by default, so the reference run leaves its last one at frame 100, 5 Myr. The example is already set up to restart from it; switch the restart on, give the run another two million years and stop the push: is_restarting = yes restarting_from_modelname = model-subduction restarting_from_frame = 100 max_time_in_yr = 7e6 vbc_val_x0 = 0 # the left plate is held still The restart runs in the same directory as the parent, reads its frame 100 and checkpoint, and writes frames 100 to 140 of its own; the extra two million years take about two minutes. The question it answers is which parts of the model were driven by the push and which carry on by themselves once convergence stops, as after a collision or a plate reorganisation. The slab stops. Its tip sank 13 km per million years while pushed and less than 1 km in the two million years after. There is no slab pull to speak of here: the plate it hangs from is held at the wall, and sinking further would mean stretching a plate at the 10²⁴ Pa s viscosity cap. This model subducts because it is pushed. The peak speed in the domain falls from 19 to 1 cm/yr. The surface rebounds first, then smooths. Within the first million years the trench shallows from 3.8 to 1.8 km and the forearc high rises from 2.6 to 5.3 km; the whole overriding plate between x = 100 and 300 km comes up by 1.5 to 2.5 km. That is isostatic rebound: the shear on the plate interface that was holding the overriding plate down is gone. After that the levels hardly move, the high eases back to 4.6 km, and surface diffusion takes over: at surface_diffusivity = 5e-7 it reaches √(κt) ≈ 6 km in two million years, enough to cut the root-mean-square slope between x = 60 and 340 km by a third while the overall relief stays near 6 km. Diffusion rounds the slopes; it does not remove the relief. The incoming plate next to the held wall sags by up to 6 km, a wall effect to be aware of. The slab warms and reacts until it runs out of crust. Below 60 km the slab's mean temperature rises by 50 °C over the two million years, because nothing cold arrives any more. Eclogite is the one thing that speeds up: 381 markers at 5 Myr become 588 by 5.75 Myr as the stationary crust heats across the basalt–eclogite boundary and the eclogite front climbs from 87 to 71 km depth. Then it stops, at 610 markers by 7 Myr: the crust above 71 km is too shallow to cross the boundary however warm it gets, so a stationary slab saturates. Serpentinite grows by 190 markers in the first half million years, then stops too: its rule is geometric and needs new mantle to be brought over crust. Two cautions. Pick a restart frame that is not a remesh step, since a checkpoint written on one is not bit-recoverable. And a restart is a new realization of a chaotic run, so compare it with the parent's trend, as the bottom row does, rather than with a single frame. Change one parameter at a time, and keep a log of what you changed.
documents.s: Restart case: stop the convergence and see what carries on

documents.t: The rows marked "observed" come from runs made for this tutorial; the others are the usual causes. Symptom Part Cause and fix Strain stays diffuse, no single fault 1 The band cannot be narrower than its elements: smallest_size too large (observed at 1, Exercise 2) or resolution too coarse. Or softening is too slow: pls1 large, or weakzone_plstrain below pls1 so the seed is not pre-softened Fault dies and a new one forms 1 Slow softening or a thick layer favours several short-lived faults over one long-lived one; lower pls1 or thin the layer (Lavier, Buck & Poliakov 2000) Time step shrinks and the run slows both dt follows the smallest element; the mesh has refined more than you want. Raise smallest_size or lower mmg_metric_refine_coeff (observed: 0.017 yr at the stock 0.01 against 0.11 yr at 1) Stops at input with a mattype_* message 2 Each active rule needs its source and target set to distinct, valid materials; check the mattype_* lines against num_materials Stops at input: serpentinization_thickness too small 2 It must be at least one grid cell, resolution × vt_size remeshing_option 13 refused 2 Restored side walls need an MMG build: make ndims=2 usemmg=1 Serpentinite appears far from the slab 2 The rule has no temperature gate below 150 km; a slab bend can make a whole grid column crust-dominant. Set serpentinization_wet_crust_margin >= 0 to confine it Slab stalls, plates thicken and buckle 2 The interface is too strong: this is the has_serpentinization = no case of Exercise 3. Check mattype_serpentinite is set and the sediment and serpentinite friction angles are low. Such a run also piles up bottom-drift remeshes and can end in [DES exit 41]; to carry it on, restart from the last checkpoint with max_boundary_distortion halved to 0.5
