With usemmg = 1 in Makefile, MMG is pulled in as a git submodule and built automatically; no separate MMG install or MMG_INCLUDE/MMG_LIB_DIR setup is needed. mesh.smallest_size and mesh.largest_size set MMG's minimum and maximum element edge length, as a multiple of mesh.resolution (the same two parameters also bound meshing_option = 2's coarse zone): largest_size = 30 (default): the largest element has edge length largest_size^(1/NDIMS) * resolution smallest_size = 0.01 (default): the smallest element has edge length smallest_size^(1/NDIMS) * resolution Remeshing with MMG is conservative by default: a remesh freezes (keeps as-is) every quiet element and only refines, repairs, or coarsens the elements that a specific rule flags, chiefly ones whose plastic strain grew since the last remesh. This replaces an earlier, simpler scheme that rebuilt the whole mesh from a plastic-strain-scaled size field every remesh. See Conservative remeshing below. mmg_hmin_factor and mmg_hmax_factor are retired These two parameters no longer exist; using them now exits with "unknown or retired key." Use mesh.smallest_size/mesh.largest_size instead. To keep the same element sizes as before, convert the old values: largest_size = mmg_hmax_factor^NDIMS and smallest_size = mmg_hmin_factor^NDIMS / mmg_remesh_defensive_tiny_ratio (the old defaults, mmg_hmax_factor = 2.0/mmg_hmin_factor = 0.2, convert to largest_size = 4/smallest_size = 0.0267 in 2D and largest_size = 8/ smallest_size = 0.00533 in 3D, using the new default mmg_remesh_defensive_tiny_ratio = 1.5).
examples/tectonics/core-complex-mmg.cfg param.mesh.resolution: 1 km

mmg_debug: Turn on/off debug mode. In debug mode, MMG checks if all structures are allocated. mmg_verbose: Level of verbosity, -1 to 10, for MMG's own library output. mesh.meshing_verbosity: Screen output of DES's own remesh bookkeeping (not MMG's). At the default -1, a remesh prints only its trigger line, "Remeshing starts", "New mesh" and "Remeshing finished"; each MMG quality retry still prints one line naming the bad elements and what was unfrozen. Set it to 0 to restore the full stage-by-stage log ([metric], [collapse], [freeze], [unfreeze], [require], [corner], [mmg], [restore], [GPU mem], [quality]), useful when tuning the mmg_remesh_* parameters below. 1-3 add Triangle/TetGen's own -V verbosity on top. mesh.smallest_size/mesh.largest_size: set MMG's minimum/maximum element edge length (see above); not MMG-specific, they also bound meshing_option = 2's coarse zone. mmg_hausd_factor: Global Hausdorff distance (on all boundaries in the mesh), as a factor of mesh.resolution. Roughly speaking, the allowed difference between the boundary before and after mesh refinement or optimization. At the default 0.01, MMG refines a sharply bent free surface down to its size floor and can trigger the tiny-element check at nearly every quality pass; use 0.02-0.05 along a 3D fault scarp and 0.1 on the top/wall ridges next to restored side walls. For more MMG parameters, refer to https://mmgtools.github.io/libmmg3d_8h.html#a964a06109019542d04f12263c3fae24d For instance, mmg_debug = 0 mmg_verbose = 0 mmg_hausd_factor = 0.01

With usemmg = 1, every remesh now defaults to conservative: it starts by assuming every element is frozen (kept exactly as it is) and only refines, repairs, or frees the elements a specific rule flags. This replaces an earlier scheme that rebuilt the whole mesh from a plastic-strain-scaled size field at every remesh, which diffused and coarsened the quiet far field over time. In plain terms, by default: An element whose plastic strain grew by more than mmg_remesh_active_plstrain since the last remesh is split (its existing nodes are kept, so the band's strain carries over exactly). A distorted or tiny element is repaired by moving its nodes. An element far from its current size target is freed to coarsen or split. Most boundary nodes stay pinned; remeshing_option = 13's restored side walls and the bottom boundary never move except through the specific rules that are allowed to. Parameter Default Effect mmg_remesh_active_plstrain 0.01 Plastic-strain increment since the last remesh above which an element is split. Raise it to freeze more of a band; lower it (keep it > 0) to split more. mmg_remesh_defensive_quality_ratio 1.5 Repairs an element once its quality falls below min_quality times this ratio, before it hits the remesh-triggering min_quality itself. 1 repairs only once the trigger is reached. mmg_remesh_defensive_tiny_ratio 1.5 Gap, in element size, between the tiny-element remesh trigger and the smallest element MMG will build. Lower (minimum 1) means less of a gap, so back-to-back remeshes are more likely. mmg_remesh_size_recovery_ratio 1.4 A quiet element finer than this factor times its size target is freed to coarsen. 0 disables size recovery (and the t = 0 weak-zone refinement); values above 1 free fewer fossil-fine elements. mmg_metric_refine_coeff 5 Plastic-strain sensitivity of the target element size: target volume scales by 1/(1 + coeff * plastic_strain). 0 disables plastic refinement from a fresh start. Higher meshes a strained zone finer, at the cost of more elements and often a shorter time step. mmg_metric_refine_recover no no (default): once refined, a node keeps its finest size target even as plastic strain there drops. yes: the target tracks the current plastic strain instead, so a refined zone can coarsen again. mmg_aniso_wall_ratio 0 (off) At a remeshing_option = 13 restored inflow wall, >= 1 coarsens elements normal to the wall while keeping them fine along it (an aspect ratio), so an incoming column is carried by fewer, wider elements. Start from examples/tectonics/core-complex-mmg.cfg, which lists every MMG key with a one-line hint. mmg_metric_refine_coeff and mmg_remesh_active_plstrain are the two most worth tuning first; in 3D, also mmg_hausd_factor. Breaking: old checkpoints cannot restart Conservative remeshing persists new per-node/per-element state (plastic strain since the last remesh, size targets) in the checkpoint. A checkpoint written before this change does not have that state, and restarting from it exits with a restart-mismatch error (see Checkpointing and restart). Finish or discard runs on the old binary before upgrading.

One needs to set usemmg to 1 in Makefile: usemmg = 1 make prepare then pulls MMG in as a git submodule and builds it under mmg/build automatically, no manual MMG install or path configuration needed. Makefile points the build at that submodule: ifeq ($(usemmg), 1) # path to MMG3D header files MMG_INCLUDE = ./mmg/build/include # path of MMG3D library files MMG_LIB_DIR = ./mmg/build/lib MMG_CXXFLAGS = -I$(MMG_INCLUDE) -DUSEMMG ifeq ($(ndims), 3) MMG_LDFLAGS = -L$(MMG_LIB_DIR) -lmmg3d else MMG_LDFLAGS = -L$(MMG_LIB_DIR) -lmmg2d endif ifneq ($(OSNAME), Darwin) # Apple's ld doesn't support -rpath MMG_LDFLAGS += -Wl,-rpath=$(MMG_LIB_DIR) endif endif ifeq ($(usemmg), 1) CXXFLAGS += $(MMG_CXXFLAGS) LDFLAGS += $(MMG_LDFLAGS) endif When USEMMG is defined during the build process with -DUSEMMG, remesh() function calls optimize_mesh(), not new_mesh(). void remesh(const Param &param, Variables &var, int bad_quality) { ... #ifdef THREED #if defined ADAPT || defined USEMMG optimize_mesh(param, var, bad_quality, old_coord, old_connectivity, old_segment, old_segflag); #else new_mesh(param, var, bad_quality, old_coord, old_connectivity, old_segment, old_segflag); #endif ...

Options for the bottom boundary​ The option param.mesh.remeshing_option determines what to do to the bottom boundary during remeshing. However, it does not directly control how MMG performs mesh optimization. /* choosing which way to remesh the boundary */ switch (param.mesh.remeshing_option) { case 0: // DO NOT change the boundary excl_func = &is_boundary; break; case 1: excl_func = &is_boundary; flatten_bottom(old_bcflag, qcoord, -param.mesh.zlength, points_to_delete, min_dist); break; case 2: excl_func = &is_boundary; new_bottom(old_bcflag, qcoord, -param.mesh.zlength, points_to_delete, min_dist, qsegment, qsegflag, old_nseg); break; case 10: excl_func = &is_corner; break; case 11: excl_func = &is_corner; flatten_bottom(old_bcflag, qcoord, -param.mesh.zlength, points_to_delete, min_dist); break; case 12: flatten_x0(old_bcflag, qcoord, points_to_delete); break; default: std::cerr << "Error: unknown remeshing_option: " << param.mesh.remeshing_option << '\n'; std::exit(1); } Workflow during remeshing with MMG​ Initialization Mesh building in MMG5 format Metric field building: each node's target element size comes from the freeze/required policy described in Conservative remeshing above, not a single global formula. Mesh optimization Mesh-related data update using the optimized MMG5 mesh

For large 3D models (roughly >5 million elements), TetGen can be slow or crash during the initial mesh generation step. DES3D supports an optional two-stage initialization that uses TetGen to create a coarse seed mesh and then refines it with MMG to the target resolution. Enable it in your config file: use_mmg_init = 1 mmg_init_coarsening_factor = 10.0 # TetGen seed element volumes scaled by factor^NDIMS use_mmg_init is only effective when DES3D is compiled with usemmg = 1. If MMG support is absent, the parameter is silently ignored and the standard TetGen path is used. Parameter Default Description use_mmg_init 0 Set to 1 to enable two-stage MMG initialization (requires usemmg = 1) mmg_init_coarsening_factor 10.0 TetGen builds its coarse seed mesh with element volumes scaled by factor^NDIMS; MMG then refines it to the target resolution. Higher = smaller coarse mesh = faster TetGen but more MMG work. When to use Enable use_mmg_init when your 3D model has more than ~2 million target elements and TetGen initialization takes more than a few minutes or produces memory errors.
documents.s: Using MMG for initial mesh generation

documents.t: To have multiple material types, regions can be defined in a poly file for triangle or tetgen. In this case, material properties in a config file (.cfg) must correspond to the regions defined in the poly file in terms of the number of materials and the order by which the materials and parameters are listed. This technical requirement is illustrated by a multi-material 2D rifting example. A pair of input parameter files are provided: DynEarthSol/examples/tectonics/rifting-2d.cfg: input file for DynEarthSol. DynEarthSol/examples/tectonics/rifting-2d.poly: input file for the mesh generator, triangle.
documents.s: Making a complex mesh with .poly file

documents.t: In [mesh] section, set meshing_option to 90 and specify poly_filename: e.g., meshing_option = 90 poly_filename = rifting-2d.poly In [mat] section, specify num_materials: e.g., num_materials = 4 Provide as many values as num_materials for all the material properties (e.g. rho0, lambda, mu, etc): e.g., rho0 = [ 2800, 2900, 3210, 3300 ] We recommend you draw a schematic such as the one in rifting-2d.poly to illustrate your layers with labeled nodal points (shown below):

In this file, you will define node coordinates segments connecting coordinates regions Node coordinates As in the example .poly file, specify the number of total nodes and number of dimensions. Then specify the node number (starting from 0) and the x- and y-coordinates. #### node coordinates #### # npoints ndims 0 0 13 2 0 0 # i xi yi 0 0.0 0.0 1 0.0 -35.0e3 2 0.0 -150.0e3 3 500.0e3 -150.0e3 4 500.0e3 -35.0e3 5 500.0e3 0.0 6 150.0e3 -150.0e3 7 350.0e3 -150.0e3 8 380.0e3 -35.0e3 9 250.0e3 -39.0e3 10 120.0e3 -35.0e3 11 300.0e3 -35.0e3 12 200.0e3 -35.0e3 Segments As in the example .poly file, specify the number of total segments connecting any 2 nodes. Then specify the segment number (starting from 0) and the nodes it connects (e.g. in the picture of rifting-2d.poly's scheme above, segment 0 connects nodes 0 and 1. Segment 9 connects nodes 10 and 12.) Finally, assign a boundary flag. Flags: 0: not a boundary 1: left boundary (x0) 2: right boundary (x1) 16: bottom boundary (z0) 32: top boundary (z1) #### segments #### # nsegments 1 16 1 # j pj0 pj1 bdry_flag 0 0 1 1 # 1: left (x0) 1 1 2 1 2 2 6 16 # 16: bottom (z0) 3 6 7 16 4 7 3 16 5 3 4 2 # 2: right (x1) 6 4 5 2 7 5 0 32 # 32: top (z1) 8 1 10 0 # 0: not a boundary 9 10 12 0 10 12 9 0 11 9 11 0 12 11 8 0 13 8 4 0 14 10 6 0 15 8 7 0 Holes In tectonic moeling, there is no reason to deal with an undergroun empty space. #### holes, must be 0 #### 0 Regions As in the example .poly file, specify the number of total regions. Then specify the region number (starting from 0) and a point within that region (we recommend choosing a fairly central node here). The mattype specifies which value in the .cfg file [mat] paramter should be applied to the region. Finally, specify the max element size (m^2) for the region. If there is no upper limit on element size, use -1. #### regions #### # nregions 4 # k xk zk mattype size 0 250e3 -20e3 0 2e7 # max. element size (in m^2) 1 250e3 -80e3 1 4e7 2 1e3 -80e3 1 -1 # no upper limit on elem size 3 450e3 -80e3 1 -1

Each lateral face of a 3D model (x0, x1, y0, y1) can be assigned an independent velocity boundary condition (VBC) case. The case number is set via bc.vbc_x0, bc.vbc_x1, bc.vbc_y0, bc.vbc_y1. For the full reference across all six faces, 2D and 3D, and the traction (Neumann) and automatic gravity-driven boundary conditions, see Velocity and traction boundary conditions. Case Normal component Lateral-shear component Vertical 0 Free Free Free 1 Fixed (vbc_val_*) Free Free 2 Free Fixed (0) Free 3 Fixed Fixed (0) Free 4 Free Free Fixed (0) 5 Fixed Fixed Free 6 Fixed (vbc_val_*) Fixed (vbc_val_*_l) Free

Case 6 (added in 2026) allows setting both the normal and lateral-shear velocities on a face to independent non-zero values, with the vertical component free. It is useful for transtensional or transpressional boundary conditions. bc.vbc_x0 = 6 bc.vbc_val_x0 = -0.01 # normal velocity (m/yr) bc.vbc_val_x0_l = 0.005 # lateral-shear velocity (m/yr) bc.vbc_x1 = 6 bc.vbc_val_x1 = 0.01 bc.vbc_val_x1_l = -0.005 See examples/tectonics/oblique-rift-3d.cfg for a complete transtensional rifting example using case 6.
documents.s: Case 6 — independent normal and lateral-shear velocities

documents.t: DES3D supports several ways to define fault-like weak zones that focus deformation in a model, selected with weakzone_option in the [ic] section: weakzone_option What it creates 0 No weak zone 1 A single planar weak zone: azimuth, inclination, half-width, depth range and center location 2 An ellipsoidal weak zone: center location and semi-axes 3 A Gaussian-distribution point weak zone: center location and standard deviation 4 A single planar fault whose map-view position bulges along strike following a Gaussian — see below 5 Multiple general planar segments — see below weakzone_azimuth is measured relative to the model's +y axis, not geographic north, and weakzone_inclination relative to the horizontal plane — both in degrees.

For models that require more than one pre-existing fault (e.g., conjugate normal faults or a step-over fault system), use weakzone_option = 5. This option accepts any number of planar fault segments, each with its own center, orientation, half-width and spatial bounds; a point belongs to the weak zone if any segment contains it. Each segment uses a General_planar_zone formulation with a proper unit-normal, avoiding the tan(azimuth) numerical singularity of the single-fault Planar_zone (option 1).

Every weakzone_segments_* parameter is an array with one entry per segment, [v0, v1, ...], of length weakzone_num_segments: [ic] weakzone_option = 5 weakzone_plstrain = 0.5 # plastic strain assigned inside any segment weakzone_num_segments = 2 # number of fault segments # Segment centers (normalized 0-1, in units of mesh.xlength/ylength/zlength) weakzone_segments_xcenter = [0.35, 0.65] weakzone_segments_ycenter = [0.5, 0.5] # 3D only weakzone_segments_zcenter = [0.5, 0.5] # Opposite dip directions, same dip angle weakzone_segments_azimuth = [0, 180] # degrees, relative to +y axis weakzone_segments_inclination = [60, 60] # degrees, relative to horizontal weakzone_segments_halfwidth = [1.5, 1.5] # in units of mesh.resolution # Bounding box per segment (normalized 0-1) weakzone_segments_x_min = [0.0, 0.5] weakzone_segments_x_max = [0.5, 1.0] weakzone_segments_y_min = [0.0, 0.0] # 3D only weakzone_segments_y_max = [1.0, 1.0] # 3D only weakzone_segments_depth_min = [0.0, 0.0] weakzone_segments_depth_max = [1.0, 1.0] See examples/tectonics/conjugate-faults-3d.cfg for this two-segment conjugate normal-fault setup in full. Number of segments weakzone_num_segments can be set to any positive integer; every weakzone_segments_* array above must then have exactly that many entries.

weakzone_option = 4 places a single planar fault — geometrically the same as option 1 (azimuth, inclination, half-width, depth range, center) — but shifts its map-view x-position along strike by a Gaussian bulge: x(y)=x0​+Aexp(−2σ2(y−y0​)2​) where A is weakzone_gaussian_amplitude and σ is weakzone_standard_deviation. This is useful for localizing the initial failure to the center of the model domain while tapering to a straight fault toward the lateral edges. [ic] weakzone_option = 4 weakzone_azimuth = 0.0 # relative to +y axis (degrees) weakzone_inclination = -45.0 # relative to horizontal plane (degrees) weakzone_halfwidth = 1.2 # in units of mesh.resolution weakzone_depth_min = 0.5 weakzone_depth_max = 1.0 weakzone_xcenter = 0.5 weakzone_ycenter = 0.5 # 3D only weakzone_zcenter = 1.0 weakzone_y_min = 0.0 # 3D only weakzone_y_max = 1.0 # 3D only weakzone_plstrain = 0.5 weakzone_gaussian_amplitude = -4000 # x-shift at peak (m) weakzone_standard_deviation = 1e4 # sigma along y (m) See gospl_driver/examples/gaussian-weakzone-3d-with-gospl.cfg for this exact configuration, combined with GoSPL surface-process coupling — see Coupling with GoSPL.

If you would rather not install the dependencies yourself, build a Docker image from the repository root. build.sh sets the dimension (NDIMS=2) and the compiler (gcc-11; also gcc-8 and clang-14) at its top: edit them there or pass them in the environment. ./build.sh docker run --rm -it dynearthsol/gcc-11 GOSPL=1 ./build.sh builds dynearthsol/gcc-11-gospl instead: a 3D executable with GoSPL coupling, the gospl conda environment and gospl_extensions included, so no conda setup is needed on the host. See Coupling with GoSPL for how to run it. The rest of this page covers building from source.

A C++17 compiler: GNU g++ 8 or newer, NVIDIA nvc++ 25.7 or newer, or Clang 5 or newer. Apple Clang is also supported. The Intel classic icpc and PGI pgc++ compilers are no longer supported: make CXX=icpc (or CXX=pgc++) now stops at check-deps instead of building. Make and Git. The CLI11 config parser is vendored in the source tree. Python 3 with NumPy and SciPy for the Python tools. Add h5py to read VTKHDF output and Matplotlib for the PT tutorial figures. On macOS, an OpenMP runtime such as Homebrew's libomp. Optional libraries: MMG for adaptive remeshing (bundled as a submodule), ExodusII from SEACAS for 3D mesh import, and HDF5 for VTKHDF output. These requirements describe Latest. For an older release, select its manual version and use the dependencies in that release's README. See the current solver README for platform package commands.

mmg, nanoflann, and knn-bvh are bundled as git submodules and built automatically by make; no separate installation or path configuration is required. After cloning, initialize them once: git submodule update --init --recursive make will also auto-initialize stale submodules, but running the command above explicitly after cloning is recommended.

Parameter Name Possible Values Description ndims 2, 3 Choose 2 for two-dimensional models (dynearthsol2d) or 3 for three-dimensional models (dynearthsol3d). opt 0, 1, 2, 3 Integer value for optimization level. openacc 0, 1 Disable (0) or enable (1) OpenACC build. GPU_CC compute capability, e.g. 80, 90 GPU compute capability to target when openacc=1. Defaults to the capability of the GPU detected on the host (via nvidia-smi), or 80 if none is detected. make config prints the value in use. openmp 0, 1 Disable (0) or enable (1) OpenMP build. nprof 0, 1 Disable (0) or enable (1) profiling with nprof. gprof 0, 1 Disable (0) or enable (1) profiling with gprof. usemmg 0, 1 Disable (0) or enable (1) mesh optimization during remeshing with mmg. usegwb 0, 1 Disable (0) or enable (1) initial conditions from a Geodynamic World Builder world. Needs an installed GWB; GWB_DIR names it (default ~/opt/WorldBuilder). useexo 0, 1 Disable (0) or enable (1) import of an .exo mesh, usually created with the meshing software, CUBIT. Note: Only a 3D mesh can be imported currently. hdf5 0, 1 Enable HDF5-based VTKHDF output (see Visualizing outputs). Paths are auto-detected on Linux and macOS via pkg-config and the usual install layouts; override with HDF5_INCLUDE_DIR / HDF5_LIB_DIR if the wrong install is picked up or the build stops with install advice.

ExodusII​ If you want to import an ExodusII mesh (.exo), install SEACAS enabling exodus support set useexo = 1 and ndims = 3. Only 3D exodus mesh can be imported. set EXO_INCLUDE and EXO_LIB_DIR in Makefile based on the SEACAS installation path. MMG​ MMG is bundled as a git submodule and built automatically; no manual installation or path configuration is needed. To enable it: set usemmg = 1 (both ndims=2 and ndims=3 are supported). For further information, see Adaptive mesh refinement with MMG. Geodynamic World Builder​ To set the initial temperature, marker materials or weak zone from a Geodynamic World Builder world (ic.temperature_option, ic.mattype_option or ic.weakzone_option 936): build GWB (CMake 3.5 or newer, a C++14 compiler) as a shared library and install it: git clone https://github.com/GeodynamicWorldBuilder/WorldBuilder.git cmake -S WorldBuilder -B WorldBuilder/build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \ -DBUILD_SHARED_LIBS=ON -DWB_ENABLE_TESTS=OFF -DWB_ENABLE_PYTHON=OFF \ -DWB_MAKE_FORTRAN_WRAPPER=OFF -DCMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX=$HOME/opt/WorldBuilder cmake --build WorldBuilder/build -j 4 cmake --install WorldBuilder/build set usegwb = 1, and GWB_DIR if GWB is installed elsewhere. GWB puts its library in bin/, which GWB_LIB_DIR overrides. See Initial conditions from Geodynamic World Builder. HDF5​ For outputting model results in the HDF5-based VTKHDF format (compressed, often ~50% smaller, and viewable directly in ParaView without conversion): install HDF5 with your package manager (brew install hdf5 on macOS, apt install libhdf5-dev on Debian/Ubuntu, dnf install hdf5-devel on Fedora/RHEL); it is commonly pre-installed already. set hdf5 = 1. make locates the include/lib paths itself via pkg-config and standard install layouts; set HDF5_INCLUDE_DIR and HDF5_LIB_DIR to override. See Visualizing outputs for the VTKHDF file format and the 2vtk.py --update-vtkhdf workflow.

$ make Build options can be set on the command line without editing Makefile: e.g., To build optimized executable (default optimization level, 2): make To build a debugging executable: make opt=0 To build the executable without OpenMP: make openmp=0 This build is necessary to debug the code under valgrind.

Apple's built-in Clang supports OpenMP compilation but ships no OpenMP runtime. Install the runtime with Homebrew: brew install libomp Then a plain build finds everything on its own, no paths to edit and none to pass on the command line: make ndims=2 OpenMP is searched at the Homebrew prefix matching the machine's architecture (/opt/homebrew on Apple Silicon, /usr/local on Intel), not via PATH; this matters on a Mac that has ever used both prefixes, where PATH often points at an install of the wrong architecture. If a build picks up something unexpected: make config # prints the compiler and every resolved dependency path make check-deps # validates dependencies (fatal on macOS) without building OPENMP_ROOT_DIR can be set on the command line to force a specific runtime install when the search doesn't find the right one. At startup, DES3D automatically sets OMP_WAIT_POLICY=active on macOS to avoid a performance regression caused by libomp's default zero-blocktime on Apple Silicon. You can override this by setting the variable in your environment before running the executable.

DES3D's six box faces, x0/x1 (west/east), y0/y1 (south/north, 3D only), and z0/z1 (bottom/top), each take an independent boundary condition, set entirely in the [bc] section. Three systems can act on a face, and they compose additively rather than replacing one another: Velocity (Dirichlet): vbc_* fixes components of velocity outright. Traction (Neumann): stress_bc_* adds a prescribed force. Automatic gravity-driven support: applied wherever a face's normal direction is left free, so "free" under gravity is not the same as "zero force" (see Automatic boundary support under gravity). A custom (non-rectangular) mesh can also define up to four extra "slant" boundary planes, n0–n3, covered at the end.

Each face takes a vbc_<face> type code and a vbc_val_<face> value (m/s). The default model (vbc_x0 = vbc_x1 = 1, with opposite-signed values) is a divergent box: both side walls move apart. [bc] vbc_x0 = 1 vbc_val_x0 = -1e-9 # m/s vbc_x1 = 1 vbc_val_x1 = 1e-9 # m/s vbc_x0/vbc_x1 (and, in 3D, vbc_y0/vbc_y1) are lateral faces: their normal is horizontal, and in 3D they distinguish three independent components: the normal direction, the in-plane lateral-shear direction, and the vertical (z) direction. vbc_z0/vbc_z1 are the top/bottom faces and use a different, smaller set of codes, covered in their own table below.

In 2D there is no separate out-of-plane direction, so the "z" column below doesn't apply; the single non-normal component is the "lateral-shear" column, which in 2D is the vertical (z) direction itself. Type Normal component Lateral-shear component z component (3D only) 0 Free Free Free 1 Fixed (vbc_val_*) Free Free 2 Free Fixed at 0 Fixed at 0 3 Fixed (vbc_val_*) Fixed at 0 Fixed at 0 4 2D: normal fixed at 0, lateral-shear (=z) fixed (vbc_val_*). 3D: normal free, lateral-shear fixed (vbc_val_*), z fixed at 0 5 (3D only) Fixed at 0 Fixed (vbc_val_*) Fixed at 0 6 Fixed (vbc_val_*) Fixed (vbc_val_*_l) Free 7 (3D only) Fixed (vbc_val_*) Fixed at 0 Free Type 4 means different things in 2D and 3D Every other type keeps the same meaning in 2D and 3D, but 4 doesn't: in 2D it's a "tangential loading" mode (normal pinned to 0, the single tangential/vertical component prescribed); in 3D the normal is left free instead, and it's the lateral-shear component that gets prescribed while z is pinned to 0. Don't reuse a 2D type-4 config verbatim in 3D. Types 11 and 13 don't apply here 11 and 13 exist only for the slant boundaries (vbc_n0–vbc_n3, below) and are silently ignored (the face stays fully free) if set on vbc_x0, vbc_x1, vbc_y0, or vbc_y1. Unlike vbc_n0–vbc_n3, these six parameters aren't validated at startup, so a typo here doesn't stop the run; check that the boundary actually moved as intended. Sign convention: literal axis direction, not inward/outward Unlike the slant-boundary values below, vbc_val_x0, vbc_val_x1, etc. are the literal signed velocity along the global axis, not relative to inward/outward. A positive vbc_val_x1 moves the east wall further east (outward, extension); a positive vbc_val_x0 moves the west wall further east too, i.e. inward (convergence), since x0 is already at the low-x end. The divergent-box default above uses a negative value on x0 and a positive one on x1 precisely because both push outward.

vbc_z0/vbc_z1 use their own, smaller set of codes, not the lateral table above: Type Horizontal component(s) Normal (z) component 0 Free Free 1 Free Fixed (vbc_val_*) 2 Fixed at 0 Free 3 Fixed at 0 Fixed (vbc_val_*) 4 Fixed (vbc_val_*) Fixed at 0 In 3D, type 4 fixes both horizontal components (x and y) to the same scalar vbc_val_*, so it's only meaningful for a uniformly-sliding lid, not independent x/y rates. vbc_z0 = 4 is 2D only Unlike vbc_z1, vbc_z0's type 4 only exists in the 2D build; a 3D build silently ignores it (the face stays free), the same trap as types 11/13 above.

Type 6 is the only one that lets you set both the normal and lateral-shear velocity to independent non-zero values, useful for transtensional/transpressional setups. See Velocity boundary conditions (3D) for a worked example with examples/tectonics/oblique-rift-3d.cfg.
documents.s: Case 6: independent normal and lateral-shear velocity

documents.t: Any lateral face, x0/x1 and, in 3D, y0/y1, can ramp through a sequence of rate multipliers over time. Each face has its own independent period table: [bc] num_vbc_period_x0 = 2 vbc_period_x0_time_in_yr = [1e6, 2e6] # end time of each period vbc_period_x0_ratio = [1., 0.5] # vbc_val_x0 multiplier during each period In 3D, the same three parameters exist for y0/y1: num_vbc_period_y0/y1, vbc_period_y0/y1_time_in_yr, vbc_period_y0/y1_ratio. Only the normal-component types are scaled by the period table The period table scales the velocity that types 1, 3, and 6 prescribe for the normal component (also type 7 in 3D). It does not apply to type 4 or 5's tangential/shear value, which stays at the raw vbc_val_*/vbc_val_*_l you set.

The normal velocity on x0/x1 (types 1, 3, 6) can also vary piecewise-linearly with depth, as a fraction of vbc_val_x0/vbc_val_x1, using two interior break points as a fraction of the boundary's height (0 = top, 1 = bottom): [bc] vbc_val_division_x0_min = 0.3 # upper break point (fraction of height from the top) vbc_val_division_x0_max = 0.7 # lower break point vbc_val_x0_ratio0 = 1.0 # ratio at the top vbc_val_x0_ratio1 = 1.0 # ratio at vbc_val_division_x0_min vbc_val_x0_ratio2 = 0.5 # ratio at vbc_val_division_x0_max vbc_val_x0_ratio3 = 0.5 # ratio at the bottom

Parameter Effect bottom_shear_zone_thickness For vbc_x0 = 3, 2D only: ramps the x-velocity linearly to zero within this thickness (m) of the bottom, instead of a step. vbc_val_z1_loading_period After this much model time, vbc_z1 is forced to 0 (free) regardless of its configured type. Useful for a loading phase followed by free relaxation.

Each face also takes a stress_bc_<face> type and stress_val_<face> magnitude (Pa): [bc] stress_bc_x1 = 1 # traction in the x direction stress_val_x1 = -1e8 # Pa; negative = compression (pushes inward) Type Meaning 0 (default) No traction boundary condition 1 Traction in the x direction 2 (3D only) Traction in the y direction 3 Traction in the z direction Match the type to the face's own normal direction The traction is resolved onto the facet through its outward normal, so it only has an effect when the type matches the face's own normal axis: type 1 on x0/x1, type 2 on y0/y1, type 3 on z0/z1. Any other combination computes a force along a direction the face has no normal component in, and silently applies zero force. With the type matched to the face, the sign is consistent with ordinary stress convention: a positive value is tension (pulls the boundary outward), a negative value is compression (pushes it inward), on both the "low" (x0/y0/z0) and "high" (x1/y1/z1) side of each axis, since the outward normal itself flips sign between them. A traction BC only matters where the corresponding vbc_* leaves that face's normal component free (type 0 or 2); if the normal is Dirichlet-fixed, the velocity solve overwrites it regardless of any force applied there.

With gravity on (control.gravity != 0), the lateral faces (x0, x1, y0, y1) automatically receive a lithostatic ("Archimedes") support pressure from the exterior column (via control.ref_pressure_option) whenever their normal is free; otherwise a merely "free" sidewall would let material flow out under its own weight with nothing pushing back. z0 and z1 work differently: each gets support only if its own flag is on, and nothing at all (not even the lithostatic default) if that flag is off and the face is otherwise free. Face Support Controlled by z0 (bottom) Winkler foundation: hydrostatic pressure from a virtual fluid of the local material's density (+ winkler_delta_rho) below the model has_winkler_foundation (default on), winkler_delta_rho (kg/m³) z1 (top) Hydrostatic water load on any part of the surface below control.surf_base_level has_water_loading (default on), sea_water_density (kg/m³, default 1030) Winkler and water loading override vbc_z0/vbc_z1 If has_winkler_foundation is on, vbc_z0 is forced to 0 (with a warning) regardless of what you set, because the foundation needs the bottom free to supply its own support. The same happens to vbc_z1 when has_water_loading is on. Turn the relevant flag off first if you need a Dirichlet velocity BC on that face instead, and if you do, remember z0/z1 then has no automatic support at all, unlike the lateral faces. An alternative (or additional) bottom support is a simple elastic foundation: a restoring force proportional to each bottom node's total vertical displacement from its initial position: [bc] has_elastic_foundation = yes elastic_foundation_constant = 1e11 # default It is off by default and, unlike Winkler/water loading, does not force vbc_z0 to free; the two can be combined with an explicit Dirichlet condition if you choose to. See Solution scheme in DES3D for the Neumann boundary force derivation these all feed into.

A mesh with non-rectangular boundaries (e.g. imported .poly/.exo geometry) can define up to four additional planar boundaries, n0–n3, each independently of the box faces above: [bc] vbc_n0 = 1 # only 1, 3, 11, 13 are supported vbc_val_n0 = -1e-9 # m/s, outward normal direction is positive Only types 1, 3, 11, and 13 are supported (anything else is rejected at startup, unlike the axis-aligned faces above): Type Normal component Tangential component 1 Fixed (vbc_val_n*) Free 3 Fixed (vbc_val_n*) Fixed at 0 11 (3D only) Fixed, horizontal part of the normal only (vbc_val_n*) Free (including z) 13 (3D only) Fixed, horizontal part of the normal only (vbc_val_n*) Fixed at 0 (including z) Unlike the axis-aligned faces above, the sign here is relative to the outward normal: a positive value always points out of the domain.

DES3D offers two mechanical solution paths. The default, control.has_PT = no, advances the explicit momentum equation using the configured damping and mass scaling. With control.has_PT = yes, a pseudo-transient (PT) solve seeks mechanical equilibrium within each physical timestep. PT is useful when each physical increment should satisfy a stated force balance tolerance. Its pseudo iterations are a numerical relaxation process; they do not resolve physical wave propagation. Assess a dynamic problem using the explicit momentum formulation and appropriate inertia, mass scaling and timestep choices. This page covers solver selection and controls. The theory explains the method; the tutorials progress from elastic loading and equilibrium to Maxwell creep under a held load.

A physical step has a physical duration, controlled by the usual timestep settings such as control.fixed_dt (seconds). Thermal diffusion, when enabled, advances temperature once before the PT solve; temperature then remains fixed during the mechanical trials. During the PT solve: The reference mesh and the physical-start material history are held fixed. Each candidate velocity is constrained by the velocity boundary conditions. The constitutive law evaluates the candidate over the same physical dt, starting again from the physical-start history. The solver accepts one candidate when its projected force residual meets the tolerance. Hydraulic transport, mesh motion and stress rotation then follow in their physical update stages. Increasing the number of pseudo iterations does not repeatedly advance plastic strain, viscous relaxation or frictional aging. It also does not improve physical-time resolution; check the physical timestep separately. See PT mechanics for the equations and acceptance contract.

These options belong in the input file's existing [control] section: [control] has_PT = yes PT_option = 0 PT_max_iter = 5000 PT_relative_tolerance = 1e-6 PT_absolute_tolerance = 0 Parameter Default Meaning has_PT no Use a PT mechanical solve for each physical step. PT_option 0 0: localized dual-time stress/velocity relaxation; 1: adaptive dynamic relaxation (ADR). PT_max_iter 5000 Maximum loop passes in one mechanical solve. PT_CFL 0.25 Pseudo-time relaxation control for option 0. Unused by option 1. PT_Re 14.90188239869415 Dual-time relaxation control for option 0. Unused by option 1. PT_relative_tolerance 1e-6 Relative force tolerance in the default convergence mode. PT_absolute_tolerance 0 Absolute force tolerance, in N/m in 2D or N in 3D. PT_use_running_scale no Use the alternative load-history scale for physical solves. PT_stagnation_window 500 Warn after this many iterations without a new best residual; 0 disables the warning. Both schemes use the same constitutive candidates, force residual, acceptance test and failure handling. Option 1 derives fictitious masses from an elastic/viscous reference stiffness and adapts its damping. Compare the options on a checked model; an iteration advantage in one example does not establish a general speedup. The legacy damping_factor is not a PT convergence control: artificial damping is excluded from the PT residual. control.PT_jump has been removed. Delete it from older input files. The parameter reference is examples/defaults.cfg, also available through ./dynearthsol2d --help.
documents.s: Enable PT and choose an iteration scheme

documents.t: The solver assembles undamped nodal forces, including gravity, applied tractions and foundation loads. It projects these forces onto the velocity directions the boundary conditions leave free. Constrained support reactions therefore do not count as disequilibrium. The residual is the root mean square (RMS) force over the free rank; an entirely constrained model has zero free residual. With the default PT_use_running_scale = no, acceptance requires R≤PT_absolute_tolerance+PT_relative_toleranceRwarm​. Rwarm​ is the first candidate's force imbalance, using the preceding physical velocity. It is not the gross prestress. If that trial does not converge, the solver may compare it with a candidate having zero free velocity and retain the smaller finite residual. That comparison does not change the relative-tolerance reference. Absolute tolerance is a nodal force RMS, not a traction or stress in Pa. Its meaning depends on dimension and mesh. A relative-only target can become smaller than floating-point cancellation permits as the warm residual shrinks. Inspect the printed residual and threshold when diagnosing a failure near an already equilibrated state.

The elastic and Maxwell tutorials explicitly set: [control] PT_use_running_scale = yes For physical steps this replaces the default criterion with R≤max(10−6Rn​,1000ϵdouble​Fabs​). Rn​ tracks the largest first warm residual of accepted physical solves, including the current candidate when eligible. Fabs​ is an absolute assembled element-force magnitude scale from the first trial, held fixed during that solve. The second term is a heuristic roundoff allowance, not a bound on stress or displacement error. Initial equilibration still uses the absolute/relative criterion. Explicitly setting either tolerance with running scale enabled prints a warning because those settings no longer control physical-step convergence. Initial equilibration does not enter the running history. Remeshing retains the history but excludes the first successful post-remesh solve from increasing it. An earlier large load can make this criterion too permissive for a later small perturbation. Its general use with history-dependent plastic, viscous or rate-and-state laws remains unvalidated beyond the documented examples. Use it with a known reference response and assess sensitivity to the loads, timestep and mesh. The solver default remains no.

With sim.info_display_step_interval = 1 and mesh.quality_check_step_interval = 1, every physical step prints a record: PT step=2 status=converged iterations=1 residual=0.0342014 initial=0.0342014 threshold=0.0353553 warm_initial=35355.3 evaluations=2 stage=before_physical_updates This shortened record comes from the 2D elastic tutorial, option 0. Field Interpretation step Physical simulation step. status converged, max_iterations or nonfinite. iterations PT loop passes. A value of 1 means no relaxation update was needed. evaluations Full constitutive/force trials, including candidate comparisons and restoration. initial Residual of the selected starting candidate. warm_initial First warm candidate's residual; the reference for default relative convergence. residual, threshold Accepted residual and its acceptance limit. stage For physical steps: after any thermal update, before hydraulic transport, mesh motion and stress rotation. The accepted vector is saved as PT residual force, supported by Dynearthsol.py and 2vtk.py. Legacy force retains damping and support reactions. See PT force output before comparing these fields or recomputing force from saved stress.

A stagnation warning does not stop the solve or relax the tolerance. Reaching PT_max_iter without convergence exits with 54; a nonfinite candidate exits with 50. Mechanical history is restored and the failed candidate does not proceed to output, hydraulic transport or mesh motion. This restores mechanical history; an earlier thermal update is not rolled back. Review the loading, constraints, physical timestep and attainable tolerance before changing the iteration limit. Restart requires an explicitly selected checkpoint. With unchanged controls, PT restores the saved velocity, next-step dt and velocity scale without repeating completed initial equilibration. Running scale also requires its checkpointed history; old checkpoints without that history cannot restart with it enabled. Hydraulic checkpoints require the pending pressure increment consumed by the next mechanical step. Use one OpenMP thread for byte-exact continuation; multi-thread ADR reductions can differ in the last bits. PT establishes equilibrium on the reference configuration. It does not guarantee equilibrium after mesh motion, convergence through strain softening, or accuracy for arbitrary hydraulic coupling. Start with the elastic tutorial, then the Maxwell creep tutorial. The solver notes and validation limits describe the available qualification in detail.

dynearthsol2d input.cfg or dynearthsol3d input.cfg Several example input files are provided under examples/ directory. The format of the input file is described in examples/defaults.cfg. Benchmark cases with analytical solution can be found under benchmarks/ directory. Execute the executable with -h flag to see the available input parameters and their descriptions. For a force-balanced mechanical solve within each physical timestep, see Choosing a mechanical solver (PT) and the elastic-loading tutorial.

The sim.info_display_step_interval parameter controls how often DES3D prints a status line to the screen: info_display_step_interval = 10 # print progress every 10 simulation steps This parameter replaced the older info_display_interval (which was wall-clock seconds) as of 2026. The value must be a positive multiple of mesh.quality_check_step_interval; DES3D will round it up automatically and notify you if an adjustment is made.
Restarting from a checkpoint Provenance, warnings and exit codes Initial stress Choosing a mechanical solver

control.has_thermal_diffusion = yes enables conduction (the default). Fluid heat advection, shear heating and point heat injection also use the temperature update; disabling conduction alone does not disable those features. See Heat transport.

Each face can be insulated (bc.tbc_* = 0) or held at a prescribed temperature (1). The default holds the top at bc.surface_temperature and insulates the base and sides. To hold a hot base and cold top: [bc] tbc_z0 = 1 tbc_val_z0 = 1600 tbc_z1 = 1 tbc_val_z1 = 273 Use tbc_x0, tbc_x1 and, in 3D, tbc_y0, tbc_y1 for the sides, with matching tbc_val_* values in K. Intersecting fixed-temperature faces must agree at shared nodes. There is no prescribed heat-flux boundary option. An explicit thermal boundary is applied at initialization and after remeshing as well as during transport. It can therefore change an initial profile immediately. Without custom thermal boundary settings, the legacy initial profile is retained until the first transport update applies the default top value. bc.mantle_temperature shapes the initial profiles and supplies the fallback value for a fixed base (tbc_z0 = 1) when tbc_val_z0 is unset. It does not hold an insulated base fixed. Other fixed faces use surface_temperature when their explicit value is unset.

ic.temperature_option selects how the initial temperature field is built: temperature_option Profile 0 (default) Uniform half-space cooling 1 Continental thermal gradient 2 Equilibrium temperature for crustal radiogenic heating 3 Continental thermal gradient with adiabatic mantle 4 Uniform background with a Gaussian perturbation 5 Linear top-to-base profile with a Gaussian perturbation 90 Read from an external grid (e.g., generated by COMSOL)

The classic error-function cooling profile between surface_temperature and mantle_temperature, using the thermal diffusivity of material 0 (therm_cond[0] / (rho0[0] * heat_capacity[0])): [ic] temperature_option = 0 oceanic_plate_age_in_yr = 60e6 # age of the plate, used in the half-space cooling profile

A steady-state continental geotherm (crust over mantle) with an exponentially decaying radiogenic heat source in the crust, relaxed toward temperature_option = 0's initial condition over the plate's age: [ic] temperature_option = 1 continental_plate_age_in_yr = 100.e6 # age of the plate radiogenic_heating_of_crust = 1.e-9 # W/kg radiogenic_crustal_thickness = 30.e3 # m lithospheric_thickness = 100.e3 # m radiogenic_folding_depth = 10.e3 # m; e-folding depth of radiogenic heating (shared with option 2)

Like option 1, but for an arbitrary stack of radiogenic-heating layers instead of a single crustal layer, each with its own material (and therefore its own therm_cond, rho0, radiogenic_heat_prod): [ic] temperature_option = 2 num_radiogenic_heat_layer = 1 # number of layers radiogenic_heat_boundry = [-1,-1] # depth of each layer boundary, top to bottom (m); -1 = model top/bottom radiogenic_heat_mat_in_layer = [0] # material index of each layer radiogenic_folding_depth = 10.e3 # m; e-folding depth of radiogenic heating (shared with option 1)
documents.s: temperature_option = 2: equilibrium temperature for crustal radiogenic heating

documents.t: A radiogenic continental geotherm, using the same layered [mat] properties as option 2, capped by an adiabatic mantle below (via mantle_temperature and gravity). The radiogenic heating of the top layer is driven by the heat flux parameters below instead of radiogenic_heat_prod, and can be localized under an elliptical "dome" in map view instead of applied uniformly: [ic] temperature_option = 3 num_radiogenic_heat_layer = 1 # number of layers (shared with option 2) radiogenic_heat_boundry = [-1,-1] # layer boundary depths, top to bottom (m); -1 = model top/bottom radiogenic_heat_mat_in_layer = [0] # material index of each layer radiogenic_heat_dome_center_x = 0.5 # dome center, fraction of mesh.xlength radiogenic_heat_dome_center_y = 0.5 # dome center, fraction of mesh.ylength (3D) surface_heat_flux = 70e-3 # W/m^2, background surface heat flux away from the dome radiogenic_heat_dome_amplitude = 0 # extra surface heat flux at the dome center radiogenic_heat_dome_width = 0 # dome half-width (m); required (> 0) when this option is used radiogenic_heat_dome_width_y = 0 # dome half-width in y (3D): 0 = same as x (circular), <0 = infinite (ridge/hinge) radiogenic_heat_dome_azimuth = 0 # dome rotation (degrees, 3D)
documents.s: temperature_option = 3: continental thermal gradient with adiabatic mantle

documents.t: Option 4 starts at ic.temp_background; option 5 uses the linear profile between bc.surface_temperature and bc.mantle_temperature over mesh.zlength. Both add a Gaussian of amplitude ic.temp_anomaly_amplitude, centred at ic.temp_anomaly_xcenter/ycenter/zcenter, with positive ic.temp_anomaly_xsemi_axis/ysemi_axis/zsemi_axis lengths. The y parameters apply in 3D. Zero amplitude gives the unperturbed profile. The initial profile and active thermal boundaries should describe the same problem; see the convection benchmark.

Reads a precomputed temperature field on its own mesh, interpolated onto the DES3D mesh at startup, typically generated by COMSOL: [ic] temperature_option = 90 Temp_filename = Thermal.dat # rows of "x [y] z temperature" Nodes_filename = Coord.dat # rows of "x [y] z", may be ordered differently than Temp_filename Connectivity_filename = Connectivity.dat # rows of node indices per element (4 per row in 3D)
documents.s: temperature_option = 90: read from an external grid

documents.t: The thermal diffusivity used above, and the diffusion solved every step, both come from each material's properties in [mat] (one value per material, or a single value broadcast to all materials): [mat] heat_capacity = [1e3] # J/(kg.K) therm_cond = [3] # W/(m.K) radiogenic_heat_prod = [0] # W/kg; internal heat source for temperature_option = 1-3 mat.max_thermal_diffusivity (default 5e-6 m²/s) supplies the outer timestep's diffusion estimate; it does not clip a material's conductivity or its physical diffusivity. Thermal substeps have an additional bound assembled from the actual transport operator and nodal heat capacity.

To convert the binary output files to VTU files, run 2vtk.py modelname modelname should be the one defined in the config file. To see full usage information (including options for marker data VTP files), run 2vtk.py -h The processed VTU (node and cell data) and VTP (marker data) files can be visualized with ParaView or VisIt. Choose saved fields with the [sim] output settings in examples/defaults.cfg, such as has_marker_output and is_outputting_averaged_fields.

Accepted PT solves can save an optional nodal vector, PT residual force. The Python reader and 2vtk.py support this field. Field Meaning force Legacy force, including artificial damping and constrained reactions. PT residual force Accepted undamped force projected onto admissible velocity perturbations. The PT vector's free-rank RMS is the reported residual, in N/m in 2D or N in 3D. It describes the accepted solve on its reference geometry, before hydraulic transport, mesh motion and stress rotation. For physical steps with thermal diffusion enabled, temperature has already been advanced; the report's stage=before_physical_updates does not precede that thermal stage. This diagnostic time level is retained even when other output fields are averaged. Force reassembled from saved post-rotation stress can therefore differ from this diagnostic. The vector is absent before any accepted solve, after remeshing until a new solve is accepted, and at failed solves. New saves preserve it across restart; older saves remain readable and acquire it after the next accepted solve. It adds no checkpoint requirement. During binary-to-VTU conversion, 2vtk.py reports once if selected frames lack it and preserves the field where available. An initial-frame notice can be expected in the elastic tutorial.

2vtk.py follows a restarted model's .manifest back to its parent, so the whole series converts as one: 2vtk.py modelname-r Without -g, frames from the parent that were already converted are linked in under the restarted name (modelname-r.000000.vtu -> modelname.000000.vtu, and so on); any parent frame with no .vtu yet prints a warning naming it, instead of being silently skipped. 2vtk.py -g modelname-r converts the parent's frames first, so the series runs from frame 0. Each frame also carries its own origin — which model and machine wrote it, and, on a restart, what it restarted from — as described in Provenance.

DES3D can write output in the VTKHDF format (.vtkhdf), a self-contained HDF5-based format supported by ParaView 5.11+. VTKHDF files bundle all time steps into a single file, making them easier to manage for long runs than the equivalent per-step VTU collection.

The -u / --update-vtkhdf flag lets you add or recompute derived fields (e.g., strain-rate invariants, second invariant of stress) in an existing .vtkhdf file without regenerating it from scratch. This is useful when you want to add a newly supported output quantity to a completed run. 2vtk.py --update-vtkhdf modelname.vtkhdf Combined with -g on a restarted model, 2vtk.py -u -g modelname-r.vtkhdf writes a .vtkhdf.series file in place alongside it, one entry per frame across the whole restart chain, so ParaView opens the run as a single series instead of one file per restart leg. Requirements: h5py must be installed (pip install h5py or conda install h5py). Safety: The update is performed in-place. Back up your file before running if it is large or irreplaceable. The script prints a warning and exits if the target file does not look like a valid VTKHDF file. HDF5 file locking On some parallel or network filesystems, HDF5 file locking can cause a BlockingIOError. DES3D disables HDF5 locking automatically when writing VTKHDF output, so ParaView can open a frame while a run is still writing it. If you encounter this error when running 2vtk.py externally, set HDF5_USE_FILE_LOCKING=FALSE in your environment. The trade-off: with locking off, two runs that share a modelname are no longer refused, and will corrupt each other's file. Give every run its own modelname.
Every run records where it came from, and stops with a numbered exit code when something goes wrong.

Every build, run and frame records where it came from: What Where The build in the executable, as a build.snapshot block: strings <exe> | grep '^build\.snapshot\.' The run in <modelname>.manifest, beside the model's output Each frame or checkpoint a /provenance group (HDF5) or a provenance record (des-binary) in the file itself The manifest uses the cfg format: [runtime.model], [runtime.host], [runtime.device], [runtime.threads] and [runtime.env] first, then the build's own [build.*] sections, closed by [runtime.end] once the time loop ends (a record without it died, was killed, or is still running). Its first fields, end_time, stopped_by and wall_time, are enough to see how every run of a sweep ended: grep -A3 '^[runtime.end]' */*.manifest A restart appends its record rather than starting the file over. The same sections print to the screen once at run start, one line each as [build][...] then [runtime][...]; set sim.has_runtime_info_display = no to silence them: [sim] has_runtime_info_display = no make snapshot_diff=1 (off by default) also embeds the working-tree diff in the executable, so build.code-changes in the manifest is more than a note that it wasn't captured. A GPU build that finds no device exits 52 (see Exit codes) after appending its manifest record, so the attempt is on record even though the run never started. The full field-by-field reference is doc/provenance.md in the DynEarthSol repository.

While running, DES3D might print warnings on screen. An example is the warning about the potential race condition: e.g., **************************************************************** * Warning: egroup-0 and egroup-2 might share common nodes. * There is some risk of racing conditions. * Please either increase the resolution or * decrease the number OpenMP threads. **************************************************************** Please do pay attention and follow given suggestions if any.

DES3D exits with a two-digit code that is printed together with its category. The first digit is the category (1x is yours to fix, 2x the environment, 3x–6x the code itself) and the second the specific cause: Code Meaning 0 Normal exit 10 / 11 Config error / bad value or unknown option 12 Malformed .poly or .exo file 20 / 21 / 22 Cannot open file / read or write failed (HDF5) / restart mismatch 30 / 31 Unsupported in this NDIMS / library not built in 40 / 41 / 42 Triangle or TetGen / MMG / mesh quality or topology 50 / 51 / 52 NaN or non-finite value / marker or geometry lookup / resource exhausted 53 GoSPL coupling step failed 54 PT mechanical solve did not converge 60 / 61 Assertion violated / unreachable branch Errors in the configuration file stop the run with 10 or 11 and a message naming the problem. For example, every mattype_* index is checked against num_materials at startup, and an out-of-range one exits with 11 naming the parameter. A NaN velocity stops the run with 50 instead of continuing to write frames. The run prints a single line summarizing the affected fields, their counts and the first bad element and node. A GPU build that finds no device at startup exits 52, after appending its manifest record; see Provenance. A failed GoSPL coupling step (built with usegospl=1) stops the run with 53 instead of silently dropping that interval's erosion; see Coupling with GoSPL. PT reaching its iteration limit exits with 54 after restoring the physical-start mechanical history; a nonfinite PT candidate exits with 50. Stagnation warnings alone do not stop a PT solve. See PT controls. Scripts that test for specific exit statuses need updating: earlier builds used 1, 2, 10, 11 and 12 with different meanings.

By default (initial_stress_option = 0) the historical initialization is used. For zero-gravity models, set initial_stress_option = 1 in the [ic] section to prescribe a homogeneous absolute stress tensor with initial_stress: [ic] initial_stress_option = 1 # 2-D: [sxx, szz, sxz] 3-D: [sxx, syy, szz, sxy, sxz, syz] initial_stress = [sxx, szz, sxz] # replace with your values (Pa)

DES3D writes checkpoint files at regular intervals so that a simulation can be resumed after interruption. With unchanged controls, the restart tests compare saved physical state with uninterrupted runs. Use one OpenMP thread for byte-exact PT continuation; multi-thread ADR reductions can change the last bits. The following state is persisted in the checkpoint: dt and dt_PT (time step) max_global_vel_mag reference_frame_time info_display_next_step dhacc (surface marker correction) strain_rate, viscosity, volume_old plastic strain-rate (delta_plstrain), so a restarted run's diagnostic output matches a continuous one Copy the original config and edit its existing [sim] section to select a checkpoint explicitly, giving the restart a distinct output name: [sim] modelname = result-r is_restarting = yes restarting_from_modelname = result restarting_from_frame = 10 Replace result and 10 with your original model prefix and an output frame that has both save and checkpoint files, then run the executable with that edited config. Checkpoint frame numbers are output-frame indices, not necessarily physical step numbers. Retain the original physical controls and set the stopping step/time to permit continuation. DES3D requires both restart-selection parameters; rerunning an unchanged fresh config does not automatically find a checkpoint. PT restores saved velocity, next-step dt and velocity scale, and does not repeat completed initial equilibration. Its optional running scale requires the stored history; old checkpoints without it cannot silently start a new history. Hydraulic checkpoints also require the raw signed pressure increment and the saved ordering that determines whether it has already been consumed. Dry checkpoints do not require that hydraulic record. See PT restart and limits. Checkpoint/output format revision 4 The checkpoint and frame file format was bumped from revision 3 to 4. A revision (or dimensionality) mismatch between the file and the running binary is now a hard error with a diagnostic naming the expected and actual values, previously it was accepted silently and could be misread. A checkpoint with the earlier revision cannot be restarted by the newer solver. Preserve the original executable, configuration and data to continue it. This restart restriction does not imply that every older saved field is unreadable by Python: Dynearthsol.py reads frame metadata and available fields separately, subject to the schema that reader supports. Conservative MMG remeshing adds new checkpoint records Checkpoints now also carry nremesh, plstrain_remesh, and, in MMG builds, surface dh and refined_elem_size_n (plus, with remeshing_option = 13, side_prof_*). A checkpoint written before this change does not have these records, and restarting from it is a restart-mismatch error (21/22). Continue such checkpoints with their matching executable and preserve the original data; the new state is not inferred automatically. See Conservative remeshing for what changed in MMG remeshing itself. The optional finite-density hydraulic model also saves the physical inventories, numerical split buffer, EOS temperature origin and pending thermal/pressure increments. Accepted shear heat is saved as energy, so a changed timestep must not reinterpret an old power as a new energy. The current shear-heating checkpoint stores its version, pending extensive energy and accepted power together; missing members or an unsupported version are rejected. A power-only intermediate checkpoint is not converted. These model-specific guards apply in addition to the file-format revision. See Poromechanics. Frame files (HDF5 and plain binary) now also embed the full .info row (steps, time, dt, walltime, node/element/segment counts). If a run's .info file is lost, utils/recreate_info.py rebuilds it from the frame files alone; restart() also falls back to this embedded metadata automatically when .info is missing.
